item.html:
The 10 Best Claude Fable 5 Website Prompts for SEO & Sales

Claude Fable 5 is at its most valuable right now for one specific job: building your website. From July 20, 2026, Fable 5 is included in Max and Team Premium plans at 50% of limits, while Pro and Team Standard move to usage credits — so on any plan, Fable 5 time is worth rationing. The smartest way to spend it is not on random one-off answers — it’s on Claude Fable 5 website prompts that produce reusable assets: SEO pages, landing pages, and sales pages you can ship, reuse, and turn into repeatable skills. This guide gives you the best website prompts for each, ready to copy, paste, and adapt.

New to the model? Read What Claude Fable 5 Is first. Want the general library instead of website-specific prompts? See The 15 Best Claude Fable 5 Prompts. This page assumes you know what Fable 5 is and want to build website assets with it before the credit window changes.

Quick answer

What are the best Claude Fable 5 website prompts?

The best Claude Fable 5 website prompts are structured, reusable workflows that produce a full website asset in one pass — an SEO landing page blueprint, a lead-gen landing page, a long-form sales page, or a pricing page — instead of a vague paragraph. Each one gives Fable 5 a clear goal, your real context, and an exact output format, so you build the page once and rerun the same prompt for every future page. Start with the master template below, then jump to the prompt you need.

Why Website Prompts Are the Smartest Use of Your Fable 5 Window

Most people spend a powerful model on throwaway questions. That’s the wrong move for Claude Fable 5, especially with a usage-credit window closing in. Fable 5 is built for complex, long-context, multi-step work — exactly what a good website page requires. A homepage, an SEO landing page, or a sales page isn’t one sentence; it’s positioning, structure, proof, objections, search intent, metadata, and copy, all working together.

So instead of asking Fable 5 for “some website copy,” use this window to produce reusable website assets: a page you can publish today and a prompt you can rerun for the next page, and the one after that. That’s the difference between spending credits and investing them. Every prompt below is written so the output is a finished page asset and the prompt itself becomes a template you keep.

One-Off Outputs vs Reusable Website Assets

Here’s the mindset shift in one table. The left column is how most people burn a Fable 5 session. The right column is how you turn the same session into something you use for months.

One-off output (avoid) Reusable website asset (do this)
“Write me a hero headline.” A homepage messaging prompt that returns positioning, hero, subhead, CTA, and section order you can reuse for any page.
“Give me SEO tips for this page.” An SEO landing page blueprint: H1, section outline, FAQ, internal links, and metadata mapped to one keyword and intent.
“Make my sales page better.” A full sales page structure plus a repeatable conversion-audit prompt you rerun after every change.
Copy lives in a chat you’ll lose next week. Copy and the prompt both saved as a skill you rerun for the next page in seconds.

Credit-smart tip

Fable 5 is a heavier model, so batch related website work into one longer session instead of many small prompts, and reserve it for the structural pages here. Use a lighter model like Sonnet 5 for quick edits. For a full strategy, read The 9 Best Ways To Reduce Claude Fable 5 Credit Usage.

The Master Claude Fable 5 Website Prompt Template

Every website prompt in this guide is built on the same skeleton. Learn it once and you can write a strong Fable 5 prompt for any page type. Paste this template and fill in the brackets, or jump to a ready-made prompt below.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert website strategist and conversion copywriter.

GOAL
Produce a complete, ready-to-build [page type: SEO landing page / homepage / sales page] for my business.

CONTEXT
- Business: [what you sell and to whom]
- Primary audience: [who this page is for and what they want]
- Offer: [the product, service, or action this page drives]
- Brand voice: [e.g. friendly, beginner-first, no hype]
- Primary keyword or goal: [target keyword OR the single action the page should drive]

INPUTS
[Paste existing copy, notes, competitor URLs, proof, testimonials, or product details]

CONSTRAINTS
- One clear primary call to action
- Match the brand voice above
- No invented claims, stats, or testimonials — mark anything I must supply as [NEEDS INPUT]

PROCESS
1. Clarify the page's single goal and target reader in one sentence.
2. Map the page section by section, in order.
3. Draft the copy for each section.
4. Add the metadata and any FAQ the page needs.
5. Flag anything missing that would make the page stronger.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Page goal (one sentence)
- Section-by-section outline with a short label for each
- Full draft copy under each section
- Suggested SEO title and meta description
- List of anything marked [NEEDS INPUT]

QUALITY CHECK
Before finishing, confirm the primary CTA is obvious, the value is clear in the first screen, and no claims are invented.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me the single highest-impact thing to finalize first.

Best for: Turning one target keyword and search intent into a complete, ready-to-build SEO page — H1, section outline, on-page copy, FAQ, internal links, and metadata.

Use when: You want a page that ranks and reads well, not a keyword-stuffed draft.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert SEO strategist and on-page content designer.

GOAL
Design a complete SEO landing page that can rank for one primary keyword and satisfy its search intent.

CONTEXT
- Primary keyword: [keyword]
- Search intent: [informational / commercial / transactional]
- Business and offer: [what you sell and the action this page should drive]
- Audience: [who is searching and what they need]

INPUTS
[Paste any existing page copy, competitor URLs, or notes. If none, say "none".]

CONSTRAINTS
- Write for the reader first, then optimize — no keyword stuffing
- One primary CTA
- Do not invent statistics or testimonials — mark as [NEEDS INPUT]

PROCESS
1. Confirm the dominant search intent in one sentence.
2. Propose the single best H1.
3. Outline the page as ordered H2 and H3 sections that fully answer the intent.
4. Draft concise on-page copy under each section.
5. Write 4 to 6 FAQ questions real searchers ask, with short answers.
6. Suggest 3 to 5 internal links by descriptive anchor text.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Search intent (one sentence)
- Recommended H1
- Full H2/H3 outline with draft copy
- FAQ block (question + short answer)
- Internal link suggestions (anchor + where it should point)
- SEO title and meta description

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm every section maps to the search intent and the primary keyword appears naturally in the H1, first 100 words, one H2, and the meta description.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me which section to write in full first for the biggest ranking impact.

How to customize it

Paste one or two competitor URLs that already rank so Fable 5 can spot gaps and cover what they miss instead of repeating them.

What output to expect: A build-ready page blueprint: intent, H1, full outline with copy, FAQ, internal links, and metadata.

Next step: Run the SEO Metadata & Schema Prompt to finish the title tag, meta description, and FAQ schema.

Best for: The metadata layer that decides your click-through rate and how AI answer engines quote your page — title tags, meta descriptions, and FAQ content designed to be extractable.

Use when: A page is written but its metadata is an afterthought, or you want it quotable by AI search.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert technical SEO and metadata specialist.

GOAL
Write the metadata and answer-ready content that improve this page's click-through rate and make it easy for AI answer engines to quote.

CONTEXT
- Page topic and primary keyword: [topic / keyword]
- Page URL or working title: [url or title]
- Audience: [who this page is for]

INPUTS
[Paste the page copy or a summary of its main sections]

CONSTRAINTS
- SEO title under about 60 characters, meta description under about 155 characters
- Lead every FAQ answer with a direct, quotable first sentence
- No invented facts

PROCESS
1. Summarize the page's core promise in one sentence.
2. Write 3 SEO title options and note which you recommend and why.
3. Write 2 meta description options with the keyword used naturally.
4. Write 5 FAQ questions with concise, self-contained answers.
5. Suggest which single fact or definition on the page is most likely to be quoted by an AI answer engine, and how to phrase it clearly.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Core promise (one sentence)
- 3 SEO titles (recommended one marked)
- 2 meta descriptions
- 5 FAQ items (question + answer)
- One "most quotable" sentence, rewritten for clarity

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm each FAQ answer makes sense on its own, out of context, and the title reflects what the page actually delivers.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me which title to test first.

How to customize it

Ask Fable 5 to output the FAQ as a plain question-and-answer list so you can paste it into a Rank Math FAQ block or your own schema. Confirm current field limits before publishing.

What output to expect: Ready-to-paste titles, meta descriptions, and a quotable FAQ block built for both classic search and AI answers.

Next step: Feed the FAQ into the Objection-Handling & FAQ Prompt to make sure it also answers buying objections.

Best for: A reusable brief that turns a topic into a blog post or resource page designed to rank and support your money pages.

Use when: You publish content regularly and want a consistent, repeatable brief instead of starting each post from scratch.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert SEO content strategist.

GOAL
Create a complete content brief for one article that can rank and support my main offer pages.

CONTEXT
- Topic or primary keyword: [topic / keyword]
- Business and offer this content should support: [offer]
- Audience and their knowledge level: [audience]

INPUTS
[Paste any related pages you already have so we can internal-link and avoid overlap]

CONSTRAINTS
- Match the search intent, not just the keyword
- Recommend internal links to my existing pages by descriptive anchor
- No fabricated data

PROCESS
1. State the search intent and the one question the article must answer.
2. Recommend the working title and H1.
3. Outline the article as ordered H2/H3 headings.
4. For each heading, list the key points to cover.
5. List entities, subtopics, and related questions to include for topical depth.
6. Suggest internal links and one clear CTA to a money page.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Search intent + core question
- Title and H1
- Full heading outline with key points
- Entities and related questions to cover
- Internal links (anchor + target)
- Recommended CTA

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm the brief would let a writer produce the article without guessing, and that it links to at least one relevant offer page.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me whether to draft the introduction or the highest-intent section first.

How to customize it

List the URLs of pages you want the article to link to so Fable 5 can build the internal-linking plan around your real site.

What output to expect: A writer-ready brief with intent, outline, key points, entities, internal links, and a CTA.

Next step: Turn the brief into a saved skill so every future post starts here — see turning these prompts into a skill.

Best for: Fixing the most-visited page on your site — clear positioning, a hero that states who it’s for and why it matters, and a single obvious CTA.

Use when: Visitors land on your homepage and can’t tell what you do in five seconds.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert brand messaging strategist and homepage copywriter.

GOAL
Create clear homepage messaging and a hero section that tells the right visitor what I do, who it's for, and why it matters — fast.

CONTEXT
- Business: [what you sell]
- Ideal visitor: [who you most want to reach]
- Main action you want them to take: [book, buy, sign up, download]
- Brand voice: [tone]

INPUTS
[Paste current homepage copy or describe your offer in a few sentences]

CONSTRAINTS
- The hero must be understandable in about five seconds
- One primary CTA, with an optional secondary CTA
- No jargon or hype; no invented claims

PROCESS
1. Write a one-sentence positioning statement: for [who], we [do what] so they [outcome].
2. Draft 3 hero headline options with matching subheadlines.
3. Recommend the primary CTA wording and one secondary CTA.
4. Propose the homepage section order below the hero.
5. Note the single proof element that would most increase trust.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Positioning statement
- 3 hero options (headline + subheadline), recommended one marked
- Primary and secondary CTA wording
- Homepage section order
- One recommended proof element

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm a first-time visitor would understand the offer and the next step without scrolling.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me which hero option to publish first and what to test against it.

How to customize it

Give Fable 5 one competitor homepage and ask it to make your positioning clearly different, not just cleaner.

What output to expect: A positioning statement, three hero options, CTA wording, and a section order you can build immediately.

Next step: Run the Landing Page A/B Variant Prompt to generate versions to test.

Best for: A focused landing page for one offer — a lead magnet, webinar, waitlist, free trial, or booking — with copy for every section.

Use when: You’re running traffic to a dedicated page and need it to convert on one action.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert direct-response landing page copywriter.

GOAL
Write a complete lead-gen landing page focused on one conversion action.

CONTEXT
- Offer: [lead magnet, webinar, trial, booking, waitlist]
- Who it's for: [audience and the problem it solves]
- The one action: [what a visitor should do]
- Brand voice: [tone]

INPUTS
[Paste details about the offer, benefits, and any proof you have]

CONSTRAINTS
- Keep the page focused on the single action — no competing links
- Lead with the visitor's problem and desired outcome, not your features
- Mark any proof, stat, or testimonial you need from me as [NEEDS INPUT]

PROCESS
1. State the one action and the promise in a sentence.
2. Draft the hero: headline, subheadline, and CTA.
3. Draft the "what you get" and "who it's for" sections.
4. Draft a short benefits or outcomes section.
5. Draft an objection-reducing section and a proof section.
6. Draft a closing CTA that restates the promise.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- One-line promise
- Hero (headline + subheadline + CTA)
- What you get / who it's for
- Benefits or outcomes
- Objection reducer + proof (with [NEEDS INPUT] where needed)
- Closing CTA

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm the page drives only one action and the value is clear before any scroll.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me the one section most likely to lose conversions and how to strengthen it.

How to customize it

Tell Fable 5 the traffic source (ads, email, social) so it matches the page’s message to what the visitor just clicked.

What output to expect: Full landing page copy, section by section, focused on one conversion action.

Next step: Pressure-test it with the Sales Page Conversion Audit Prompt before you send traffic.

Best for: Generating distinct, testable variants of a hero or CTA — different angles, not reworded copies.

Use when: A page gets traffic and you want structured options to A/B test.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert conversion optimization strategist.

GOAL
Create distinct, testable variants of my hero and CTA based on different persuasion angles.

CONTEXT
- Page and offer: [what the page sells or asks for]
- Audience: [who lands here]
- Current hero and CTA: [paste them]

CONSTRAINTS
- Each variant must use a genuinely different angle, not reworded copy
- Keep every variant honest — no invented claims
- One clear CTA per variant

PROCESS
1. Name 3 persuasion angles that fit this audience (for example: outcome, speed, risk-reversal, status quo cost, social proof).
2. For each angle, write a hero headline, subheadline, and CTA.
3. Explain in one line what each variant is testing.
4. Recommend which variant to run first and why.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 3 angles named
- 3 variants (headline + subheadline + CTA)
- One-line test hypothesis per variant
- Recommended first test

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm the three variants are meaningfully different and each could plausibly win.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me what metric to watch and how long to run the first test.

How to customize it

Add your current conversion rate or traffic volume so Fable 5 can suggest a realistic test order and priority.

What output to expect: Three angle-based variants with a test hypothesis for each and a recommended starting test.

Next step: Once a winner emerges, feed it back into the Homepage Messaging Prompt to align the rest of the site.

Best for: A complete long-form sales page structure and draft — the kind of multi-section page Fable 5’s long-context strength is genuinely suited to.

Use when: You’re selling a product, course, service, or offer that needs more than a short page to convert.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert long-form sales page copywriter.

GOAL
Write a complete long-form sales page that moves a warm reader from interest to purchase.

CONTEXT
- Offer and price: [what you sell and the price]
- Audience and core desire: [who buys and what they really want]
- Main objections: [what makes them hesitate]
- Brand voice: [tone]

INPUTS
[Paste offer details, features, outcomes, guarantees, and any real testimonials or results]

CONSTRAINTS
- Lead with the reader's desired outcome, not the feature list
- Use only proof I provide — mark gaps as [NEEDS INPUT]
- One primary offer and CTA, repeated at natural decision points

PROCESS
1. State the core promise and the transformation the offer delivers.
2. Draft the sales page section by section: hook, problem, promise, offer, what's included, benefits/outcomes, proof, objections, guarantee, pricing, FAQ, and final CTA.
3. Keep each section tight and skimmable with clear subheads.
4. Place the CTA at the hero, after the offer, and at the close.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Core promise (one sentence)
- Full section-by-section draft with subheads
- CTA wording (used at 3 points)
- List of [NEEDS INPUT] items I must supply

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm every claim is supported or marked for input, the offer is unmistakable, and a skimmer could still follow the argument from subheads alone.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me which section most needs real proof before this page goes live.

How to customize it

Batch this in one Fable 5 session with your offer details already pasted in — a full sales page is exactly the multi-step work worth spending a Fable 5 session on.

What output to expect: A full sales page draft with every section, CTA placement, and a clear list of proof you still need to add.

Next step: Run the Sales Page Conversion Audit Prompt on the finished draft.

Best for: A prioritized, specific fix list for a page that gets traffic but doesn’t convert — the reusable audit you rerun after every change.

Use when: You have a live page and want targeted fixes, not a full rewrite.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert conversion rate optimization consultant.

GOAL
Audit this page and give me specific, prioritized fixes to improve conversions.

CONTEXT
- Page purpose: [sell, sign up, book, download]
- Audience: [who lands here and why]
- Known performance: [traffic, conversion rate, drop-off point, if known]

INPUTS
[Paste the full page copy, or describe each section in order]

CONSTRAINTS
- Do not suggest a full rewrite unless the offer itself is unclear
- Focus on clarity, proof, objection handling, and CTA
- Every fix must be specific enough to implement today

PROCESS
1. Judge whether the offer is clear in the first screen.
2. Find proof gaps and where trust breaks down.
3. List the unanswered objections a skeptical buyer would have.
4. Review CTA wording, placement, and frequency.
5. Rank all fixes by likely impact.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Offer clarity (rated + why)
- Proof gaps (list)
- Unanswered objections (list)
- CTA review (specific fixes)
- Top 5 fixes in priority order

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm no fix is vague — I should be able to act on each one without asking a follow-up.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me the single fix to make first if I only have 30 minutes.

How to customize it

Paste real traffic or conversion numbers if you have them so Fable 5 can prioritize by likely impact instead of guessing.

What output to expect: A ranked, specific fix list covering clarity, proof, objections, and CTA.

Note: For a broader page audit including layout and UX, the general Fable 5 prompts library has a dedicated Website Design & UX Review Prompt.

Best for: Surfacing the real objections a buyer has and turning them into a proof section and FAQ that also helps you get quoted in AI answers.

Use when: A page explains the offer well but still loses people at the decision point.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert conversion copywriter who specializes in objections and trust.

GOAL
Surface the real objections that stop my buyer and turn them into a proof section and an FAQ that reassures readers and reads well to AI answer engines.

CONTEXT
- Offer and price: [what you sell]
- Audience: [who buys]
- Known hesitations: [anything you already hear from prospects]

INPUTS
[Paste the current page copy or offer details]

CONSTRAINTS
- Base objections on this audience, not generic ones
- Answer honestly; never dismiss a real concern
- Keep every FAQ answer self-contained and quotable

PROCESS
1. List the top 6 objections this specific buyer would have.
2. For each, write a short, honest response that reduces the risk.
3. Turn the strongest 5 into FAQ questions with concise, standalone answers.
4. Recommend which objections deserve a visible proof element on the page.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Top 6 objections with responses
- 5 FAQ items (question + self-contained answer)
- Proof elements to add, mapped to specific objections

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm each FAQ answer makes sense on its own and no response overpromises.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me which objection is costing me the most conversions and where to address it on the page.

How to customize it

Paste real questions from sales calls, emails, or comments so the objections reflect what your buyers actually say.

What output to expect: A ranked objection list, honest responses, a quotable FAQ, and proof elements mapped to each concern.

Next step: Turn your top cost objections into a real page with the Pricing Page Prompt.

Best for: Turning your pricing into a clear, decision-ready page — plan comparison, an obvious recommended tier, and the cost objections a buyer is silently asking before they reach checkout.

Use when: Your offer is priced but the pricing page still reads like a spreadsheet instead of a sales tool.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert pricing strategist and conversion copywriter.

GOAL
Write a complete pricing page that makes the right plan obvious and removes hesitation at the moment of decision.

CONTEXT
- Offer and pricing tiers: [list plans/tiers and prices, or a single price]
- Audience: [who is deciding and what they compare you against]
- Recommended plan: [the tier you want most buyers to pick, if any]
- Brand voice: [tone]

INPUTS
[Paste your plan details, features per tier, guarantee terms, and any competitor pricing you're aware of]

CONSTRAINTS
- Make the recommended plan visually and logically obvious without pressure tactics
- Answer the top 3 cost objections before the reader has to ask
- No invented guarantees, refund terms, or comparisons — mark as [NEEDS INPUT]

PROCESS
1. State the pricing page's single goal and which plan you want most visitors to choose.
2. Draft the pricing header and a one-line value reminder above the plans.
3. Draft each plan's name, price, best-for line, and feature list.
4. Write the "why this plan" nudge for the recommended tier.
5. Draft a short FAQ answering cost, billing, and guarantee questions.
6. Draft the final CTA and any risk-reversal line beneath it.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Pricing page goal (one sentence)
- Header + value reminder
- Plan-by-plan breakdown (name, price, best-for, features)
- Recommended-plan nudge
- Pricing FAQ (question + short answer)
- Final CTA + risk-reversal line

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm the recommended plan is obvious within the first screen and every likely cost objection is answered before the FAQ.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me which plan is underperforming and the single change most likely to fix it.

How to customize it

Tell Fable 5 which plan you actually want most customers to pick — it will design the visual and copy emphasis around that tier instead of presenting every option equally.

What output to expect: A complete pricing page: header, plan-by-plan breakdown, a nudge toward your recommended tier, a cost FAQ, and a closing CTA.

Next step: Run the Sales Page Conversion Audit Prompt on the finished pricing page before it goes live.

Turn These Website Prompts Into a Reusable Skill

A prompt is one request. A skill is the saved, reusable version of that process — same inputs, same steps, same output format every time — so you build your next SEO page, landing page, or sales page in seconds instead of starting over. The SEO Metadata skill does what the metadata prompt does on any finished page, the Landing Page Creator skill turns one offer into a full conversion page like the landing and sales-page prompts above, and the Website Copy Refresh skill audits an existing page the way the conversion-audit prompt does.

Final takeaway

The best Claude Fable 5 website prompts aren’t clever wording — they’re structure that produces a finished, reusable page asset. With the credit window closing soon, the highest-return move is to build the pages that carry your business (SEO pages, landing pages, and sales pages) and save the prompts behind them as skills. Frequently asked questions

What are the best Claude Fable 5 website prompts?

The best Claude Fable 5 website prompts are structured, reusable workflows that produce a full page asset in one pass — an SEO landing page blueprint, a homepage or lead-gen landing page, a long-form sales page, or a pricing page — instead of a one-line answer. Each gives Fable 5 a clear goal, your real context, the page’s purpose and audience, a process, and an exact output format. The master template and 10 prompts above cover SEO, landing pages, and sales pages.

Is Claude Fable 5 good for building website pages?

Yes. Building a page is exactly the complex, long-context, multi-step work Fable 5 is designed for — positioning, structure, proof, objections, search intent, and copy all at once. That makes it a strong fit for SEO pages, landing pages, and sales pages, especially when you paste in real context and ask for a full section-by-section draft.

Should I use my Fable 5 window on website prompts before usage credits start?

It’s one of the highest-return ways to spend it. Anthropic restored Fable 5 globally on July 1, 2026, and from July 20 it’s included in Max and Team Premium plans at 50% of limits, with Pro and Team Standard moving to usage credits. Website pages are durable assets that keep working long after any credit balance runs down, and the prompts behind them become reusable skills — so you get lasting value instead of one-off answers. Confirm your own plan’s limits in Claude before planning around them.

What is the difference between these website prompts and the general Fable 5 prompts?

These prompts are specialized to produce full website assets — SEO pages, landing pages, and sales pages. The general 15 Best Claude Fable 5 Prompts library covers a wider range of business, research, and AI agent tasks. Use this page when your goal is a page you can publish; use the general library for everything else.

Can these prompts help my pages get quoted by AI search?

Yes, indirectly. The SEO metadata and objection/FAQ prompts ask Fable 5 to write self-contained, quotable answers with a clear first sentence, which is the kind of content AI answer engines tend to extract. Combine that with a clear page structure and honest, specific claims for the best results.

Do I need coding to use these Claude Fable 5 website prompts?

No. Copy a prompt, replace the bracketed placeholders with your real details, and run it in Claude. The output is page copy and structure you paste into your website builder. No code required.

How do I turn a website prompt into a reusable skill?

Save the prompt that produced your best page, then standardize its inputs, steps, and output format so you can rerun it for the next page. The free Claude Credit Saver Skill helps you tighten and reuse each prompt, and What an AI Agent Skill Is explains the full prompt-to-skill process.

Is Claude Fable 5 better than Sonnet 5 for website copy?

For full pages, usually yes — Fable 5 handles the long, multi-section reasoning a page needs. For quick edits, single headlines, or small rewrites, Sonnet 5 is faster and lighter on credits. A good rule: draft the whole page with Fable 5, then make small tweaks with Sonnet 5.

**What to paste into Claude:**

**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert brand messaging strategist and homepage copywriter.
GOAL Create clear homepage messaging and a hero section that tells the right visitor what I do, who it's for, and why it matters — fast.
CONTEXT - Business: \[what you sell\] - Ideal visitor: \[who you most want to reach\] - Main action you want them to take: \[book, buy, sign up, download\] - Brand voice: \[tone\]
INPUTS \[Paste current homepage copy or describe your offer in a few sentences\]
CONSTRAINTS - The hero must be understandable in about five seconds - One primary CTA, with an optional secondary CTA - No jargon or hype; no invented claims
PROCESS 1. Write a one-sentence positioning statement: for \[who\], we \[do what\] so they \[outcome\]. 2. Draft 3 hero headline options with matching subheadlines. 3. Recommend the primary CTA wording and one secondary CTA. 4. Propose the homepage section order below the hero. 5. Note the single proof element that would most increase trust.
OUTPUT FORMAT - Positioning statement - 3 hero options (headline + subheadline), recommended one marked - Primary and secondary CTA wording - Homepage section order - One recommended proof element
QUALITY CHECK Confirm a first-time visitor would understand the offer and the next step without scrolling.
NEXT ACTION Tell me which hero option to publish first and what to test against it.
**How to customize it**
Give Fable 5 one competitor homepage and ask it to make your positioning clearly different, not just cleaner.
**What output to expect:** A positioning statement, three hero options, CTA wording, and a section order you can build immediately.
**Next step:** Run the [Landing Page A/B Variant Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-website-prompts/#prompt-landing-variants) to generate versions to test.
**Best for:** A focused landing page for one offer — a lead magnet, webinar, waitlist, free trial, or booking — with copy for every section.
**Use when:** You’re running traffic to a dedicated page and need it to convert on one action.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert direct-response landing page copywriter.
GOAL Write a complete lead-gen landing page focused on one conversion action.
CONTEXT - Offer: \[lead magnet, webinar, trial, booking, waitlist\] - Who it's for: \[audience and the problem it solves\] - The one action: \[what a visitor should do\] - Brand voice: \[tone\]
INPUTS \[Paste details about the offer, benefits, and any proof you have\]
CONSTRAINTS - Keep the page focused on the single action — no competing links - Lead with the visitor's problem and desired outcome, not your features - Mark any proof, stat, or testimonial you need from me as \[NEEDS INPUT\]
PROCESS 1. State the one action and the promise in a sentence. 2. Draft the hero: headline, subheadline, and CTA. 3. Draft the "what you get" and "who it's for" sections. 4. Draft a short benefits or outcomes section. 5. Draft an objection-reducing section and a proof section. 6. Draft a closing CTA that restates the promise.
OUTPUT FORMAT - One-line promise - Hero (headline + subheadline + CTA) - What you get / who it's for - Benefits or outcomes - Objection reducer + proof (with \[NEEDS INPUT\] where needed) - Closing CTA
QUALITY CHECK Confirm the page drives only one action and the value is clear before any scroll.
NEXT ACTION Tell me the one section most likely to lose conversions and how to strengthen it.
**How to customize it**
Tell Fable 5 the traffic source (ads, email, social) so it matches the page’s message to what the visitor just clicked.
**What output to expect:** Full landing page copy, section by section, focused on one conversion action.
**Next step:** Pressure-test it with the [Sales Page Conversion Audit Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-website-prompts/#prompt-sales-audit) before you send traffic.
**Best for:** Generating distinct, testable variants of a hero or CTA — different angles, not reworded copies.
**Use when:** A page gets traffic and you want structured options to A/B test.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert conversion optimization strategist.
GOAL Create distinct, testable variants of my hero and CTA based on different persuasion angles.
CONTEXT - Page and offer: \[what the page sells or asks for\] - Audience: \[who lands here\] - Current hero and CTA: \[paste them\]
CONSTRAINTS - Each variant must use a genuinely different angle, not reworded copy - Keep every variant honest — no invented claims - One clear CTA per variant
PROCESS 1. Name 3 persuasion angles that fit this audience (for example: outcome, speed, risk-reversal, status quo cost, social proof). 2. For each angle, write a hero headline, subheadline, and CTA. 3. Explain in one line what each variant is testing. 4. Recommend which variant to run first and why.
OUTPUT FORMAT - 3 angles named - 3 variants (headline + subheadline + CTA) - One-line test hypothesis per variant - Recommended first test
QUALITY CHECK Confirm the three variants are meaningfully different and each could plausibly win.
NEXT ACTION Tell me what metric to watch and how long to run the first test.
**How to customize it**
Add your current conversion rate or traffic volume so Fable 5 can suggest a realistic test order and priority.
**What output to expect:** Three angle-based variants with a test hypothesis for each and a recommended starting test.
**Next step:** Once a winner emerges, feed it back into the [Homepage Messaging Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-website-prompts/#prompt-homepage) to align the rest of the site.
**Best for:** A complete long-form sales page structure and draft — the kind of multi-section page Fable 5’s long-context strength is genuinely suited to.
**Use when:** You’re selling a product, course, service, or offer that needs more than a short page to convert.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert long-form sales page copywriter.
GOAL Write a complete long-form sales page that moves a warm reader from interest to purchase.
CONTEXT - Offer and price: \[what you sell and the price\] - Audience and core desire: \[who buys and what they really want\] - Main objections: \[what makes them hesitate\] - Brand voice: \[tone\]
INPUTS \[Paste offer details, features, outcomes, guarantees, and any real testimonials or results\]
CONSTRAINTS - Lead with the reader's desired outcome, not the feature list - Use only proof I provide — mark gaps as \[NEEDS INPUT\] - One primary offer and CTA, repeated at natural decision points
PROCESS 1. State the core promise and the transformation the offer delivers. 2. Draft the sales page section by section: hook, problem, promise, offer, what's included, benefits/outcomes, proof, objections, guarantee, pricing, FAQ, and final CTA. 3. Keep each section tight and skimmable with clear subheads. 4. Place the CTA at the hero, after the offer, and at the close.
OUTPUT FORMAT - Core promise (one sentence) - Full section-by-section draft with subheads - CTA wording (used at 3 points) - List of \[NEEDS INPUT\] items I must supply
QUALITY CHECK Confirm every claim is supported or marked for input, the offer is unmistakable, and a skimmer could still follow the argument from subheads alone.
NEXT ACTION Tell me which section most needs real proof before this page goes live.
**How to customize it**
Batch this in one Fable 5 session with your offer details already pasted in — a full sales page is exactly the multi-step work worth spending a Fable 5 session on.
**What output to expect:** A full sales page draft with every section, CTA placement, and a clear list of proof you still need to add.
**Next step:** Run the [Sales Page Conversion Audit Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-website-prompts/#prompt-sales-audit) on the finished draft.
**Best for:** A prioritized, specific fix list for a page that gets traffic but doesn’t convert — the reusable audit you rerun after every change.
**Use when:** You have a live page and want targeted fixes, not a full rewrite.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert conversion rate optimization consultant.
GOAL Audit this page and give me specific, prioritized fixes to improve conversions.
CONTEXT - Page purpose: \[sell, sign up, book, download\] - Audience: \[who lands here and why\] - Known performance: \[traffic, conversion rate, drop-off point, if known\]
INPUTS \[Paste the full page copy, or describe each section in order\]
CONSTRAINTS - Do not suggest a full rewrite unless the offer itself is unclear - Focus on clarity, proof, objection handling, and CTA - Every fix must be specific enough to implement today
PROCESS 1. Judge whether the offer is clear in the first screen. 2. Find proof gaps and where trust breaks down. 3. List the unanswered objections a skeptical buyer would have. 4. Review CTA wording, placement, and frequency. 5. Rank all fixes by likely impact.
OUTPUT FORMAT - Offer clarity (rated + why) - Proof gaps (list) - Unanswered objections (list) - CTA review (specific fixes) - Top 5 fixes in priority order
QUALITY CHECK Confirm no fix is vague — I should be able to act on each one without asking a follow-up.
NEXT ACTION Tell me the single fix to make first if I only have 30 minutes.
**How to customize it**
Paste real traffic or conversion numbers if you have them so Fable 5 can prioritize by likely impact instead of guessing.
**What output to expect:** A ranked, specific fix list covering clarity, proof, objections, and CTA.
**Note:** For a broader page audit including layout and UX, the [general Fable 5 prompts library](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-prompts/) has a dedicated Website Design & UX Review Prompt.
**Best for:** Surfacing the real objections a buyer has and turning them into a proof section and FAQ that also helps you get quoted in AI answers.
**Use when:** A page explains the offer well but still loses people at the decision point.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert conversion copywriter who specializes in objections and trust.
GOAL Surface the real objections that stop my buyer and turn them into a proof section and an FAQ that reassures readers and reads well to AI answer engines.
CONTEXT - Offer and price: \[what you sell\] - Audience: \[who buys\] - Known hesitations: \[anything you already hear from prospects\]
INPUTS \[Paste the current page copy or offer details\]
CONSTRAINTS - Base objections on this audience, not generic ones - Answer honestly; never dismiss a real concern - Keep every FAQ answer self-contained and quotable
PROCESS 1. List the top 6 objections this specific buyer would have. 2. For each, write a short, honest response that reduces the risk. 3. Turn the strongest 5 into FAQ questions with concise, standalone answers. 4. Recommend which objections deserve a visible proof element on the page.
OUTPUT FORMAT - Top 6 objections with responses - 5 FAQ items (question + self-contained answer) - Proof elements to add, mapped to specific objections
QUALITY CHECK Confirm each FAQ answer makes sense on its own and no response overpromises.
NEXT ACTION Tell me which objection is costing me the most conversions and where to address it on the page.
**How to customize it**
Paste real questions from sales calls, emails, or comments so the objections reflect what your buyers actually say.
**What output to expect:** A ranked objection list, honest responses, a quotable FAQ, and proof elements mapped to each concern.
**Next step:** Turn your top cost objections into a real page with the [Pricing Page Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-website-prompts/#prompt-pricing).
**Best for:** Turning your pricing into a clear, decision-ready page — plan comparison, an obvious recommended tier, and the cost objections a buyer is silently asking before they reach checkout.
**Use when:** Your offer is priced but the pricing page still reads like a spreadsheet instead of a sales tool.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert pricing strategist and conversion copywriter.
GOAL Write a complete pricing page that makes the right plan obvious and removes hesitation at the moment of decision.
CONTEXT - Offer and pricing tiers: \[list plans/tiers and prices, or a single price\] - Audience: \[who is deciding and what they compare you against\] - Recommended plan: \[the tier you want most buyers to pick, if any\] - Brand voice: \[tone\]
INPUTS \[Paste your plan details, features per tier, guarantee terms, and any competitor pricing you're aware of\]
CONSTRAINTS - Make the recommended plan visually and logically obvious without pressure tactics - Answer the top 3 cost objections before the reader has to ask - No invented guarantees, refund terms, or comparisons — mark as \[NEEDS INPUT\]
PROCESS 1. State the pricing page's single goal and which plan you want most visitors to choose. 2. Draft the pricing header and a one-line value reminder above the plans. 3. Draft each plan's name, price, best-for line, and feature list. 4. Write the "why this plan" nudge for the recommended tier. 5. Draft a short FAQ answering cost, billing, and guarantee questions. 6. Draft the final CTA and any risk-reversal line beneath it.
OUTPUT FORMAT - Pricing page goal (one sentence) - Header + value reminder - Plan-by-plan breakdown (name, price, best-for, features) - Recommended-plan nudge - Pricing FAQ (question + short answer) - Final CTA + risk-reversal line
QUALITY CHECK Confirm the recommended plan is obvious within the first screen and every likely cost objection is answered before the FAQ.
NEXT ACTION Tell me which plan is underperforming and the single change most likely to fix it.
**How to customize it**
Tell Fable 5 which plan you actually want most customers to pick — it will design the visual and copy emphasis around that tier instead of presenting every option equally.
**What output to expect:** A complete pricing page: header, plan-by-plan breakdown, a nudge toward your recommended tier, a cost FAQ, and a closing CTA.
**Next step:** Run the [Sales Page Conversion Audit Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-website-prompts/#prompt-sales-audit) on the finished pricing page before it goes live.
## Turn These Website Prompts Into a Reusable Skill
A prompt is one request. A skill is the saved, reusable version of that process — same inputs, same steps, same output format every time — so you build your next SEO page, landing page, or sales page in seconds instead of starting over. This is the whole point of using your Fable 5 window well: the page you ship today is valuable, but the reusable prompt behind it compounds.
Start by saving your best-performing website prompt above, then see how to [build a website with one reusable AI skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-create-a-website-with-ai-skill/) for the finished version of exactly that — one reusable skill that produces a site map, hero copy, SEO metadata, and FAQs on every run, in Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. If you want the underlying theory first, [What an AI Agent Skill Is](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent-skill/) covers prompts versus skills versus agents. To skip the blank page, browse the free [AI Website & Design skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/web-design/) — the reusable, cross-platform versions of the prompts on this page. The [SEO Metadata skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/seo-metadata/) does what the metadata prompt does on any finished page, the [Landing Page Creator skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/landing-page/) turns one offer into a full conversion page like the landing and sales-page prompts above, and the [Website Copy Refresh skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/website-copy-refresh/) audits an existing page the way the conversion-audit prompt does.
## Final takeaway
The best Claude Fable 5 website prompts aren’t clever wording — they’re structure that produces a finished, reusable page asset. With the credit window closing soon, the highest-return move is to build the pages that carry your business (SEO pages, landing pages, and sales pages) and save the prompts behind them as skills. Pick one prompt above, build one real page this week, then save it so the next page takes minutes. For a deeper usage strategy, read [The 9 Best Ways To Reduce Claude Fable 5 Credit Usage](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/save-claude-fable-5-credits/).
[Free skills **AI Website & Design Skills** _The reusable, cross-platform versions of these prompts — website, landing page, SEO, and brand._](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/web-design/) [Free skill **Get the Claude Credit Saver Skill** _Tighten and reuse every prompt so you waste fewer credits on back-and-forth._](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/free-claude-credit-saver-skill/) [Skill library **Browse Claude Skills** _Find reusable Claude workflows for research, SEO, content, and business tasks._](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/claude/) [More prompts **The 15 Best Claude Fable 5 Prompts** _The full library for business, SEO, research, and AI agent workflows._](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-prompts/)
## Frequently asked questions
What are the best Claude Fable 5 website prompts?
The best Claude Fable 5 website prompts are structured, reusable workflows that produce a full page asset in one pass — an SEO landing page blueprint, a homepage or lead-gen landing page, a long-form sales page, or a pricing page — instead of a one-line answer. Each gives Fable 5 a clear goal, your real context, the page’s purpose and audience, a process, and an exact output format. The master template and 10 prompts above cover SEO, landing pages, and sales pages.
Is Claude Fable 5 good for building website pages?
Yes. Building a page is exactly the complex, long-context, multi-step work Fable 5 is designed for — positioning, structure, proof, objections, search intent, and copy all at once. That makes it a strong fit for SEO pages, landing pages, and sales pages, especially when you paste in real context and ask for a full section-by-section draft.
Should I use my Fable 5 window on website prompts before usage credits start?
It’s one of the highest-return ways to spend it. Anthropic restored Fable 5 globally on July 1, 2026, and from July 20 it’s included in Max and Team Premium plans at 50% of limits, with Pro and Team Standard moving to usage credits. Website pages are durable assets that keep working long after any credit balance runs down, and the prompts behind them become reusable skills — so you get lasting value instead of one-off answers. Confirm your own plan’s limits in Claude before planning around them.
What is the difference between these website prompts and the general Fable 5 prompts?
These prompts are specialized to produce full website assets — SEO pages, landing pages, and sales pages. The general [15 Best Claude Fable 5 Prompts](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-prompts/) library covers a wider range of business, research, and AI agent tasks. Use this page when your goal is a page you can publish; use the general library for everything else.
Can these prompts help my pages get quoted by AI search?
Yes, indirectly. The SEO metadata and objection/FAQ prompts ask Fable 5 to write self-contained, quotable answers with a clear first sentence, which is the kind of content AI answer engines tend to extract. Combine that with a clear page structure and honest, specific claims for the best results.
Do I need coding to use these Claude Fable 5 website prompts?
No. Copy a prompt, replace the bracketed placeholders with your real details, and run it in Claude. The output is page copy and structure you paste into your website builder. No code required.
How do I turn a website prompt into a reusable skill?
Save the prompt that produced your best page, then standardize its inputs, steps, and output format so you can rerun it for the next page. The free [Claude Credit Saver Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/free-claude-credit-saver-skill/) helps you tighten and reuse each prompt, and [What an AI Agent Skill Is](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent-skill/) explains the full prompt-to-skill process.
Is Claude Fable 5 better than Sonnet 5 for website copy?
For full pages, usually yes — Fable 5 handles the long, multi-section reasoning a page needs. For quick edits, single headlines, or small rewrites, Sonnet 5 is faster and lighter on credits. A good rule: draft the whole page with Fable 5, then make small tweaks with Sonnet 5.

Share a ChatGPT skill with a teammate, publish it to your workspace, install one shared with you, or upload a skill MD file. Step by step, with permissions.

item.name: AI Agents Blog: Beginner Guides, AI Skills, No-Code Workflows
How to Share & Install ChatGPT Skills in a Workspace

item.text: How to Share & Install ChatGPT Skills in Workspace (2026) A skill only has to be built once. After that, the useful question is how to get it to everyone else. ChatGPT lets you hand a skill to one teammate, publish it to your whole workspace, install one somebody sent you, or upload a skill file you downloaded — and each of those is a slightly different action in a slightly different place. This guide covers all four, plus what happens after you share: changing who has access, transferring ownership, and pulling a skill back. If you’re still deciding what to build, start with how to create a ChatGPT skill instead. How do you share a ChatGPT skill? Open the ChatGPT sidebar, select Plugins, then the Skills tab. Find the skill you want to share, open its more-options menu (•••), and choose Share. From there you can search for people or groups in your workspace, or copy a sharing link. You can also set access permissions so only you or specific people can use it. To go the other direction — installing something shared with you — look under Shared with me or Shared by your workspace, open the (•••) menu, and select Install. Sharing, publishing, installing, and uploading are four different actions — all of them live in the Skills tab under Plugins. Who Can Share and Install ChatGPT Skills Sharing is a workspace feature, so two things have to be true before any of the steps below work: your plan has to include Skills, and your workspace has to allow the specific action you’re trying to take. OpenAI lists Personal Skills as generally available for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu. If you’re not sure whether your account qualifies — or the Skills tab isn’t there at all — that’s a separate question with its own answer: ChatGPT Skills availability, plans, and why the tab isn’t showing. Official source: OpenAI’s Skills in ChatGPT documentation. Last checked July 21, 2026. Sharing a skill isn’t the only way to hand one over A skill is ultimately just instructions. If your workspace blocks sharing — or the person you’re helping is on a different plan entirely — you can paste the same text into a chat or a Project and it still works. That portability is why every skill in our library is written as plain text first. This is the most common direction: somebody built something good and sent it your way. Installing it takes about five seconds. Open the ChatGPT sidebar and select Plugins. In the Plugin Directory, select the Skills tab. Look under Shared with me, or Shared by your workspace name — these are separate groupings from Installed and Created by me. Open the more-options menu (•••) next to the skill you want. Select Install. Once installed, ChatGPT can apply the skill automatically when a task matches, or you can explicitly select it by @-mentioning the skill. Both methods are covered properly in how to use ChatGPT skills. Shared with me vs. Installed A skill being shared with you doesn’t mean it’s running. Sharing grants access; installing is what puts it to work. If a teammate insists they sent you something and it isn’t behaving, this is usually why — it’s sitting in “Shared with me,” waiting. Going the other way — handing your skill to a specific colleague or team — starts from the same place. Open the sidebar, select Plugins, then the Skills tab. Find the skill you want to share and open its more-options menu (•••). Select Share. Search for the people or groups in your workspace you want to give access to — or copy the sharing link and send it yourself. Set the access permissions, so the skill stays limited to you or to the specific people you picked. Sharing grants access but does not automatically install the skill. The recipient normally installs it from their own Skills page, unless an authorized workspace admin installs it on their behalf. Worth mentioning when you send it, because it saves a “nothing happened” message later. Share the working version, not the first draft A skill that’s been used and tightened a few times behaves very differently from one written in a single sitting. Run yours on real, messy work before you hand it around — a shared skill that produces mediocre output tends to get quietly uninstalled, and you rarely hear why. How to Publish a Skill to Your Workspace Publishing is the broader version of sharing. Instead of picking individuals, you put the skill in the workspace library so anyone with access can find and install it themselves — useful for the workflows you want standardized rather than passed around informally. It runs through the same Share flow, with the workspace chosen as the audience rather than named people. The difference worth understanding is one of intent: Action Who gets access Best for Share with people or groups Only the individuals or groups you select A skill built for one team, one client, or one role Copy a sharing link Authorized workspace members who can access the link Handing something over quickly, outside a formal rollout Publish to the workspace Everyone in the workspace who can browse the library Processes you want done the same way company-wide Publishing is often gated separately from ordinary sharing, so it’s possible to be allowed to share a skill with a colleague but not to publish it to everyone. If the option isn’t there, that’s a permissions question rather than a bug — see what admins control below. How to Upload a Skill File You Downloaded Skills follow the open Agent Skills standard, which means a skill exported from one supporting product can be brought into another. If someone hands you a skill file rather than a workspace share, you upload it: Go to Plugins → Skills. Select Create, then Upload from your computer. Choose the skill file and confirm. ChatGPT scans uploaded skills before making them available. Most clear straight away. Some come back marked Needs Review, meaning you’ll need to look at additional information before using it, and a few are marked Blocked and can’t be used at all. Read a skill before you install it This matters more than it sounds. A skill can contain instructions, supporting files, and code — so an uploaded skill from an external source or another organization deserves the same scrutiny you’d give any downloaded file. The automatic scan is a safety net, not a substitute for reading what you’re about to let run on your work. If you didn’t write it and don’t trust where it came from, open it first. Managing a Skill After You’ve Shared It Sharing isn’t a one-way door. Once a skill is out in a workspace, it can be reviewed and adjusted. When available for your workspace, the admin Skills page is separate from Permissions & roles. Permissions decide who is allowed to do what; the Skills page is where the skills that already exist get managed. It lists each skill’s owner, access level, how many people use it, and how many times it’s been invoked in the last 30 days. From there, the actions that matter for anyone who has shared something: Change who has access — widen or narrow the users, groups, or workspace members who can use the skill. Change owner — hand a skill to someone else. The previous owner keeps their access after the transfer, so nothing breaks for them. Download — pull a copy of the skill back out, which is also how you move one between workspaces. Delete skill — remove it permanently. Everyone who currently has access loses it. Deleting a shared skill affects everyone, not just you This is the one to be careful with. Deleting removes the skill for every person who had access to it — not only from your own list. If you just don’t want to use it anymore, uninstalling it on your end is the safer move. Check whether anyone else depends on it before deleting a skill you shared or published. What Admins Control About Sharing On workspace plans, sharing is governed by role-based permissions rather than being on for everyone by default. The controls relevant to moving skills around are typically separate switches, which is why you can end up able to do one thing and not another: Enable skills — whether members can create and use skills at all. Enable skill uploading — whether members can upload skill files from their own computer. Share skills — whether members can share with other members or groups. Publish skills to workspace — whether members can publish to the whole workspace. Enable skills installing — whether members can install skills for other members so they’re used automatically. A common configuration is allowing workspace-published skills while blocking arbitrary uploads, so only reviewed skills reach people. Control names and grouping have shifted during rollout, so check your current admin settings before writing internal policy against them. For the full picture of admin controls and plan eligibility, see the ChatGPT Skills availability guide. Shared a Skill and It Hasn’t Appeared? Three things explain most sharing-specific cases: They haven’t installed it yet. Sharing grants access but does not automatically install the skill. It may be sitting under “Shared with me” unless they install it or an authorized workspace admin installs it on their behalf. Sharing is restricted for their role. Workspace permissions can allow you to share while preventing them from installing. An admin can confirm. They’re on a different device than they installed it on. Personal Skills are added per surface and don’t sync automatically between desktop and web/mobile. If the Skills tab isn’t appearing for them at all — rather than one specific skill missing — that’s an access question, not a sharing one. The availability troubleshooting checklist covers all five causes. The Short Version Everything happens in Plugins → Skills. The (•••) menu next to a skill is where sharing and installing both live. Share grants access; install is what makes it run; publish puts it in front of the whole workspace; upload brings in a file from outside. And the part worth remembering: the value was never the sharing mechanism. It’s whether the skill is good enough that people keep it. Start from a skill worth sharing. How do I share a ChatGPT skill with someone? Open the sidebar, select Plugins, then the Skills tab. Find your skill, open its more-options menu (•••), and select Share. You can search for people or groups in your workspace, or copy a sharing link to send yourself. You can also set access permissions so only specific people can use it. How do I install a ChatGPT skill someone shared with me? Go to Plugins → Skills and look under “Shared with me” or “Shared by” your workspace. Open the more-options menu (•••) next to the skill and select Install. Once installed, ChatGPT applies it automatically whenever a task matches what it’s built for. Does sharing a skill install it for the other person? Not automatically. Sharing grants access, and the recipient normally installs the skill from their own Skills page. An authorized workspace admin can also install it on the recipient’s behalf. If a shared skill appears to “do nothing,” it may still be sitting under Shared with me, not yet installed. What’s the difference between sharing and publishing a ChatGPT skill? Sharing gives access to specific people or groups you choose. Publishing puts the skill in your workspace library so anyone with access can find and install it themselves. Sharing suits a skill built for one team or role; publishing suits a process you want done consistently across the whole company. How do I upload a ChatGPT skill file? Go to Plugins → Skills, select Create, then Upload from your computer, and choose the file. ChatGPT scans uploads before making them available — most clear immediately, some are marked Needs Review, and a few are Blocked and can’t be used. Review any skill from an outside source before installing it. Can I take back a ChatGPT skill I shared? Yes. Access can be changed after the fact — on workspace plans there’s an admin Skills page where access, ownership, and removal are managed. Be careful with Delete, though: deleting a skill removes it for everyone who had access, not just for you. If you simply want to stop using it, uninstall it instead. item.html:
How to Share & Install ChatGPT Skills in Workspace (2026)

A skill only has to be built once. After that, the useful question is how to get it to everyone else. ChatGPT lets you hand a skill to one teammate, publish it to your whole workspace, install one somebody sent you, or upload a skill file you downloaded — and each of those is a slightly different action in a slightly different place.

This guide covers all four, plus what happens after you share: changing who has access, transferring ownership, and pulling a skill back. If you’re still deciding what to build, start with how to create a ChatGPT skill instead.

Quick answer

How do you share a ChatGPT skill?

Open the ChatGPT sidebar, select Plugins, then the Skills tab. Find the skill you want to share, open its more-options menu (•••), and choose Share. From there you can search for people or groups in your workspace, or copy a sharing link. You can also set access permissions so only you or specific people can use it.

To go the other direction — installing something shared with you — look under Shared with me or Shared by your workspace, open the (•••) menu, and select Install.

Who Can Share and Install ChatGPT Skills

Sharing is a workspace feature, so two things have to be true before any of the steps below work: your plan has to include Skills, and your workspace has to allow the specific action you’re trying to take.

OpenAI lists Personal Skills as generally available for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu. If you’re not sure whether your account qualifies — or the Skills tab isn’t there at all — that’s a separate question with its own answer: ChatGPT Skills availability, plans, and why the tab isn’t showing.

Official source: OpenAI’s Skills in ChatGPT documentation. Last checked July 21, 2026.

Sharing a skill isn’t the only way to hand one over

A skill is ultimately just instructions. If your workspace blocks sharing — or the person you’re helping is on a different plan entirely — you can paste the same text into a chat or a Project and it still works. That portability is why every skill in our library is written as plain text first.

This is the most common direction: somebody built something good and sent it your way. Installing it takes about five seconds.

  1. Open the ChatGPT sidebar and select Plugins.
  2. In the Plugin Directory, select the Skills tab.
  3. Look under Shared with me, or Shared by your workspace name — these are separate groupings from Installed and Created by me.
  4. Open the more-options menu (•••) next to the skill you want.
  5. Select Install.

Once installed, ChatGPT can apply the skill automatically when a task matches, or you can explicitly select it by @-mentioning the skill. Both methods are covered properly in how to use ChatGPT skills.

Shared with me vs. Installed

A skill being shared with you doesn’t mean it’s running. Sharing grants access; installing is what puts it to work. If a teammate insists they sent you something and it isn’t behaving, this is usually why — it’s sitting in “Shared with me,” waiting.

Going the other way — handing your skill to a specific colleague or team — starts from the same place.

  1. Open the sidebar, select Plugins, then the Skills tab.
  2. Find the skill you want to share and open its more-options menu (•••).
  3. Select Share.
  4. Search for the people or groups in your workspace you want to give access to — or copy the sharing link and send it yourself.
  5. Set the access permissions, so the skill stays limited to you or to the specific people you picked.

Sharing grants access but does not automatically install the skill. The recipient normally installs it from their own Skills page, unless an authorized workspace admin installs it on their behalf. Worth mentioning when you send it, because it saves a “nothing happened” message later.

Share the working version, not the first draft

A skill that’s been used and tightened a few times behaves very differently from one written in a single sitting. Run yours on real, messy work before you hand it around — a shared skill that produces mediocre output tends to get quietly uninstalled, and you rarely hear why.

How to Publish a Skill to Your Workspace

Publishing is the broader version of sharing. Instead of picking individuals, you put the skill in the workspace library so anyone with access can find and install it themselves — useful for the workflows you want standardized rather than passed around informally.

It runs through the same Share flow, with the workspace chosen as the audience rather than named people. The difference worth understanding is one of intent:

Action Who gets access Best for
Share with people or groups Only the individuals or groups you select A skill built for one team, one client, or one role
Copy a sharing link Authorized workspace members who can access the link Handing something over quickly, outside a formal rollout
Publish to the workspace Everyone in the workspace who can browse the library Processes you want done the same way company-wide

Publishing is often gated separately from ordinary sharing, so it’s possible to be allowed to share a skill with a colleague but not to publish it to everyone. If the option isn’t there, that’s a permissions question rather than a bug — see what admins control below.

How to Upload a Skill File You Downloaded

Skills follow the open Agent Skills standard, which means a skill exported from one supporting product can be brought into another. If someone hands you a skill file rather than a workspace share, you upload it:

  1. Go to Plugins → Skills.
  2. Select Create, then Upload from your computer.
  3. Choose the skill file and confirm.

ChatGPT scans uploaded skills before making them available. Most clear straight away. Some come back marked Needs Review, meaning you’ll need to look at additional information before using it, and a few are marked Blocked and can’t be used at all.

Read a skill before you install it

This matters more than it sounds. A skill can contain instructions, supporting files, and code — so an uploaded skill from an external source or another organization deserves the same scrutiny you’d give any downloaded file. The automatic scan is a safety net, not a substitute for reading what you’re about to let run on your work. If you didn’t write it and don’t trust where it came from, open it first.

Managing a Skill After You’ve Shared It

Sharing isn’t a one-way door. Once a skill is out in a workspace, it can be reviewed and adjusted.

When available for your workspace, the admin Skills page is separate from Permissions & roles. Permissions decide who is allowed to do what; the Skills page is where the skills that already exist get managed. It lists each skill’s owner, access level, how many people use it, and how many times it’s been invoked in the last 30 days.

From there, the actions that matter for anyone who has shared something:

  • Change who has access — widen or narrow the users, groups, or workspace members who can use the skill.
  • Change owner — hand a skill to someone else. The previous owner keeps their access after the transfer, so nothing breaks for them.
  • Download — pull a copy of the skill back out, which is also how you move one between workspaces.
  • Delete skill — remove it permanently. Everyone who currently has access loses it.

Deleting a shared skill affects everyone, not just you

This is the one to be careful with. Deleting removes the skill for every person who had access to it — not only from your own list. If you just don’t want to use it anymore, uninstalling it on your end is the safer move. Check whether anyone else depends on it before deleting a skill you shared or published.

What Admins Control About Sharing

On workspace plans, sharing is governed by role-based permissions rather than being on for everyone by default. The controls relevant to moving skills around are typically separate switches, which is why you can end up able to do one thing and not another:

  • Enable skills — whether members can create and use skills at all.
  • Enable skill uploading — whether members can upload skill files from their own computer.
  • Share skills — whether members can share with other members or groups.
  • Publish skills to workspace — whether members can publish to the whole workspace.
  • Enable skills installing — whether members can install skills for other members so they’re used automatically.

A common configuration is allowing workspace-published skills while blocking arbitrary uploads, so only reviewed skills reach people. Control names and grouping have shifted during rollout, so check your current admin settings before writing internal policy against them. For the full picture of admin controls and plan eligibility, see the ChatGPT Skills availability guide.

Shared a Skill and It Hasn’t Appeared?

Three things explain most sharing-specific cases:

  1. They haven’t installed it yet. Sharing grants access but does not automatically install the skill. It may be sitting under “Shared with me” unless they install it or an authorized workspace admin installs it on their behalf.
  2. Sharing is restricted for their role. Workspace permissions can allow you to share while preventing them from installing. An admin can confirm.
  3. They’re on a different device than they installed it on. Personal Skills are added per surface and don’t sync automatically between desktop and web/mobile.

If the Skills tab isn’t appearing for them at all — rather than one specific skill missing — that’s an access question, not a sharing one. The availability troubleshooting checklist covers all five causes.

The Short Version

Everything happens in Plugins → Skills. The (•••) menu next to a skill is where sharing and installing both live. Share grants access; install is what makes it run; publish puts it in front of the whole workspace; upload brings in a file from outside.

And the part worth remembering: the value was never the sharing mechanism. It’s whether the skill is good enough that people keep it. Start from a skill worth sharing.

Frequently asked questions

Open the sidebar, select Plugins, then the Skills tab. Find your skill, open its more-options menu (•••), and select Share. You can search for people or groups in your workspace, or copy a sharing link to send yourself. You can also set access permissions so only specific people can use it.

How do I install a ChatGPT skill someone shared with me?

Go to Plugins → Skills and look under “Shared with me” or “Shared by” your workspace. Open the more-options menu (•••) next to the skill and select Install. Once installed, ChatGPT applies it automatically whenever a task matches what it’s built for.

Does sharing a skill install it for the other person?

Not automatically. Sharing grants access, and the recipient normally installs the skill from their own Skills page. An authorized workspace admin can also install it on the recipient’s behalf. If a shared skill appears to “do nothing,” it may still be sitting under Shared with me, not yet installed.

What’s the difference between sharing and publishing a ChatGPT skill?

Sharing gives access to specific people or groups you choose. Publishing puts the skill in your workspace library so anyone with access can find and install it themselves. Sharing suits a skill built for one team or role; publishing suits a process you want done consistently across the whole company.

How do I upload a ChatGPT skill file?

Go to Plugins → Skills, select Create, then Upload from your computer, and choose the file. ChatGPT scans uploads before making them available — most clear immediately, some are marked Needs Review, and a few are Blocked and can’t be used. Review any skill from an outside source before installing it.

Can I take back a ChatGPT skill I shared?

Yes. Access can be changed after the fact — on workspace plans there’s an admin Skills page where access, ownership, and removal are managed. Be careful with Delete, though: deleting a skill removes it for everyone who had access, not just for you. If you simply want to stop using it, uninstall it instead.

Why can’t I share or publish a skill?

Sharing, uploading, publishing, and installing are governed by separate workspace permissions, so it’s normal to be able to do one and not another. If the option is missing, ask whoever administers your workspace — these are set per role under Permissions & roles rather than per person.

Can I share a ChatGPT skill with someone outside my workspace?

Workspace sharing is designed for people inside your workspace. To get a skill to someone outside it, export or download the skill file and let them upload it on their end — Skills follow the open Agent Skills standard, so they transfer between supporting products. Simplest of all: a skill is just instructions, so the plain text can be sent and pasted into a chat or Project on any plan.
