item.text: Free AI Overdue Invoice Follow-Up Skill (2026) The free AI Overdue Invoice Follow-Up skill Paste the invoice details and how long it’s been — get a firm, polite payment reminder that doesn’t torch the relationship, plus a four-stage escalation ladder so you know exactly what to send next week, and the week after, in Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT. Free copy-and-use prompt · No credit card · Optional setup help This Overdue Invoice Follow-Up skill is a free AI skill that turns an unpaid invoice and a few details about the client into a payment reminder that’s firm enough to get paid and warm enough to keep the client. Paste in the amount, the due date, how far overdue it is, and anything you know about why — and the skill writes the email at the right temperature for that stage, tells you which stage you’re actually at, and gives you the escalation ladder for what to send if this one goes unanswered. It never invents an amount, never threatens, and never sends. Copy the skill prompt and use it in Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT in seconds — or save the same instructions as a reusable workflow using the setup option in your preferred AI tool. No coding required. The Overdue Invoice Follow-Up skill writes a payment reminder email from the invoice details you paste in, matched to how overdue it is — gentle nudge at 7 days, direct at 30, firm at 60+. It returns the email, the escalation ladder, and a suggested send date. It has no access to your accounting software, so it will never invent an invoice number, amount, or due date. It does not give legal or debt-collection advice, it never threatens or implies legal action, and it never sends anything — you review and send every email yourself. One awkward email, written for you By the end of this AI skill guide, you’ll have the Overdue Invoice Follow-Up skill ready to use — either as a quick copy-and-paste prompt in any AI chat or saved as a reusable workflow using your preferred platform’s setup option. It handles the email most business owners rewrite five times and then don’t send: the one that asks for money you’re already owed, without sounding either apologetic or aggressive. INVOICE FOLLOW-UP — $4,200, 34 days overdue, good client (example) Where you are: Stage 2 of 4 — Direct. Past the “it slipped” window, not yet a payment problem. This is the email that usually works. Subject: “Invoice #1042 — 34 days overdue” The email: 74 words. States the invoice, amount, and date it was due as plain facts. One line asking for a payment date — not an apology, not a threat. Offers a way out (“if something’s changed, tell me and we’ll sort it”). Escalation ladder: Stage 1 · 1–14 days — Gentle. Assume it slipped. Stage 2 · 15–45 days — Direct. Ask for a date. ← you are here Stage 3 · 46–75 days — Firm. Name the impact, pause new work. Stage 4 · 75+ days — Final notice from you, then stop emailing and get advice. Plus a reply for each objection: “We never received it” — warm re-send, no accusation, confirms the right billing contact. “We dispute it” — acknowledges, asks what’s wrong, moves it to a call. Doesn’t argue the amount in writing. Send: Tuesday morning. Next follow-up in 7 days if there’s no reply. Before you send: “You didn’t give me your late-fee terms — I’ve left fees out entirely rather than claim a fee you may not be owed. Check your contract before mentioning one.” How to use the Overdue Invoice Follow-Up AI skill in 3 steps The Overdue Invoice Follow-Up skill is an AI skill — a reusable set of instructions written in skill format. You don’t have to install anything to use it: copy the skill prompt below and paste it into Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT to run it instantly, exactly like a normal prompt. When chasing invoices becomes a monthly ritual, follow the platform-specific setup below to save the instructions for reuse. Paste it in with your invoice details Paste it into Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT — or upload it as a SKILL.md — then add the amount, due date, days overdue, and what the relationship is like. Get your email and your ladder Your AI returns the stage you’re at, a ready-to-send email, the escalation ladder, a send date, and anything it refused to assume. You are an experienced accounts-receivable specialist who writes payment reminders for small businesses. Your job is to turn the invoice details the user pastes in into a follow-up email that is firm enough to get paid and warm enough to keep the client. PROCESS 1. Identify the invoice from what the user provides: amount, invoice number, issue date, due date, and days overdue. 2. Copy the skill prompt and use it in Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT in seconds — or save the same instructions as a reusable workflow using the setup option in your preferred AI tool. No coding required.

Quick answer

The Overdue Invoice Follow-Up skill writes a payment reminder email from the invoice details you paste in, matched to how overdue it is — gentle nudge at 7 days, direct at 30, firm at 60+. It returns the email, the escalation ladder, and a suggested send date. It has no access to your accounting software, so it will never invent an invoice number, amount, or due date. Your results

One awkward email, written for you

By the end of this AI skill guide, you’ll have the Overdue Invoice Follow-Up skill ready to use — either as a quick copy-and-paste prompt in any AI chat or saved as a reusable workflow using your preferred platform’s setup option. Where you are: Stage 2 of 4 — Direct. Past the “it slipped” window, not yet a payment problem. This is the email that usually works.

The email: 74 words. States the invoice, amount, and date it was due as plain facts. One line asking for a payment date — not an apology, not a threat. Offers a way out (“if something’s changed, tell me and we’ll sort it”).

Escalation ladder:

  • Stage 1 · 1–14 days — Gentle. Assume it slipped.
  • Stage 2 · 15–45 days — Direct. Ask for a date. ← you are here
  • Stage 3 · 46–75 days — Firm. Name the impact, pause new work.
  • Stage 4 · 75+ days — Final notice from you, then stop emailing and get advice.

Plus a reply for each objection:

  • “We never received it” — warm re-send, no accusation, confirms the right billing contact.
  • “We dispute it” — acknowledges, asks what’s wrong, moves it to a call. Doesn’t argue the amount in writing.

Send: Tuesday morning. Next follow-up in 7 days if there’s no reply.

Before you send: “You didn’t give me your late-fee terms — I’ve left fees out entirely rather than claim a fee you may not be owed. Check your contract before mentioning one.”

You are an experienced accounts-receivable specialist who writes payment reminders for small businesses. Your job is to turn the invoice details the user pastes in into a follow-up email that is firm enough to get paid and warm enough to keep the client.

PROCESS
1. Identify the invoice from what the user provides: amount, invoice number, issue date, due date, and days overdue.
2. Work out which escalation stage this is, based on days overdue:
   - Stage 1 (1-14 days): Gentle. Assume it genuinely slipped. No pressure.
   - Stage 2 (15-45 days): Direct. State the facts, ask for a specific payment date.
   - Stage 3 (46-75 days): Firm. Name the business impact. Reasonable to pause further work.
   - Stage 4 (75+ days): Final notice from the user, then stop and recommend they get professional advice.
3. Factor in the relationship: a long-standing client who always pays gets more benefit of the doubt than a first-time client who has already missed a date.
4. Write ONE email for the current stage. Keep it under 120 words.
5. State the invoice number, amount, and due date as plain facts. Do not apologise for asking to be paid, and do not over-explain.
6. Ask for one specific thing: a payment date. Not "let me know your thoughts."
7. MAKE IT EASY TO PAY. If the user provided a payment link, bank details reference, or preferred payment method, include it in the email. Never make someone hunt for how to pay you — friction is a genuine cause of late payment, not just an excuse. If the user gave you no payment method, put it in "What I would not assume" and tell them to add one.

   - "We never received it" — re-send warmly, no accusation, attach/reference the invoice again and confirm the correct billing address or contact. This is usually true, and treating it as a lie costs you the client.

10. Show the full 4-stage ladder so the user knows what comes next.
11. Recommend a send date and when to follow up again.
12. List anything you refused to assume.

RULES
- Use ONLY the details the user provides. NEVER invent an invoice number, amount, due date, payment term, or late fee.
- You have no access to accounting software, banking, Stripe, QuickBooks, Xero, or any payment record. You cannot check whether an invoice was paid. Never imply you can.
- NEVER mention late fees, interest, or penalties unless the user tells you those terms exist and what they are. If they do not, leave fees out entirely and flag it.
- NEVER give legal advice, quote debt-collection law, or threaten legal action, court, collections, or a credit report. If the user seems to be heading there, say plainly that this is the point to get professional advice, and stop.
- No guilt-tripping, no passive aggression, no fake deadlines, no manufactured urgency. Firm and factual beats emotional every time.

The stage, the reasoning, and what this email is trying to achieve.

### The Email (Draft)
Under 120 words. Ready to review and send. Include the payment method/link if one was provided.

A short, warm re-send reply. No accusation.

A short reply that acknowledges, asks what specifically is wrong, and moves it to a call. Do not argue the amount in writing.
### The Escalation Ladder
All 4 stages, with the current one marked. What to send next and when.
### When To Send
A suggested send date, and when to follow up if there is no reply.
### What I Would Not Assume
Anything missing — payment terms, late fees, payment method, prior contact — that you deliberately left out rather than invented.

By the end of this AI skill guide, you’ll have the Overdue Invoice Follow-Up skill ready to use — either as a quick copy-and-paste prompt in any AI chat or saved as a reusable workflow using your preferred platform’s setup option. It handles the email most business owners rewrite five times and then don’t send: the one that asks for money you’re already owed, without sounding either apologetic or aggressive.
#### INVOICE FOLLOW-UP — $4,200, 34 days overdue, good client (example)
**Where you are:** Stage 2 of 4 — Direct. Past the “it slipped” window, not yet a payment problem. This is the email that usually works.
**Subject:** “Invoice #1042 — 34 days overdue”
**The email:** 74 words. States the invoice, amount, and date it was due as plain facts. One line asking for a payment date — not an apology, not a threat. Offers a way out (“if something’s changed, tell me and we’ll sort it”).
**Escalation ladder:**
* **Stage 1 · 1–14 days —** Gentle. Assume it slipped. * **Stage 2 · 15–45 days —** Direct. Ask for a date. ← _you are here_ * **Stage 3 · 46–75 days —** Firm. Name the impact, pause new work. * **Stage 4 · 75+ days —** Final notice from you, then stop emailing and get advice.
**Plus a reply for each objection:**
* **“We never received it” —** warm re-send, no accusation, confirms the right billing contact. * **“We dispute it” —** acknowledges, asks what’s wrong, moves it to a call. Doesn’t argue the amount in writing.
**Send:** Tuesday morning. Next follow-up in 7 days if there’s no reply.
**Before you send:** “You didn’t give me your late-fee terms — I’ve left fees out entirely rather than claim a fee you may not be owed. Check your contract before mentioning one.”
## How to use the Overdue Invoice Follow-Up AI skill in 3 steps
The Overdue Invoice Follow-Up skill is an **AI skill** — a reusable set of instructions written in skill format. You don’t have to install anything to use it: copy the **skill prompt** below and paste it into Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT to run it instantly, exactly like a normal prompt. When chasing invoices becomes a monthly ritual, follow the platform-specific setup below to save the instructions for reuse.
1. 1
**Copy the AI skill**
Click the copy button on the AI skill prompt below — it’s already formatted and ready to run.
2. 2
**Paste it in with your invoice details**
Paste it into Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT — or upload it as a SKILL.md — then add the amount, due date, days overdue, and what the relationship is like.
3. 3
**Get your email and your ladder**
Your AI returns the stage you’re at, a ready-to-send email, the escalation ladder, a send date, and anything it refused to assume.
Formatted as an AI skill or use instantly as a prompt · no installation required
``` You are an experienced accounts-receivable specialist who writes payment reminders for small businesses. Your job is to turn the invoice details the user pastes in into a follow-up email that is firm enough to get paid and warm enough to keep the client.
PROCESS 1. Identify the invoice from what the user provides: amount, invoice number, issue date, due date, and days overdue. 2. Work out which escalation stage this is, based on days overdue: - Stage 1 (1-14 days): Gentle. Assume it genuinely slipped. No pressure. - Stage 2 (15-45 days): Direct. State the facts, ask for a specific payment date. - Stage 3 (46-75 days): Firm. Name the business impact. Reasonable to pause further work. - Stage 4 (75+ days): Final notice from the user, then stop and recommend they get professional advice. 3. Factor in the relationship: a long-standing client who always pays gets more benefit of the doubt than a first-time client who has already missed a date. 4. Write ONE email for the current stage. Keep it under 120 words. 5. State the invoice number, amount, and due date as plain facts. Do not apologise for asking to be paid, and do not over-explain. 6. Ask for one specific thing: a payment date. Not "let me know your thoughts." 7. MAKE IT EASY TO PAY. If the user provided a payment link, bank details reference, or preferred payment method, include it in the email. Never make someone hunt for how to pay you — friction is a genuine cause of late payment, not just an excuse. If the user gave you no payment method, put it in "What I would not assume" and tell them to add one. 8. Always give the client a dignified way out: an invitation to say if something has changed or if there is a problem. 9. HANDLE THE TWO COMMON OBJECTIONS. Alongside the main email, give the user a short response for each: - "We never received it" — re-send warmly, no accusation, attach/reference the invoice again and confirm the correct billing address or contact. This is usually true, and treating it as a lie costs you the client. - "We dispute it / something's wrong with it" — do NOT argue in writing and do NOT restate the demand. Acknowledge, ask what specifically is wrong, and move it to a call. A disputed invoice is a conversation, not an email thread. 10. Show the full 4-stage ladder so the user knows what comes next. 11. Recommend a send date and when to follow up again. 12. List anything you refused to assume.
RULES - Use ONLY the details the user provides. NEVER invent an invoice number, amount, due date, payment term, or late fee. - You have no access to accounting software, banking, Stripe, QuickBooks, Xero, or any payment record. You cannot check whether an invoice was paid. Never imply you can. - NEVER mention late fees, interest, or penalties unless the user tells you those terms exist and what they are. If they do not, leave fees out entirely and flag it. - NEVER give legal advice, quote debt-collection law, or threaten legal action, court, collections, or a credit report. If the user seems to be heading there, say plainly that this is the point to get professional advice, and stop. - No guilt-tripping, no passive aggression, no fake deadlines, no manufactured urgency. Firm and factual beats emotional every time. - Never write in a way that assumes bad faith. Most late invoices are admin failures, not theft. - Do not send anything. Produce drafts for human review only.
OUTPUT FORMAT ### Where You Are The stage, the reasoning, and what this email is trying to achieve. ### Subject Line ### The Email (Draft) Under 120 words. Ready to review and send. Include the payment method/link if one was provided. ### If They Say They Never Received It A short, warm re-send reply. No accusation. ### If They Dispute The Invoice A short reply that acknowledges, asks what specifically is wrong, and moves it to a call. Do not argue the amount in writing. ### The Escalation Ladder All 4 stages, with the current one marked. What to send next and when. ### When To Send A suggested send date, and when to follow up if there is no reply. ### What I Would Not Assume Anything missing — payment terms, late fees, payment method, prior contact — that you deliberately left out rather than invented.
MY INVOICE: [Paste the details: amount, invoice number, when it was issued, when it was due, how many days overdue, whether you have chased already, what the client relationship is like, your payment terms if you have them, and how they can pay — a payment link, bank reference, or preferred method.] ```

## Overdue Invoice Follow-Up skill: frequently asked questions
Is the Overdue Invoice Follow-Up skill free?
Yes. The copy-and-use AI skill prompt is completely free. Optional reusable features may depend on the AI tool and plan you use. ChatGPT Projects are available on free and paid plans, Claude skills are available when code execution is enabled, and Gemini Spark skills currently require Google AI Ultra.
What’s the difference between this and the Follow-Up Email skill?
This one is **only about money** — an invoice that’s past its due date. It works from the invoice number, amount, original due date, days overdue, and your payment terms, and it changes tone by how overdue the payment is. The [Follow-Up Email skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/ai-follow-up-email-generator/) is for **everything else that went quiet**: an unanswered proposal, a client thread, a networking intro, a stalled project. Rule of thumb — if you’re owed _money_, use this page. If you’re owed a _reply_, use that one.
What if they say they never received the invoice, or dispute it?
The skill drafts both replies alongside the main email. For **“we never received it”** it writes a warm re-send with no accusation — that claim is usually true, and treating it as a lie is an expensive way to be right. For **“we dispute it”** it deliberately does _not_ argue the amount in writing or restate the demand: it acknowledges, asks what specifically is wrong, and moves the conversation to a call. A disputed invoice is a conversation, not an email thread — and written arguments about money have a way of being screenshotted.
Does it give legal advice or handle debt collection?
**No — and it is specifically instructed not to.** The skill will never quote debt-collection law, threaten court or collections, or imply legal consequences. If an invoice reaches the point where those things are on the table, the skill says so plainly and tells you to get professional advice. It writes emails; it is not a lawyer and does not pretend to be one.
Can it check whether the invoice was actually paid?
No. It has no connection to Stripe, QuickBooks, Xero, your bank, or any accounting tool, and it will never claim otherwise. It only knows what you paste in — which also means it will never invent an invoice number, an amount, or a due date. Check the payment landed before you send; nothing damages a client relationship faster than chasing money they already sent.
Will it mention late fees or interest?
Only if you tell it those terms exist and what they are. If you don’t provide them, the skill leaves fees out entirely and flags it in the “What I would not assume” section, rather than claiming a fee you may not be contractually owed. That guardrail exists because inventing a late fee is the fastest way to turn a slow payer into a dispute.
How does it decide how firm the email should be?
By days overdue, moderated by the relationship you describe. It uses a 4-stage ladder: gentle at 1–14 days (assume it slipped), direct at 15–45 (ask for a date), firm at 46–75 (name the impact, reasonable to pause work), and final notice at 75+. A long-standing client who always pays gets more benefit of the doubt than a first-timer who’s already missed a date — so tell it which you’re dealing with.
Can it send the reminders and chase automatically?
No — the free skill writes drafts and stops there. That’s deliberate: an email about money should never go out under your name without you reading it first. If you want AI connected to your invoicing tool and inbox to track what’s outstanding and prompt you when it’s time to chase, that’s the connected agent version we teach inside the [AI Agents Academy](https://www.skool.com/ai-agents-for-beginners/about).

item.text: The 15 Best Claude Fable 5 Prompts for Business In 2026 Claude Fable 5 is back. Anthropic restored global access starting July 1, 2026, after the export controls that paused it were lifted — see the official Anthropic update. If you still need the basics, read what Claude Fable 5 is first. If you want ideas before prompts, read the 12 best Claude Fable 5 use cases. This page assumes you already know what Fable 5 is and want the 15 best Claude Fable 5 prompts for business in 2026 — ready to copy, paste, and use. Update — July 13, 2026 Anthropic has now settled Fable 5’s access permanently. From July 20, Fable 5 is included in all Max and Team Premium plans at 50% of limits. Pro and Team Standard keep access through usage credits and receive a one-time $100 credit, after which Fable 5 bills at API rates ($10 per million input tokens, $50 per million output). See Anthropic’s guide to managing usage credits. The 50% Claude Code rate-limit boost also ends July 20, so standard weekly limits shrink the same day. The strategy is still the same: use cheaper models to plan, draft, and refine, then save Fable 5 for final high-value outputs. Full write-up: what the Fable 5 access change means for your plan. Why do most Claude Fable 5 prompts underperform? Most people use Claude Fable 5 like a normal chatbot — one short line, one quick answer. That is the wrong approach for a model built for complex, long-running, ambiguous work. The best Claude Fable 5 prompts are structured workflows: a clear goal, real context, actual inputs, constraints, a process, an exact output format, and a quality check — not a one-line request. Every prompt below follows that structure. If your goal is to get better results without wasting usage on retries, start with our guide on how to save Claude Fable 5 credits. The 15 best Claude Fable 5 prompts in this guide cover business strategy, SEO content, research, website design, and AI agent workflows — each one ready to copy, paste, and use. How to Decide If Claude Fable 5 Is the Right Fit If you’re deciding whether Claude Fable 5 is the right fit, use it for complex research, strategy, and workflow tasks that need deeper reasoning, not every quick question. Anthropic’s own prompting documentation for Claude Fable 5 notes that it may need updated prompt scaffolding compared with prior Claude models. In practice, that means giving Fable 5 a real job instead of a quick question. Every strong Claude Fable 5 prompt includes these eight parts. 1 Goal One clear sentence describing exactly what you want and why it matters. 2 Context What Claude needs to know: your business, audience, situation, and offer. 3 Inputs The source material you’re handing over: notes, data, URLs, exports, transcripts. 4 Constraints Tone, length, what to avoid, and what must be included. 5 Process The steps Claude should think through, in order — not just the final answer. 6 Output format The exact shape of what comes back: a table, outline, checklist, or brief. 7 Quality check A rule Claude uses to review its own answer before handing it to you. 8 Next action The single next step you should take once you have the output. Instead of asking: Help me with SEO. A structured Claude Fable 5 prompt reviews your keywords, checks for cannibalization against your existing pages, clusters opportunities by intent, and hands back a prioritized table — not a paragraph of generic advice. That difference is the entire point of this library. A quick safety note Fable 5 includes updated safety classifiers. A small number of benign coding or debugging requests can get flagged or rerouted to Claude Opus 4.8 instead of answered directly — this is expected behavior, not a broken prompt. Every prompt in this library stays in normal business, content, design, research, and workflow territory, so you’re unlikely to see it, but it’s worth knowing about if you adapt these prompts for engineering tasks. Details are in Anthropic’s Fable 5 prompting docs. A quick tip on managing your Fable 5 credits Fable 5 is a heavier, more capable model, and running every single prompt through it — including quick one-liners — burns through usage credits faster than it needs to. As a simple rule: save Fable 5 for the harder work in this library (deep research, business strategy, prompt-to-skill conversion, and other multi-step or high-stakes prompts), and use a lighter model like Sonnet 5 for quick drafts, small edits, and everyday questions. Batching related work into one longer Fable 5 session, instead of many small separate prompts, also stretches your credits further. Best Claude Fable 5 Prompt Template Save this master template and reuse it as a starting point for any new Claude Fable 5 prompt. It bakes in all eight parts from above. Every specialized prompt further down this page is a filled-in version of this same structure. What to paste into Claude: You are an expert [ROLE] working on this task with me. GOAL [One clear sentence describing exactly what you want and why it matters.] CONTEXT - Business/brand: [name, niche, audience] - Situation: [what's happening right now that makes this task necessary] - Audience: [who this is for] INPUTS - [Paste source material: notes, data, URLs, transcripts, screenshots, exports] - [Add a second input if relevant] CONSTRAINTS - Tone: [describe voice/style] - Length: [word count, section count, etc.] - Must avoid: [things to exclude] - Must include: [non-negotiables] PROCESS 1. [First thinking step] 2. [Second thinking step] 3. [Third thinking step] 4. [Continue until the final step] [Exact format you want back: table, outline, numbered list, etc.] QUALITY CHECK Before giving me the final answer, check your own work against [criteria] and flag anything you are unsure about. NEXT ACTION End with one clear recommended next step I should take. How to customize it Fill in every bracket with your real details before you paste it — a template with placeholders still in it will read like a template to Claude too. Delete any section that genuinely doesn’t apply rather than leaving it blank. 15 Copy-Paste Claude Fable 5 Prompts Below are 15 ready-to-use Claude Fable 5 prompts for business, SEO, research, content, website design, and AI agent workflows. Each one follows the same structure: who it’s best for, when to use it, the exact prompt to paste, how to customize it, what output to expect, and the next step once you have it. Best for: Business owners who need a practical strategy, not vague ideas. This is one of the strongest Fable 5 prompts for business decisions where the cost of guessing wrong is real. Use when: You need a decision-ready plan for a specific choice — pricing, a growth bottleneck, a new offer, or where to put limited time and budget next. What to paste into Claude: You are an expert business strategist for [your industry or website URL] who has helped small businesses grow profitably. GOAL Help me decide [specific decision, e.g. "whether to raise prices," "which service to cut," "how to grow revenue in the next 90 days"] with a clear, practical recommendation — not a list of generic options. CONTEXT - Business: [what you sell, who you sell to, how you make money] - Current situation: [revenue range, team size, main constraint right now] - What has already been tried: [list anything relevant] - Risk tolerance: [conservative / moderate / aggressive] INPUTS [Paste any relevant numbers, notes, past strategy docs, or customer feedback here] CONSTRAINTS - Timeframe: [e.g. decide and act within 30/60/90 days] - Budget: [rough range or "no new budget"] - Must not: [anything off the table, e.g. "no layoffs," "no new hires"] PROCESS 1. Identify the real constraint holding the business back right now, not just the symptom. 2. List 3 realistic strategic options, with the tradeoffs of each. 3. Recommend ONE option and explain why it beats the others for this specific situation. 4. Break the recommendation into a first-30-days action plan. 5. Flag the biggest risk in the plan and how to reduce it. - Section 1: The real constraint (2-3 sentences) - Section 2: Three options in a short table (option, tradeoff, timeframe) - Section 3: Recommendation and reasoning - Section 4: 30-day action plan as a numbered list - Section 5: Biggest risk and mitigation QUALITY CHECK Before finalizing, check whether your recommendation actually matches my stated risk tolerance and budget. If it doesn't, revise it. NEXT ACTION End with the single next task I should do this week. How to customize it Swap in the real decision, numbers, and constraints — the sharper your revenue and cost details, the less generic the recommendation. What output to expect: A structured decision brief — a stated constraint, three weighed options, one clear recommendation, and a first-30-days plan — not a brainstorm. Next step: Turn the 30-day plan into a weekly checklist, or feed progress into the Business Brief Prompt. Best for: Finding content opportunities from keyword lists, Search Console exports, or competitor pages. This is one of the most useful Fable 5 prompts for SEO because it can hold an entire keyword export in context at once. Use when: You have a pile of keywords or topics and want a prioritized, clustered plan instead of a raw list. What to paste into Claude: You are an expert SEO content strategist for [your site/niche]. Turn the data below into a prioritized list of content opportunities I can act on this month — not just a list of keywords. CONTEXT - Site: [URL, niche, audience] - Current content: [rough number of articles, main topics already covered] - Goal: [rank for a niche, capture more clicks, fill a content gap] INPUTS [Paste your keyword list, GSC export, or competitor URLs/topics here] CONSTRAINTS - Only suggest topics that fit [your niche/audience] - Flag anything that overlaps with existing content: [list URLs of existing articles to avoid cannibalizing] - Prioritize topics with clear buyer or reader intent over vanity keywords PROCESS 1. Group the raw keywords/topics into themed clusters. 2. For each cluster, identify the likely search intent (informational, commercial, navigational). 3. Score each cluster on estimated opportunity (low competition + clear intent + fits my niche). 4. Flag any cluster that risks cannibalizing an existing page I listed. 5. Recommend the top 5 clusters to write next, in priority order. A table with columns: Cluster, Search intent, Opportunity score (1-5), Cannibalization risk, Recommended next step. QUALITY CHECK Double-check that none of your top 5 recommendations duplicate the intent of an existing page I listed. If one does, replace it or suggest a merge instead. NEXT ACTION Tell me which single cluster to write first and why. How to customize it Paste your actual keyword export and list your real existing URLs so Claude can flag cannibalization instead of guessing. What output to expect: A prioritized, clustered table of content opportunities with intent and cannibalization risk flagged — ready to hand to a writer. Next step: Feed the top cluster into the Blog Outline Prompt to build the actual article structure. Best for: Analyzing competitor articles and finding a stronger angle instead of just writing a longer copy of the same thing. Use when: A competitor outranks you, or is about to, and you want to know exactly what to do differently. You are an expert competitive content strategist for [your website]. Analyze the competitor content below and tell me exactly how to create a stronger, more useful version — not just a longer one. CONTEXT - My site/brand: [name, angle, audience] - My existing page on this topic, if any: [URL or "none yet"] - Why this competitor matters: [they outrank me / direct competitor / new entrant] [Paste the competitor's URL, or paste their article text/outline] CONSTRAINTS - Do not recommend copying their structure directly - Focus on gaps: missing sections, weak examples, outdated info, unanswered questions - Consider search intent, not just word count PROCESS 1. Summarize what the competitor's content actually covers and how it's structured. 2. Identify what it does well. 3. Identify concrete gaps: missing subtopics, weak or generic sections, outdated claims, unanswered reader questions. 4. Identify a distinct angle I can own that they have not covered. 5. Recommend a structure for my version that is better, not just bigger. - Their structure (bulleted) - What they do well (short list) - Gaps and weaknesses (short list) - My differentiated angle (1-2 sentences) - Recommended outline for my version (numbered headings) QUALITY CHECK Check that your recommended outline actually addresses the gaps you found — not a generic "better" version. NEXT ACTION Tell me the one thing that would make my version clearly worth ranking above theirs. Paste the actual competitor URL or full text, and add notes on your own unique data, results, or experience to sharpen the differentiation. What output to expect: A gap analysis plus a differentiated outline you can hand straight to a writer. Next step: Run the recommended outline through the Blog Outline Prompt to finalize headings without cannibalizing your own content. Best for: Creating an SEO article outline that fits cleanly alongside your existing content instead of competing with it. Use when: You know the topic and target keyword, but need a full outline that avoids cannibalizing an existing page. You are an expert SEO content strategist and outline writer. Create a complete article outline for the target keyword below that will not compete with my existing articles for the same intent. - Target keyword: [keyword] - Search intent: [informational / comparison / how-to / commercial] - Audience: [who is searching this] - My existing related articles (title + URL + one-line topic for each): [list them] - Any notes, data, or examples I want included: [paste here] - The new article must target a clearly different angle or intent than any URL I listed - If overlap is unavoidable, tell me directly instead of forcing a workaround - Keep headings specific, not generic ("5 tips" style headings are not allowed) 1. Compare the target keyword's intent against each existing article I listed. 2. Confirm there is a distinct angle for this new article, or flag the overlap. 3. Draft an H1, meta description, and full H2/H3 outline. 4. Suggest 2-3 internal links to my existing articles where they naturally fit. 5. Suggest FAQ questions that match real search queries for this topic. - Cannibalization check (one paragraph) - H1 - Meta description - Full outline (H2s with H3s nested underneath) - Suggested internal links (anchor text + target URL) - FAQ questions (5-8) Re-read the outline and confirm no H2 duplicates the primary angle of an existing article I listed. Tell me which section of the outline is hardest to write, so I know where to start research first. List your real existing article URLs and topics so Claude can genuinely check for overlap, not just assume there isn’t any. What output to expect: A cannibalization-safe H1, meta description, full heading structure, internal link suggestions, and FAQ ideas. Next step: Draft the article section by section, then run the finished draft through the Quality Check Prompt before publishing. Best for: Updating an existing article without shifting its intent, URL, or existing internal links too far. Use when: An article is losing rankings, has outdated information, or needs expansion — but doesn’t need a full rebuild. You are an expert SEO editor refreshing an existing article. Update this article to be more accurate, complete, and competitive — while keeping its original intent and URL intact. - Target keyword: [keyword] - Why it needs a refresh: [rankings dropped / outdated info / new competitor / thin content] - What must NOT change: [URL, core angle, existing internal links pointing to it] [Paste the full existing article text] - Do not change the article's core search intent or target keyword - Preserve any existing internal/external links unless they are broken or outdated - Flag outdated claims, prices, dates, or product names instead of guessing new ones 1. Identify what is outdated, thin, or missing compared to current best practices for this topic. 2. Identify sections that are still strong and should stay mostly as-is. 3. Recommend specific additions, deletions, and rewrites, section by section. 4. Suggest an updated meta description if the old one is weak. 5. Suggest 1-2 new FAQ questions based on what readers likely ask now. A section-by-section table: Section, Keep / Rewrite / Add / Cut, Reasoning, Suggested new copy (where applicable). Confirm the refreshed version still targets the same primary keyword and intent as the original — flag it if your suggestions drift. Tell me the single change most likely to recover rankings fastest. Paste the real, full article text rather than a summary, and note any known ranking-drop dates so Claude can weigh what likely changed. What output to expect: A section-by-section refresh plan — keep, rewrite, add, or cut — instead of a full rewrite. Next step: Apply the changes, then check performance directly in Google Search Console after a few weeks, or fold the results into your Business Brief Prompt. Best for: Anyone reviewing a website, landing page, or app screen for layout, clarity, and usability — creators, consultants, agencies, and small business owners in any industry, not just tech companies. Use when: A page looks fine to you, but visitors seem confused, bounce quickly, or don’t take the action you expect, and you want a structured design critique instead of a vague “make it look nicer.” You are an expert website designer and UX consultant who has reviewed hundreds of small business and creator websites. Review the website or page described below and give me a structured critique of its layout, clarity, and usability — not just a list of visual opinions. - Type of site/page: [homepage, landing page, portfolio, online store, app screen] - Primary goal of this page: [get a sign-up, sell a product, book a call, get a download] - Audience: [who typically lands here and why] [Paste the page copy section by section, describe each section in order top to bottom, or paste a link plus a description of what's on it] - Focus on structure, clarity, hierarchy, and flow — not code or technical implementation - Call out anything that would confuse a first-time visitor within the first 5 seconds - Keep every suggestion specific enough to act on today 1. Identify whether the page's main goal is obvious within the first few seconds. 2. Review visual and content hierarchy — is the most important thing actually first? 3. Review the navigation and flow from top to bottom. 4. Identify friction points: confusing sections, missing information, or unclear next steps. 5. Rank the fixes by likely impact on visitor experience. - First impression (1-2 sentences) - Hierarchy issues (short list) - Friction points (short list) - Top 5 fixes in priority order Make sure every fix is a specific structural or content change, not a vague note like "make it more modern." Tell me the single change most likely to reduce visitor confusion this week. Describe your actual page section by section, or paste real copy, and be specific about what action you want visitors to take so Claude can judge whether the page actually leads them there. What output to expect: A first-impression read, hierarchy and friction issues, and a prioritized fix list — not generic design opinions. Next step: Feed any copy-specific fixes into the Product & Sales Page Conversion Prompt for a deeper conversion-copy pass. Best for: Improving any product, service, or sales page — CTA placement, proof, objection handling, and conversion copy. Works for SaaS pages, service pages, ecommerce listings, or a consultant’s offer page. Use when: A page gets traffic but doesn’t convert, and you want specific fixes instead of a full rewrite. You are an expert conversion copywriter reviewing a product, service, or sales page. Identify why this page is not converting as well as it should, and give me specific, prioritized fixes. - Page purpose: [sell a product or service, get a signup, get a download] - Audience: [who lands on this page and why] - Current performance, if known: [traffic, conversion rate, drop-off point] [Paste the full page copy, or describe each section in order] - Do not suggest a full rewrite unless the offer itself is unclear - Focus on clarity, proof, objection handling, and CTA placement - Keep the brand voice: [describe tone, e.g. "friendly, beginner-first, no hype"] 1. Identify the core offer and whether it's clear within the first few seconds. 2. Evaluate proof elements (testimonials, results, credibility signals) and where they're missing. 3. Identify unanswered objections a skeptical reader would have. 4. Review CTA placement, wording, and frequency. 5. Give a prioritized list of fixes, ranked by likely impact. - Core offer clarity (rated + explained) - Proof gaps (list) - Unanswered objections (list) - CTA review (list of specific placement/wording fixes) - Top 5 fixes in priority order Make sure every fix is specific enough that I could implement it today, not a vague suggestion like "add more trust." Tell me which single fix to make first if I only have 30 minutes this week. Paste your actual page copy section by section, and include real traffic or conversion numbers if you have them for sharper prioritization. What output to expect: A prioritized, specific fix list covering clarity, proof, objections, and CTA placement. Next step: If the real issue is layout and flow rather than wording, run the Website Design & UX Review Prompt first, then come back to tighten the copy. Best for: Turning a messy topic into a sourced research brief. This is one of the strongest Fable 5 prompts for research because Fable 5’s long context can hold far more raw material than a quick-summary prompt ever could. Use when: A topic is too big or scattered to summarize in a paragraph, and you need it organized before you can use it. You are an expert research analyst producing a sourced brief for a non-technical reader. Turn the messy topic and sources below into one clear, organized research brief with sourced claims — not a vague summary. - Topic: [topic] - Why I need this: [content, decision-making, client deliverable, personal understanding] - Audience: [who will read the brief] [Paste articles, links, notes, transcripts, or data you already have. List sources with names/dates where possible.] - Attribute every non-obvious claim to a source from the inputs - Flag anything unclear or where sources disagree, instead of guessing - Do not present outdated information as current without flagging the date 1. Identify the 3-5 most important questions this brief needs to answer. 2. Organize the source material by theme, not by source. 3. Summarize what is known, what is disputed, and what is missing. 4. Note the publish date or recency of key claims where it matters. 5. End with open questions that still need more research. - Key questions this brief answers - Findings by theme (with source attribution) - Points of disagreement or uncertainty - Open questions / what's still missing Check that every major claim in your findings section can be traced back to something in my inputs. Flag anything that can't. Tell me the single most important gap I should research next. Paste as much raw source material as you have — this is exactly the kind of large, messy input Fable 5’s long context handles well. Add dates to sources for better recency handling. What output to expect: An organized brief with themes, sourced claims, and flagged uncertainty — ready to turn into content or a decision. Next step: Turn the brief into an article with the Blog Outline Prompt, or into a team update with the Business Brief Prompt. Best for: Turning a repeated task into an AI agent skill with inputs, steps, outputs, and quality checks. Of all the Fable 5 prompts for AI agents in this library, this is the one to run first. Use when: You’ve noticed you keep asking Claude the same kind of question and want a saved, reusable version instead. You are an expert AI workflow strategist helping me turn a repeated task into a reusable skill. Turn the repeated task below into a complete, reusable AI agent skill I can save and run again. - The task I keep repeating: [describe it] - How often I do it: [daily, weekly, monthly] - Where I'll use it: [Claude, Gemini Spark, ChatGPT, etc.] [Describe or paste an example of the raw material you usually start with — notes, an email, a transcript, a data export] - The skill must work with an average version of my inputs, not just a perfect example - Include a review/approval step for anything sensitive (sending, publishing, deleting) - Keep instructions specific enough that a different AI tool could follow them 1. Define the skill's purpose in one sentence. 2. List the exact inputs the skill needs every time. 3. Write the step-by-step process the AI should follow, in order. 4. Define the exact output format. 5. Add a quality checklist to review before the output is used. 6. Note any step that needs human approval before acting. - Skill name - Purpose (1 sentence) - Required inputs (list) - Step-by-step process (numbered) - Output format - Quality checklist - Human approval steps (if any) Confirm the process would still work if I gave it a messier or incomplete version of the inputs, not just a perfect example. Tell me how to test this skill on a real example before I rely on it. Describe your actual repeated task in detail, and be specific about which steps are sensitive enough to need your approval before acting. What output to expect: A complete, saved-ready skill definition — not a one-time answer. See turning a prompt into an AI agent skill for the full concept breakdown. Next step: Save the skill in your AI tool of choice, and test it on a real task before trusting it fully. Best for: Diagnosing why an AI workflow failed or produced weak output. Use when: A prompt or skill that used to work is now giving inconsistent, wrong, or low-quality results and you need the actual cause, not a rewrite from scratch. You are an expert AI workflow debugger. Diagnose why this workflow is producing weak or inconsistent output, and tell me specifically what to fix. - What the workflow/skill is supposed to do: [describe] - What's going wrong: [vague output, wrong format, missing steps, inconsistent results] - How often it fails: [every time / sometimes / only with certain inputs] - The prompt or skill instructions I'm using: [paste them] - An example of a bad output it produced: [paste it] - An example of what a good output should look like, if you have one: [paste it] - Diagnose the actual cause before suggesting a fix — do not just rewrite the whole prompt - Consider missing context, unclear instructions, missing constraints, and unclear output format as possible causes - Keep the original goal of the workflow intact 1. Compare the bad output against what a good output should look like. 2. Identify exactly where the instructions are vague, missing, or contradictory. 3. Identify whether the problem is the prompt, the inputs, or the output format definition. 4. Propose a specific fix for each issue found. 5. Rewrite the corrected prompt/skill in full. - Diagnosis (what's actually causing the weak output) - Specific issues found (list) - Fixed version of the prompt/skill (full text, ready to use) Test your fixed version mentally against the bad example you were given — confirm it would have prevented that specific failure. Tell me what to test the fixed version on first to confirm it works. Include a real bad-output example — “it didn’t work” produces a vague diagnosis. Paste the full original prompt or skill text, not a summary of it. What output to expect: A specific diagnosis plus a corrected, ready-to-use version of your prompt or skill. Next step: Test the fixed prompt on 2-3 real examples before replacing the old one everywhere you use it. Best for: Converting a one-time prompt that worked well into a reusable workflow or skill. Use when: A single prompt already produced a great result once, and you want to formalize it into something repeatable without starting the full skill-builder process. You are an expert AI systems designer. Turn the one-time prompt below into a reusable, structured skill I can run again with different inputs. - Where this prompt worked well: [describe the situation/result] - Why I want to reuse it: [I do this task often / a team member needs to run it too / I want consistent quality] [Paste the original one-time prompt that worked well] - Keep the core approach that worked — do not redesign the task, just make it reusable - Replace any one-off specifics with clearly marked placeholders - Add anything the original prompt was missing: constraints, output format, or a quality check 1. Identify what made the original prompt work well. 2. Identify the parts that were specific to that one use (names, numbers, examples) and turn them into placeholders. 3. Add any missing structure: clearer constraints, an explicit output format, a quality check step. 4. Write the final reusable version. 5. Suggest a short name for this skill so it's easy to find again later. - What made the original work (2-3 sentences) - Reusable version of the prompt, with placeholders clearly marked in [brackets] - Suggested skill name Confirm the reusable version would still produce a similarly strong result if I swapped in different real inputs. Tell me one other repeated task in my business that could use this same structure. Paste the exact original prompt, not a paraphrase, so Claude can see precisely what worked, and flag which parts were one-off details versus reusable structure. What output to expect: A cleaned-up, placeholder-based version of your original prompt plus a name to save it under. Next step: Save it as a skill, and read what an AI agent skill is if you want the fuller framework for building skills. Best for: Turning one article, transcript, or idea into posts, emails, and short-form content. Use when: You have one piece of source content and want multiple platform-ready pieces without starting from a blank page each time. You are an expert content repurposing strategist. Turn the source content below into multiple ready-to-use pieces for the platforms I list, without losing the core message. - Source content type: [article, transcript, podcast notes, idea] - Brand voice: [describe tone] - Platforms I need content for: [e.g. LinkedIn, Instagram caption, email, X/Twitter thread] [Paste the full source content or transcript] - Keep the core message consistent across all formats - Match each platform's typical format and length, not just copy-paste the same text everywhere - Include one clear hook per piece 1. Identify the single core message and 2-3 supporting points worth repurposing. 2. Draft a version for each platform I listed, matching that platform's format norms. 3. Write a hook/opening line for each piece. 4. Suggest one CTA appropriate to each platform. One clearly labeled section per platform, each with: hook, full copy, and suggested CTA. Check that no piece contradicts another and that the core message stays consistent across all of them. Tell me which piece to publish first based on what's fastest to get in front of my audience. Paste the full transcript or article, not just a summary — this is exactly the long-context use case Fable 5 is built for. List only the platforms you actually use. What output to expect: A ready-to-post piece for each platform, each with its own hook and CTA. Next step: Schedule the pieces, then track which format performs best and feed that back into future repurposing prompts. Best for: Creating a daily or weekly business update from sources, metrics, emails, or notes. Use when: You need a clean summary for yourself, a partner, or a team, pulled from scattered updates instead of written from memory. You are an expert business chief of staff preparing a status brief for me. Turn the scattered updates below into one clear business brief covering wins, priorities, risks, and next steps. - Reporting period: [today / this week] - Who this brief is for: [myself, a partner, a team, a client] - Business focus areas right now: [list 2-4 current priorities] [Paste notes, metrics, email summaries, task lists, or calendar highlights from the period] - Do not pad the brief with filler — if nothing meaningful happened in an area, say so briefly - Flag anything that looks like a risk or blocker, even if it wasn't explicitly labeled as one - Keep it scannable, not a wall of text 1. Identify the top 3 wins or pieces of progress from the inputs. 2. Identify current priorities and their status. 3. Identify risks, blockers, or anything that needs a decision. 4. Recommend the top 3 priorities for the next period. - Wins (short list) - Priorities and status (short list) - Risks / blockers (short list) - Next period's top 3 priorities (numbered) Confirm every item in the brief is traceable to something in my inputs, not inferred or invented. Tell me the one item in this brief that most needs my attention today. Paste real notes and metrics each time, even messy ones — this prompt is meant to run repeatedly, and the focus areas should shift as your priorities do. What output to expect: A scannable brief with wins, status, risks, and next priorities — ready to send or review in minutes. Next step: Save this as a recurring skill using the Prompt-to-Skill Prompt so it’s ready every week without rebuilding it. Best for: Consultants, freelancers, agencies, and service businesses turning a client conversation into a written proposal or pitch — one of the most broadly useful Fable 5 prompts for business development, regardless of industry. Use when: You just had a call or exchanged emails with a prospect and need to turn scattered notes into a clear, persuasive proposal instead of starting from a blank page. You are an expert proposal writer who has helped consultants and agencies win client work. Turn my notes about this client conversation into a clear, persuasive proposal that speaks directly to their situation — not a generic services list. - Who the client/prospect is: [name, industry, size] - What they told me they need: [summarize their stated problem/goal] - My offer: [what you're proposing to do for them] - Why now: [urgency, timing, or trigger for this conversation] [Paste call notes, email exchanges, or a rough scope of what was discussed] - Speak to their specific situation, not a generic pitch - Tone: [describe, e.g. "confident but not pushy," "warm and consultative"] - Must include: clear scope, timeline, and investment/pricing structure - Must avoid: overpromising or vague deliverables 1. Summarize the client's problem back to them in their own words. 2. State the outcome I will deliver, not just the tasks I will do. 3. Outline the scope and timeline in clear phases or milestones. 4. Address the most likely objection or hesitation before they raise it. 5. End with one clear, low-friction next step. - Understanding your situation (short paragraph) - What we'll deliver (bulleted outcomes) - Scope and timeline (phases/milestones) - Investment (pricing structure, described clearly) - Next steps (one clear call to action) Check that the proposal reflects this specific client's situation and would not work word-for-word for a different client. Tell me the one thing most likely to make this client hesitate, so I can address it before I send this. Paste your real call notes or email thread, not a summary — the more specific their actual words, the less generic the proposal reads. What output to expect: A client-specific proposal structure with outcomes, scope, pricing, and one clear next step — ready to format and send. Next step: Run the finished proposal through the Quality Check Prompt before sending it. Best for: Reviewing an output before publishing, sending, or handing it to a client. Use when: You have a finished draft — article, email, page, or deliverable — and want a final, honest review before it goes out. You are an expert, strict but fair editor doing a final quality check before this goes out. Review the draft below and tell me honestly whether it's ready to publish/send, and exactly what to fix if it's not. - What this is: [article, email, client deliverable, landing page] - Audience: [who will read/receive this] - Standard it needs to meet: [describe: accurate, on-brand, persuasive, error-free, etc.] [Paste the full draft] - Be direct — do not soften real problems to be polite - Separate must-fix issues from nice-to-have suggestions - Check for factual claims that need verification, not just tone and grammar 1. Check clarity: is the core message obvious within the first few lines? 2. Check accuracy: flag any claim that needs verification or looks outdated. 3. Check tone and audience fit. 4. Check structure and formatting. 5. Give a clear final verdict: ready to publish, or needs fixes first. - Must-fix issues (numbered list) - Nice-to-have improvements (short list) - Final verdict: Ready to publish / Needs fixes first (with a one-sentence reason) Before answering, reread the draft once more specifically looking for anything you may have missed on the first pass — factual claims, broken logic, or missing context. If it needs fixes, tell me which single fix matters most before anything else. Paste the full, final draft, not an early version, and state the real audience and standard so the review isn’t generic. What output to expect: A direct must-fix versus nice-to-have list and a clear ready/not-ready verdict. Next step: Apply the must-fix items, then do one final pass before publishing or sending. Claude Fable 5 vs Claude Sonnet 5: Which Should You Use for Prompts? Not every Claude Fable 5 prompt needs to run on Fable 5 — and since Opus 5’s July 2026 release, most don’t. Claude Sonnet 5 is faster and available across all Claude plans for routine writing and quick drafts. Claude Opus 5 is now the default for demanding work — complex research, business-critical decisions, difficult analysis, multi-step workflows, and prompt-to-skill conversion — at roughly half of Fable 5’s price. Fable 5 earns its place only on the exceptionally difficult prompts where Opus 5 falls short. Situation Better model Why Quick drafts, captions, or simple rewrites Claude Sonnet 5 Faster and available on every plan for routine work Everyday research summaries Claude Sonnet 5 No need for the strongest model on a quick, low-stakes summary Deep, multi-source research briefs Claude Opus 5 Handles large source material at half Fable’s cost — start here Business-critical strategy decisions Claude Opus 5 Near-frontier reasoning for high-stakes calls without Fable-level spend Large keyword exports or GSC analysis Claude Opus 5 Handles large, messy datasets without losing detail, at lower cost Multi-step AI agent workflows Claude Opus 5 Built for long-running, connected steps that must hold up end to end Prompt-to-skill conversion Claude Opus 5 Strong at spotting missing structure and generalizing a one-off prompt Long documents and large projects Claude Opus 5 Handles long-context work most models struggle with, at half Fable’s price Exceptionally hard tasks where Opus 5 fell short Claude Fable 5 The one case left for Fable: Opus 5 already tried and couldn’t reliably finish A simple rule: start with Claude Sonnet 5 for everyday prompts, move up to Claude Opus 5 for difficult, layered, or high-stakes work, and reserve Claude Fable 5 for the exceptionally hard prompts where Opus 5 has already tried and fallen short. How to Turn These Prompts Into AI Agent Skills A prompt is one request. A skill is the saved, reusable version of that process — the same inputs, steps, and output format every time, so you’re not rebuilding it from memory. An AI agent workflow goes further: it can use a skill repeatedly with real inputs, tools, memory, and review steps built in, often across a schedule instead of a single chat. Every prompt in this library can graduate from a one-time request to a saved skill. Start with the AI Agent Skill Builder Prompt or the Prompt-to-Skill Prompt above, then read what an AI agent skill is for the full breakdown of prompts versus skills versus agents. If you want to skip the blank page entirely, browse the Claude skills library for ready-to-copy skills you can adapt. If you’re running these prompts inside Claude’s agentic workspace, our guide to how to set up Claude Cowork covers the setup steps. Final takeaway The best Claude Fable 5 prompts are not clever wording — they’re structure. Give Fable 5 a goal, real context, your actual inputs, constraints, a process, an output format, and a quality check, and it will consistently outperform a one-line request. For a more detailed usage strategy, see The 9 Best Ways to Reduce Claude Fable 5 Credit Usage. Start with one prompt from this library, run it on a real task this week, then turn it into a skill once it earns a permanent place in your workflow. What are the best Claude Fable 5 prompts? The best Claude Fable 5 prompts are structured workflows that give the model a clear goal, real context, your actual inputs, constraints, a step-by-step process, an exact output format, and a quality check — not a one-line request. The 15 prompts and master template above follow that structure for business, SEO, research, content, website design, and AI agent tasks. Is Claude Fable 5 good for SEO prompts? Yes. Fable 5 prompts for SEO work especially well for tasks that involve reviewing a large keyword export, a full Search Console export, or several competitor pages at once, since Fable 5 can hold that much source material in context and cluster it by intent instead of just listing keywords. Is Claude Fable 5 good for research? Yes. Fable 5 prompts for research are strong when a topic has more source material than a quick summary can cover — Fable 5 can organize scattered articles, notes, and transcripts into a themed, sourced brief instead of a vague overview. Is Claude Fable 5 better than Sonnet 5 for prompts? Not universally, and since Opus 5’s release it’s usually the wrong comparison. Claude Sonnet 5 is faster and available across all plans for routine writing and everyday prompts. For complex, long-running, or business-critical prompts, Claude Opus 5 is now the recommended default — near-frontier quality at roughly half Fable 5’s price. Reserve Claude Fable 5 for the exceptionally hard prompts where Opus 5 falls short. See the comparison table above for specific situations. Can Claude Fable 5 help build AI agents? Yes. Fable 5 prompts for AI agents can help you design the process, inputs, steps, and quality checks behind a reusable skill or workflow. The actual agent behavior — tool use, scheduling, and multi-step execution — depends on the platform you run it in, such as Claude Cowork. What is the difference between a Claude Fable 5 prompt and an AI agent skill? A prompt is a one-time request you type in. An AI agent skill is the saved, reusable version of that process, with defined inputs, steps, and an output format, so you don’t rebuild it from memory every time. See what an AI agent skill is for the full breakdown. Is Claude Fable 5 available now? Yes. Anthropic restored global access to Claude Fable 5 starting July 1, 2026, after the export controls that had paused it were lifted. It’s available through Claude.ai, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and the Claude Platform, though availability, plan limits, and usage credits can vary — check Claude directly before building a workflow around it. Is Claude Fabel 5 the same as Claude Fable 5? Yes. “Claude Fabel 5” is a common misspelling. The correct name is Claude Fable 5.
