The 15 Best Claude Fable 5 Prompts for Business In 2026

Claude Fable 5 is back. Anthropic restored global access starting July 1, 2026, after the export controls that paused it were lifted — see the official Anthropic update. If you still need the basics, read what Claude Fable 5 is first. If you want ideas before prompts, read the 12 best Claude Fable 5 use cases. This page assumes you already know what Fable 5 is and want the 15 best Claude Fable 5 prompts for business in 2026 — ready to copy, paste, and use.

Update — July 13, 2026

Anthropic has now settled Fable 5’s access permanently. From July 20, Fable 5 is included in all Max and Team Premium plans at 50% of limits. Pro and Team Standard keep access through usage credits and receive a one-time $100 credit, after which Fable 5 bills at API rates ($10 per million input tokens, $50 per million output). See Anthropic’s guide to managing usage credits. The 50% Claude Code rate-limit boost also ends July 20, so standard weekly limits shrink the same day. The strategy is still the same: use cheaper models to plan, draft, and refine, then save Fable 5 for final high-value outputs. Full write-up: what the Fable 5 access change means for your plan.

Quick answer

Why do most Claude Fable 5 prompts underperform?

Most people use Claude Fable 5 like a normal chatbot — one short line, one quick answer. That is the wrong approach for a model built for complex, long-running, ambiguous work. The best Claude Fable 5 prompts are structured workflows: a clear goal, real context, actual inputs, constraints, a process, an exact output format, and a quality check — not a one-line request. Every prompt below follows that structure. If your goal is to get better results without wasting usage on retries, start with our guide on how to save Claude Fable 5 credits.

How to Decide If Claude Fable 5 Is the Right Fit

If you’re deciding whether Claude Fable 5 is the right fit, use it for complex research, strategy, and workflow tasks that need deeper reasoning, not every quick question. Anthropic’s own prompting documentation for Claude Fable 5 notes that it may need updated prompt scaffolding compared with prior Claude models. In practice, that means giving Fable 5 a real job instead of a quick question. Every strong Claude Fable 5 prompt includes these eight parts.

1 Goal

One clear sentence describing exactly what you want and why it matters.

2 Context

What Claude needs to know: your business, audience, situation, and offer.

3 Inputs

The source material you’re handing over: notes, data, URLs, exports, transcripts.

4 Constraints

Tone, length, what to avoid, and what must be included.

5 Process

The steps Claude should think through, in order — not just the final answer.

6 Output format

The exact shape of what comes back: a table, outline, checklist, or brief.

7 Quality check

A rule Claude uses to review its own answer before handing it to you.

8 Next action

The single next step you should take once you have the output.

Instead of asking:

Help me with SEO.

A structured Claude Fable 5 prompt reviews your keywords, checks for cannibalization against your existing pages, clusters opportunities by intent, and hands back a prioritized table — not a paragraph of generic advice. That difference is the entire point of this library.

A quick safety note

Fable 5 includes updated safety classifiers. A small number of benign coding or debugging requests can get flagged or rerouted to Claude Opus 4.8 instead of answered directly — this is expected behavior, not a broken prompt. Every prompt in this library stays in normal business, content, design, research, and workflow territory, so you’re unlikely to see it, but it’s worth knowing about if you adapt these prompts for engineering tasks. Details are in Anthropic’s Fable 5 prompting docs.

A quick tip on managing your Fable 5 credits

Fable 5 is a heavier, more capable model, and running every single prompt through it — including quick one-liners — burns through usage credits faster than it needs to. As a simple rule: save Fable 5 for the harder work in this library (deep research, business strategy, prompt-to-skill conversion, and other multi-step or high-stakes prompts), and use a lighter model like Sonnet 5 for quick drafts, small edits, and everyday questions. Batching related work into one longer Fable 5 session, instead of many small separate prompts, also stretches your credits further.

Best Claude Fable 5 Prompt Template

Save this master template and reuse it as a starting point for any new Claude Fable 5 prompt. It bakes in all eight parts from above. Every specialized prompt further down this page is a filled-in version of this same structure.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert [ROLE] working on this task with me.

GOAL
[One clear sentence describing exactly what you want and why it matters.]

CONTEXT
- Business/brand: [name, niche, audience]
- Situation: [what's happening right now that makes this task necessary]
- Audience: [who this is for]

INPUTS
- [Paste source material: notes, data, URLs, transcripts, screenshots, exports]
- [Add a second input if relevant]

CONSTRAINTS
- Tone: [describe voice/style]
- Length: [word count, section count, etc.]
- Must avoid: [things to exclude]
- Must include: [non-negotiables]

PROCESS
1. [First thinking step]
2. [Second thinking step]
3. [Third thinking step]
4. [Continue until the final step]

OUTPUT FORMAT
[Exact format you want back: table, outline, numbered list, etc.]

QUALITY CHECK
Before giving me the final answer, check your own work against [criteria] and flag anything you are unsure about.

NEXT ACTION
End with one clear recommended next step I should take.

How to customize it

Fill in every bracket with your real details before you paste it — a template with placeholders still in it will read like a template to Claude too. Delete any section that genuinely doesn’t apply rather than leaving it blank.

15 Copy-Paste Claude Fable 5 Prompts

Below are 15 ready-to-use Claude Fable 5 prompts for business, SEO, research, content, website design, and AI agent workflows. Each one follows the same structure: who it’s best for, when to use it, the exact prompt to paste, how to customize it, what output to expect, and the next step once you have it.

Best for: Business owners who need a practical strategy, not vague ideas. This is one of the strongest Fable 5 prompts for business decisions where the cost of guessing wrong is real.

Use when: You need a decision-ready plan for a specific choice — pricing, a growth bottleneck, a new offer, or where to put limited time and budget next.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert business strategist for [your industry or website URL] who has helped small businesses grow profitably.

GOAL
Help me decide [specific decision, e.g. "whether to raise prices," "which service to cut," "how to grow revenue in the next 90 days"] with a clear, practical recommendation — not a list of generic options.

CONTEXT
- Business: [what you sell, who you sell to, how you make money]
- Current situation: [revenue range, team size, main constraint right now]
- What has already been tried: [list anything relevant]
- Risk tolerance: [conservative / moderate / aggressive]

INPUTS
[Paste any relevant numbers, notes, past strategy docs, or customer feedback here]

CONSTRAINTS
- Timeframe: [e.g. decide and act within 30/60/90 days]
- Budget: [rough range or "no new budget"]
- Must not: [anything off the table, e.g. "no layoffs," "no new hires"]

PROCESS
1. Identify the real constraint holding the business back right now, not just the symptom.
2. List 3 realistic strategic options, with the tradeoffs of each.
3. Recommend ONE option and explain why it beats the others for this specific situation.
4. Break the recommendation into a first-30-days action plan.
5. Flag the biggest risk in the plan and how to reduce it.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Section 1: The real constraint (2-3 sentences)
- Section 2: Three options in a short table (option, tradeoff, timeframe)
- Section 3: Recommendation and reasoning
- Section 4: 30-day action plan as a numbered list
- Section 5: Biggest risk and mitigation

QUALITY CHECK
Before finalizing, check whether your recommendation actually matches my stated risk tolerance and budget. If it doesn't, revise it.

NEXT ACTION
End with the single next task I should do this week.

How to customize it

Swap in the real decision, numbers, and constraints — the sharper your revenue and cost details, the less generic the recommendation.

What output to expect: A structured decision brief — a stated constraint, three weighed options, one clear recommendation, and a first-30-days plan — not a brainstorm.

Next step: Turn the 30-day plan into a weekly checklist, or feed progress into the Business Brief Prompt.

Best for: Finding content opportunities from keyword lists, Search Console exports, or competitor pages. This is one of the most useful Fable 5 prompts for SEO because it can hold an entire keyword export in context at once.

Use when: You have a pile of keywords or topics and want a prioritized, clustered plan instead of a raw list.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert SEO content strategist for [your site/niche].

GOAL
Turn the data below into a prioritized list of content opportunities I can act on this month — not just a list of keywords.

CONTEXT
- Site: [URL, niche, audience]
- Current content: [rough number of articles, main topics already covered]
- Goal: [rank for a niche, capture more clicks, fill a content gap]

INPUTS
[Paste your keyword list, GSC export, or competitor URLs/topics here]

CONSTRAINTS
- Only suggest topics that fit [your niche/audience]
- Flag anything that overlaps with existing content: [list URLs of existing articles to avoid cannibalizing]
- Prioritize topics with clear buyer or reader intent over vanity keywords

PROCESS
1. Group the raw keywords/topics into themed clusters.
2. For each cluster, identify the likely search intent (informational, commercial, navigational).
3. Score each cluster on estimated opportunity (low competition + clear intent + fits my niche).
4. Flag any cluster that risks cannibalizing an existing page I listed.
5. Recommend the top 5 clusters to write next, in priority order.

OUTPUT FORMAT
A table with columns: Cluster, Search intent, Opportunity score (1-5), Cannibalization risk, Recommended next step.

QUALITY CHECK
Double-check that none of your top 5 recommendations duplicate the intent of an existing page I listed. If one does, replace it or suggest a merge instead.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me which single cluster to write first and why.

How to customize it

Paste your actual keyword export and list your real existing URLs so Claude can flag cannibalization instead of guessing.

What output to expect: A prioritized, clustered table of content opportunities with intent and cannibalization risk flagged — ready to hand to a writer.

Next step: Feed the top cluster into the Blog Outline Prompt to build the actual article structure.

Best for: Analyzing competitor articles and finding a stronger angle instead of just writing a longer copy of the same thing.

Use when: A competitor outranks you, or is about to, and you want to know exactly what to do differently.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert competitive content strategist for [your website].

GOAL
Analyze the competitor content below and tell me exactly how to create a stronger, more useful version — not just a longer one.

CONTEXT
- My site/brand: [name, angle, audience]
- My existing page on this topic, if any: [URL or "none yet"]
- Why this competitor matters: [they outrank me / direct competitor / new entrant]

INPUTS
[Paste the competitor's URL, or paste their article text/outline]

CONSTRAINTS
- Do not recommend copying their structure directly
- Focus on gaps: missing sections, weak examples, outdated info, unanswered questions
- Consider search intent, not just word count

PROCESS
1. Summarize what the competitor's content actually covers and how it's structured.
2. Identify what it does well.
3. Identify concrete gaps: missing subtopics, weak or generic sections, outdated claims, unanswered reader questions.
4. Identify a distinct angle I can own that they have not covered.
5. Recommend a structure for my version that is better, not just bigger.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Their structure (bulleted)
- What they do well (short list)
- Gaps and weaknesses (short list)
- My differentiated angle (1-2 sentences)
- Recommended outline for my version (numbered headings)

QUALITY CHECK
Check that your recommended outline actually addresses the gaps you found — not a generic "better" version.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me the one thing that would make my version clearly worth ranking above theirs.

How to customize it

Paste the actual competitor URL or full text, and add notes on your own unique data, results, or experience to sharpen the differentiation.

What output to expect: A gap analysis plus a differentiated outline you can hand straight to a writer.

Next step: Run the recommended outline through the Blog Outline Prompt to finalize headings without cannibalizing your own content.

Best for: Creating an SEO article outline that fits cleanly alongside your existing content instead of competing with it.

Use when: You know the topic and target keyword, but need a full outline that avoids cannibalizing an existing page.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert SEO content strategist and outline writer.

GOAL
Create a complete article outline for the target keyword below that will not compete with my existing articles for the same intent.

CONTEXT
- Target keyword: [keyword]
- Search intent: [informational / comparison / how-to / commercial]
- Audience: [who is searching this]

INPUTS
- My existing related articles (title + URL + one-line topic for each): [list them]
- Any notes, data, or examples I want included: [paste here]

CONSTRAINTS
- The new article must target a clearly different angle or intent than any URL I listed
- If overlap is unavoidable, tell me directly instead of forcing a workaround
- Keep headings specific, not generic ("5 tips" style headings are not allowed)

PROCESS
1. Compare the target keyword's intent against each existing article I listed.
2. Confirm there is a distinct angle for this new article, or flag the overlap.
3. Draft an H1, meta description, and full H2/H3 outline.
4. Suggest 2-3 internal links to my existing articles where they naturally fit.
5. Suggest FAQ questions that match real search queries for this topic.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Cannibalization check (one paragraph)
- H1
- Meta description
- Full outline (H2s with H3s nested underneath)
- Suggested internal links (anchor text + target URL)
- FAQ questions (5-8)

QUALITY CHECK
Re-read the outline and confirm no H2 duplicates the primary angle of an existing article I listed.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me which section of the outline is hardest to write, so I know where to start research first.

How to customize it

List your real existing article URLs and topics so Claude can genuinely check for overlap, not just assume there isn’t any.

What output to expect: A cannibalization-safe H1, meta description, full heading structure, internal link suggestions, and FAQ ideas.

Next step: Draft the article section by section, then run the finished draft through the Quality Check Prompt before publishing.

Best for: Updating an existing article without shifting its intent, URL, or existing internal links too far.

Use when: An article is losing rankings, has outdated information, or needs expansion — but doesn’t need a full rebuild.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert SEO editor refreshing an existing article.

GOAL
Update this article to be more accurate, complete, and competitive — while keeping its original intent and URL intact.

CONTEXT
- Target keyword: [keyword]
- Why it needs a refresh: [rankings dropped / outdated info / new competitor / thin content]
- What must NOT change: [URL, core angle, existing internal links pointing to it]

INPUTS
[Paste the full existing article text]

CONSTRAINTS
- Do not change the article's core search intent or target keyword
- Preserve any existing internal/external links unless they are broken or outdated
- Flag outdated claims, prices, dates, or product names instead of guessing new ones

PROCESS
1. Identify what is outdated, thin, or missing compared to current best practices for this topic.
2. Identify sections that are still strong and should stay mostly as-is.
3. Recommend specific additions, deletions, and rewrites, section by section.
4. Suggest an updated meta description if the old one is weak.
5. Suggest 1-2 new FAQ questions based on what readers likely ask now.

OUTPUT FORMAT
A section-by-section table: Section, Keep / Rewrite / Add / Cut, Reasoning, Suggested new copy (where applicable).

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm the refreshed version still targets the same primary keyword and intent as the original — flag it if your suggestions drift.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me the single change most likely to recover rankings fastest.

How to customize it

Paste the real, full article text rather than a summary, and note any known ranking-drop dates so Claude can weigh what likely changed.

What output to expect: A section-by-section refresh plan — keep, rewrite, add, or cut — instead of a full rewrite.

Next step: Apply the changes, then check performance directly in Google Search Console after a few weeks, or fold the results into your Business Brief Prompt.

Best for: Anyone reviewing a website, landing page, or app screen for layout, clarity, and usability — creators, consultants, agencies, and small business owners in any industry, not just tech companies.

Use when: A page looks fine to you, but visitors seem confused, bounce quickly, or don’t take the action you expect, and you want a structured design critique instead of a vague “make it look nicer.”

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert website designer and UX consultant who has reviewed hundreds of small business and creator websites.

GOAL
Review the website or page described below and give me a structured critique of its layout, clarity, and usability — not just a list of visual opinions.

CONTEXT
- Type of site/page: [homepage, landing page, portfolio, online store, app screen]
- Primary goal of this page: [get a sign-up, sell a product, book a call, get a download]
- Audience: [who typically lands here and why]

INPUTS
[Paste the page copy section by section, describe each section in order top to bottom, or paste a link plus a description of what's on it]

CONSTRAINTS
- Focus on structure, clarity, hierarchy, and flow — not code or technical implementation
- Call out anything that would confuse a first-time visitor within the first 5 seconds
- Keep every suggestion specific enough to act on today

PROCESS
1. Identify whether the page's main goal is obvious within the first few seconds.
2. Review visual and content hierarchy — is the most important thing actually first?
3. Review the navigation and flow from top to bottom.
4. Identify friction points: confusing sections, missing information, or unclear next steps.
5. Rank the fixes by likely impact on visitor experience.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- First impression (1-2 sentences)
- Hierarchy issues (short list)
- Friction points (short list)
- Top 5 fixes in priority order

QUALITY CHECK
Make sure every fix is a specific structural or content change, not a vague note like "make it more modern."

NEXT ACTION
Tell me the single change most likely to reduce visitor confusion this week.

How to customize it

Describe your actual page section by section, or paste real copy, and be specific about what action you want visitors to take so Claude can judge whether the page actually leads them there.

What output to expect: A first-impression read, hierarchy and friction issues, and a prioritized fix list — not generic design opinions.

Next step: Feed any copy-specific fixes into the Product & Sales Page Conversion Prompt for a deeper conversion-copy pass.

Best for: Improving any product, service, or sales page — CTA placement, proof, objection handling, and conversion copy. Works for SaaS pages, service pages, ecommerce listings, or a consultant’s offer page.

Use when: A page gets traffic but doesn’t convert, and you want specific fixes instead of a full rewrite.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert conversion copywriter reviewing a product, service, or sales page.

GOAL
Identify why this page is not converting as well as it should, and give me specific, prioritized fixes.

CONTEXT
- Page purpose: [sell a product or service, get a signup, get a download]
- Audience: [who lands on this page and why]
- Current performance, if known: [traffic, conversion rate, drop-off point]

INPUTS
[Paste the full page copy, or describe each section in order]

CONSTRAINTS
- Do not suggest a full rewrite unless the offer itself is unclear
- Focus on clarity, proof, objection handling, and CTA placement
- Keep the brand voice: [describe tone, e.g. "friendly, beginner-first, no hype"]

PROCESS
1. Identify the core offer and whether it's clear within the first few seconds.
2. Evaluate proof elements (testimonials, results, credibility signals) and where they're missing.
3. Identify unanswered objections a skeptical reader would have.
4. Review CTA placement, wording, and frequency.
5. Give a prioritized list of fixes, ranked by likely impact.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Core offer clarity (rated + explained)
- Proof gaps (list)
- Unanswered objections (list)
- CTA review (list of specific placement/wording fixes)
- Top 5 fixes in priority order

QUALITY CHECK
Make sure every fix is specific enough that I could implement it today, not a vague suggestion like "add more trust."

NEXT ACTION
Tell me which single fix to make first if I only have 30 minutes this week.

How to customize it

Paste your actual page copy section by section, and include real traffic or conversion numbers if you have them for sharper prioritization.

What output to expect: A prioritized, specific fix list covering clarity, proof, objections, and CTA placement.

Next step: If the real issue is layout and flow rather than wording, run the Website Design & UX Review Prompt first, then come back to tighten the copy.

Best for: Turning a messy topic into a sourced research brief. This is one of the strongest Fable 5 prompts for research because Fable 5’s long context can hold far more raw material than a quick-summary prompt ever could.

Use when: A topic is too big or scattered to summarize in a paragraph, and you need it organized before you can use it.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert research analyst producing a sourced brief for a non-technical reader.

GOAL
Turn the messy topic and sources below into one clear, organized research brief with sourced claims — not a vague summary.

CONTEXT
- Topic: [topic]
- Why I need this: [content, decision-making, client deliverable, personal understanding]
- Audience: [who will read the brief]

INPUTS
[Paste articles, links, notes, transcripts, or data you already have. List sources with names/dates where possible.]

CONSTRAINTS
- Attribute every non-obvious claim to a source from the inputs
- Flag anything unclear or where sources disagree, instead of guessing
- Do not present outdated information as current without flagging the date

PROCESS
1. Identify the 3-5 most important questions this brief needs to answer.
2. Organize the source material by theme, not by source.
3. Summarize what is known, what is disputed, and what is missing.
4. Note the publish date or recency of key claims where it matters.
5. End with open questions that still need more research.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Key questions this brief answers
- Findings by theme (with source attribution)
- Points of disagreement or uncertainty
- Open questions / what's still missing

QUALITY CHECK
Check that every major claim in your findings section can be traced back to something in my inputs. Flag anything that can't.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me the single most important gap I should research next.

How to customize it

Paste as much raw source material as you have — this is exactly the kind of large, messy input Fable 5’s long context handles well. Add dates to sources for better recency handling.

What output to expect: An organized brief with themes, sourced claims, and flagged uncertainty — ready to turn into content or a decision.

Next step: Turn the brief into an article with the Blog Outline Prompt, or into a team update with the Business Brief Prompt.

Best for: Turning a repeated task into an AI agent skill with inputs, steps, outputs, and quality checks. Of all the Fable 5 prompts for AI agents in this library, this is the one to run first.

Use when: You’ve noticed you keep asking Claude the same kind of question and want a saved, reusable version instead.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert AI workflow strategist helping me turn a repeated task into a reusable skill.

GOAL
Turn the repeated task below into a complete, reusable AI agent skill I can save and run again.

CONTEXT
- The task I keep repeating: [describe it]
- How often I do it: [daily, weekly, monthly]
- Where I'll use it: [Claude, Gemini Spark, ChatGPT, etc.]

INPUTS
[Describe or paste an example of the raw material you usually start with — notes, an email, a transcript, a data export]

CONSTRAINTS
- The skill must work with an average version of my inputs, not just a perfect example
- Include a review/approval step for anything sensitive (sending, publishing, deleting)
- Keep instructions specific enough that a different AI tool could follow them

PROCESS
1. Define the skill's purpose in one sentence.
2. List the exact inputs the skill needs every time.
3. Write the step-by-step process the AI should follow, in order.
4. Define the exact output format.
5. Add a quality checklist to review before the output is used.
6. Note any step that needs human approval before acting.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Skill name
- Purpose (1 sentence)
- Required inputs (list)
- Step-by-step process (numbered)
- Output format
- Quality checklist
- Human approval steps (if any)

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm the process would still work if I gave it a messier or incomplete version of the inputs, not just a perfect example.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me how to test this skill on a real example before I rely on it.

How to customize it

Describe your actual repeated task in detail, and be specific about which steps are sensitive enough to need your approval before acting.

What output to expect: A complete, saved-ready skill definition — not a one-time answer. See turning a prompt into an AI agent skill for the full concept breakdown.

Next step: Save the skill in your AI tool of choice, and test it on a real task before trusting it fully.

Best for: Diagnosing why an AI workflow failed or produced weak output.

Use when: A prompt or skill that used to work is now giving inconsistent, wrong, or low-quality results and you need the actual cause, not a rewrite from scratch.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert AI workflow debugger.

GOAL
Diagnose why this workflow is producing weak or inconsistent output, and tell me specifically what to fix.

CONTEXT
- What the workflow/skill is supposed to do: [describe]
- What's going wrong: [vague output, wrong format, missing steps, inconsistent results]
- How often it fails: [every time / sometimes / only with certain inputs]

INPUTS
- The prompt or skill instructions I'm using: [paste them]
- An example of a bad output it produced: [paste it]
- An example of what a good output should look like, if you have one: [paste it]

CONSTRAINTS
- Diagnose the actual cause before suggesting a fix — do not just rewrite the whole prompt
- Consider missing context, unclear instructions, missing constraints, and unclear output format as possible causes
- Keep the original goal of the workflow intact

PROCESS
1. Compare the bad output against what a good output should look like.
2. Identify exactly where the instructions are vague, missing, or contradictory.
3. Identify whether the problem is the prompt, the inputs, or the output format definition.
4. Propose a specific fix for each issue found.
5. Rewrite the corrected prompt/skill in full.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Diagnosis (what's actually causing the weak output)
- Specific issues found (list)
- Fixed version of the prompt/skill (full text, ready to use)

QUALITY CHECK
Test your fixed version mentally against the bad example you were given — confirm it would have prevented that specific failure.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me what to test the fixed version on first to confirm it works.

How to customize it

Include a real bad-output example — “it didn’t work” produces a vague diagnosis. Paste the full original prompt or skill text, not a summary of it.

What output to expect: A specific diagnosis plus a corrected, ready-to-use version of your prompt or skill.

Next step: Test the fixed prompt on 2-3 real examples before replacing the old one everywhere you use it.

Best for: Converting a one-time prompt that worked well into a reusable workflow or skill.

Use when: A single prompt already produced a great result once, and you want to formalize it into something repeatable without starting the full skill-builder process.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert AI systems designer.

GOAL
Turn the one-time prompt below into a reusable, structured skill I can run again with different inputs.

CONTEXT
- Where this prompt worked well: [describe the situation/result]
- Why I want to reuse it: [I do this task often / a team member needs to run it too / I want consistent quality]

INPUTS
[Paste the original one-time prompt that worked well]

CONSTRAINTS
- Keep the core approach that worked — do not redesign the task, just make it reusable
- Replace any one-off specifics with clearly marked placeholders
- Add anything the original prompt was missing: constraints, output format, or a quality check

PROCESS
1. Identify what made the original prompt work well.
2. Identify the parts that were specific to that one use (names, numbers, examples) and turn them into placeholders.
3. Add any missing structure: clearer constraints, an explicit output format, a quality check step.
4. Write the final reusable version.
5. Suggest a short name for this skill so it's easy to find again later.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- What made the original work (2-3 sentences)
- Reusable version of the prompt, with placeholders clearly marked in [brackets]
- Suggested skill name

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm the reusable version would still produce a similarly strong result if I swapped in different real inputs.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me one other repeated task in my business that could use this same structure.

How to customize it

Paste the exact original prompt, not a paraphrase, so Claude can see precisely what worked, and flag which parts were one-off details versus reusable structure.

What output to expect: A cleaned-up, placeholder-based version of your original prompt plus a name to save it under.

Next step: Save it as a skill, and read what an AI agent skill is if you want the fuller framework for building skills.

Best for: Turning one article, transcript, or idea into posts, emails, and short-form content.

Use when: You have one piece of source content and want multiple platform-ready pieces without starting from a blank page each time.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert content repurposing strategist.

GOAL
Turn the source content below into multiple ready-to-use pieces for the platforms I list, without losing the core message.

CONTEXT
- Source content type: [article, transcript, podcast notes, idea]
- Brand voice: [describe tone]
- Platforms I need content for: [e.g. LinkedIn, Instagram caption, email, X/Twitter thread]

INPUTS
[Paste the full source content or transcript]

CONSTRAINTS
- Keep the core message consistent across all formats
- Match each platform's typical format and length, not just copy-paste the same text everywhere
- Include one clear hook per piece

PROCESS
1. Identify the single core message and 2-3 supporting points worth repurposing.
2. Draft a version for each platform I listed, matching that platform's format norms.
3. Write a hook/opening line for each piece.
4. Suggest one CTA appropriate to each platform.

OUTPUT FORMAT
One clearly labeled section per platform, each with: hook, full copy, and suggested CTA.

QUALITY CHECK
Check that no piece contradicts another and that the core message stays consistent across all of them.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me which piece to publish first based on what's fastest to get in front of my audience.

How to customize it

Paste the full transcript or article, not just a summary — this is exactly the long-context use case Fable 5 is built for. List only the platforms you actually use.

What output to expect: A ready-to-post piece for each platform, each with its own hook and CTA.

Next step: Schedule the pieces, then track which format performs best and feed that back into future repurposing prompts.

Best for: Creating a daily or weekly business update from sources, metrics, emails, or notes.

Use when: You need a clean summary for yourself, a partner, or a team, pulled from scattered updates instead of written from memory.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert business chief of staff preparing a status brief for me.

GOAL
Turn the scattered updates below into one clear business brief covering wins, priorities, risks, and next steps.

CONTEXT
- Reporting period: [today / this week]
- Who this brief is for: [myself, a partner, a team, a client]
- Business focus areas right now: [list 2-4 current priorities]

INPUTS
[Paste notes, metrics, email summaries, task lists, or calendar highlights from the period]

CONSTRAINTS
- Do not pad the brief with filler — if nothing meaningful happened in an area, say so briefly
- Flag anything that looks like a risk or blocker, even if it wasn't explicitly labeled as one
- Keep it scannable, not a wall of text

PROCESS
1. Identify the top 3 wins or pieces of progress from the inputs.
2. Identify current priorities and their status.
3. Identify risks, blockers, or anything that needs a decision.
4. Recommend the top 3 priorities for the next period.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Wins (short list)
- Priorities and status (short list)
- Risks / blockers (short list)
- Next period's top 3 priorities (numbered)

QUALITY CHECK
Confirm every item in the brief is traceable to something in my inputs, not inferred or invented.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me the one item in this brief that most needs my attention today.

How to customize it

Paste real notes and metrics each time, even messy ones — this prompt is meant to run repeatedly, and the focus areas should shift as your priorities do.

What output to expect: A scannable brief with wins, status, risks, and next priorities — ready to send or review in minutes.

Next step: Save this as a recurring skill using the Prompt-to-Skill Prompt so it’s ready every week without rebuilding it.

Best for: Consultants, freelancers, agencies, and service businesses turning a client conversation into a written proposal or pitch — one of the most broadly useful Fable 5 prompts for business development, regardless of industry.

Use when: You just had a call or exchanged emails with a prospect and need to turn scattered notes into a clear, persuasive proposal instead of starting from a blank page.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert proposal writer who has helped consultants and agencies win client work.

GOAL
Turn my notes about this client conversation into a clear, persuasive proposal that speaks directly to their situation — not a generic services list.

CONTEXT
- Who the client/prospect is: [name, industry, size]
- What they told me they need: [summarize their stated problem/goal]
- My offer: [what you're proposing to do for them]
- Why now: [urgency, timing, or trigger for this conversation]

INPUTS
[Paste call notes, email exchanges, or a rough scope of what was discussed]

CONSTRAINTS
- Speak to their specific situation, not a generic pitch
- Tone: [describe, e.g. "confident but not pushy," "warm and consultative"]
- Must include: clear scope, timeline, and investment/pricing structure
- Must avoid: overpromising or vague deliverables

PROCESS
1. Summarize the client's problem back to them in their own words.
2. State the outcome I will deliver, not just the tasks I will do.
3. Outline the scope and timeline in clear phases or milestones.
4. Address the most likely objection or hesitation before they raise it.
5. End with one clear, low-friction next step.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Understanding your situation (short paragraph)
- What we'll deliver (bulleted outcomes)
- Scope and timeline (phases/milestones)
- Investment (pricing structure, described clearly)
- Next steps (one clear call to action)

QUALITY CHECK
Check that the proposal reflects this specific client's situation and would not work word-for-word for a different client.

NEXT ACTION
Tell me the one thing most likely to make this client hesitate, so I can address it before I send this.

How to customize it

Paste your real call notes or email thread, not a summary — the more specific their actual words, the less generic the proposal reads.

What output to expect: A client-specific proposal structure with outcomes, scope, pricing, and one clear next step — ready to format and send.

Next step: Run the finished proposal through the Quality Check Prompt before sending it.

Best for: Reviewing an output before publishing, sending, or handing it to a client.

Use when: You have a finished draft — article, email, page, or deliverable — and want a final, honest review before it goes out.

What to paste into Claude:

You are an expert, strict but fair editor doing a final quality check before this goes out.

GOAL
Review the draft below and tell me honestly whether it's ready to publish/send, and exactly what to fix if it's not.

CONTEXT
- What this is: [article, email, client deliverable, landing page]
- Audience: [who will read/receive this]
- Standard it needs to meet: [describe: accurate, on-brand, persuasive, error-free, etc.]

INPUTS
[Paste the full draft]

CONSTRAINTS
- Be direct — do not soften real problems to be polite
- Separate must-fix issues from nice-to-have suggestions
- Check for factual claims that need verification, not just tone and grammar

PROCESS
1. Check clarity: is the core message obvious within the first few lines?
2. Check accuracy: flag any claim that needs verification or looks outdated.
3. Check tone and audience fit.
4. Check structure and formatting.
5. Give a clear final verdict: ready to publish, or needs fixes first.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- Must-fix issues (numbered list)
- Nice-to-have improvements (short list)
- Final verdict: Ready to publish / Needs fixes first (with a one-sentence reason)

QUALITY CHECK
Before answering, reread the draft once more specifically looking for anything you may have missed on the first pass — factual claims, broken logic, or missing context.

NEXT ACTION
If it needs fixes, tell me which single fix matters most before anything else.

How to customize it

Paste the full, final draft, not an early version, and state the real audience and standard so the review isn’t generic.

What output to expect: A direct must-fix versus nice-to-have list and a clear ready/not-ready verdict.

Next step: Apply the must-fix items, then do one final pass before publishing or sending.

Claude Fable 5 vs Claude Sonnet 5: Which Should You Use for Prompts?

Not every Claude Fable 5 prompt needs to run on Fable 5 — and since Opus 5’s July 2026 release, most don’t. Claude Sonnet 5 is faster and available across all Claude plans for routine writing and quick drafts. Claude Opus 5 is now the default for demanding work — complex research, business-critical decisions, difficult analysis, multi-step workflows, and prompt-to-skill conversion — at roughly half of Fable 5’s price. Fable 5 earns its place only on the exceptionally difficult prompts where Opus 5 falls short.

Situation Better model Why
Quick drafts, captions, or simple rewrites Claude Sonnet 5 Faster and available on every plan for routine work
Everyday research summaries Claude Sonnet 5 No need for the strongest model on a quick, low-stakes summary
Deep, multi-source research briefs Claude Opus 5 Handles large source material at half Fable’s cost — start here
Business-critical strategy decisions Claude Opus 5 Near-frontier reasoning for high-stakes calls without Fable-level spend
Large keyword exports or GSC analysis Claude Opus 5 Handles large, messy datasets without losing detail, at lower cost
Multi-step AI agent workflows Claude Opus 5 Built for long-running, connected steps that must hold up end to end
Prompt-to-skill conversion Claude Opus 5 Strong at spotting missing structure and generalizing a one-off prompt
Long documents and large projects Claude Opus 5 Handles long-context work most models struggle with, at half Fable’s price
Exceptionally hard tasks where Opus 5 fell short Claude Fable 5 The one case left for Fable: Opus 5 already tried and couldn’t reliably finish

A simple rule: start with Claude Sonnet 5 for everyday prompts, move up to Claude Opus 5 for difficult, layered, or high-stakes work, and reserve Claude Fable 5 for the exceptionally hard prompts where Opus 5 has already tried and fallen short.

How to Turn These Prompts Into AI Agent Skills

A prompt is one request. A skill is the saved, reusable version of that process — the same inputs, steps, and output format every time, so you’re not rebuilding it from memory. An AI agent workflow goes further: it can use a skill repeatedly with real inputs, tools, memory, and review steps built in, often across a schedule instead of a single chat.

Every prompt in this library can graduate from a one-time request to a saved skill. Start with the AI Agent Skill Builder Prompt or the Prompt-to-Skill Prompt above, then read what an AI agent skill is for the full breakdown of prompts versus skills versus agents. If you want to skip the blank page entirely, browse the Claude skills library for ready-to-copy skills you can adapt. If you’re running these prompts inside Claude’s agentic workspace, our guide to how to set up Claude Cowork covers the setup steps.

Final takeaway

The best Claude Fable 5 prompts are not clever wording — they’re structure. Give Fable 5 a goal, real context, your actual inputs, constraints, a process, an output format, and a quality check, and it will consistently outperform a one-line request. For a more detailed usage strategy, see The 9 Best Ways to Reduce Claude Fable 5 Credit Usage. Start with one prompt from this library, run it on a real task this week, then turn it into a skill once it earns a permanent place in your workflow.

Frequently asked questions

What are the best Claude Fable 5 prompts?

The best Claude Fable 5 prompts are structured workflows that give the model a clear goal, real context, your actual inputs, constraints, a step-by-step process, an exact output format, and a quality check — not a one-line request. The 15 prompts and master template above follow that structure for business, SEO, research, content, website design, and AI agent tasks.

Is Claude Fable 5 good for SEO prompts?

Yes. Fable 5 prompts for SEO work especially well for tasks that involve reviewing a large keyword export, a full Search Console export, or several competitor pages at once, since Fable 5 can hold that much source material in context and cluster it by intent instead of just listing keywords.

Is Claude Fable 5 good for research?

Yes. Fable 5 prompts for research are strong when a topic has more source material than a quick summary can cover — Fable 5 can organize scattered articles, notes, and transcripts into a themed, sourced brief instead of a vague overview.

Is Claude Fable 5 better than Sonnet 5 for prompts?

Not universally, and since Opus 5’s release it’s usually the wrong comparison. Claude Sonnet 5 is faster and available across all plans for routine writing and everyday prompts. For complex, long-running, or business-critical prompts, Claude Opus 5 is now the recommended default — near-frontier quality at roughly half Fable 5’s price. Reserve Claude Fable 5 for the exceptionally hard prompts where Opus 5 falls short. See the comparison table above for specific situations.

Can Claude Fable 5 help build AI agents?

Yes. Fable 5 prompts for AI agents can help you design the process, inputs, steps, and quality checks behind a reusable skill or workflow. The actual agent behavior — tool use, scheduling, and multi-step execution — depends on the platform you run it in, such as Claude Cowork.

What is the difference between a Claude Fable 5 prompt and an AI agent skill?

A prompt is a one-time request you type in. An AI agent skill is the saved, reusable version of that process, with defined inputs, steps, and an output format, so you don’t rebuild it from memory every time. See what an AI agent skill is for the full breakdown.

Is Claude Fable 5 available now?

Yes. Anthropic restored global access to Claude Fable 5 starting July 1, 2026, after the export controls that had paused it were lifted. It’s available through Claude.ai, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and the Claude Platform, though availability, plan limits, and usage credits can vary — check Claude directly before building a workflow around it.

Is Claude Fabel 5 the same as Claude Fable 5?

Yes. “Claude Fabel 5” is a common misspelling. The correct name is Claude Fable 5.

## Why do most Claude Fable 5 prompts underperform?
Most people use Claude Fable 5 like a normal chatbot — one short line, one quick answer. That is the wrong approach for a model built for complex, long-running, ambiguous work. The best Claude Fable 5 prompts are structured workflows: a clear goal, real context, actual inputs, constraints, a process, an exact output format, and a quality check — not a one-line request. Every prompt below follows that structure. If your goal is to get better results without wasting usage on retries, start with our guide on [how to save Claude Fable 5 credits](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/save-claude-fable-5-credits/).
The 15 best Claude Fable 5 prompts in this guide cover business strategy, SEO content, research, website design, and AI agent workflows — each one ready to copy, paste, and use.
## How to Decide If Claude Fable 5 Is the Right Fit
If you’re deciding whether Claude Fable 5 is the right fit, use it for complex research, strategy, and workflow tasks that need deeper reasoning, not every quick question. Anthropic’s own [prompting documentation for Claude Fable 5](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-fable-5) notes that it may need updated prompt scaffolding compared with prior Claude models. In practice, that means giving Fable 5 a real job instead of a quick question. Every strong Claude Fable 5 prompt includes these eight parts.
1 **Goal**
One clear sentence describing exactly what you want and why it matters.
2 **Context**
What Claude needs to know: your business, audience, situation, and offer.
3 **Inputs**
The source material you’re handing over: notes, data, URLs, exports, transcripts.
4 **Constraints**
Tone, length, what to avoid, and what must be included.
5 **Process**
The steps Claude should think through, in order — not just the final answer.
6 **Output format**
The exact shape of what comes back: a table, outline, checklist, or brief.
7 **Quality check**
A rule Claude uses to review its own answer before handing it to you.
8 **Next action**
The single next step you should take once you have the output.
Instead of asking:
> Help me with SEO.
A structured Claude Fable 5 prompt reviews your keywords, checks for cannibalization against your existing pages, clusters opportunities by intent, and hands back a prioritized table — not a paragraph of generic advice. That difference is the entire point of this library.
**A quick safety note**
Fable 5 includes updated safety classifiers. A small number of benign coding or debugging requests can get flagged or rerouted to Claude Opus 4.8 instead of answered directly — this is expected behavior, not a broken prompt. Every prompt in this library stays in normal business, content, design, research, and workflow territory, so you’re unlikely to see it, but it’s worth knowing about if you adapt these prompts for engineering tasks. Details are in [Anthropic’s Fable 5 prompting docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-fable-5).
**A quick tip on managing your Fable 5 credits**
Fable 5 is a heavier, more capable model, and running every single prompt through it — including quick one-liners — burns through usage credits faster than it needs to. As a simple rule: save Fable 5 for the harder work in this library (deep research, business strategy, prompt-to-skill conversion, and other multi-step or high-stakes prompts), and use a lighter model like Sonnet 5 for quick drafts, small edits, and everyday questions. Batching related work into one longer Fable 5 session, instead of many small separate prompts, also stretches your credits further.
## Best Claude Fable 5 Prompt Template
Save this master template and reuse it as a starting point for any new Claude Fable 5 prompt. It bakes in all eight parts from above. Every specialized prompt further down this page is a filled-in version of this same structure.

## 15 Copy-Paste Claude Fable 5 Prompts
Below are 15 ready-to-use Claude Fable 5 prompts for business, SEO, research, content, website design, and AI agent workflows. **Best for:** Business owners who need a practical strategy, not vague ideas. This is one of the strongest Fable 5 prompts for business decisions where the cost of guessing wrong is real.
**Use when:** You need a decision-ready plan for a specific choice — pricing, a growth bottleneck, a new offer, or where to put limited time and budget next.

**Next step:** Turn the 30-day plan into a weekly checklist, or feed progress into the [Business Brief Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-prompts/#prompt-business-brief).

QUALITY CHECK Make sure every fix is specific enough that I could implement it today, not a vague suggestion like "add more trust."
NEXT ACTION Tell me which single fix to make first if I only have 30 minutes this week.
**How to customize it**
Paste your actual page copy section by section, and include real traffic or conversion numbers if you have them for sharper prioritization.
**What output to expect:** A prioritized, specific fix list covering clarity, proof, objections, and CTA placement.
**Next step:** If the real issue is layout and flow rather than wording, run the [Website Design & UX Review Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-prompts/#prompt-website-design) first, then come back to tighten the copy.
**Best for:** Turning a messy topic into a sourced research brief. This is one of the strongest Fable 5 prompts for research because Fable 5’s long context can hold far more raw material than a quick-summary prompt ever could.
**Use when:** A topic is too big or scattered to summarize in a paragraph, and you need it organized before you can use it.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert research analyst producing a sourced brief for a non-technical reader.
GOAL Turn the messy topic and sources below into one clear, organized research brief with sourced claims — not a vague summary.
CONTEXT - Topic: \[topic\] - Why I need this: \[content, decision-making, client deliverable, personal understanding\] - Audience: \[who will read the brief\]
INPUTS \[Paste articles, links, notes, transcripts, or data you already have. List sources with names/dates where possible.\]
CONSTRAINTS - Attribute every non-obvious claim to a source from the inputs - Flag anything unclear or where sources disagree, instead of guessing - Do not present outdated information as current without flagging the date
PROCESS 1. Identify the 3-5 most important questions this brief needs to answer. 2. Organize the source material by theme, not by source. 3. Summarize what is known, what is disputed, and what is missing. 4. Note the publish date or recency of key claims where it matters. 5. End with open questions that still need more research.
OUTPUT FORMAT - Key questions this brief answers - Findings by theme (with source attribution) - Points of disagreement or uncertainty - Open questions / what's still missing
QUALITY CHECK Check that every major claim in your findings section can be traced back to something in my inputs. Flag anything that can't.
NEXT ACTION Tell me the single most important gap I should research next.
**How to customize it**
Paste as much raw source material as you have — this is exactly the kind of large, messy input Fable 5’s long context handles well. Add dates to sources for better recency handling.
**What output to expect:** An organized brief with themes, sourced claims, and flagged uncertainty — ready to turn into content or a decision.
**Next step:** Turn the brief into an article with the [Blog Outline Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-prompts/#prompt-blog-outline), or into a team update with the [Business Brief Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-prompts/#prompt-business-brief).
**Best for:** Turning a repeated task into an AI agent skill with inputs, steps, outputs, and quality checks. Of all the Fable 5 prompts for AI agents in this library, this is the one to run first.
**Use when:** You’ve noticed you keep asking Claude the same kind of question and want a saved, reusable version instead.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert AI workflow strategist helping me turn a repeated task into a reusable skill.
GOAL Turn the repeated task below into a complete, reusable AI agent skill I can save and run again.
CONTEXT - The task I keep repeating: \[describe it\] - How often I do it: \[daily, weekly, monthly\] - Where I'll use it: \[Claude, Gemini Spark, ChatGPT, etc.\]
INPUTS \[Describe or paste an example of the raw material you usually start with — notes, an email, a transcript, a data export\]
CONSTRAINTS - The skill must work with an average version of my inputs, not just a perfect example - Include a review/approval step for anything sensitive (sending, publishing, deleting) - Keep instructions specific enough that a different AI tool could follow them
PROCESS 1. Define the skill's purpose in one sentence. 2. List the exact inputs the skill needs every time. 3. Write the step-by-step process the AI should follow, in order. 4. Define the exact output format. 5. Add a quality checklist to review before the output is used. 6. Note any step that needs human approval before acting.
OUTPUT FORMAT - Skill name - Purpose (1 sentence) - Required inputs (list) - Step-by-step process (numbered) - Output format - Quality checklist - Human approval steps (if any)
QUALITY CHECK Confirm the process would still work if I gave it a messier or incomplete version of the inputs, not just a perfect example.
NEXT ACTION Tell me how to test this skill on a real example before I rely on it.
**How to customize it**
Describe your actual repeated task in detail, and be specific about which steps are sensitive enough to need your approval before acting.
**What output to expect:** A complete, saved-ready skill definition — not a one-time answer. See [turning a prompt into an AI agent skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent-skill/) for the full concept breakdown.
**Next step:** Save the skill in your AI tool of choice, and test it on a real task before trusting it fully.
**Best for:** Diagnosing why an AI workflow failed or produced weak output.
**Use when:** A prompt or skill that used to work is now giving inconsistent, wrong, or low-quality results and you need the actual cause, not a rewrite from scratch.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert AI workflow debugger.
GOAL Diagnose why this workflow is producing weak or inconsistent output, and tell me specifically what to fix.
CONTEXT - What the workflow/skill is supposed to do: \[describe\] - What's going wrong: \[vague output, wrong format, missing steps, inconsistent results\] - How often it fails: \[every time / sometimes / only with certain inputs\]
INPUTS - The prompt or skill instructions I'm using: \[paste them\] - An example of a bad output it produced: \[paste it\] - An example of what a good output should look like, if you have one: \[paste it\]
CONSTRAINTS - Diagnose the actual cause before suggesting a fix — do not just rewrite the whole prompt - Consider missing context, unclear instructions, missing constraints, and unclear output format as possible causes - Keep the original goal of the workflow intact
PROCESS 1. Compare the bad output against what a good output should look like. 2. Identify exactly where the instructions are vague, missing, or contradictory. 3. Identify whether the problem is the prompt, the inputs, or the output format definition. 4. Propose a specific fix for each issue found. 5. Rewrite the corrected prompt/skill in full.
OUTPUT FORMAT - Diagnosis (what's actually causing the weak output) - Specific issues found (list) - Fixed version of the prompt/skill (full text, ready to use)
QUALITY CHECK Test your fixed version mentally against the bad example you were given — confirm it would have prevented that specific failure.
NEXT ACTION Tell me what to test the fixed version on first to confirm it works.
**How to customize it**
Include a real bad-output example — “it didn’t work” produces a vague diagnosis. Paste the full original prompt or skill text, not a summary of it.
**What output to expect:** A specific diagnosis plus a corrected, ready-to-use version of your prompt or skill.
**Next step:** Test the fixed prompt on 2-3 real examples before replacing the old one everywhere you use it.
**Best for:** Converting a one-time prompt that worked well into a reusable workflow or skill.
**Use when:** A single prompt already produced a great result once, and you want to formalize it into something repeatable without starting the full skill-builder process.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert AI systems designer.
GOAL Turn the one-time prompt below into a reusable, structured skill I can run again with different inputs.
CONTEXT - Where this prompt worked well: \[describe the situation/result\] - Why I want to reuse it: \[I do this task often / a team member needs to run it too / I want consistent quality\]
INPUTS \[Paste the original one-time prompt that worked well\]
CONSTRAINTS - Keep the core approach that worked — do not redesign the task, just make it reusable - Replace any one-off specifics with clearly marked placeholders - Add anything the original prompt was missing: constraints, output format, or a quality check
PROCESS 1. Identify what made the original prompt work well. 2. Identify the parts that were specific to that one use (names, numbers, examples) and turn them into placeholders. 3. Add any missing structure: clearer constraints, an explicit output format, a quality check step. 4. Write the final reusable version. 5. Suggest a short name for this skill so it's easy to find again later.
OUTPUT FORMAT - What made the original work (2-3 sentences) - Reusable version of the prompt, with placeholders clearly marked in \[brackets\] - Suggested skill name
QUALITY CHECK Confirm the reusable version would still produce a similarly strong result if I swapped in different real inputs.
NEXT ACTION Tell me one other repeated task in my business that could use this same structure.
**How to customize it**
Paste the exact original prompt, not a paraphrase, so Claude can see precisely what worked, and flag which parts were one-off details versus reusable structure.
**What output to expect:** A cleaned-up, placeholder-based version of your original prompt plus a name to save it under.
**Next step:** Save it as a skill, and read [what an AI agent skill is](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent-skill/) if you want the fuller framework for building skills.
**Best for:** Turning one article, transcript, or idea into posts, emails, and short-form content.
**Use when:** You have one piece of source content and want multiple platform-ready pieces without starting from a blank page each time.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert content repurposing strategist.
GOAL Turn the source content below into multiple ready-to-use pieces for the platforms I list, without losing the core message.
CONTEXT - Source content type: \[article, transcript, podcast notes, idea\] - Brand voice: \[describe tone\] - Platforms I need content for: \[e.g. LinkedIn, Instagram caption, email, X/Twitter thread\]
INPUTS \[Paste the full source content or transcript\]
CONSTRAINTS - Keep the core message consistent across all formats - Match each platform's typical format and length, not just copy-paste the same text everywhere - Include one clear hook per piece
PROCESS 1. Identify the single core message and 2-3 supporting points worth repurposing. 2. Draft a version for each platform I listed, matching that platform's format norms. 3. Write a hook/opening line for each piece. 4. Suggest one CTA appropriate to each platform.
OUTPUT FORMAT One clearly labeled section per platform, each with: hook, full copy, and suggested CTA.
QUALITY CHECK Check that no piece contradicts another and that the core message stays consistent across all of them.
NEXT ACTION Tell me which piece to publish first based on what's fastest to get in front of my audience.
**How to customize it**
Paste the full transcript or article, not just a summary — this is exactly the long-context use case Fable 5 is built for. List only the platforms you actually use.
**What output to expect:** A ready-to-post piece for each platform, each with its own hook and CTA.
**Next step:** Schedule the pieces, then track which format performs best and feed that back into future repurposing prompts.
**Best for:** Creating a daily or weekly business update from sources, metrics, emails, or notes.
**Use when:** You need a clean summary for yourself, a partner, or a team, pulled from scattered updates instead of written from memory.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert business chief of staff preparing a status brief for me.
GOAL Turn the scattered updates below into one clear business brief covering wins, priorities, risks, and next steps.
CONTEXT - Reporting period: \[today / this week\] - Who this brief is for: \[myself, a partner, a team, a client\] - Business focus areas right now: \[list 2-4 current priorities\]
INPUTS \[Paste notes, metrics, email summaries, task lists, or calendar highlights from the period\]
CONSTRAINTS - Do not pad the brief with filler — if nothing meaningful happened in an area, say so briefly - Flag anything that looks like a risk or blocker, even if it wasn't explicitly labeled as one - Keep it scannable, not a wall of text
PROCESS 1. Identify the top 3 wins or pieces of progress from the inputs. 2. Identify current priorities and their status. 3. Identify risks, blockers, or anything that needs a decision. 4. Recommend the top 3 priorities for the next period.
OUTPUT FORMAT - Wins (short list) - Priorities and status (short list) - Risks / blockers (short list) - Next period's top 3 priorities (numbered)
QUALITY CHECK Confirm every item in the brief is traceable to something in my inputs, not inferred or invented.
NEXT ACTION Tell me the one item in this brief that most needs my attention today.
**How to customize it**
Paste real notes and metrics each time, even messy ones — this prompt is meant to run repeatedly, and the focus areas should shift as your priorities do.
**What output to expect:** A scannable brief with wins, status, risks, and next priorities — ready to send or review in minutes.
**Next step:** Save this as a recurring skill using the [Prompt-to-Skill Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-prompts/#prompt-to-skill) so it’s ready every week without rebuilding it.
**Best for:** Consultants, freelancers, agencies, and service businesses turning a client conversation into a written proposal or pitch — one of the most broadly useful Fable 5 prompts for business development, regardless of industry.
**Use when:** You just had a call or exchanged emails with a prospect and need to turn scattered notes into a clear, persuasive proposal instead of starting from a blank page.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert proposal writer who has helped consultants and agencies win client work.
GOAL Turn my notes about this client conversation into a clear, persuasive proposal that speaks directly to their situation — not a generic services list.
CONTEXT - Who the client/prospect is: \[name, industry, size\] - What they told me they need: \[summarize their stated problem/goal\] - My offer: \[what you're proposing to do for them\] - Why now: \[urgency, timing, or trigger for this conversation\]
INPUTS \[Paste call notes, email exchanges, or a rough scope of what was discussed\]
CONSTRAINTS - Speak to their specific situation, not a generic pitch - Tone: \[describe, e.g. "confident but not pushy," "warm and consultative"\] - Must include: clear scope, timeline, and investment/pricing structure - Must avoid: overpromising or vague deliverables
PROCESS 1. Summarize the client's problem back to them in their own words. 2. State the outcome I will deliver, not just the tasks I will do. 3. Outline the scope and timeline in clear phases or milestones. 4. Address the most likely objection or hesitation before they raise it. 5. End with one clear, low-friction next step.
OUTPUT FORMAT - Understanding your situation (short paragraph) - What we'll deliver (bulleted outcomes) - Scope and timeline (phases/milestones) - Investment (pricing structure, described clearly) - Next steps (one clear call to action)
QUALITY CHECK Check that the proposal reflects this specific client's situation and would not work word-for-word for a different client.
NEXT ACTION Tell me the one thing most likely to make this client hesitate, so I can address it before I send this.
**How to customize it**
Paste your real call notes or email thread, not a summary — the more specific their actual words, the less generic the proposal reads.
**What output to expect:** A client-specific proposal structure with outcomes, scope, pricing, and one clear next step — ready to format and send.
**Next step:** Run the finished proposal through the [Quality Check Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-prompts/#prompt-quality-check) before sending it.
**Best for:** Reviewing an output before publishing, sending, or handing it to a client.
**Use when:** You have a finished draft — article, email, page, or deliverable — and want a final, honest review before it goes out.
**What to paste into Claude:**
You are an expert, strict but fair editor doing a final quality check before this goes out.
GOAL Review the draft below and tell me honestly whether it's ready to publish/send, and exactly what to fix if it's not.
CONTEXT - What this is: \[article, email, client deliverable, landing page\] - Audience: \[who will read/receive this\] - Standard it needs to meet: \[describe: accurate, on-brand, persuasive, error-free, etc.\]
INPUTS \[Paste the full draft\]
CONSTRAINTS - Be direct — do not soften real problems to be polite - Separate must-fix issues from nice-to-have suggestions - Check for factual claims that need verification, not just tone and grammar
PROCESS 1. Check clarity: is the core message obvious within the first few lines? 2. Check accuracy: flag any claim that needs verification or looks outdated. 3. Check tone and audience fit. 4. Check structure and formatting. 5. Give a clear final verdict: ready to publish, or needs fixes first.
OUTPUT FORMAT - Must-fix issues (numbered list) - Nice-to-have improvements (short list) - Final verdict: Ready to publish / Needs fixes first (with a one-sentence reason)
QUALITY CHECK Before answering, reread the draft once more specifically looking for anything you may have missed on the first pass — factual claims, broken logic, or missing context.
NEXT ACTION If it needs fixes, tell me which single fix matters most before anything else.
**How to customize it**
Paste the full, final draft, not an early version, and state the real audience and standard so the review isn’t generic.
**What output to expect:** A direct must-fix versus nice-to-have list and a clear ready/not-ready verdict.
**Next step:** Apply the must-fix items, then do one final pass before publishing or sending.
## Claude Fable 5 vs Claude Sonnet 5: Which Should You Use for Prompts?
Not every Claude Fable 5 prompt needs to run on Fable 5 — and since Opus 5’s July 2026 release, most don’t. Claude Sonnet 5 is faster and available across all Claude plans for routine writing and quick drafts. Claude Opus 5 is now the default for demanding work — complex research, business-critical decisions, difficult analysis, multi-step workflows, and prompt-to-skill conversion — at roughly half of Fable 5’s price. Fable 5 earns its place only on the exceptionally difficult prompts where Opus 5 falls short.
| Situation | Better model | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | Quick drafts, captions, or simple rewrites | Claude Sonnet 5 | Faster and available on every plan for routine work | | Everyday research summaries | Claude Sonnet 5 | No need for the strongest model on a quick, low-stakes summary | | Deep, multi-source research briefs | Claude Opus 5 | Handles large source material at half Fable’s cost — start here | | Business-critical strategy decisions | Claude Opus 5 | Near-frontier reasoning for high-stakes calls without Fable-level spend | | Large keyword exports or GSC analysis | Claude Opus 5 | Handles large, messy datasets without losing detail, at lower cost | | Multi-step AI agent workflows | Claude Opus 5 | Built for long-running, connected steps that must hold up end to end | | Prompt-to-skill conversion | Claude Opus 5 | Strong at spotting missing structure and generalizing a one-off prompt | | Long documents and large projects | Claude Opus 5 | Handles long-context work most models struggle with, at half Fable’s price | | Exceptionally hard tasks where Opus 5 fell short | Claude Fable 5 | The one case left for Fable: Opus 5 already tried and couldn’t reliably finish |
A simple rule: start with Claude Sonnet 5 for everyday prompts, move up to Claude Opus 5 for difficult, layered, or high-stakes work, and reserve Claude Fable 5 for the exceptionally hard prompts where Opus 5 has already tried and fallen short.
## How to Turn These Prompts Into AI Agent Skills
A prompt is one request. A skill is the saved, reusable version of that process — the same inputs, steps, and output format every time, so you’re not rebuilding it from memory. An AI agent workflow goes further: it can use a skill repeatedly with real inputs, tools, memory, and review steps built in, often across a schedule instead of a single chat.
Every prompt in this library can graduate from a one-time request to a saved skill. Start with the [AI Agent Skill Builder Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-prompts/#prompt-skill-builder) or the [Prompt-to-Skill Prompt](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-prompts/#prompt-to-skill) above, then read [what an AI agent skill is](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent-skill/) for the full breakdown of prompts versus skills versus agents. If you want to skip the blank page entirely, browse the [Claude skills library](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/claude/) for ready-to-copy skills you can adapt. If you’re running these prompts inside Claude’s agentic workspace, our guide to how to [set up Claude Cowork](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/setup-guides/claude-cowork/) covers the setup steps.
## Final takeaway
The best Claude Fable 5 prompts are not clever wording — they’re structure. Give Fable 5 a goal, real context, your actual inputs, constraints, a process, an output format, and a quality check, and it will consistently outperform a one-line request. For a more detailed usage strategy, see [The 9 Best Ways to Reduce Claude Fable 5 Credit Usage](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/save-claude-fable-5-credits/). Start with one prompt from this library, run it on a real task this week, then turn it into a skill once it earns a permanent place in your workflow.
## Frequently asked questions
What are the best Claude Fable 5 prompts?
The best Claude Fable 5 prompts are structured workflows that give the model a clear goal, real context, your actual inputs, constraints, a step-by-step process, an exact output format, and a quality check — not a one-line request. The 15 prompts and master template above follow that structure for business, SEO, research, content, website design, and AI agent tasks.
Is Claude Fable 5 good for SEO prompts?
Yes. Fable 5 prompts for SEO work especially well for tasks that involve reviewing a large keyword export, a full Search Console export, or several competitor pages at once, since Fable 5 can hold that much source material in context and cluster it by intent instead of just listing keywords.
Is Claude Fable 5 good for research?
Yes. Fable 5 prompts for research are strong when a topic has more source material than a quick summary can cover — Fable 5 can organize scattered articles, notes, and transcripts into a themed, sourced brief instead of a vague overview.
Is Claude Fable 5 better than Sonnet 5 for prompts?
Not universally, and since Opus 5’s release it’s usually the wrong comparison. Claude Sonnet 5 is faster and available across all plans for routine writing and everyday prompts. For complex, long-running, or business-critical prompts, Claude Opus 5 is now the recommended default — near-frontier quality at roughly half Fable 5’s price. Reserve Claude Fable 5 for the exceptionally hard prompts where Opus 5 falls short. See the comparison table above for specific situations.
Can Claude Fable 5 help build AI agents?
Yes. Fable 5 prompts for AI agents can help you design the process, inputs, steps, and quality checks behind a reusable skill or workflow. The actual agent behavior — tool use, scheduling, and multi-step execution — depends on the platform you run it in, such as Claude Cowork.
What is the difference between a Claude Fable 5 prompt and an AI agent skill?
A prompt is a one-time request you type in. An AI agent skill is the saved, reusable version of that process, with defined inputs, steps, and an output format, so you don’t rebuild it from memory every time. See [what an AI agent skill is](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent-skill/) for the full breakdown.
Is Claude Fable 5 available now?
Yes. Anthropic restored global access to Claude Fable 5 starting July 1, 2026, after the export controls that had paused it were lifted. It’s available through Claude.ai, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and the Claude Platform, though availability, plan limits, and usage credits can vary — check Claude directly before building a workflow around it.
Is Claude Fabel 5 the same as Claude Fable 5?
Yes. “Claude Fabel 5” is a common misspelling. The correct name is Claude Fable 5.
