item.text: Free AI Client Onboarding Skill (2026) The free AI Client Onboarding skill Paste what you sold and who you sold it to — get the whole first two weeks written for you: a welcome email, the exact questions to ask before you start, a kickoff call agenda, and a 30-day plan with milestones, in Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT. Free copy-and-use prompt · No credit card · Optional setup help This Client Onboarding skill is a free AI skill that turns a signed client into a confident first two weeks — the welcome email, the intake questions, the kickoff agenda, and the 30-day plan, written in one pass. Paste in what you sold, who bought it, and what happens next, and the skill builds the client-facing package you actually send: a welcome email that sets expectations instead of just saying thanks, the specific questions you need answered before work starts, an agenda that stops the kickoff call becoming a second discovery call, and milestones with dates. It won’t invent your pricing, your scope, or your contract terms — anything you leave vague comes back as a direct question. Copy the skill prompt and use it in Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT in seconds — or save the same instructions as a reusable workflow. No coding required. The Client Onboarding skill turns the details of a newly signed client into a client-facing onboarding package: a welcome email, the intake questions to ask before work starts, a kickoff call agenda, a 30-day milestone plan, and the risks worth heading off early. It cannot see your CRM, contract, project tool, or calendar, and it will never invent your scope, pricing, payment terms, or deadlines. Anything you leave vague is returned as a direct question rather than a confident guess, and it never sends anything — every email and agenda is a draft for you to review. Your results One signed client, one confident first two weeks By the end of this AI skill guide, you’ll have the Client Onboarding skill ready to use — either as a quick copy-and-paste prompt in any AI chat or saved as a reusable workflow using your preferred platform’s setup option. It fixes the gap that quietly costs the most: the week between “yes” and “started,” where a client’s confidence is highest and most businesses go silent. ONBOARDING PACKAGE — new website client, 6-week build (example) Welcome email: 96 words. Confirms what was bought, names their point of contact, tells them the one thing they need to do this week — and when they’ll next hear from you. No “excited to work with you!” filler. Ask before you start: Who signs off — and is that one person or a committee? Do you have brand assets, or are we creating them? (scope risk) What does “done” look like to you? Any date that can’t move — a launch, an event, a board meeting? Kickoff agenda: 30 min — confirm the goal (5), walk the timeline (10), agree how we communicate and how often (5), name the risks (5), confirm next actions and owners (5). First 30 days: Week 1 kickoff + assets in · Week 2 first draft · Week 3 revisions · Week 4 sign-off checkpoint. Each with who owes what. Watch out for: “Sign-off wasn’t named. On a 6-week build, an unnamed approver is the single most likely reason this slips — ask in the kickoff, not in week 5.” Gaps to fill: “You didn’t give me payment terms or a revision limit — I left both out rather than inventing them. Both belong in the welcome email.” How to use the Client Onboarding AI skill in 3 steps The Client Onboarding skill is an AI skill — a reusable set of instructions written in skill format. You don’t have to install anything to use it: copy the skill prompt below and paste it into Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT to run it instantly, exactly like a normal prompt. Once you’re onboarding clients regularly, follow the platform-specific setup below to save the instructions for reuse. Paste it in with the client and what you sold Paste it into Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT — or upload it as a SKILL.md — then add who the client is, what they bought, and what happens next. Get your onboarding package Your AI returns the welcome email, intake questions, kickoff agenda, 30-day plan, the risks worth naming early, and the gaps you still need to fill. You are an experienced client services lead. Your job is to turn the details of a newly signed client into the client-facing onboarding package the user will actually send and run: a welcome email, intake questions, a kickoff agenda, and a 30-day plan. PROCESS 1. Identify the client, what they bought, and what outcome they are expecting, from the material provided. 2. Write a WELCOME EMAIL under 120 words. It must do four things: confirm what they bought, name their point of contact, give them the ONE thing they need to do this week, and tell them when they will next hear from you. No filler enthusiasm. 3. Write the INTAKE QUESTIONS the user needs answered BEFORE work starts. Prioritise the questions that prevent scope and timeline problems later: who signs off, what "done" looks like, what assets exist, what dates cannot move. 4. Write a KICKOFF CALL AGENDA with time boxes. The kickoff must confirm and align — it is not a second discovery call. 5. Build a FIRST 30 DAYS plan with milestones. For each milestone, say who owes what. Only use dates and durations the user actually provided. 6. Identify the RISKS most likely to derail this specific engagement, based on what the user described. 7. List the GAPS — anything vague or missing that must be settled before this package is client-ready. RULES - Use ONLY what the user provides. NEVER invent pricing, payment terms, scope, deliverables, revision limits, deadlines, team names, or contract terms. - You cannot see the user's CRM, contract, proposal, project tool, calendar, or files. You know nothing about their business beyond what is pasted in. Never imply otherwise. - Do NOT write contract or legal language. You are not drafting an agreement. If something belongs in a contract (liability, IP, termination, payment enforcement), say so and leave it out. - When something is vague ("then we get started"), do NOT smooth it into professional-sounding filler. Put it in Gaps and ask the exact question. A confident-sounding invented deliverable is how scope disputes start. - Write for the client to read. Plain, warm, specific. No jargon, no corporate padding. - Focus on what the user does WITH the client. Do not produce an internal step-by-step process document — that is a different job. - Do not send anything. Produce drafts for human review only. OUTPUT FORMAT ### Welcome Email (Draft) Under 120 words. Ready to review and send. ### Ask Before You Start The intake questions, most important first. Mark the ones that are scope or timeline risks. ### Kickoff Call Agenda Time-boxed. With the goal of the call stated in one line. ### First 30 Days Milestones with owners. Only dates the user actually gave you. ### Watch Out For The risks most likely to derail THIS engagement, and when to raise each one. ### Gaps To Fill Direct questions. What is missing before this is client-ready — and what you deliberately left out rather than invent. MY NEW CLIENT: [Paste the details: who the client is, what they bought, the price and terms if you want them referenced, the timeline, who is involved on both sides, and what happens next. The free AI Client Onboarding skill

Paste what you sold and who you sold it to — get the whole first two weeks written for you: a welcome email, the exact questions to ask before you start, a kickoff call agenda, and a 30-day plan with milestones, in Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT.

Free copy-and-use prompt · No credit card · Optional setup help

This Client Onboarding skill is a free AI skill that turns a signed client into a confident first two weeks — the welcome email, the intake questions, the kickoff agenda, and the 30-day plan, written in one pass. Paste in what you sold, who bought it, and what happens next, and the skill builds the client-facing package you actually send: a welcome email that sets expectations instead of just saying thanks, the specific questions you need answered before work starts, an agenda that stops the kickoff call becoming a second discovery call, and milestones with dates. It won’t invent your pricing, your scope, or your contract terms — anything you leave vague comes back as a direct question. Copy the skill prompt and use it in Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT in seconds — or save the same instructions as a reusable workflow. No coding required.

Quick answer

The Client Onboarding skill turns the details of a newly signed client into a client-facing onboarding package: a welcome email, the intake questions to ask before work starts, a kickoff call agenda, a 30-day milestone plan, and the risks worth heading off early. It cannot see your CRM, contract, project tool, or calendar, and it will never invent your scope, pricing, payment terms, or deadlines. Anything you leave vague is returned as a direct question rather than a confident guess, and it never sends anything — every email and agenda is a draft for you to review.

Your results

One signed client, one confident first two weeks

By the end of this AI skill guide, you’ll have the Client Onboarding skill ready to use — either as a quick copy-and-paste prompt in any AI chat or saved as a reusable workflow using your preferred platform’s setup option. It fixes the gap that quietly costs the most: the week between “yes” and “started,” where a client’s confidence is highest and most businesses go silent.

ONBOARDING PACKAGE — new website client, 6-week build (example)

Welcome email: 96 words. Confirms what was bought, names their point of contact, tells them the one thing they need to do this week — and when they’ll next hear from you. No “excited to work with you!” filler.

Ask before you start:

  • Who signs off — and is that one person or a committee?
  • Do you have brand assets, or are we creating them? (scope risk)
  • What does “done” look like to you?
  • Any date that can’t move — a launch, an event, a board meeting?

Kickoff agenda: 30 min — confirm the goal (5), walk the timeline (10), agree how we communicate and how often (5), name the risks (5), confirm next actions and owners (5).

First 30 days: Week 1 kickoff + assets in · Week 2 first draft · Week 3 revisions · Week 4 sign-off checkpoint. Each with who owes what.

Watch out for: “Sign-off wasn’t named. On a 6-week build, an unnamed approver is the single most likely reason this slips — ask in the kickoff, not in week 5.”

Gaps to fill: “You didn’t give me payment terms or a revision limit — I left both out rather than inventing them. Both belong in the welcome email.”

How to use the Client Onboarding AI skill in 3 steps

The Client Onboarding skill is an AI skill — a reusable set of instructions written in skill format. You don’t have to install anything to use it: copy the skill prompt below and paste it into Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT to run it instantly, exactly like a normal prompt.     Copy the AI skill

    Click the copy button on the AI skill prompt below — it’s already formatted and ready to run.

  2. 2

    Paste it in with the client and what you sold

    Paste it into Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT — or upload it as a SKILL.md — then add who the client is, what they bought, and what happens next.

    Get your onboarding package

    Your AI returns the welcome email, intake questions, kickoff agenda, 30-day plan, the risks worth naming early, and the gaps you still need to fill.

Formatted as an AI skill or use instantly as a prompt · no installation required

You are an experienced client services lead. Your job is to turn the details of a newly signed client into the client-facing onboarding package the user will actually send and run: a welcome email, intake questions, a kickoff agenda, and a 30-day plan.

PROCESS
1. Identify the client, what they bought, and what outcome they are expecting, from the material provided.
2. Write a WELCOME EMAIL under 120 words. It must do four things: confirm what they bought, name their point of contact, give them the ONE thing they need to do this week, and tell them when they will next hear from you. No filler enthusiasm.
3. Write the INTAKE QUESTIONS the user needs answered BEFORE work starts. Prioritise the questions that prevent scope and timeline problems later: who signs off, what "done" looks like, what assets exist, what dates cannot move.
4. Write a KICKOFF CALL AGENDA with time boxes. The kickoff must confirm and align — it is not a second discovery call.
5. Build a FIRST 30 DAYS plan with milestones. For each milestone, say who owes what. Only use dates and durations the user actually provided.
6. Identify the RISKS most likely to derail this specific engagement, based on what the user described.
7. List the GAPS — anything vague or missing that must be settled before this package is client-ready.

RULES
- Use ONLY what the user provides. NEVER invent pricing, payment terms, scope, deliverables, revision limits, deadlines, team names, or contract terms.
- You cannot see the user's CRM, contract, proposal, project tool, calendar, or files. You know nothing about their business beyond what is pasted in. Never imply otherwise.
- Do NOT write contract or legal language. You are not drafting an agreement. If something belongs in a contract (liability, IP, termination, payment enforcement), say so and leave it out.
- When something is vague ("then we get started"), do NOT smooth it into professional-sounding filler. Put it in Gaps and ask the exact question. A confident-sounding invented deliverable is how scope disputes start.
- Write for the client to read. Plain, warm, specific. No jargon, no corporate padding.
- Focus on what the user does WITH the client. Do not produce an internal step-by-step process document — that is a different job.
- Do not send anything. Produce drafts for human review only.

OUTPUT FORMAT
### Welcome Email (Draft)
Under 120 words. Ready to review and send.
### Ask Before You Start
The intake questions, most important first. Mark the ones that are scope or timeline risks.
### Kickoff Call Agenda
Time-boxed. With the goal of the call stated in one line.
### First 30 Days
Milestones with owners. Only dates the user actually gave you.
### Watch Out For
The risks most likely to derail THIS engagement, and when to raise each one.
### Gaps To Fill
Direct questions. What is missing before this is client-ready — and what you deliberately left out rather than invent.

Your AI returns the welcome email, intake questions, kickoff agenda, 30-day plan, the risks worth naming early, and the gaps you still need to fill.
Formatted as an AI skill or use instantly as a prompt · no installation required
``` You are an experienced client services lead. Your job is to turn the details of a newly signed client into the client-facing onboarding package the user will actually send and run: a welcome email, intake questions, a kickoff agenda, and a 30-day plan.
PROCESS 1. Identify the client, what they bought, and what outcome they are expecting, from the material provided. 2. Write a WELCOME EMAIL under 120 words. It must do four things: confirm what they bought, name their point of contact, give them the ONE thing they need to do this week, and tell them when they will next hear from you. No filler enthusiasm. 3. Write the INTAKE QUESTIONS the user needs answered BEFORE work starts. Prioritise the questions that prevent scope and timeline problems later: who signs off, what "done" looks like, what assets exist, what dates cannot move. 4. Write a KICKOFF CALL AGENDA with time boxes. The kickoff must confirm and align — it is not a second discovery call. 5. Build a FIRST 30 DAYS plan with milestones. For each milestone, say who owes what. Only use dates and durations the user actually provided. 6. Identify the RISKS most likely to derail this specific engagement, based on what the user described. 7. List the GAPS — anything vague or missing that must be settled before this package is client-ready.
RULES - Use ONLY what the user provides. NEVER invent pricing, payment terms, scope, deliverables, revision limits, deadlines, team names, or contract terms. - You cannot see the user's CRM, contract, proposal, project tool, calendar, or files. You know nothing about their business beyond what is pasted in. Never imply otherwise. - Do NOT write contract or legal language. You are not drafting an agreement. If something belongs in a contract (liability, IP, termination, payment enforcement), say so and leave it out. - When something is vague ("then we get started"), do NOT smooth it into professional-sounding filler. Put it in Gaps and ask the exact question. A confident-sounding invented deliverable is how scope disputes start. - Write for the client to read. Plain, warm, specific. No jargon, no corporate padding. - Focus on what the user does WITH the client. Do not produce an internal step-by-step process document — that is a different job. - Do not send anything. Produce drafts for human review only.
OUTPUT FORMAT ### Welcome Email (Draft) Under 120 words. Ready to review and send. ### Ask Before You Start The intake questions, most important first. Mark the ones that are scope or timeline risks. ### Kickoff Call Agenda Time-boxed. With the goal of the call stated in one line. ### First 30 Days Milestones with owners. Only dates the user actually gave you. ### Watch Out For The risks most likely to derail THIS engagement, and when to raise each one. ### Gaps To Fill Direct questions. What is missing before this is client-ready — and what you deliberately left out rather than invent.
MY NEW CLIENT: [Paste the details: who the client is, what they bought, the price and terms if you want them referenced, the timeline, who is involved on both sides, and what happens next. Rough notes are fine.] ```
## AI skill or prompt? Which one beginners should use
The core instructions stay the same either way. You can paste them directly into a chat or save them using the reusable setup available in your preferred AI tool:
**Use it as a prompt**
Paste the skill into any AI chat and it works right away. This is perfect for getting started. Saving it as a reusable workflow means your AI already knows the instructions — no repeated pasting or re-explaining. [If you need help, we can get you set up for free in 7 days](https://www.skool.com/ai-agents-for-beginners/about) so every new client gets the same strong start.
**Save it as a reusable workflow**
Claude and Gemini Spark support native skills, while ChatGPT lets you save the instructions inside a dedicated Project. This is the skill where saving pays off most: onboarding should be identical for every client, and a saved workflow is what makes that true without you rewriting it each time. [If you need help, we can get you set up for free in 7 days](https://www.skool.com/ai-agents-for-beginners/about).
[How to Install It](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/client-onboarding/#install)
## How to save or install the Client Onboarding skill in Claude, Gemini Spark & ChatGPT
The copy-and-use prompt works in Claude, Gemini Spark, and ChatGPT. Saving it as a reusable workflow works differently in each platform, so choose your preferred setup below.
**Claude — Use Instantly**
1. Copy the AI skill prompt above. 2. Open a new Claude chat. 3. Paste the prompt, then add your new client’s details below it. 4. Ask Claude to build your onboarding package.
Native Claude installation requires a packaged skill ZIP. The copy-and-use prompt above works immediately without one. [Browse all free Claude skills →](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/claude/)
**Gemini Spark**
1. Open Gemini Spark and go to the **Skills** page. 2. Choose **Create manually** and paste the skill instructions, or upload a supported SKILL.md or ZIP file. 3. Review the name, description, and instructions, then save the skill. 4. Select it in a Spark task with `/` or `@`, or let Spark apply it when relevant.
Gemini Spark skills currently require Google AI Ultra and an eligible account and region. [Browse all free Gemini Spark skills →](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gemini-spark/)
**ChatGPT**
1. Create a new ChatGPT Project. 2. Open the Project menu and select **Project settings**. 3. Paste the AI skill prompt into the Project instructions. 4. Return to the Project every time you sign a new client.
ChatGPT Projects are available on free and paid plans. Native ChatGPT Skills are also available in beta on eligible work and education plans. [Browse all free ChatGPT skills →](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/chatgpt/)
**Add your standard terms once, reuse them forever**
If you save this as a reusable workflow, paste your real payment terms, revision limits, and communication norms into the saved instructions. The skill will then build them into every welcome email instead of listing them as gaps — which is exactly how onboarding becomes consistent across every client without you thinking about it.
## How to onboard a new client in any AI tool
Once the workflow is saved, ask for your package in plain language — for example, “Onboard this new client.” Gemini Spark can apply an active skill automatically or let you select it with `/` or `@`. Claude can apply an enabled native skill when relevant. In ChatGPT, open your Client Onboarding Project and start a new chat.
* Open Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT and start a new chat. * Ask for a client onboarding package in plain language, or select the skill. * Paste who the client is, what they bought, and what happens next. * Answer the questions in “Gaps to fill,” then re-run it for a client-ready package.
**New to AI assistants?** Start with our [free AI setup guides](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/setup-guides/) to get Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT ready first — then come back and add this skill in minutes.
Try this starter request — copy it, paste it, then add your details below:
``` Use my Client Onboarding skill on this new client:
CLIENT: [Who they are, what business they're in, who I'll be dealing with] WHAT THEY BOUGHT: [The service or package, and the outcome they're expecting] TIMELINE: [Start date, key dates, how long it runs] WHAT HAPPENS NEXT: [Kickoff call? Deposit? Assets needed?]
Give me the welcome email, intake questions, kickoff agenda, and 30-day plan. Don't invent scope, pricing, or terms I didn't give you — ask me instead.
[Replace with your own client details] ```
## 6 common client onboarding mistakes (and what to do instead)
The skill is built to catch these, but they’re worth knowing on their own — most onboarding problems are one of the six below, and every one of them is cheaper to fix in week one than in week five.
**1\. Going quiet between “yes” and “started”**
A client’s confidence peaks the moment they sign — and then most businesses disappear for a week to “get set up.” Send the welcome email the same day. It doesn’t need the whole plan, it needs to prove you’re already moving.
**2\. Booking the kickoff before intake comes back**
If the intake answers aren’t in, the kickoff call _becomes_ the intake form — and you’ve burned the one meeting where you were supposed to align on the actual work. Send questions first, book the call second.
**3\. Never asking who signs off**
This is the single most common reason a project slips. “The client” is often three people, and the one with approval authority was never in the room. Ask in the kickoff — not in week five when a deadline is on the line.
**4\. Leaving payment terms to “we’ll sort that out”**
Terms feel awkward to restate once someone has said yes, so they get skipped — and that’s precisely how you end up writing an [overdue invoice email](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/overdue-invoice-follow-up/) later. Put terms in the welcome email, where they read as organized rather than confrontational.
**5\. Assuming the client knows what happens next**
You’ve run this a hundred times; they haven’t run it once. Every message should answer “what do I do now, and when do I hear from you again?” — silence gets read as a problem, even when everything is fine.
**6\. Onboarding from memory, differently every time**
If it lives in your head, it changes with your mood and your week — and it can’t be handed to anyone. That’s the whole reason to save this as a reusable skill: same standard, every client, whether or not you’re the one running it.
## Want the automated version instead?
This page is the **free, portable version**: you paste the details in, it drafts the package, and it works in any AI chat with nothing connected. That’s deliberate — it means nothing touches your files or inbox unless you choose to paste it.
There’s also a **connected version**, where the AI reads the signed proposal straight from a folder, scans the client email thread for outstanding questions, and saves the welcome email as a draft in your inbox — no pasting at all. **Which should you start with?**
Start here. The skill on this page is the same thinking without the setup — get it producing packages you’re happy with first, then automate it once you know what “good” looks like. Automating a process you haven’t settled yet just gets you the wrong output faster.

## Client Onboarding skill: frequently asked questions
Is the Client Onboarding skill free?
Yes. The copy-and-use AI skill prompt is completely free. Optional reusable features may depend on the AI tool and plan you use. ChatGPT Projects are available on free and paid plans, Claude skills are available when code execution is enabled, and Gemini Spark skills currently require Google AI Ultra.
What’s the difference between this and the SOP Generator skill?
This one is **client-facing** — the welcome email, questions, agenda, and plan you send to and run with the client. item.text: Free AI Monthly Business Review Skill (2026) The free AI Monthly Business Review skill Paste last month’s numbers and a few notes on what happened — get an honest monthly business review: what moved, what worked, what didn’t, the most likely reason why, and the three things worth doing next month, in Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT. Free copy-and-use prompt · No credit card · Optional setup help This Monthly Business Review skill is a free AI skill that turns the numbers you already track and a few notes about what happened into a clear, honest monthly business review — the kind most small businesses never actually sit down and write. Paste in your revenue, leads, traffic, churn, spend, or whatever you measure, add a line or two about launches, outages, campaigns, or a slow holiday week, and the skill separates what genuinely moved from what just wobbled, tells you what’s worth repeating, names the biggest miss, offers the most likely explanation as a clearly-labelled hypothesis, and gives you three ranked priorities for next month. Copy the skill prompt and use it in Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT in seconds — or save the same instructions as a reusable workflow using the setup option in your preferred AI tool. No coding required. The Monthly Business Review skill turns the numbers and notes you paste in for one month into a structured review: headline figures, what actually moved, wins worth repeating, the biggest miss, a labelled hypothesis for why, three ranked priorities for next month, and the one number to watch. It cannot connect to your analytics, accounting software, CRM, or Stripe — you provide the numbers. It will do the arithmetic on what you give it and show its working, but it will never invent a metric, and if you haven’t given it a prior month to compare against, it says “no comparison provided” instead of making one up. Your results One month, one honest read on the business By the end of this AI skill guide, you’ll have the Monthly Business Review skill ready to use — either as a quick copy-and-paste prompt in any AI chat or saved as a reusable workflow using your preferred platform’s setup option. It handles the review most owners keep meaning to do and never quite get to: an hour of honest reflection on what the month actually said, compressed into about five minutes. MONTHLY BUSINESS REVIEW — March, small service business (example) The month in one line: Revenue was flat, but that hides the real story — leads were up 31% and closing got worse. What moved: Leads: 42 → 55 (+31%) Closed deals: 9 → 8 (−11%) Close rate: 21% → 15% (9/42 vs 8/55 — arithmetic shown so you can check it) Wins: The referral push worked — it drove most of the lead jump at zero ad spend. Biggest miss: Close rate fell 6 points while lead volume rose. Most likely explanation (hypothesis): More leads, but lower intent — referral leads may need a different first call. To confirm: split close rate by lead source. One month is not proof. Next month’s top 3: 1) Tag leads by source. 2) Rework the first call for referrals. 3) Keep the referral push running — it’s free. What was missing: “You didn’t provide close rate by source or average deal size — either would have made this review much sharper.” How to use the Monthly Business Review AI skill in 3 steps The Monthly Business Review skill is an AI skill — a reusable set of instructions written in skill format. You don’t have to install anything to use it: copy the skill prompt below and paste it into Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT to run it instantly, exactly like a normal prompt. When you start running it at the end of every month, follow the platform-specific setup below to save the instructions for reuse. Paste it in with your month’s numbers Paste it into Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT — or upload it as a SKILL.md — then add whatever you track, plus a few notes on what actually happened. Get your review Your AI returns headline numbers, what moved, wins, the biggest miss, a labelled hypothesis, three ranked priorities, and the one number to watch. You are an experienced business analyst writing a monthly business review for a small business owner. Your job is to turn the numbers and notes the user pastes in into an honest, useful review they can read in five minutes and act on. PROCESS 1. Identify the month being reviewed and the type of business from the material provided. 2. Restate the headline numbers exactly as the user gave them. Do not round in a way that flatters or alarms. 3. Compare to the prior period or to a target ONLY if the user provided those figures. If they did not, write "No comparison provided" — do not invent a baseline. 4. Identify what actually moved. Distinguish a meaningful change from normal month-to-month noise, and say which is which. 5. Separate WINS (worked, worth repeating) from MISSES (underperformed, worth fixing). 6. For the single biggest miss, give the most likely explanation — labelled clearly as a HYPOTHESIS, not a fact — and state exactly what data would confirm or disprove it. 7. Recommend 3 priorities for next month, ranked, each tied to something specific in this month's data. 8. Name the ONE number to watch next month. 9. List what was missing from the input that would have made the review sharper. RULES - Use ONLY the numbers and notes the user provides. NEVER invent revenue, traffic, leads, conversion rates, churn, headcount, ad spend, or any other metric. - You cannot connect to Google Analytics, Stripe, QuickBooks, a CRM, or any dashboard. You have no data unless the user pastes it in. Never imply otherwise. - You MAY do arithmetic on the numbers provided — differences, percentages, ratios, totals. Show the calculation in one short line so the user can check it. Never estimate a number that was not provided. - Always label an explanation of "why" as a hypothesis. One month of data does not establish a cause. - Do not soften a bad month; an honest review is the entire point. Equally, do not manufacture alarm about ordinary variation. - If the user provides too little to review properly, say so plainly and list exactly what to gather before next month. OUTPUT FORMAT ### The Month in One Line The honest headline — including when a flat top-line number is hiding something. ### Headline Numbers As provided. Include a comparison only if a baseline was given. ### What Moved Meaningful changes vs. normal noise. ### Wins — Worth Repeating ### Misses — Worth Fixing ### Most Likely Explanation (Hypothesis) For the biggest miss. Include what would confirm or disprove it. ### Next Month's Top 3 Priorities Ranked. Each tied to something above. ### The One Number To Watch ### What Was Missing Data that would have made this review sharper. MY MONTH: [Paste whatever you track — revenue, leads, traffic, close rate, churn, ad spend, hours delivered. Include last month's figures too if you have them. Then add a few notes on what happened: launches, campaigns, outages, hires, holidays, anything unusual.] Paste the skill into any AI chat and it works right away. This is perfect for getting started. Saving it as a reusable workflow means your AI already knows the instructions — no repeated pasting or re-explaining. If you need help, we can get you set up for free in 7 days so you can run an honest review at the end of every month. Claude and Gemini Spark support native skills, while ChatGPT lets you save the instructions inside a dedicated Project. Each option keeps the workflow ready for next month without adding the full prompt again — and because the format stays identical, your reviews become comparable month over month. If you need help, we can get you set up for free in 7 days. How to save or install the Monthly Business Review skill in Claude, Gemini Spark & ChatGPT Paste the prompt, then paste your month’s numbers and notes below it. Ask Claude to run your monthly business review. Gemini Spark skills currently require Google AI Ultra and an eligible account and region. Return to the Project at the end of each month with fresh numbers. Keep last month’s review in the same place Because the output format never changes, saving each month’s review in the same Project or chat makes them directly comparable — you can paste last month’s review in alongside this month’s numbers and ask what changed. That comparison is where the real insight usually shows up. How to run a monthly business review in any AI tool Once the workflow is saved, ask for your review in plain language — for example, “Run my monthly business review.” Gemini Spark can apply an active skill automatically or let you select it with / or @. Claude can apply an enabled native skill when relevant. In ChatGPT, open your Monthly Business Review Project and start a new chat. Ask for your monthly business review in plain language, or select the skill. Paste your numbers and a few notes on what happened, then let the skill do the read. Use my Monthly Business Review skill on this month: THIS MONTH'S NUMBERS: [revenue, leads, traffic, close rate, churn, ad spend — whatever you track] LAST MONTH (if you have it): [the same figures, so it can compare] WHAT HAPPENED: [launches, campaigns, outages, hires, holidays, anything unusual] Be honest. Don't invent any number I didn't give you, and tell me what data was missing. [Replace with your own numbers and notes] Free Copy/Paste Skill vs Free 7-Day Setup Help The free copy/paste skill gives you the Monthly Business Review workflow immediately. The free 7-day setup help gives you guided access to more AI skills and beginner-friendly support inside the Academy. Included Free Copy/Paste Skill Free 7-Day Setup Help Monthly Business Review skill prompt Yes Yes Wins, misses, hypothesis, and ranked next-month priorities Yes Yes Help deciding which numbers are actually worth tracking No Yes Choose your path Choose How You Want to Use This Free AI Skill Copy the free skill when you want the instructions now. Choose the free 7-day setup help when you want support building a monthly review you’ll actually keep doing. Free Copy/Paste Skill Reusable Monthly Business Review skill Copy-and-use prompt workflow Claude, Gemini Spark, and ChatGPT setup notes Academy access Free 7-Day Setup Help Guided help applying this skill Access to more practical AI skills Beginner setup support Training for turning repeat tasks into workflows $0 today – then Academy pricing applies Copy the Free Monthly Business Review Skill Use this free skill at the end of your next month. It turns your numbers and a few notes into an honest read on what moved, what worked, what didn’t, and the three things worth doing next — with no invented data and its arithmetic shown so you can check it. Start Free 7-Day Trial → Monthly Business Review skill: frequently asked questions Is the Monthly Business Review skill free? Yes. The copy-and-use AI skill prompt is completely free. Optional reusable features may depend on the AI tool and plan you use. ChatGPT Projects are available on free and paid plans, Claude skills are available when code execution is enabled, and Gemini Spark skills currently require Google AI Ultra. Does it connect to my analytics, Stripe, or accounting software? No. The skill has no connection to Google Analytics, Stripe, QuickBooks, your CRM, or any dashboard. It only knows what you paste in. That’s a deliberate boundary: it means nothing leaves your tools without you choosing to share it, and it means the review is only ever built on numbers you’ve actually checked. What numbers should I paste in? Whatever you already track — there’s no required list. Revenue, leads, traffic, close rate, churn, ad spend, hours delivered, units shipped. Include last month’s figures too if you have them, so the skill can compare rather than guess. Then add a few notes on what happened: a launch, an outage, a campaign, a holiday week. The notes are what turn numbers into a story. Will it invent numbers or make up a reason my revenue dropped? No. It uses only the figures you provide and will never fabricate a metric. It will do arithmetic on what you give it — percentages, differences, ratios — and it shows the calculation in one line so you can check it. Any explanation of “why” is clearly labelled as a hypothesis, with a note on what data would confirm or disprove it, because one month of numbers doesn’t establish a cause. The copy-and-use prompt works in Claude, Gemini Spark, ChatGPT, and most general AI chat tools. Claude and Gemini Spark support native skills, while ChatGPT lets you save the instructions inside a dedicated Project or, on eligible paid plans, a custom GPT. Can it pull my numbers and run the review automatically each month? No — the free skill runs when you paste your month in. If you want AI connected to your analytics and accounting tools to gather the numbers, run the review, and drop it in your inbox on the first of every month, that’s the connected agent version we teach inside the AI Agents Academy.

You are an experienced business analyst writing a monthly business review for a small business owner. Your job is to turn the numbers and notes the user pastes in into an honest, useful review they can read in five minutes and act on.

PROCESS
1. Identify the month being reviewed and the type of business from the material provided.
2. Restate the headline numbers exactly as the user gave them. Do not round in a way that flatters or alarms.
3. Compare to the prior period or to a target ONLY if the user provided those figures. If they did not, write "No comparison provided" — do not invent a baseline.
4. Identify what actually moved. Distinguish a meaningful change from normal month-to-month noise, and say which is which.
5. Separate WINS (worked, worth repeating) from MISSES (underperformed, worth fixing).
6. For the single biggest miss, give the most likely explanation — labelled clearly as a HYPOTHESIS, not a fact — and state exactly what data would confirm or disprove it.
7. Recommend 3 priorities for next month, ranked, each tied to something specific in this month's data.
8. Name the ONE number to watch next month.
9. List what was missing from the input that would have made the review sharper.

RULES
- Use ONLY the numbers and notes the user provides. NEVER invent revenue, traffic, leads, conversion rates, churn, headcount, ad spend, or any other metric.
- You cannot connect to Google Analytics, Stripe, QuickBooks, a CRM, or any dashboard. You have no data unless the user pastes it in. Never imply otherwise.
- You MAY do arithmetic on the numbers provided — differences, percentages, ratios, totals. Show the calculation in one short line so the user can check it. Never estimate a number that was not provided.
- Always label an explanation of "why" as a hypothesis. One month of data does not establish a cause.
- Do not soften a bad month; an honest review is the entire point. Equally, do not manufacture alarm about ordinary variation.
- If the user provides too little to review properly, say so plainly and list exactly what to gather before next month.

The honest headline — including when a flat top-line number is hiding something.
### Headline Numbers
As provided. Include a comparison only if a baseline was given.
### What Moved
Meaningful changes vs. normal noise.
### Wins — Worth Repeating
### Misses — Worth Fixing
### Most Likely Explanation (Hypothesis)
For the biggest miss. Include what would confirm or disprove it.
### Next Month's Top 3 Priorities
Ranked. Each tied to something above.
### The One Number To Watch
### What Was Missing
Data that would have made this review sharper.

MY MONTH:
[Paste whatever you track — revenue, leads, traffic, close rate, churn, ad spend, hours delivered. Include last month's figures too if you have them. Then add a few notes on what happened: launches, campaigns, outages, hires, holidays, anything unusual.]

item.text: Claude Fable 5 Access by Plan: What Changed on July 20 After three extensions in five weeks, Anthropic has settled Claude Fable 5’s access for good — and the answer now depends on which plan you’re on. From July 20, 2026, Fable 5 becomes a permanent part of Max and Team Premium plans at 50% of weekly limits. Pro and Team Standard subscribers keep access through usage credits instead, starting with a one-time $100 credit. This is a short explainer, not a giant guide. If you use Fable 5 for website copy, SEO strategy, landing pages, sales pages, or reusable Claude workflows, what matters now is knowing which side of the split you’re on and adjusting how you spend Fable 5 runs. For practical starting points, use the Claude Fable 5 website prompts, the full Claude Fable 5 prompt list, and the Fable 5 credit saver guide before you spend credits on trial and error. What changed with Claude Fable 5 access? The promotional period ended on Sunday, July 19 at 11:59 pm PT, and Anthropic replaced it with a permanent structure rather than another extension. Max and Team Premium: Fable 5 is now included in your plan at 50% of weekly limits, indefinitely. Pro and Team Standard: Fable 5 moves to usage credits, starting with a one-time $100 credit; after that it bills at API rates of $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. One easy-to-miss detail: the 50% Claude Code weekly rate-limit boost also ends July 20, so if you’re on Max or Team Premium, your standard limits shrink on the same day your Fable access becomes permanent. See What Changed ↓ Anthropic’s email confirming the final extension through July 19. Two days later the company replaced the rolling deadlines with a permanent, plan-based structure. What changed? The deadline stopped moving. item.text: How to Create a Claude Skill in 2026: Beginner Guide A ChatGPT skill is a reusable workflow that gives ChatGPT task-specific instructions, resources, and tools so it can repeat the same process reliably. Instead of pasting the same prompt, template, brand rules, or checklist into every chat, you save the workflow once and let ChatGPT use it when the task matches. Important: OpenAI uses several related customization features. A ChatGPT Skill is not the same as a custom GPT, a Project, or a plugin. This guide focuses on Personal Skills in ChatGPT. OpenAI also supports the Agent Skills format in Codex and the API. If you want the universal framework first, start with How to Create an AI Skill. Already have a prompt you reuse? Use how to turn a prompt into an AI skill first, then come back here to shape it into a ChatGPT skill. Not sure what to build first? See the 15 best ChatGPT skills for business owners for real examples, then come back here to build your own. ChatGPT Skills availability Personal Skills are generally available for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu users. Skills are also supported in Codex and the API. Skills do not automatically sync between desktop/web and mobile — you may need to install a Skill in each place you use ChatGPT. How do you create a ChatGPT skill? To create a ChatGPT skill, choose one repeatable workflow, describe when the skill should run, write clear step-by-step instructions, define the expected output, add any templates or examples, test it with a real request, and refine the description until ChatGPT can recognize when to use it. OpenAI’s current guidance says you can ask ChatGPT to build the skill by starting a chat with “Build me a skill…” and explaining the goal, steps, format, and rules. Advanced users can also author a SKILL.md file with a name and description. A strong ChatGPT skill starts with one repeatable workflow, clear instructions, and a testable output format. What Is a ChatGPT Skill? A ChatGPT skill is a reusable workflow for a focused task. OpenAI describes skills as packages of instructions and supporting resources that help ChatGPT complete repeatable work with the right process, context, and tools. A skill can include a name, a description, workflow instructions, templates, examples, brand guidance, schemas, or connected tools. The key idea is simple: a prompt asks once; a skill saves the process. Once a skill is created and installed, OpenAI says ChatGPT can automatically use one or more skills when they are helpful. Once yours is set up, how to use ChatGPT skills walks through installing, running, editing, and removing them. For official context, see OpenAI’s Skills in ChatGPT help page and Build Skills guide. For the beginner-friendly definition of skills across every platform, read What Is an AI Agent Skill?. What You Need Before You Start Before you create a ChatGPT skill, make sure you have: A ChatGPT account with Skills access – Personal Skills are generally available for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu accounts — keep an eye out as availability expands to more plans over time. In Enterprise and Edu workspaces, an admin may need to enable Skills and related permissions. One repeatable task – choose a weekly update, client follow-up, research brief, content QA pass, documentation review, or another workflow you already repeat. A clear output format – define what “done” looks like before you build anything. Example inputs or templates – one real example makes the skill much easier to test and refine. Is a ChatGPT Skill the Same as a Custom GPT? No. They overlap, but they are not the same surface. OpenAI’s Help Center describes GPTs as custom versions of ChatGPT configured for a specific purpose, with instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, and actions. A skill is more like a reusable workflow package that ChatGPT or Codex can use when a task matches. Simple rule Use a skill when you want ChatGPT to reuse a process. Use a custom GPT when you want a named assistant experience that users can open, share, or publish in the GPT Store. How to Create a ChatGPT Skill: 7 Steps The best first ChatGPT skill is boring in the best way: one job, one process, one predictable output. Do not start with “help me with marketing.” Start with “turn raw campaign notes into a launch brief” or “draft a warm follow-up email from meeting notes.” Finish this sentence first: This skill should always ___ when I ___. That sentence becomes the foundation for the skill’s description, trigger, and test cases. The description is how ChatGPT understands when the skill applies. Make it specific, action-oriented, and full of the words you actually use when asking for the task. Weak: Helps with emails. Better: Use this skill when I provide meeting notes and ask for a client follow-up email. Turn the notes into a short, warm email with a recap, next step, and three subject line options. Clear beats clever A plain, descriptive name and description help both you and ChatGPT recognize when the skill applies. “Client Follow-Up Email” works; “Inbox Ninja” doesn’t. Save the clever name for when the purpose is already obvious. Write the process like you are training a new assistant. Include the goal, required inputs, ordered steps, output format, rules, and a review checklist. ChatGPT skill planning template: SKILL NAME [Short, specific name] WHEN TO USE THIS SKILL Use this skill when I ask you to [repeatable task] and provide [required inputs]. GOAL Produce [specific result] using the same process and format every time. REQUIRED INPUTS - [Input 1] - [Input 2] - [Input 3] WORKFLOW 1. Review the inputs and identify the goal. 2. Ask one clarifying question only if a required input is missing. 3. Follow this process: - [Step A] - [Step B] - [Step C] 4. Create the output in the format below. 5. Run the review checklist before finalizing. OUTPUT FORMAT - [Section 1] - [Section 2] - [Section 3] RULES - Do not invent facts, quotes, dates, sources, or numbers. - Use [tone/style]. - Keep the output [length]. - Flag anything that needs human review. EXAMPLE Input: [Example input] Strong output: [Example output] REVIEW CHECKLIST - Did I use all required inputs? - Did I follow the workflow? - Did I match the output format? - Did I flag uncertainty instead of guessing? A ChatGPT skill can be instruction-only, but the strongest skills often include support material: a brand voice guide, a formatting template, an example output, a checklist, a schema, or a source policy. Use instructions for behavior, tone, rules, steps, and output format. Use examples to show what good output looks like. Use resources for templates, reference material, brand guidelines, or reusable checklists. Use an app when the workflow needs access to external systems, data, or actions. Use a plugin when you want to package and distribute Skills with an app or other shared workflow capabilities. Start simple. Add tools only after the instruction-only version works. Most bad skills fail because the instructions are vague, not because they lack integrations. Open ChatGPT, select Plugins in the sidebar, and open the Skills tab in the Plugin Directory. Select Create, then choose Create with chat, Create with editor, or Upload from your computer. Create with chat: Describe the workflow and let ChatGPT’s Skill Creator guide you. Create with editor: Write or edit the Skill directly in the Skills editor. Upload from your computer: Upload an existing Skill package. Switch from Plugins to the Skills tab, then use the add (+) menu to pick how you want to build it — chat, editor, or upload. For the simplest method, choose Create with chat and paste the planning template below. Starter prompt: Build me a ChatGPT skill for this repeatable workflow: [Paste your completed skill planning template.] Make it focused on one task. Keep it instruction-only unless a supporting template or example would make the workflow more reliable. Before finalizing, point out any vague trigger language, missing inputs, weak output formatting, or rules that need human review. You do not need to write a SKILL.md manually when using ChatGPT’s Create with chat or Skills editor. If you are authoring manually for Codex, the API, or an uploadable skill folder, OpenAI’s build-skills documentation says a skill directory includes a required SKILL.md file with name and description, plus optional scripts, references, assets, and metadata. How to Create a ChatGPT Skill With Chat Create with chat is the fastest way to create a ChatGPT skill, especially for beginners. You describe the workflow, and ChatGPT’s skill creator walks you through name, description, instructions, and any supporting resources. It’s the closest thing OpenAI ships to a guided “ask ChatGPT to create a skill” flow — no manual template writing required. Open Plugins → Skills. Select Create → Create with chat. Describe the workflow you want the Skill to handle. Answer ChatGPT’s follow-up questions (audience, inputs, output format). Review the generated name, description, instructions, and resources. Install the completed Skill. Test it with two or three realistic inputs before rolling it out. Every eligible account includes a built-in skill-creator Skill. When you ask ChatGPT to create, modify, or troubleshoot a Skill, ChatGPT automatically uses it to generate, update, or debug the Skill — even if you never install it manually. How to Create a ChatGPT Skill With the Editor The Skills editor is the “manual mode” for people who want direct control. Use it when Create with chat gets you 80% of the way there but you need to tighten specific pieces yourself, or when you’re revising an already-installed Skill. The editor gives you a form-style interface with every field the Skill uses. Inside the editor you can control: Skill name — how the Skill is referenced and displayed. How to Create a Claude Skill in 2026: Beginner Guide

A ChatGPT skill is a reusable workflow that gives ChatGPT task-specific instructions, resources, and tools so it can repeat the same process reliably. Instead of pasting the same prompt, template, brand rules, or checklist into every chat, you save the workflow once and let ChatGPT use it when the task matches.

Important: OpenAI uses several related customization features. A ChatGPT Skill is not the same as a custom GPT, a Project, or a plugin. This guide focuses on Personal Skills in ChatGPT. OpenAI also supports the Agent Skills format in Codex and the API. If you want the universal framework first, start with How to Create an AI Skill.

Already have a prompt you reuse? Use how to turn a prompt into an AI skill first, then come back here to shape it into a ChatGPT skill.

Not sure what to build first? See the 15 best ChatGPT skills for business owners for real examples, then come back here to build your own.

ChatGPT Skills availability

Personal Skills are generally available for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu users. Skills are also supported in Codex and the API. Skills do not automatically sync between desktop/web and mobile — you may need to install a Skill in each place you use ChatGPT.

Quick answer

How do you create a ChatGPT skill?

To create a ChatGPT skill, choose one repeatable workflow, describe when the skill should run, write clear step-by-step instructions, define the expected output, add any templates or examples, test it with a real request, and refine the description until ChatGPT can recognize when to use it. OpenAI’s current guidance says you can ask ChatGPT to build the skill by starting a chat with “Build me a skill…” and explaining the goal, steps, format, and rules. Advanced users can also author a SKILL.md file with a name and description.

What Is a ChatGPT Skill?

A ChatGPT skill is a reusable workflow for a focused task. OpenAI describes skills as packages of instructions and supporting resources that help ChatGPT complete repeatable work with the right process, context, and tools. A skill can include a name, a description, workflow instructions, templates, examples, brand guidance, schemas, or connected tools.

The key idea is simple: a prompt asks once; a skill saves the process. Once a skill is created and installed, OpenAI says ChatGPT can automatically use one or more skills when they are helpful. Once yours is set up, how to use ChatGPT skills walks through installing, running, editing, and removing them.

For official context, see OpenAI’s Skills in ChatGPT help page and Build Skills guide. For the beginner-friendly definition of skills across every platform, read What Is an AI Agent Skill?.

What You Need Before You Start

Before you create a ChatGPT skill, make sure you have:

  • A ChatGPT account with Skills access – Personal Skills are generally available for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu accounts — keep an eye out as availability expands to more plans over time. In Enterprise and Edu workspaces, an admin may need to enable Skills and related permissions.
  • One repeatable task – choose a weekly update, client follow-up, research brief, content QA pass, documentation review, or another workflow you already repeat.
  • A clear output format – define what “done” looks like before you build anything.
  • Example inputs or templates – one real example makes the skill much easier to test and refine.

Is a ChatGPT Skill the Same as a Custom GPT?

No. They overlap, but they are not the same surface. OpenAI’s Help Center describes GPTs as custom versions of ChatGPT configured for a specific purpose, with instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, and actions. A skill is more like a reusable workflow package that ChatGPT or Codex can use when a task matches.

Simple rule

Use a skill when you want ChatGPT to reuse a process. Use a custom GPT when you want a named assistant experience that users can open, share, or publish in the GPT Store.

How to Create a ChatGPT Skill: 7 Steps

The best first ChatGPT skill is boring in the best way: one job, one process, one predictable output. Do not start with “help me with marketing.” Start with “turn raw campaign notes into a launch brief” or “draft a warm follow-up email from meeting notes.”

Finish this sentence first: This skill should always ___ when I ___.

That sentence becomes the foundation for the skill’s description, trigger, and test cases.

The description is how ChatGPT understands when the skill applies. Make it specific, action-oriented, and full of the words you actually use when asking for the task.

Weak: Helps with emails.

Better: Use this skill when I provide meeting notes and ask for a client follow-up email. Turn the notes into a short, warm email with a recap, next step, and three subject line options.

Clear beats clever

A plain, descriptive name and description help both you and ChatGPT recognize when the skill applies. “Client Follow-Up Email” works; “Inbox Ninja” doesn’t. Save the clever name for when the purpose is already obvious.

Write the process like you are training a new assistant. Include the goal, required inputs, ordered steps, output format, rules, and a review checklist.

ChatGPT skill planning template:

SKILL NAME
[Short, specific name]

WHEN TO USE THIS SKILL
Use this skill when I ask you to [repeatable task] and provide [required inputs].

GOAL
Produce [specific result] using the same process and format every time.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- [Input 1]
- [Input 2]
- [Input 3]

WORKFLOW
1. Review the inputs and identify the goal.
2. Ask one clarifying question only if a required input is missing.
3. Follow this process:
   - [Step A]
   - [Step B]
   - [Step C]
4. Create the output in the format below.
5. Run the review checklist before finalizing.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- [Section 1]
- [Section 2]
- [Section 3]

RULES
- Do not invent facts, quotes, dates, sources, or numbers.
- Use [tone/style].
- Keep the output [length].
- Flag anything that needs human review.

EXAMPLE
Input:
[Example input]

Strong output:
[Example output]

REVIEW CHECKLIST
- Did I use all required inputs?
- Did I follow the workflow?
- Did I match the output format?
- Did I flag uncertainty instead of guessing?

A ChatGPT skill can be instruction-only, but the strongest skills often include support material: a brand voice guide, a formatting template, an example output, a checklist, a schema, or a source policy.

  • Use instructions for behavior, tone, rules, steps, and output format.
  • Use examples to show what good output looks like.
  • Use resources for templates, reference material, brand guidelines, or reusable checklists.
  • Use an app when the workflow needs access to external systems, data, or actions. Use a plugin when you want to package and distribute Skills with an app or other shared workflow capabilities.

Start simple. Add tools only after the instruction-only version works. Most bad skills fail because the instructions are vague, not because they lack integrations.

Open ChatGPT, select Plugins in the sidebar, and open the Skills tab in the Plugin Directory. Select Create, then choose Create with chat, Create with editor, or Upload from your computer.

  1. Create with chat: Describe the workflow and let ChatGPT’s Skill Creator guide you.
  2. Create with editor: Write or edit the Skill directly in the Skills editor.
  3. Upload from your computer: Upload an existing Skill package.

For the simplest method, choose Create with chat and paste the planning template below.

Starter prompt:

Build me a ChatGPT skill for this repeatable workflow:

[Paste your completed skill planning template.]

Make it focused on one task. Keep it instruction-only unless a supporting template or example would make the workflow more reliable. Before finalizing, point out any vague trigger language, missing inputs, weak output formatting, or rules that need human review.

You do not need to write a SKILL.md manually when using ChatGPT’s Create with chat or Skills editor. If you are authoring manually for Codex, the API, or an uploadable skill folder, OpenAI’s build-skills documentation says a skill directory includes a required SKILL.md file with name and description, plus optional scripts, references, assets, and metadata.

How to Create a ChatGPT Skill With Chat

Create with chat is the fastest way to create a ChatGPT skill, especially for beginners. You describe the workflow, and ChatGPT’s skill creator walks you through name, description, instructions, and any supporting resources. It’s the closest thing OpenAI ships to a guided “ask ChatGPT to create a skill” flow — no manual template writing required.

  1. Open Plugins → Skills.
  2. Select Create → Create with chat.
  3. Describe the workflow you want the Skill to handle.
  4. Answer ChatGPT’s follow-up questions (audience, inputs, output format).
  5. Review the generated name, description, instructions, and resources.
  6. Install the completed Skill.
  7. Test it with two or three realistic inputs before rolling it out.

Every eligible account includes a built-in skill-creator Skill. When you ask ChatGPT to create, modify, or troubleshoot a Skill, ChatGPT automatically uses it to generate, update, or debug the Skill — even if you never install it manually.

How to Create a ChatGPT Skill With the Editor

The Skills editor is the “manual mode” for people who want direct control. Use it when Create with chat gets you 80% of the way there but you need to tighten specific pieces yourself, or when you’re revising an already-installed Skill. The editor gives you a form-style interface with every field the Skill uses.

Inside the editor you can control:

  • Skill name — how the Skill is referenced and displayed.
  • Description and triggering language — the phrasing ChatGPT matches against a user’s request.
  • Instructions — the step-by-step workflow ChatGPT follows.
  • Output format — the shape and structure of the result.
  • Examples — sample inputs and strong outputs.
  • Supporting resources — templates, checklists, brand guidelines, or schemas.
  • Later revisions — you can return to the editor any time to refine an installed Skill.

Pick the method that matches how you like to work — beginners should start with chat, and precision-minded builders should default to the editor.

Method Best for
Create with Chat Beginners and fast first drafts
Create with Editor Precise control and manual refinement
Upload Existing skill packages, Codex/API, or external files
Install Shared Skill Reusing a teammate’s approved workflow

How to Upload an Existing ChatGPT Skill

Upload is for Skills you already have as a file — for example, a package you exported from Codex, one you authored against the OpenAI API, or a Skill shared with you outside of your workspace. It takes seconds, but you should always review what you’re importing.

  1. Open Plugins → Skills → Create → Upload from your computer.
  2. Select the Skill file from your computer.
  3. Verify the imported name, description, and instructions match what you expected.
  4. Install the Skill and run a quick test.

Uploaded Skills are scanned automatically, but you should still review them yourself before installing, since a Skill may contain instructions, supporting files, or code that changes how ChatGPT behaves.

Do not trust a skill after one clean test. Test it on three examples:

  • Easy test: a clean input where the expected output is obvious.
  • Real test: the messy kind of notes, files, or requests you actually use.
  • Edge test: missing information, conflicting instructions, or a task the skill should refuse or flag.

Watch for two things: whether ChatGPT chooses or accepts the skill for the right request, and whether the output follows the process without drifting.

Install and Test Your ChatGPT Skill

After creating the Skill, install it when prompted or manage it from your ChatGPT Skills page. Once installed, test it again with two or three realistic requests to confirm that ChatGPT selects it for the intended tasks and avoids using it for unrelated ones. Watch for both trigger accuracy and output quality — a Skill that fires on the wrong request is just as much of a problem as one that ignores the right request.

Depending on your permissions, you can keep a Skill private, share it with specific people or groups, or publish it to your workspace so teammates can install it themselves. The full walkthrough — sharing, publishing, uploading, and managing access afterward — is in how to share and install ChatGPT skills.

Refine the Skill When Results Drift

If ChatGPT misses the Skill entirely, tighten the description and triggering language. If it uses the Skill but the output drifts, fix the workflow instructions, output format, rules, or examples in the editor — or ask ChatGPT to modify the Skill for you. Do not broaden the Skill every time you notice a new use case; create a second focused Skill instead. Five small Skills are easier to trigger and maintain than one giant “business assistant” Skill.

Advanced Example: An Uploadable ChatGPT SKILL.md

You do not need to write a SKILL.md manually when using ChatGPT’s Create with chat or Skills editor. The following example is for people creating an uploadable Agent Skills package or working with Codex or the API.

---
name: client-follow-up-email
description: Use this skill when I provide meeting notes and ask for a client follow-up email. Turn the notes into a short, warm, professional email with a recap, next step, and three subject line options.
---

Goal:
Draft a client follow-up email from meeting notes.

Required inputs:
- Client name
- Meeting notes or call summary
- Desired next step

Workflow:
1. Review the notes and identify the client's goal, concern, or open question.
2. Choose the clearest next step.
3. Draft one email under 180 words.
4. Add three subject line options.
5. If a required detail is missing, list it under "Needs review" instead of guessing.

Output format:
Subject line options:
1.
2.
3.

Email draft:
[Email]

Needs review:
- [Only include if something is missing or uncertain.]

Rules:
- Do not invent pricing, dates, promises, or deliverables.
- Keep the tone warm, direct, and useful.
- Make the call to action clear.

ChatGPT Skills vs. Custom GPTs vs. Projects

If the terminology feels crowded, use the job-to-be-done:

  • Create a ChatGPT skill when you want a reusable task workflow that can be selected or triggered when needed.
  • Create a custom GPT when you want a named assistant experience with its own instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, or actions.
  • Create a Project when you want a persistent workspace for long-running work, shared files, project instructions, and related chats.
  • Create a plugin when you want an installable package containing one or more Skills, an app, or both.
Surface Best for What you create
ChatGPT skill A repeatable workflow ChatGPT should follow consistently. Instructions, resources, examples, and optionally a SKILL.md package.
Custom GPT A reusable ChatGPT assistant experience with its own name and settings. A GPT with instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, or actions.
Project Long-running work with shared files, chats, and project-specific instructions. A workspace that keeps context together across related chats.
Plugin Installing or distributing a packaged workflow across ChatGPT or Codex. An installable bundle containing one or more Skills, an app, or both; it may also include app templates.

For official GPT details, see OpenAI’s GPTs in ChatGPT and Creating and editing GPTs docs. For Projects, see OpenAI’s Projects in ChatGPT guide.

Common Mistakes When Creating a ChatGPT Skill

Mistake Better approach
Making the skill too broad Give it one job, one trigger, and one expected output.
Writing a prompt instead of a workflow Separate the goal, inputs, steps, output format, rules, and review checklist.
Using a vague description State exactly when the skill should run and what it should produce.
Adding tools before the instructions work Test the instruction-only version first, then add apps, actions, or plugins only when needed.
Skipping real-world tests Test with messy inputs, missing details, and edge cases before trusting the skill.
Confusing skills with custom GPTs Use skills for workflows and custom GPTs for named assistant experiences.

Where to Find and Reuse AI Skills

You do not have to build every workflow from scratch. Browse the ChatGPT skills gallery for examples that work in ChatGPT, or compare platform-specific formats with the Claude skills gallery and Gemini Spark skills gallery. Even when the setup steps differ, the core pattern is the same: one job, clear trigger, ordered steps, defined output, and testing.

See the Free AI News Agent Skill for an example of a reusable workflow that can be run in ChatGPT to create a structured AI update brief. Keep it labeled Works in ChatGPT until a native ChatGPT Skill package has been uploaded and tested.

For a longer build written to run in ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini without changes, see this no-code AI website skill — a single skill that returns a site map, hero copy, SEO metadata, and FAQs on every run.

Final Takeaway

A ChatGPT skill is your repeatable process, saved so ChatGPT can follow it again. Pick a task you repeat, write the trigger and workflow clearly, add one example, test it on real work, and refine until it behaves consistently. If you need a named assistant experience, build a custom GPT instead. If you need an installable package that bundles Skills with an app or other workflow capabilities, use a plugin.

Frequently Asked Questions

No. A skill is best for a repeatable workflow. A custom GPT is a named ChatGPT experience with its own instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, or actions, and it can be shared or published depending on eligibility.
