## Is a ChatGPT Skill the Same as a Custom GPT?
No. They overlap, but they are not the same surface. OpenAI’s Help Center describes GPTs as custom versions of ChatGPT configured for a specific purpose, with instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, and actions. A skill is more like a reusable workflow package that ChatGPT or Codex can use when a task matches.
**Simple rule**
Use a **skill** when you want ChatGPT to reuse a process. Use a **custom GPT** when you want a named assistant experience that users can open, share, or publish in the GPT Store.
## How to Create a ChatGPT Skill: 7 Steps
The best first ChatGPT skill is boring in the best way: one job, one process, one predictable output. Do not start with “help me with marketing.” Start with “turn raw campaign notes into a launch brief” or “draft a warm follow-up email from meeting notes.”
**Finish this sentence first:** _This skill should always \_\_\_ when I \_\_\_._
That sentence becomes the foundation for the skill’s description, trigger, and test cases.
The description is how ChatGPT understands when the skill applies. Make it specific, action-oriented, and full of the words you actually use when asking for the task.
**Weak:** Helps with emails.
**Better:** Use this skill when I provide meeting notes and ask for a client follow-up email. Turn the notes into a short, warm email with a recap, next step, and three subject line options.
**Clear beats clever**
A plain, descriptive name and description help both you and ChatGPT recognize when the skill applies. “Client Follow-Up Email” works; “Inbox Ninja” doesn’t. Save the clever name for when the purpose is already obvious.
Write the process like you are training a new assistant. Include the goal, required inputs, ordered steps, output format, rules, and a review checklist.
**ChatGPT skill planning template:**
SKILL NAME \[Short, specific name\]
WHEN TO USE THIS SKILL Use this skill when I ask you to \[repeatable task\] and provide \[required inputs\].
GOAL Produce \[specific result\] using the same process and format every time.
REQUIRED INPUTS - \[Input 1\] - \[Input 2\] - \[Input 3\]
WORKFLOW 1. Review the inputs and identify the goal. 2. Ask one clarifying question only if a required input is missing. 3. Follow this process: - \[Step A\] - \[Step B\] - \[Step C\] 4. Create the output in the format below. 5. Run the review checklist before finalizing.
OUTPUT FORMAT - \[Section 1\] - \[Section 2\] - \[Section 3\]
RULES - Do not invent facts, quotes, dates, sources, or numbers. - Use \[tone/style\]. - Keep the output \[length\]. - Flag anything that needs human review.
EXAMPLE Input: \[Example input\]
Strong output: \[Example output\]
REVIEW CHECKLIST - Did I use all required inputs? - Did I follow the workflow? - Did I match the output format? - Did I flag uncertainty instead of guessing?
A ChatGPT skill can be instruction-only, but the strongest skills often include support material: a brand voice guide, a formatting template, an example output, a checklist, a schema, or a source policy.
* **Use instructions** for behavior, tone, rules, steps, and output format. * **Use examples** to show what good output looks like. * **Use resources** for templates, reference material, brand guidelines, or reusable checklists. * **Use an app** when the workflow needs access to external systems, data, or actions. Use a **plugin** when you want to package and distribute Skills with an app or other shared workflow capabilities.
Start simple. Add tools only after the instruction-only version works. Most bad skills fail because the instructions are vague, not because they lack integrations.
Open ChatGPT, select **Plugins** in the sidebar, and open the **Skills** tab in the Plugin Directory. Select **Create**, then choose **Create with chat**, **Create with editor**, or **Upload from your computer**.
1. **Create with chat:** Describe the workflow and let ChatGPT’s Skill Creator guide you. 2. **Create with editor:** Write or edit the Skill directly in the Skills editor. 3. **Upload from your computer:** Upload an existing Skill package.
Switch from Plugins to the Skills tab, then use the add (+) menu to pick how you want to build it — chat, editor, or upload.
For the simplest method, choose **Create with chat** and paste the planning template below.
**Starter prompt:**
Build me a ChatGPT skill for this repeatable workflow:
\[Paste your completed skill planning template.\]
Make it focused on one task. Keep it instruction-only unless a supporting template or example would make the workflow more reliable. Before finalizing, point out any vague trigger language, missing inputs, weak output formatting, or rules that need human review.
You do not need to write a `SKILL.md` manually when using ChatGPT’s Create with chat or Skills editor. If you are authoring manually for Codex, the API, or an uploadable skill folder, OpenAI’s build-skills documentation says a skill directory includes a required `SKILL.md` file with `name` and `description`, plus optional scripts, references, assets, and metadata.
## How to Create a ChatGPT Skill With Chat
Create with chat is the fastest way to create a ChatGPT skill, especially for beginners. You describe the workflow, and ChatGPT’s skill creator walks you through name, description, instructions, and any supporting resources. It’s the closest thing OpenAI ships to a guided “ask ChatGPT to create a skill” flow — no manual template writing required.
1. Open Plugins → Skills. 2. Select Create → Create with chat. 3. Describe the workflow you want the Skill to handle. 4. Answer ChatGPT’s follow-up questions (audience, inputs, output format). 5. Review the generated name, description, instructions, and resources. 6. Install the completed Skill. 7. Test it with two or three realistic inputs before rolling it out.
Every eligible account includes a built-in **skill-creator Skill**. When you ask ChatGPT to create, modify, or troubleshoot a Skill, ChatGPT automatically uses it to generate, update, or debug the Skill — even if you never install it manually.
## How to Create a ChatGPT Skill With the Editor
The Skills editor is the “manual mode” for people who want direct control. Use it when Create with chat gets you 80% of the way there but you need to tighten specific pieces yourself, or when you’re revising an already-installed Skill. The editor gives you a form-style interface with every field the Skill uses.
Inside the editor you can control:
* **Skill name** — how the Skill is referenced and displayed. * **Description and triggering language** — the phrasing ChatGPT matches against a user’s request. * **Instructions** — the step-by-step workflow ChatGPT follows. * **Output format** — the shape and structure of the result. * **Examples** — sample inputs and strong outputs. * **Supporting resources** — templates, checklists, brand guidelines, or schemas. * **Later revisions** — you can return to the editor any time to refine an installed Skill.
Pick the method that matches how you like to work — beginners should start with chat, and precision-minded builders should default to the editor.
| Method | Best for | | --- | --- | | **Create with Chat** | Beginners and fast first drafts | | **Create with Editor** | Precise control and manual refinement | | **Upload** | Existing skill packages, Codex/API, or external files | | **Install Shared Skill** | Reusing a teammate’s approved workflow |
## How to Upload an Existing ChatGPT Skill
Upload is for Skills you already have as a file — for example, a package you exported from Codex, one you authored against the OpenAI API, or a Skill shared with you outside of your workspace. It takes seconds, but you should always review what you’re importing.
1. Open Plugins → Skills → Create → Upload from your computer. 2. Select the Skill file from your computer. 3. Verify the imported name, description, and instructions match what you expected. 4. Install the Skill and run a quick test.
Uploaded Skills are scanned automatically, but you should still review them yourself before installing, since a Skill may contain instructions, supporting files, or code that changes how ChatGPT behaves.
Do not trust a skill after one clean test. Test it on three examples:
* **Easy test:** a clean input where the expected output is obvious. * **Real test:** the messy kind of notes, files, or requests you actually use. * **Edge test:** missing information, conflicting instructions, or a task the skill should refuse or flag.
Watch for two things: whether ChatGPT chooses or accepts the skill for the right request, and whether the output follows the process without drifting.
## Install and Test Your ChatGPT Skill
After creating the Skill, install it when prompted or manage it from your ChatGPT Skills page. Once installed, test it again with two or three realistic requests to confirm that ChatGPT selects it for the intended tasks and avoids using it for unrelated ones. Watch for both trigger accuracy and output quality — a Skill that fires on the wrong request is just as much of a problem as one that ignores the right request.
Depending on your permissions, you can keep a Skill private, share it with specific people or groups, or publish it to your workspace so teammates can install it themselves. The full walkthrough — sharing, publishing, uploading, and managing access afterward — is in [how to share and install ChatGPT skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-share-chatgpt-skills/).
## Refine the Skill When Results Drift
If ChatGPT misses the Skill entirely, tighten the description and triggering language. If it uses the Skill but the output drifts, fix the workflow instructions, output format, rules, or examples in the editor — or ask ChatGPT to modify the Skill for you. Do not broaden the Skill every time you notice a new use case; create a second focused Skill instead. Five small Skills are easier to trigger and maintain than one giant “business assistant” Skill.
## Advanced Example: An Uploadable ChatGPT SKILL.md
You do not need to write a `SKILL.md` manually when using ChatGPT’s Create with chat or Skills editor. The following example is for people creating an uploadable Agent Skills package or working with Codex or the API.
\--- name: client-follow-up-email description: Use this skill when I provide meeting notes and ask for a client follow-up email. Turn the notes into a short, warm, professional email with a recap, next step, and three subject line options. ---
Goal: Draft a client follow-up email from meeting notes.
Required inputs: - Client name - Meeting notes or call summary - Desired next step
Workflow: 1. Review the notes and identify the client's goal, concern, or open question. 2. Choose the clearest next step. 3. Draft one email under 180 words. 4. Add three subject line options. 5. If a required detail is missing, list it under "Needs review" instead of guessing.
Output format: Subject line options: 1. 2. 3.
Email draft: \[Email\]
Needs review: - \[Only include if something is missing or uncertain.\]
Rules: - Do not invent pricing, dates, promises, or deliverables. - Keep the tone warm, direct, and useful. - Make the call to action clear.
## ChatGPT Skills vs. Custom GPTs vs. Projects
If the terminology feels crowded, use the job-to-be-done:
* **Create a ChatGPT skill** when you want a reusable task workflow that can be selected or triggered when needed. * **Create a custom GPT** when you want a named assistant experience with its own instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, or actions. * **Create a Project** when you want a persistent workspace for long-running work, shared files, project instructions, and related chats. * **Create a plugin** when you want an installable package containing one or more Skills, an app, or both.
| Surface | Best for | What you create | | --- | --- | --- | | **ChatGPT skill** | A repeatable workflow ChatGPT should follow consistently. | Instructions, resources, examples, and optionally a `SKILL.md` package. | | **Custom GPT** | A reusable ChatGPT assistant experience with its own name and settings. | A GPT with instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, or actions. | | **Project** | Long-running work with shared files, chats, and project-specific instructions. | A workspace that keeps context together across related chats. | | **Plugin** | Installing or distributing a packaged workflow across ChatGPT or Codex. | An installable bundle containing one or more Skills, an app, or both; it may also include app templates. |
For official GPT details, see OpenAI’s [GPTs in ChatGPT](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8554407) and [Creating and editing GPTs](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8554397-creating-a-gpt) docs. For Projects, see OpenAI’s [Projects in ChatGPT](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-using-projects-in-chatgpt) guide.
## Common Mistakes When Creating a ChatGPT Skill
| Mistake | Better approach | | --- | --- | | Making the skill too broad | Give it one job, one trigger, and one expected output. | | Writing a prompt instead of a workflow | Separate the goal, inputs, steps, output format, rules, and review checklist. | | Using a vague description | State exactly when the skill should run and what it should produce. | | Adding tools before the instructions work | Test the instruction-only version first, then add apps, actions, or plugins only when needed. | | Skipping real-world tests | Test with messy inputs, missing details, and edge cases before trusting the skill. | | Confusing skills with custom GPTs | Use skills for workflows and custom GPTs for named assistant experiences. |
## Where to Find and Reuse AI Skills
You do not have to build every workflow from scratch. Browse the [ChatGPT skills gallery](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/chatgpt/) for examples that work in ChatGPT, or compare platform-specific formats with the [Claude skills gallery](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/claude/) and [Gemini Spark skills gallery](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gemini-spark/). Even when the setup steps differ, the core pattern is the same: one job, clear trigger, ordered steps, defined output, and testing.
See the [Free AI News Agent Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/ai-news-agent/) for an example of a reusable workflow that can be run in ChatGPT to create a structured AI update brief. Keep it labeled **Works in ChatGPT** until a native ChatGPT Skill package has been uploaded and tested.
For a longer build written to run in ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini without changes, see this [no-code AI website skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-create-a-website-with-ai-skill/) — a single skill that returns a site map, hero copy, SEO metadata, and FAQs on every run.
## Final Takeaway
A ChatGPT skill is your repeatable process, saved so ChatGPT can follow it again. Pick a task you repeat, write the trigger and workflow clearly, add one example, test it on real work, and refine until it behaves consistently. If you need a named assistant experience, build a custom GPT instead. If you need an installable package that bundles Skills with an app or other workflow capabilities, use a plugin.
## Frequently Asked Questions
What is a ChatGPT skill?
A ChatGPT skill is a reusable workflow that gives ChatGPT task-specific instructions, resources, and tools for repeatable work. It helps ChatGPT follow the same process each time instead of relying on a prompt you paste manually.
How do I create a ChatGPT skill?
Choose one focused workflow, write when the skill should apply, define the steps and output format, add examples or resources, ask ChatGPT to build the skill, test it with realistic inputs, and refine it until it works consistently.
Is a ChatGPT skill the same as a custom GPT?
No. A skill is best for a repeatable workflow. A custom GPT is a named ChatGPT experience with its own instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, or actions, and it can be shared or published depending on eligibility.
Do I need to know how to code to create a ChatGPT skill?
No for a basic instruction-only skill. You can start by describing the workflow to ChatGPT. Coding becomes relevant only if the skill needs scripts, custom tools, APIs, or plugin packaging.
What should I put in a ChatGPT skill?
Include a clear name, a specific description of when to use it, required inputs, step-by-step instructions, output format, rules, examples, and a review checklist. Add supporting resources only when they make the workflow more reliable.
Can ChatGPT choose a skill automatically?
Yes. OpenAI’s Skills documentation says that after a skill is created and installed, ChatGPT can automatically use one or more skills when they are helpful.
When should I use a plugin instead of a skill?
Use a skill for reusable instructions around one focused workflow. Use a plugin when you need an installable bundle that can include one or more Skills, an app, or both.

item.text: The Complete Guide to Creating a Gemini Spark Skill A Gemini Spark skill is a saved set of reusable instructions that teaches Gemini exactly how you want a repeated job done — so you stop re-explaining your process, format, and rules every time. This guide shows you how to build one from start to finish inside Gemini Spark, whether you let Gemini draft it for you or write it yourself, even if you’ve never touched a line of code. New to what AI skills are entirely? Start with What Is an AI Agent Skill? for a clear definition and how skills differ from prompts and full AI agents. And if you haven’t opened Spark yet, the How to Use Gemini Spark guide covers the basics. This page assumes you’re ready to build a reusable Spark skill. Want the big picture? This is one platform in our complete guide on How to Create an AI Skill, which covers the universal method for every tool. Starting from a prompt you already use? First turn it into a clean skill structure with how to turn a prompt into an AI skill, then compare it with examples in the Gemini Spark skills gallery before saving and testing it inside Spark. How do you create a Gemini Spark skill? To create a Gemini Spark skill, go to gemini.google.com, switch to Spark, and open Skills. Then add a skill one of four ways: Create with Gemini (describe the job and Gemini drafts it), start from a Recommended template, Create manually, or upload a skill file. Give the skill a clear name, a description of when to use it, and step-by-step instructions with your output format and an example. Save it, then test it in a real task and refine until Spark applies it reliably. No coding required. A Gemini Spark skill saves your process once so Gemini can reuse it across every matching task. What Is a Gemini Spark Skill? A Gemini Spark skill is a saved set of reusable instructions and context that teaches Gemini how to complete a specific type of work — and which tools to use while doing it. Once a skill is active, Spark can apply it automatically when a task matches, or you can point a task at it directly. Skills are one of Spark’s three building blocks, and the easiest way to keep them straight is task = what, skill = how, schedule = when. A task is the goal (“write this week’s client update”), a skill is the repeatable method (“always format updates like this”), and a schedule is the trigger (“every Monday at 8am”). For the full breakdown, see the difference between Spark tasks, skills, and schedules. One handy difference from a Claude skill: you don’t have to write or upload a file to build a Spark skill. You create it right inside the Spark interface using a name, a description, and an instructions field — so there’s nothing to install and no format to learn. (Advanced users can upload a SKILL.md file, but most people never need to. More on that in Spark skills vs. Claude skills below.) What You Need Before You Start Building a Gemini Spark skill takes no coding. You need: Access to Gemini Spark — Spark rolls out by plan and region, so confirm you’re eligible first with our Gemini Spark availability guide. Spark already set up — if you haven’t switched it on yet, follow the free Gemini Spark setup guide, then come back here. One real, repeated task in mind — a report you format the same way, an email type you send often, a research routine. The more specific, the better your first skill will work. The most common reason a Spark skill underperforms is trying to make it do too much. A strong skill has one clear job: “format my weekly business brief,” not “help me with all my reporting.” Before you build anything, finish this sentence: “This skill should always ___ when I ___.” That single sentence becomes the skill’s description — the part Spark reads to decide when to apply it. Go to gemini.google.com and switch to Spark using the toggle in the left sidebar. Then open the Skills page — that’s where all your skills live, where Spark’s ready-made templates appear under Recommended, and where you’ll add your new one. Your saved skills show up in your Active list once they’re on. Use the Gemini Spark toggle first, then open Skills to create or manage your reusable Spark instructions. This is where Skills live in Gemini Spark — open it to create, edit, and manage every skill you build. Spark gives you four ways to add a skill. Pick the one that matches how much you want to write yourself: Create with Gemini — the easiest. On the Skills page, choose Create with Gemini, describe what the skill should do, and follow the prompts in the task thread while Gemini drafts it for you. (You can also do this from any Spark task: “Create a skill based on these instructions: …”) Start from a template — under Recommended, find a close match, choose Add skill to save it to your Active list, then open it and edit the name, description, and instructions. Create manually — choose Create manually for a blank skill you fill in yourself. Best when you know exactly how the work should be done. Upload a skill file — if you already have a skill written elsewhere, upload it directly. Beginner tip Start with Create with Gemini for your first skill, then open what it wrote and tighten it using Step 4. Seeing how Gemini structures a skill is the fastest way to learn the format. However you create the skill, its quality comes down to the instructions. Whether Gemini drafts them or you write them, a strong Spark skill spells out the same things. Use this as your checklist — or paste it straight into the instructions field and fill it in. Spark skill instructions template: PURPOSE What this skill does, in one sentence. WHEN TO USE IT The kind of task or request that should trigger this skill. STEPS 1. First thing Gemini should do. 2. Next step, in order. 3. Continue until the work is complete. TOOLS AND SOURCES Which tools or Google Workspace apps it may use (Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Drive, Tasks, Keep, or permitted Mac folders), and any sources to rely on or avoid. RULES How to evaluate information, what tone to use, and anything to never do. OUTPUT FORMAT Exactly how the result should be structured. EXAMPLE A short example of a strong result. NEEDS APPROVAL Any action Gemini should pause and ask me about before doing (sending, sharing, deleting). Keep the name short and specific, and make the description say plainly when Spark should use the skill — that description is how Spark decides to apply it automatically. The clearer it is, the more reliably the skill fires. Save the skill, make sure it’s switched on in your Active list, then run a real task it should handle — using messy, realistic input, not a clean example. Watch two things: did Spark actually apply the skill, and did the result follow your instructions? Test the task manually here; don’t put it on a schedule until it produces dependable results on its own. Need a task to test it on? Browse the Gemini Spark skills gallery for realistic workflow examples, then test your new skill on a similar task before scheduling or reusing it. If Spark didn’t apply the skill, the description is usually the culprit — make it match the words you actually use when you ask for that task. If it applied the skill but the output was off, fix the instructions: add the missing rule, tighten the output format, or add a clearer example. A fast way to do this is to ask Gemini in the thread to update the skill with your change, then test again. Most skills take two or three passes before they’re dependable — and only then is one safe to put on a schedule. Gemini Spark Skills vs. Claude Skills Both are “reusable instructions,” but they’re built and stored differently — so if you use both tools, it helps to know where they diverge. Gemini Spark skill Claude skill How it’s built In the Spark interface — a name, description, and instructions field. As a SKILL.md file with a YAML header, added under Customize. Ways to create it Create with Gemini, a template, manually, or upload a file. Write or upload SKILL.md, or let Claude create it. Where it shines Google Workspace work and scheduled, recurring automations. Documents, long-context reasoning, and coding tasks. Building on Claude too? Follow how to create a Claude skill, then compare reusable examples in the Claude skills gallery and Gemini Spark skills gallery to adapt the same workflow across platforms. Common Mistakes When Building a Spark Skill The description is too vague. “Helps with email” rarely triggers; “drafts a reply to a customer support email in my brand voice” does. The skill does too many jobs. Split it into separate, focused skills — Spark lets you reference one skill from another to build bigger workflows. No output format or example. Without a defined structure and a sample, Spark guesses — and the result drifts each run. Scheduling before testing. Automating an untested task multiplies its mistakes. Prove it manually first. No approval gate. For anything that sends, shares, or deletes, tell the skill to pause for your approval. Where to Find and Reuse Gemini Spark Skills You don’t have to build every skill from scratch. Spark’s own Recommended templates are the fastest starting point inside the app, and you can browse ready-made, beginner-friendly options in our Gemini Spark skills gallery. Already built something similar in Claude? Use the Claude skills gallery for structure examples, then adapt the instructions manually for Spark. For the official reference, Google maintains its own Create & manage skills for Gemini Apps documentation. Final Takeaway A Gemini Spark skill is just your process, saved once so Gemini repeats it perfectly every time. The hard part isn’t the tool — it’s being specific about the one job the skill does. Open Skills in Spark, pick a task you repeat weekly, let Gemini draft the skill or write it yourself, then test and refine until it fires reliably. Build one real skill this week and the next takes minutes. What is a Gemini Spark skill? A Gemini Spark skill is a saved set of reusable instructions and context that teaches Gemini how to complete a specific type of task, and which tools to use. Once it’s active, Spark can apply the skill automatically when a matching task comes up, or you can select it for a task yourself. How do I create a skill in Gemini Spark? Go to gemini.google.com, switch to Spark, and open the Skills page. Then add a skill by choosing Create with Gemini, starting from a Recommended template, creating one manually, or uploading a skill file. Give it a clear name, a description of when to use it, and detailed instructions, then save and test it. Do I need to know how to code to build a Gemini Spark skill? No. A Spark skill is written in plain language inside the Spark interface — a name, a description, and instructions. There’s no file to write and no format to learn, so it’s fully beginner-friendly. What’s the difference between a Gemini Spark task, skill, and schedule? Task equals what, skill equals how, and schedule equals when. A task is the goal you want completed, a skill is the reusable method for completing it, and a schedule is the time or condition that triggers the task automatically. Test a task manually before you save its method as a skill or put it on a schedule. Why isn’t Gemini Spark applying my skill? It’s almost always the description. If it’s vague or doesn’t match how you phrase the request, Spark won’t recognize when to apply the skill. Rewrite the description to be specific about the trigger, or select the skill manually for the task, then refine and test again. Can I turn a Claude skill into a Gemini Spark skill? Yes. The setup steps are different, but the core structure can usually transfer: one job, a trigger description, ordered instructions, rules, and an output format. Compare examples in the Claude skills gallery and Gemini Spark skills gallery, then adapt the instructions for Spark manually. Where can I find ready-made Gemini Spark skills? Inside Spark, the Recommended templates on the Skills page are the quickest starting point. You can also browse beginner-friendly, ready-to-use options in our Gemini Spark skills gallery, then customize any of them to fit your workflow.

The Complete Guide to Creating a Gemini Spark Skill

A Gemini Spark skill is a saved set of reusable instructions that teaches Gemini exactly how you want a repeated job done — so you stop re-explaining your process, format, and rules every time. This guide shows you how to build one from start to finish inside Gemini Spark, whether you let Gemini draft it for you or write it yourself, even if you’ve never touched a line of code.

New to what AI skills are entirely? Start with What Is an AI Agent Skill? for a clear definition and how skills differ from prompts and full AI agents. And if you haven’t opened Spark yet, the How to Use Gemini Spark guide covers the basics. This page assumes you’re ready to build a reusable Spark skill.

Want the big picture? This is one platform in our complete guide on How to Create an AI Skill, which covers the universal method for every tool.

Starting from a prompt you already use? First turn it into a clean skill structure with how to turn a prompt into an AI skill, then compare it with examples in the Gemini Spark skills gallery before saving and testing it inside Spark.

Quick answer

How do you create a Gemini Spark skill?

To create a Gemini Spark skill, go to gemini.google.com, switch to Spark, and open Skills. Then add a skill one of four ways: Create with Gemini (describe the job and Gemini drafts it), start from a Recommended template, Create manually, or upload a skill file. Give the skill a clear name, a description of when to use it, and step-by-step instructions with your output format and an example. Save it, then test it in a real task and refine until Spark applies it reliably. No coding required.

What Is a Gemini Spark Skill?

A Gemini Spark skill is a saved set of reusable instructions and context that teaches Gemini how to complete a specific type of work — and which tools to use while doing it. Once a skill is active, Spark can apply it automatically when a task matches, or you can point a task at it directly.

Skills are one of Spark’s three building blocks, and the easiest way to keep them straight is task = what, skill = how, schedule = when. A task is the goal (“write this week’s client update”), a skill is the repeatable method (“always format updates like this”), and a schedule is the trigger (“every Monday at 8am”). For the full breakdown, see the difference between Spark tasks, skills, and schedules.

One handy difference from a Claude skill: you don’t have to write or upload a file to build a Spark skill. You create it right inside the Spark interface using a name, a description, and an instructions field — so there’s nothing to install and no format to learn. (Advanced users can upload a SKILL.md file, but most people never need to. More on that in Spark skills vs. Claude skills below.)

What You Need Before You Start

Building a Gemini Spark skill takes no coding. You need:

  • Access to Gemini Spark — Spark rolls out by plan and region, so confirm you’re eligible first with our Gemini Spark availability guide.
  • Spark already set up — if you haven’t switched it on yet, follow the free Gemini Spark setup guide, then come back here.
  • One real, repeated task in mind — a report you format the same way, an email type you send often, a research routine. The more specific, the better your first skill will work.

The most common reason a Spark skill underperforms is trying to make it do too much. A strong skill has one clear job: “format my weekly business brief,” not “help me with all my reporting.”

Before you build anything, finish this sentence: “This skill should always ___ when I ___.” That single sentence becomes the skill’s description — the part Spark reads to decide when to apply it.

Go to gemini.google.com and switch to Spark using the toggle in the left sidebar. Then open the Skills page — that’s where all your skills live, where Spark’s ready-made templates appear under Recommended, and where you’ll add your new one. Your saved skills show up in your Active list once they’re on.

Spark gives you four ways to add a skill. Pick the one that matches how much you want to write yourself:

  • Create with Gemini — the easiest. On the Skills page, choose Create with Gemini, describe what the skill should do, and follow the prompts in the task thread while Gemini drafts it for you. (You can also do this from any Spark task: “Create a skill based on these instructions: …”)
  • Start from a template — under Recommended, find a close match, choose Add skill to save it to your Active list, then open it and edit the name, description, and instructions.
  • Create manually — choose Create manually for a blank skill you fill in yourself. Best when you know exactly how the work should be done.
  • Upload a skill file — if you already have a skill written elsewhere, upload it directly.

Beginner tip

Start with Create with Gemini for your first skill, then open what it wrote and tighten it using Step 4. Seeing how Gemini structures a skill is the fastest way to learn the format.

However you create the skill, its quality comes down to the instructions. Whether Gemini drafts them or you write them, a strong Spark skill spells out the same things. Use this as your checklist — or paste it straight into the instructions field and fill it in.

Spark skill instructions template:

PURPOSE
What this skill does, in one sentence.

WHEN TO USE IT
The kind of task or request that should trigger this skill.

STEPS
1. First thing Gemini should do.
2. Next step, in order.
3. Continue until the work is complete.

TOOLS AND SOURCES
Which tools or Google Workspace apps it may use (Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Drive, Tasks, Keep, or permitted Mac folders), and any sources to rely on or avoid.

RULES
How to evaluate information, what tone to use, and anything to never do.

OUTPUT FORMAT
Exactly how the result should be structured.

EXAMPLE
A short example of a strong result.

NEEDS APPROVAL
Any action Gemini should pause and ask me about before doing (sending, sharing, deleting).

Keep the name short and specific, and make the description say plainly when Spark should use the skill — that description is how Spark decides to apply it automatically. The clearer it is, the more reliably the skill fires.

Save the skill, make sure it’s switched on in your Active list, then run a real task it should handle — using messy, realistic input, not a clean example. Watch two things: did Spark actually apply the skill, and did the result follow your instructions? Test the task manually here; don’t put it on a schedule until it produces dependable results on its own.

Need a task to test it on?

Browse the Gemini Spark skills gallery for realistic workflow examples, then test your new skill on a similar task before scheduling or reusing it.

If Spark didn’t apply the skill, the description is usually the culprit — make it match the words you actually use when you ask for that task. If it applied the skill but the output was off, fix the instructions: add the missing rule, tighten the output format, or add a clearer example. A fast way to do this is to ask Gemini in the thread to update the skill with your change, then test again. Most skills take two or three passes before they’re dependable — and only then is one safe to put on a schedule.

Gemini Spark Skills vs. Claude Skills

Both are “reusable instructions,” but they’re built and stored differently — so if you use both tools, it helps to know where they diverge.

  Gemini Spark skill Claude skill
How it’s built In the Spark interface — a name, description, and instructions field. As a SKILL.md file with a YAML header, added under Customize.
Ways to create it Create with Gemini, a template, manually, or upload a file. Write or upload SKILL.md, or let Claude create it.
Where it shines Google Workspace work and scheduled, recurring automations. Documents, long-context reasoning, and coding tasks.

Building on Claude too? Follow how to create a Claude skill, then compare reusable examples in the Claude skills gallery and Gemini Spark skills gallery to adapt the same workflow across platforms.

Common Mistakes When Building a Spark Skill

  • The description is too vague. “Helps with email” rarely triggers; “drafts a reply to a customer support email in my brand voice” does.
  • The skill does too many jobs. Split it into separate, focused skills — Spark lets you reference one skill from another to build bigger workflows.
  • No output format or example. Without a defined structure and a sample, Spark guesses — and the result drifts each run.
  • Scheduling before testing. Automating an untested task multiplies its mistakes. Prove it manually first.
  • No approval gate. For anything that sends, shares, or deletes, tell the skill to pause for your approval.

Where to Find and Reuse Gemini Spark Skills

You don’t have to build every skill from scratch. Spark’s own Recommended templates are the fastest starting point inside the app, and you can browse ready-made, beginner-friendly options in our Gemini Spark skills gallery. Already built something similar in Claude? Use the Claude skills gallery for structure examples, then adapt the instructions manually for Spark. For the official reference, Google maintains its own Create & manage skills for Gemini Apps documentation.

Final Takeaway

A Gemini Spark skill is just your process, saved once so Gemini repeats it perfectly every time. The hard part isn’t the tool — it’s being specific about the one job the skill does. Open Skills in Spark, pick a task you repeat weekly, let Gemini draft the skill or write it yourself, then test and refine until it fires reliably. Build one real skill this week and the next takes minutes.

Frequently asked questions

What is a Gemini Spark skill?

A Gemini Spark skill is a saved set of reusable instructions and context that teaches Gemini how to complete a specific type of task, and which tools to use. Once it’s active, Spark can apply the skill automatically when a matching task comes up, or you can select it for a task yourself.

How do I create a skill in Gemini Spark?

Go to gemini.google.com, switch to Spark, and open the Skills page. Then add a skill by choosing Create with Gemini, starting from a Recommended template, creating one manually, or uploading a skill file. Give it a clear name, a description of when to use it, and detailed instructions, then save and test it.

Do I need to know how to code to build a Gemini Spark skill?

No. A Spark skill is written in plain language inside the Spark interface — a name, a description, and instructions. There’s no file to write and no format to learn, so it’s fully beginner-friendly.

What’s the difference between a Gemini Spark task, skill, and schedule?

Task equals what, skill equals how, and schedule equals when. A task is the goal you want completed, a skill is the reusable method for completing it, and a schedule is the time or condition that triggers the task automatically. Test a task manually before you save its method as a skill or put it on a schedule.

Why isn’t Gemini Spark applying my skill?

It’s almost always the description. If it’s vague or doesn’t match how you phrase the request, Spark won’t recognize when to apply the skill. Rewrite the description to be specific about the trigger, or select the skill manually for the task, then refine and test again.

Can I turn a Claude skill into a Gemini Spark skill?

Yes. The setup steps are different, but the core structure can usually transfer: one job, a trigger description, ordered instructions, rules, and an output format. Compare examples in the Claude skills gallery and Gemini Spark skills gallery, then adapt the instructions for Spark manually.

Where can I find ready-made Gemini Spark skills?

Inside Spark, the Recommended templates on the Skills page are the quickest starting point. You can also browse beginner-friendly, ready-to-use options in our Gemini Spark skills gallery, then customize any of them to fit your workflow.

How to Create an AI Skill: Complete Beginner Guide (2026)

An AI skill is a saved set of instructions that teaches an AI assistant how to do one repeatable job the same way every time. Build it once and you stop re-explaining your process, your format, and your rules in every new chat. This is the complete, beginner-friendly guide to creating one — the method is the same on every platform, and the exact clicks live in the platform-specific guides linked throughout.

Want the definition first? Read What Is an AI Agent Skill? for how a skill differs from a prompt and a full AI agent. Already know the idea and just want your platform’s exact steps? Jump to create a skill on your platform below.

Already have a prompt you like? Use how to turn a prompt into an AI skill, then compare your structure with ready-made examples in the AI agent skills library. This page is for creating a skill from the ground up.

Quick answer

How do you create an AI skill?

To create an AI skill, follow the same five steps on any platform: (1) decide the one job the skill should do, (2) write its core — a name, a description of when to use it, step-by-step instructions, an output format, and an example, (3) add it to your AI tool, (4) test it on a real task, and (5) refine the description until the AI applies it reliably. The universal method is below, and the exact steps for Claude and Gemini Spark are in their own guides. No coding required.

What Is an AI Skill?

An AI skill — sometimes called an AI agent skill — is a reusable package of instructions that tells an AI assistant exactly how to handle one specific task, and when to use it. Instead of re-typing “write it in this tone, use this format, follow these steps” every time, you save it once and the AI loads it whenever a request matches. A skill is narrower than a full AI agent and more durable than a one-off prompt: it’s the repeatable how behind a task you do again and again.

The concept is the same across tools — Claude, Gemini Spark, ChatGPT, and others all let you save reusable skills. What changes is where you put the skill and how you enter it, which is why the exact steps live in the platform guides below. For the full breakdown of skills versus prompts versus agents, see What Is an AI Agent Skill?.

Create a Skill on Your Platform (Exact Steps)

The five-step method below is universal — but the precise clicks depend on your tool. These guides walk you through building a skill in each one, screenshot by screenshot. Pick your platform, or read the universal method first and come back:

Using ChatGPT or another assistant? The same five steps still apply — save your skill wherever that tool keeps reusable instructions, then test and refine it exactly as below.

The Universal Method: 5 Steps That Work on Any Platform

Whichever tool you use, a good AI skill comes together the same way. Learn these five steps once and you can build a skill anywhere.

The most common reason a skill underperforms is trying to make it do too much. A strong skill has one clear job: “turn my meeting notes into a client follow-up email,” not “help with all my communication.”

Before you build anything, finish this sentence: “This skill should always ___ when I ___.” That single sentence becomes the skill’s description — the part the AI reads to decide when to apply it.

Every AI skill, on every platform, is built from the same parts: a name, a description of when to use it, the instructions to follow, an output format, and an example. Write these in plain language — you’re training an assistant, not writing code. Use this template as your starting point and paste it wherever your tool keeps skill instructions.

Universal AI skill template:

NAME
A short, specific name for the skill.

WHEN TO USE IT
One sentence: the kind of request that should trigger this skill.

INSTRUCTIONS
1. First thing the AI should do.
2. Next step, in order.
3. Continue until the work is complete.

RULES
Tone to use, what to always do, and what to never do.

OUTPUT FORMAT
Exactly how the finished result should be structured.

EXAMPLE
A short example of a great result.

NEEDS APPROVAL
Any action the AI should pause and ask me about first (sending, sharing, deleting).

The “when to use it” line is the most important part of the whole skill — it’s how the AI decides to apply it. Make it match the words you actually use when you ask for that task.

This is the one step that differs by platform — where the skill lives and how you enter it. Follow your tool’s guide for the exact clicks:

  • Claude — save your skill as a SKILL.md file and add it under Customize. Full walkthrough: how to create a Claude skill.
  • Gemini Spark — build it right in the Spark interface, or let Gemini draft it for you. Full walkthrough: how to create a Gemini Spark skill.
  • ChatGPT — open Plugins → Skills and create it with chat, the editor, or an upload. Full walkthrough: how to create a ChatGPT skill.
  • Any other tool — add your instructions wherever it saves reusable skills or custom instructions.

Turn the skill on, then run a real, messy version of the task — not a clean test case. Watch two things: did the AI actually apply the skill, and did the output follow your instructions? Real input is where weak instructions show up, so always test with something you’d genuinely use.

If the AI didn’t apply the skill, the “when to use it” description is almost always the fix — rewrite it to match how you phrase the request. If it applied the skill but the result was off, tighten the instructions: add the missing rule, sharpen the output format, or add a clearer example. Most skills take two or three passes before they’re dependable. Once yours is, you’ve built a reusable asset that saves time on every future task.

What Makes a Strong AI Skill

The difference between a skill that fires reliably and one that gets ignored comes down to a few things every good skill includes:

  • One clear job — narrow beats broad. Several focused skills outperform one that tries to do everything.
  • A specific trigger — the “when to use it” line should read the way you actually ask for the task.
  • A defined output format — tell the AI exactly how the result should look, so it doesn’t drift each run.
  • At least one example — a sample of a great result removes guesswork.
  • An approval gate — for anything that sends, shares, or deletes, have the skill pause for your okay.

AI Skills vs. Prompts vs. Agents

These three get mixed up constantly. The simplest way to tell them apart is by how much they do and how long they last.

Prompt AI skill AI agent
A one-time instruction typed into a single chat. A saved, reusable method the AI applies whenever a task matches. An autonomous worker that combines skills and tools to complete a goal.
You retype it every time. You write it once; it triggers itself. You set it up once; it runs multi-step work on its own.
Best for a one-off request. Best for a task you repeat often. Best for a whole workflow you want handled end to end.

In short: a prompt is a single ask, a skill is a reusable method, and an agent is a system that uses skills to get work done. Most people should start with skills — they deliver the biggest time savings for the least setup. For the deeper comparison, see What Is an AI Agent Skill?.

Common Mistakes When Creating an AI Skill

  • The trigger is too vague. “Helps with writing” rarely fires; “drafts a client follow-up email from my meeting notes” does.
  • The skill does too many jobs. Split it into separate, focused skills — they’re free to make and easier to trigger correctly.
  • No output format or example. Without both, the AI guesses, and the result drifts every run.
  • Testing on a clean example. A skill that works on tidy input often breaks on real, messy input. Test with the real thing.
  • Never refining. The first version rarely triggers perfectly. Two or three quick passes is normal — and expected.

Where to Find Ready-Made AI Skills

You don’t have to build every skill from scratch. Browse our AI agent skills library for ready-to-use skills built for solo operators and small teams, or go straight to the platform collections: Claude skills and Gemini Spark skills. Installing a ready-made skill is the fastest way to see the format before you build your own.

If you are still choosing your first repeatable workflow, see which AI Skills are worth setting up first.

To see the five steps above applied end to end on a real job, read how to create a website with an AI skill. It walks one complete skill from the single-job decision through to a finished site map, hero copy, SEO metadata, and FAQs — a useful reference for how much detail a skill actually needs before it runs reliably.

Final Takeaway

Creating an AI skill means saving your process once so the AI can follow it more consistently. The method is the same everywhere — decide the one job, write the skill’s core, add it to your tool, test, and refine — and the exact steps live in the guide for your platform. Pick a task you repeat weekly, follow the Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT guide, and build one real skill this week. The next one takes minutes.

In Claude you write a SKILL.md file and add it under Customize; in Gemini Spark you build the skill directly in the Spark interface; in ChatGPT you open Plugins → Skills and create it with chat, the editor, or an upload. Follow the Claude guide, the Gemini Spark guide, or the ChatGPT guide for the exact steps.

item.text: How to Turn a Prompt Into an AI Skill: Complete Guide (2026) A strong prompt should not stay trapped in one chat. If you use the same prompt more than once, or keep rewriting the same instructions from memory, turn it into an AI skill: a reusable process your AI tool can follow every time that task comes up. This guide shows you how to take a prompt you already like and convert it into a saved skill structure with a clear goal, inputs, steps, output format, rules, examples, and review checklist. It is the bridge between one-off prompting and building a real AI workflow. How do you turn a prompt into an AI skill? To turn a prompt into an AI skill, pull the reusable process out of the prompt. Define the one task it handles, the inputs it needs, the steps the AI should follow, the output format, the rules, one good example, and a review checklist. Then save that structure in your AI tool and test it on three real examples. If you want examples before writing your own, browse the AI agent skills library. A prompt is a one-time request. An AI skill is the reusable process behind that request. When Is a Prompt Ready to Become a Skill? A prompt is ready to become a skill when it is no longer just a question. It has become a process you repeat. You may notice that you paste the same instruction every week, keep adding the same formatting rules, or always need the AI to follow the same steps before producing an answer. Good candidates include prompts for follow-up emails, meeting summaries, content repurposing, weekly planning, research briefs, social media posts, competitor analysis, and inbox triage. These tasks have a repeatable pattern: the input changes, but the way you want the AI to work stays mostly the same. Simple rule If you have used a prompt three times and improved it each time, stop polishing the prompt and turn it into a skill. Prompt vs Reusable AI Skill The difference is not length. A long prompt can still be fragile, and a short skill can still be reliable. The difference is structure. PartPromptAI skill Purpose Get one answer now Handle one repeatable task consistently Inputs Often improvised in the chat Defined clearly so you know what to provide every time Process Mixed into the wording Separated into step-by-step instructions Output May vary unless you repeat the format Saved as a consistent format with examples Review Usually happens after the result feels wrong Built into the process before the output is trusted If you are still learning the basic definition, start with What Is an AI Agent Skill?. If you already know you want to build one from scratch, use the broader pillar guide on how to create an AI skill. This page is specifically for converting a prompt you already have. How to Turn a Prompt Into an AI Skill: Complete Guide (2026)

A strong prompt should not stay trapped in one chat. If you use the same prompt more than once, or keep rewriting the same instructions from memory, turn it into an AI skill: a reusable process your AI tool can follow every time that task comes up.

This guide shows you how to take a prompt you already like and convert it into a saved skill structure with a clear goal, inputs, steps, output format, rules, examples, and review checklist. It is the bridge between one-off prompting and building a real AI workflow.

Quick answer

How do you turn a prompt into an AI skill?

To turn a prompt into an AI skill, pull the reusable process out of the prompt. Define the one task it handles, the inputs it needs, the steps the AI should follow, the output format, the rules, one good example, and a review checklist. Then save that structure in your AI tool and test it on three real examples. If you want examples before writing your own, browse the AI agent skills library.

When Is a Prompt Ready to Become a Skill?

A prompt is ready to become a skill when it is no longer just a question. It has become a process you repeat. You may notice that you paste the same instruction every week, keep adding the same formatting rules, or always need the AI to follow the same steps before producing an answer.

Good candidates include prompts for follow-up emails, meeting summaries, content repurposing, weekly planning, research briefs, social media posts, competitor analysis, and inbox triage. These tasks have a repeatable pattern: the input changes, but the way you want the AI to work stays mostly the same.

Simple rule

If you have used a prompt three times and improved it each time, stop polishing the prompt and turn it into a skill.

Prompt vs Reusable AI Skill

The difference is not length. A long prompt can still be fragile, and a short skill can still be reliable. The difference is structure.

PartPromptAI skill
PurposeGet one answer nowHandle one repeatable task consistently
InputsOften improvised in the chatDefined clearly so you know what to provide every time
ProcessMixed into the wordingSeparated into step-by-step instructions
OutputMay vary unless you repeat the formatSaved as a consistent format with examples
ReviewUsually happens after the result feels wrongBuilt into the process before the output is trusted

If you are still learning the basic definition, start with What Is an AI Agent Skill?. If you already know you want to build one from scratch, use the broader pillar guide on how to create an AI skill. This page is specifically for converting a prompt you already have.

The 7-Step Prompt-to-Skill Method

Do not paste your prompt into a skill exactly as-is. First, unpack it. A good skill makes the hidden parts of your prompt explicit.

Write the task in one sentence. Avoid broad names like “marketing helper” or “business assistant.” Use a concrete job such as “draft a warm client follow-up email from meeting notes.”

List what the AI needs before it starts: notes, transcript, email thread, topic, audience, offer, tone, example, URL, file, or deadline. This keeps the skill from guessing.

Most prompts hide a process inside a paragraph. Pull it apart into numbered steps: review the input, identify the goal, choose the angle, draft the output, check for missing details, and flag anything uncertain.

Tell the AI exactly what the finished result should look like. Use sections, bullets, tables, subject lines, summaries, or a final checklist.

Include tone, length, source rules, style preferences, and what the AI should avoid. If the task touches real customers, publishing, private files, legal, health, finance, or account actions, add a human review step.

Examples show the AI what “good” looks like. Add one short example input and one strong example output, especially for tone-heavy tasks.

End the skill with a checklist the AI should use before giving you the final answer. This catches missing inputs, invented details, weak formatting, and unsupported claims.

Copy the Prompt-to-Skill Template

Use this template when you want to convert any working prompt into a reusable skill.

Skill name:
[Name the repeatable task.]

When to use this skill:
Use this when I ask you to [task] and provide [inputs].

Goal:
Help me complete [specific task] consistently, using the same process each time.

Required inputs:
- [Input 1]
- [Input 2]
- [Input 3]

Process:
1. Review the inputs and identify the main goal.
2. Ask one clarifying question only if a required input is missing.
3. Follow this step-by-step method:
   - [Step A]
   - [Step B]
   - [Step C]
4. Create the output in the format below.
5. Run the review checklist before finalizing.

Output format:
- [Section 1]
- [Section 2]
- [Section 3]

Rules:
- Do not invent facts, quotes, data, or source details.
- Keep the tone [tone].
- Keep the length [length].
- Flag anything that needs human review.

Example:
Input:
[Short example input]

Strong output:
[Short example output]

Review checklist:
- Did I use all required inputs?
- Did I follow the process?
- Did I match the requested format?
- Did I avoid unsupported claims?
- Did I clearly flag anything uncertain?

Example: Turn a Follow-Up Email Prompt Into an AI Skill

Here is a simple before-and-after. The original prompt works once, but the skill version is easier to reuse.

Original prompt

Write a friendly follow-up email after this meeting. Mention the next step, keep it short, and make it sound professional.

Reusable skill version

Skill name:
Client Follow-Up Email Draft

When to use this skill:
Use this when I provide meeting notes, a client name, and a desired next step.

Goal:
Draft a short, warm, professional follow-up email that reminds the client what we discussed and makes the next action clear.

Required inputs:
- Client name
- Meeting notes or call summary
- Desired next step
- Optional deadline or meeting link

Process:
1. Review the notes and identify the client's main goal, pain point, or question.
2. Choose the clearest next step.
3. Draft one email with a warm opening, a short recap, one clear CTA, and a helpful close.
4. Add three subject line options.
5. If any important detail is missing, list it under "Needs review" instead of guessing.

Output format:
Subject line options:
1.
2.
3.

Email draft:
[Email]

Needs review:
- [Only include if something is missing or uncertain.]

Rules:
- Keep the email under 180 words.
- Do not overpromise.
- Do not invent pricing, dates, or deliverables.
- Keep the tone warm, direct, and useful.

That version can become a Claude skill, a Gemini Spark skill, a ChatGPT Project instruction, a Gem-style assistant instruction, or a reusable team prompt. The exact platform setup lives in the guides below.

Before you finalize yours, compare it with examples of the best reusable AI Skills to see how proven workflows handle inputs, guardrails, and finished outputs.

Where to Save the Skill

Once you have the skill structure, save it in the tool you actually use. The structure is portable, but the setup steps are different.

If you use Gemini Gems, you can still reuse the same skill structure as saved instructions for a custom Gem. The dedicated Gem-to-skill workflow can be its own guide later; for now, treat Gems as one place where reusable instructions can live.

How to Test the Skill Before You Trust It

Do not judge a skill from one perfect test. Run it on three different examples:

  • Easy example: a clean input where the answer should be obvious.
  • Real example: the kind of messy input you actually use.
  • Edge case: missing information, conflicting context, or a task the skill should refuse or flag.

After each test, update the skill. Add missing input requirements, tighten the output format, add a rule, or include a better example.

Common Mistakes When Turning a Prompt Into a Skill

MistakeFix
Saving the original prompt without restructuring itSeparate the prompt into goal, inputs, process, output, rules, examples, and review.
Making the skill too broadPick one repeated task, not “help me with marketing” or “run my business.”
Skipping required inputsTell the AI what it needs before it starts, and what to do if something is missing.
Forgetting examplesAdd one short example that shows tone, structure, and level of detail.
Trusting the first outputTest the skill on easy, real, and edge-case inputs before using it in important work.

What to Do Next

If you already have a prompt, use the template above to turn it into a skill structure. Then compare it with ready-made examples in the AI agent skills library, or jump straight to the collection for your platform. If your prompt is a website or landing-page prompt, creating a website with an AI skill shows the finished result of this exact process.

Frequently asked questions

Can any prompt become an AI skill?

Not every prompt should become a skill. The best candidates are prompts for tasks you repeat, such as follow-up emails, summaries, research briefs, content repurposing, weekly planning, and recurring business updates.

What is the difference between a prompt and an AI skill?

A prompt is usually a one-time instruction. An AI skill is a reusable process with a defined goal, inputs, steps, output format, rules, examples, and review checklist.

Should I write the skill myself or start from an existing example?

Write the skill yourself when the workflow is specific to your business. Start from an existing example when you want to understand the structure faster, then customize the goal, inputs, steps, rules, and output format.

Can I use the same skill in Claude and Gemini Spark?

The core instructions can usually transfer, but the setup steps differ. Use the Claude guide for Claude skills and the Gemini Spark guide for Spark skills.

When should I create an AI skill from scratch instead?

Create a skill from scratch when you do not already have a working prompt. Use the broader guide on how to create an AI skill for the full build process.

Can I turn a Gemini Gem prompt into a skill?

Often, yes. A Gem instruction can be reorganized into the same skill structure: goal, inputs, process, output, rules, examples, and review checklist. A dedicated Gemini Gem-to-skill walkthrough can cover that workflow separately later.

item.text: The 9 Best Ways To Reduce Claude Fable 5 Credit Usage If you want to save Claude Fable 5 credits, the biggest lever is not one tiny prompt trick — it is learning when to reach for Fable 5 at all, when Opus 5 or Sonnet 5 will do, and how to avoid expensive retries. Since Opus 5’s July 2026 release, the smartest default is to try Opus 5 first and keep Fable 5 for the tasks Opus 5 genuinely can’t finish. In this guide, “credits” refers to Claude’s paid usage credits and the broader usage allowance people watch when running Fable 5-heavy tasks. New to the model? Start with what Claude Fable 5 is, then browse the best Claude Fable 5 use cases and the 15 best Claude Fable 5 prompts. This page assumes you already use Fable 5 and want to make the same plan go further. Update — July 24, 2026: try Opus 5 before spending Fable credits Anthropic released Claude Opus 5 on July 24, 2026, describing it as approaching Fable 5’s intelligence at roughly half the price. Opus 5 is priced at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens — half of Fable 5’s $10/$50 — and it’s now the default model on Max and the strongest model on Pro. For most demanding everyday work, Opus 5 is now the better first choice. Reach for Fable 5 only when Opus 5 can’t reliably finish the task. That single change is the biggest credit saver on this page. Access update — July 20, 2026 Anthropic has settled Fable 5’s access permanently. From July 20, Fable 5 is included in all Max and Team Premium plans at 50% of limits. Pro and Team Standard keep access through usage credits and receive a one-time $100 credit, after which Fable 5 bills at API rates ($10 per million input tokens, $50 per million output). See Anthropic’s guide to managing usage credits. The 50% Claude Code rate-limit boost also ends July 20, so standard weekly limits shrink the same day. Task Credit-smart choice Why Quick drafts, captions, small rewrites Claude Sonnet 5 Routine work doesn’t need Fable 5’s reasoning — spending its credits here is pure waste Everyday summaries and short answers Claude Sonnet 5 Fast, cheaper, and available on every plan for low-stakes tasks Outlining and first drafts Claude Sonnet 5 Do the churn cheaply, then escalate only the final step to Fable 5 Deep, multi-source research briefs Claude Opus 5 Handles long, messy source material at half Fable’s cost — try it here first Business-critical strategy decisions Claude Opus 5 Near-frontier reasoning for high-stakes calls without Fable-level spend Difficult analysis of large data Claude Opus 5 Handles big, messy datasets without losing detail, at lower cost per task Multi-step agent workflows (scoped) Claude Opus 5 Built for long-running, connected steps — just keep them bounded (tip 8) Prompt-to-skill conversion Claude Opus 5 Strong at spotting missing structure and generalizing a one-off prompt Exceptionally hard tasks where Opus 5 fell short Claude Fable 5 The one case left for Fable: Opus 5 already tried and couldn’t reliably finish A safeguard note for security and science work Opus 5 may also be the more practical choice for legitimate security research and scientific work. Claude Fable 5 Usage Credit Errors, and How to Fix Them Since the July 2026 plan changes, a lot of people meet Fable 5 through an error message rather than a settings page. Here are the ones that come up most, what each actually means, and what to do — including one that is a genuine bug rather than anything wrong with your account. “Fable 5 requires usage credits” In Claude Code the full message reads: Switched to Opus 4.8 (1M context) for this session · Fable 5 requires usage credits · /model to change Your session silently drops to Opus 4.8 and keeps going, which is why people often notice the output changed before they notice the message. Reported in Claude Code issue #79337, which was still open at the time of writing — check the thread for the current status before assuming you need to pay. “Usage credits are required for long context requests” This one is specific to long-context work and has been reported in headless or non-interactive Claude Code sessions authenticated over OAuth — including on Max, at very low usage. Enabling usage credits clears it, though users have noted no credits are actually consumed afterwards, which suggests the gate rather than the billing is the problem. Tracked in issue #62143. “Usage credits are off” — including when you just turned them on Two different situations produce this, and they need opposite responses. Genuinely off. Credits are disabled by default, so if you’ve never enabled them and you’re on a plan that needs them, this is simply telling you to switch them on. Off when you know they’re on. The toggle at claude.ai/settings/usage has been reported flipping itself to Off mid-session. The tell is that clicking it asks “Are you sure you want to turn it Off?” — meaning the server still has them on and only the interface is wrong. Dismiss the dialog, restart Claude Code, and carry on. Don’t re-purchase anything. How to turn usage credits on Credits are enabled in the Claude web app, not from a command inside Claude Code: Go to Settings → Usage at claude.ai/settings/usage. Find Usage credits and select Enable. Choose Add funds and prepay an amount. Optionally set auto-reload with a threshold. Bought your plan in the iOS or Android app? You have to enable and purchase credits on the web app — it can’t be done from mobile. This catches a lot of people who assume the option is missing from their account entirely. See Anthropic’s guide to managing usage credits for paid Claude plans. You can turn credits off again at any time from the same screen, which caps you at your plan’s included usage — a reasonable safety net if you’re worried about a long agent run quietly spending money. That’s the same instinct behind everything above: the cheapest credit is the one you never needed to spend. Final takeaway You don’t save Claude Fable 5 credits by using Fable 5 less — you save them by using it deliberately. Send routine work to a lighter model, batch related tasks into one session, prompt tightly so it lands the first time, and save your best workflows as skills. Do that, and the same plan stretches much further while Fable 5 stays free to do the heavy work it’s actually built for. How do I save Claude Fable 5 credits? The most effective way to save Claude Fable 5 credits is to use Fable 5 only for complex, high-stakes, or multi-step work and switch to a lighter model like Sonnet 5 for everyday tasks. Then batch related work into fewer sessions, write tight structured prompts to avoid retries, and trim the context you paste in. Model choice matters more than every other tip combined. Why does Claude Fable 5 use credits so fast? Fable 5 is built for complex, long-running, end-to-end work, so it does more reasoning per request than a lighter model — which uses more of your allowance per task. Credit usage climbs fastest when you run routine questions through it, paste oversized context, regenerate vague prompts, or leave agent runs unscoped. Does Claude Fable 5 cost more than Sonnet 5? In practical terms, yes — Fable 5 is the heavier, more capable model and consumes more of your usage per task, while Sonnet 5 is faster, lighter, and available across all plans. As of July 2026, Anthropic lists Claude Fable 5 API pricing at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Sonnet 5 is listed at lower API pricing, with introductory pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through August 31, 2026 ($3/$15 standard pricing afterward). Claude app usage, plan limits, and usage-credit rules can vary, so check Claude’s current pricing and your usage settings before a large run. When should I use Claude Fable 5 instead of Sonnet 5? Use Claude Fable 5 for deep research, business-critical decisions, difficult analysis, long documents, and scoped multi-step agent workflows. Use Sonnet 5 for quick drafts, summaries, outlining, and everyday questions. The comparison table above shows the credit-smart choice for common tasks. Do long prompts and large pastes use more Claude Fable 5 credits? Yes. The more context you give Fable 5, the more it processes on every turn of the conversation, and that adds up across a session. Paste only the portion of a document or export the task actually needs — but when you genuinely require a large, messy input, such as deep research, that’s the right time to spend Fable 5’s long context on purpose. Can I run out of Claude Fable 5 credits? You can reach your plan’s usage limit, after which access depends on your plan and Anthropic’s current rules. Because limits and credit rules vary and can change, check your usage before a big research job or long agent run, and route the lighter parts of the work to Sonnet 5 to stretch your allowance. Is Claude Fable 5 available now? Yes. Anthropic restored global access to Claude Fable 5 starting July 1, 2026, after the export controls that had paused it were lifted. It’s available through Claude.ai, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and the Claude Platform, though availability, plan limits, and usage credits can vary — check Claude directly before building a workflow around it. Does using Claude Fable 5 for coding waste credits? It can be inefficient in one specific way: Fable 5 includes updated safety classifiers, and a small number of benign coding or debugging requests may be flagged or rerouted to Claude Opus 4.8 rather than answered directly. That’s expected behavior, not a broken prompt, but if you mainly work on straightforward code tasks, a lighter model is often the more credit-smart choice. Why does Claude say “Fable 5 requires usage credits”? It depends on your plan. On Pro and Team Standard it’s expected — since July 20, 2026, Fable 5 runs on usage credits rather than your plan’s limits, so you need credits enabled. On Max and Team Premium it shouldn’t appear at all, because Fable 5 is included at 50% of weekly limits; users have reported it as a bug starting the day that entitlement took effect. See the fix for this error before buying anything. I’m on Max and Claude Code still asks for usage credits. Do I need to buy them? Probably not. This is a known Claude Code bug reported on July 20, 2026 — the entitlement check appears to run against the literal model string claude-fable-5[1m] instead of resolving it to claude-fable-5, so your Max inclusion never matches. The workaround is to edit ~/.claude/settings.json and remove the [1m] suffix from the model value. Full detail in the credit errors section. How do I turn on usage credits for Claude? In the Claude web app, go to Settings → Usage, find Usage credits, select Enable, then Add funds to prepay. If you bought your plan through the iOS or Android app, you must do this on the web — it isn’t available in the mobile apps. You can disable credits again from the same screen, which caps you at your plan’s included usage. My usage credits keep switching themselves off. Why? The toggle at claude.ai/settings/usage has been reported displaying Off mid-session while the server still has credits enabled. The giveaway is that clicking it asks whether you want to turn it off — which means it was on. Dismiss the dialog and restart Claude Code rather than re-purchasing. Covered in the credit errors section.
