item.text: How to Use Claude Cowork for Real Work Claude Cowork is most useful when you use it as a supervised workspace for real business tasks. Give Claude a clear outcome, the right files, a focused working area, and a good review process before you rely on the result. This guide starts after setup. If you can open Cowork inside Claude Desktop and run a task, use this walkthrough to choose better business tasks, write stronger Cowork prompts, review plans and outputs, and build repeatable workflows for research, summaries, reports, spreadsheets, file organization, recurring briefings, and project support. Still setting it up? Start with our free Claude Cowork setup guide first. This article intentionally skips installation, requirements, and starter-folder setup so it can focus on using Cowork after setup. For the broader definition, read what Claude Cowork is and how it works. How to use Claude Cowork in one workflow Use Claude Cowork by choosing one specific outcome, giving Claude only the files and context it needs, asking for a plan before actions, approving deliberately, monitoring progress, and reviewing the saved output. Use Claude Chat for quick answers. Use Cowork for multi-step work with files, saved deliverables, projects, schedules, or repeatable instructions. Once Claude Cowork is available in Claude Desktop, the real skill is learning how to assign clear, reviewable work instead of treating it like ordinary chat. When to use Claude Cowork instead of Claude Chat The easiest way to waste Cowork is to use it for work that normal Claude Chat could handle faster. Cowork is an agentic workspace. That means it is better for jobs where Claude needs to inspect files, take several steps, save a deliverable, run a recurring process, or coordinate a project over time. Use normal Claude Chat when… Use Claude Cowork when… You need a quick answer, draft, rewrite, explanation, or brainstorm. You need Claude to work across files, folders, links, notes, or project context. The final output can stay inside the chat window. The final output should be saved as a document, spreadsheet, presentation, report, or organized file. The task has one or two simple steps. The task has multiple steps, decisions, checks, and a reviewable end result. You are asking for advice or text only. You are delegating a workflow that should continue while you supervise at a higher level. You do not need folder access, project memory, plugins, schedules, or file creation. You want to turn the process into a repeatable task, project routine, or scheduled workflow. Simple rule If you only need words, use Chat. If you need Claude to work with a set of materials and return a finished work product, use Cowork. The Claude Cowork operating loop Good Cowork sessions follow a simple loop. This is the pattern to repeat until it feels natural. 1 Choose one outcome Decide exactly what should exist when Claude is done: a summary, plan, table, deck outline, cleaned folder, or report. 2 Limit the context Give Claude only the files, notes, links, and instructions that belong to this task. 3 Ask for a plan Before Claude edits or creates files, ask it to describe the work it intends to do. 4 Approve deliberately Let Claude proceed only when the plan, folder, output format, and risk level make sense. 5 Steer while it works Interrupt or redirect if Claude starts using the wrong source, scope, tone, format, or level of detail. 6 Review the result Open the output, check the facts and formatting, and decide whether the task is worth saving as a repeatable workflow. Your first real Cowork workflow should be useful, but not fragile. Avoid starting with taxes, legal decisions, client-confidential data, account changes, purchases, outbound emails, or anything difficult to undo. Look for a task that has five traits: It has a clear finish line. It uses files or notes you can safely share with Claude. The output is easy for you to inspect. A mistake would be inconvenient, not catastrophic. The process could become useful again in the future. Good first Cowork task Turn three meeting notes into a client-ready action plan saved as a Markdown or Word document. Good first Cowork task Review a folder of research notes and create a structured brief with key themes, quotes to verify, and next steps. Good first Cowork task Organize a test folder of copied documents into clear subfolders and create an index of what moved where. Do not start with your messiest task A complicated business workflow is easier after you have watched Claude complete a smaller task. Start with a workflow you can understand, inspect, and repeat. Claude Cowork works better when the workspace is not a junk drawer. Before you ask for the task, gather the source material into one clear project folder and remove anything Claude does not need. INPUTS Source files Claude should read, such as notes, transcripts, PDFs, spreadsheets, screenshots, or exports. REFERENCE Optional brand voice, examples, style rules, client notes, product details, or background information. OUTPUTS The place where Claude should save the final file, summary, table, report, or presentation draft. You do not need this exact folder structure, but you do need clear boundaries. Claude should know what to read, what to ignore, and where the finished result belongs. Project-Folder/ |-- INPUTS/ | |-- meeting-notes.md | |-- customer-feedback.csv | `-- product-background.pdf |-- REFERENCE/ | |-- brand-voice.md | `-- past-example.md `-- OUTPUTS/ Use copied files while learning When you are testing a new Cowork workflow, work from duplicate files instead of originals. Once the process is reliable, you can decide whether it is safe enough for higher-value work. A good Claude Cowork prompt gives more than a request. It gives Claude a work order. The prompt should explain the outcome, source material, process, output format, approval rules, and save location. Use this Cowork prompt formula Prompt part What to include Goal The single result you want Claude to produce. Sources The files, folders, links, notes, or connected materials Claude may use. Process The steps Claude should follow before writing or changing anything. Output The format, sections, level of detail, and filename you expect. Boundaries What Claude should avoid, ask about, or get approval for first. Review How Claude should summarize what it did when finished. Copyable Claude Cowork prompt template I want you to complete one Cowork task. Goal: [Describe the finished result I need.] Use only these sources: [Name the folder, files, links, or project context Claude may use.] Before changing or creating files: 1. Inspect the relevant sources. 2. Tell me your plan. 3. Confirm the exact output filename and location. 4. Wait for my approval. Output requirements: - Format: [Markdown, Word-style outline, spreadsheet, CSV, slide outline, etc.] - Audience: [Who this is for.] - Tone: [Plain, executive, friendly, technical, etc.] - Include: [Required sections.] - Exclude: [Anything to avoid.] Boundaries: - Do not delete files. - Do not use unrelated folders. - Ask before using web search, connected apps, plugins, or any source I did not name. - If information is missing, list the gaps instead of guessing. When finished: Save the final output in [folder] as [filename]. Then give me a short completion note with what you created, where it was saved, and what I should review. The most important line Ask Claude to confirm the output filename and location before it starts. That one sentence prevents many messy Cowork results. One of the biggest differences between chatting with Claude and using Claude Cowork is that Cowork can take actions. Do not approve a plan just because it sounds confident. Check whether it matches the actual job. Does Claude understand the goal? Is it using the correct files or project? Is it avoiding folders, apps, websites, or data you did not approve? Will the output be saved in the right place? Is the proposed format useful for the way you will use the result? Does the task require any sensitive, external, or irreversible action? If the plan is too vague, ask Claude to rewrite it before continuing. Pause before starting. Rewrite your plan as a numbered checklist with: 1. The files or sources you will inspect 2. The work you will perform 3. The files you will create or edit 4. Anything you will not touch 5. The exact output filename and folder Do not begin the task until I approve this revised plan. Watch for scope creep If Claude starts asking for broad folder access, extra apps, unrelated web sources, or permissions that do not match the task, narrow the job before approving. Claude Cowork can run for longer than a normal chat response. You do not need to micromanage every move, but you should pay attention to the shape of the work. Good signs during a Cowork task Claude is reading the files you expected. It is following the plan it proposed. It is asking before using new sources or taking broader actions. It is creating intermediate notes, outlines, or checks when the task is complex. It reports uncertainty instead of pretending every detail is known. Reasons to interrupt Wrong source Claude starts using a file, folder, website, or connector that was not part of the assignment. Wrong scope The task expands from one deliverable into broad cleanup, research, account action, or unrelated analysis. Wrong output Claude is building a response that will not be useful in the format, tone, or level of detail you need. Pause. The task is drifting from what I asked. Return to this scope only: [Restate the original task.] Use only: [Restate the approved files or sources.] Do not continue with: [Name the action, folder, source, or direction to stop.] Give me a revised plan before proceeding. Do not treat a Cowork output as finished just because Claude says the task is complete. Open the file, inspect it, and compare it against the original request. Use this review checklist The file exists in the right folder. The filename matches what you requested. The output includes every required section. The format is usable without major cleanup. Claims, numbers, names, links, dates, and quotes are marked for verification when needed. Claude did not include sensitive or irrelevant information. The completion note explains what was created and what you should check next. If the result is close but not done, give revision instructions inside the same task thread so Claude can use the context it already gathered. Revise the saved output before we consider this complete. Keep: [What is working.] Change: [What needs improvement.] Add: [Missing sections, examples, citations, tables, or details.] Remove: [Anything off-topic, redundant, risky, or too vague.] After revising, save the updated version to the same output file and summarize exactly what changed. Save the best prompt When a Cowork task works well, save the prompt that produced it. That prompt can become a reusable skill, project instruction, or scheduled workflow later. The real value of Claude Cowork appears when you stop inventing the process from scratch every time. A repeatable workflow gives Claude the same structure, rules, and output format each time you run the task. After a successful task, capture the system What source files did Claude need? What instructions made the output better? What mistakes did you have to correct? What should Claude ask before doing next time? What exact output format should repeat? Where should completed outputs be saved? Turn this successful task into a reusable workflow. Create a clean instruction file I can reuse later. Include: 1. Workflow name 2. Best use case 3. Required input files 4. Step-by-step process 5. Approval points 6. Output format 7. Quality checklist 8. Things Claude should avoid Save it in my project folder as: workflow-instructions.md Over time, these saved workflows become your personal operating system for Cowork. You can keep them as instruction files, project rules, reusable prompts, or Academy-style skills. Claude Cowork includes features that can make workflows more powerful, but each one expands what Claude can use or remember. Add them gradually. P Projects Use projects when a set of tasks belongs to the same client, business area, content engine, research theme, or recurring process. S Schedules Use schedules only after the task works manually. Start with low-risk summaries, reports, reminders, or recurring research briefs. / Skills and plugins Use skills and plugins when they clearly support the workflow. Review permissions and avoid unfamiliar sources until you trust them. Do not automate a messy task A scheduled task repeats the instructions you give it. If the manual version is unclear, unreliable, or too broad, scheduling it will make the problem repeat on a calendar. For changing product details, use Anthropic’s current documentation on Cowork projects and plugins in Claude. For the complete practical workflow, follow our guide to scheduling recurring tasks in Claude Cowork. Practical Claude Cowork examples Use these examples as starting points. Replace the folder names, audience, output format, and review requirements with your own details. Example 1: Turn meeting notes into an action plan Use the files in INPUTS/meeting-notes to create a client-ready action plan. Before writing, inspect the files and tell me: 1. Which meetings are represented 2. Any missing context 3. Your proposed structure After I approve, create a Markdown document with: - Executive summary - Decisions made - Open questions - Action items with owner and due date if available - Risks or dependencies - Recommended next meeting agenda Save the final file in OUTPUTS as client-action-plan.md. Do not invent owners or deadlines. Mark anything unclear as "Needs confirmation." Example 2: Create a weekly business briefing Create a weekly business briefing from the files in INPUTS/weekly-updates. Use only the files in this project folder unless I approve another source. The briefing should include: 1. Top priorities 2. Metrics or numbers mentioned 3. Customer or audience signals 4. Problems to address 5. Recommended next actions Write it for a busy founder who wants the important points first. Save it in OUTPUTS as weekly-business-brief.md. After saving, list any claims I should verify before sharing. Example 3: Compare research files and build a decision table Review the research files in INPUTS/vendor-research and create a comparison table. Before creating the output, identify: 1. Which vendors are represented 2. Which criteria appear in the source files 3. Which criteria are missing or inconsistent After I approve, create a table with: - Vendor - Best fit - Key strengths - Key concerns - Pricing notes if present - Missing information - My recommended next step Save the output in OUTPUTS as vendor-comparison.md. Do not browse the web unless I approve it. Example 4: Clean up a copied project folder I want you to organize the files inside TEST-FOLDER only. Before moving anything: 1. List the current file types and folder structure. 2. Recommend a new folder structure. 3. Tell me exactly which files you would move or rename. 4. Wait for approval. Rules: - Do not delete files. - Do not touch any folder outside TEST-FOLDER. - Preserve original filenames unless I approve a rename. - Create an index file explaining the final organization. After approval, organize the copied folder and save the index as TEST-FOLDER/file-index.md. How to use Claude Cowork safely Claude Cowork can read, create, edit, organize, and interact with approved resources. That is exactly why it is useful, and exactly why it deserves more care than a normal chatbot prompt. Use permission settings conservatively while you are learning. A slower review process is better than letting an unclear task run too freely. Beginner safety rules Use a dedicated working folder instead of giving broad access to your whole computer. Use copies of important files until the workflow is proven. Avoid sensitive financial, legal, health, personal, credential, or client-confidential material while testing. Ask Claude to explain the plan before it creates, edits, moves, or uses connected tools. Use “Ask before acting” for new workflows, unfamiliar sources, and anything you want to watch closely. Do not schedule tasks that send messages, make purchases, change accounts, delete files, or touch sensitive systems. Review outputs before sharing, publishing, sending, uploading, or making decisions from them. Prompt injection matters more with agents If Claude reads a website, email, document, comment, or file that contains malicious hidden instructions, those instructions may try to manipulate the task. Keep Cowork away from untrusted sources when it also has permission to take meaningful actions. For the most current safety guidance, review Anthropic’s official Use Claude Cowork safely article. Common Claude Cowork mistakes Mistake Better habit Giving Claude a broad goal like “help with my business.” Give one finished outcome, one folder, one format, and one review checklist. Letting Claude browse or inspect extra sources without a reason. Name the approved sources and require permission before adding more. Approving a vague plan. Ask for a numbered plan with files, actions, output location, and boundaries. Using Cowork for quick text answers. Use Chat for quick answers and Cowork for file-based, multi-step, saved deliverables. Scheduling a workflow before testing it manually. Run the task several times, fix the instructions, then consider scheduling. Trusting the output without checking it. Open the saved file and verify facts, formatting, sources, and omissions. What to learn next Once you can run a basic Cowork task reliably, the next step is building a small set of repeatable workflows around the work you already do every week. Start with one workflow for planning, one for research, one for document creation, and one for review. Claude Cowork FAQs What is the best way to use Claude Cowork? The best way to use Claude Cowork is to treat it like a supervised work session. Choose one outcome, provide the relevant files, ask Claude to propose a plan, approve only the actions you understand, and review the saved output before using it. What should I use Claude Cowork for first? Start with a low-risk but useful task such as summarizing meeting notes, creating a research brief, comparing documents, organizing copied files, or turning scattered notes into an action plan. Avoid sensitive or irreversible work until you trust the workflow. Is Claude Cowork better than normal Claude Chat? Claude Cowork is better for multi-step work involving files, folders, saved outputs, projects, schedules, or connected tools. Normal Claude Chat is usually better for quick questions, drafting, rewriting, brainstorming, and simple advice. How do I write better Claude Cowork prompts? Write Cowork prompts like work orders. Include the goal, approved sources, required steps, output format, save location, boundaries, and review instructions. Ask Claude to confirm its plan before it creates or edits files. Can Claude Cowork edit my files? Claude Cowork can work with files you give it permission to access, including creating, editing, organizing, and saving outputs. Use a dedicated working folder, avoid broad access, and review any planned file changes before approving them. Can Claude Cowork run recurring tasks? Yes. Claude Cowork supports scheduled tasks on eligible paid plans. Remote scheduled tasks can run without your computer awake or Claude Desktop open, but schedules that need local files, local apps, browser access, or computer use still need the desktop app connected. Test a workflow manually before scheduling it and keep scheduled tasks low-risk. Is Claude Cowork safe for business files? Claude Cowork can be useful for business files, but it should be used carefully. Start with copied, low-risk materials, avoid sensitive data while testing, grant the minimum access needed, and keep a human responsible for review and decisions. What should I do if Claude Cowork starts going in the wrong direction? Pause the task, restate the original scope, name the approved sources, tell Claude what to stop doing, and ask for a revised plan before it continues. If the task involves sensitive material or unexpected actions, stop it completely and inspect the workspace. Official Claude Cowork references Claude Cowork changes quickly, so confirm current access, safety, schedule, project, and plugin details in Anthropic’s official documentation before publishing or teaching a workflow that depends on a specific feature. Get started with Claude Cowork Use Claude Cowork safely Organize your tasks with projects in Claude Cowork Schedule recurring tasks in Claude Cowork Use plugins in Claude
item.html:
How to Use Claude Cowork for Real Work

Claude Cowork is most useful when you use it as a supervised workspace for real business tasks. Give Claude a clear outcome, the right files, a focused working area, and a good review process before you rely on the result.

This guide starts after setup. If you can open Cowork inside Claude Desktop and run a task, use this walkthrough to choose better business tasks, write stronger Cowork prompts, review plans and outputs, and build repeatable workflows for research, summaries, reports, spreadsheets, file organization, recurring briefings, and project support.

Still setting it up? Start with our free Claude Cowork setup guide first. This article intentionally skips installation, requirements, and starter-folder setup so it can focus on using Cowork after setup. For the broader definition, read what Claude Cowork is and how it works.

Quick answer

How to use Claude Cowork in one workflow

Use Claude Cowork by choosing one specific outcome, giving Claude only the files and context it needs, asking for a plan before actions, approving deliberately, monitoring progress, and reviewing the saved output. Use Claude Chat for quick answers. Use Cowork for multi-step work with files, saved deliverables, projects, schedules, or repeatable instructions.

When to use Claude Cowork instead of Claude Chat

The easiest way to waste Cowork is to use it for work that normal Claude Chat could handle faster. Cowork is an agentic workspace. That means it is better for jobs where Claude needs to inspect files, take several steps, save a deliverable, run a recurring process, or coordinate a project over time.

Use normal Claude Chat when… Use Claude Cowork when…
You need a quick answer, draft, rewrite, explanation, or brainstorm. You need Claude to work across files, folders, links, notes, or project context.
The final output can stay inside the chat window. The final output should be saved as a document, spreadsheet, presentation, report, or organized file.
The task has one or two simple steps. The task has multiple steps, decisions, checks, and a reviewable end result.
You are asking for advice or text only. You are delegating a workflow that should continue while you supervise at a higher level.
You do not need folder access, project memory, plugins, schedules, or file creation. You want to turn the process into a repeatable task, project routine, or scheduled workflow.

Simple rule

If you only need words, use Chat. If you need Claude to work with a set of materials and return a finished work product, use Cowork.

The Claude Cowork operating loop

Good Cowork sessions follow a simple loop. This is the pattern to repeat until it feels natural.

1 Choose one outcome

Decide exactly what should exist when Claude is done: a summary, plan, table, deck outline, cleaned folder, or report.

2 Limit the context

Give Claude only the files, notes, links, and instructions that belong to this task.

3 Ask for a plan

Before Claude edits or creates files, ask it to describe the work it intends to do.

4 Approve deliberately

Let Claude proceed only when the plan, folder, output format, and risk level make sense.

5 Steer while it works

Interrupt or redirect if Claude starts using the wrong source, scope, tone, format, or level of detail.

6 Review the result

Open the output, check the facts and formatting, and decide whether the task is worth saving as a repeatable workflow.

Your first real Cowork workflow should be useful, but not fragile. Avoid starting with taxes, legal decisions, client-confidential data, account changes, purchases, outbound emails, or anything difficult to undo.

Look for a task that has five traits:

  • It has a clear finish line.
  • It uses files or notes you can safely share with Claude.
  • The output is easy for you to inspect.
  • A mistake would be inconvenient, not catastrophic.
  • The process could become useful again in the future.

Good first Cowork task

Turn three meeting notes into a client-ready action plan saved as a Markdown or Word document.

Good first Cowork task

Review a folder of research notes and create a structured brief with key themes, quotes to verify, and next steps.

Good first Cowork task

Organize a test folder of copied documents into clear subfolders and create an index of what moved where.

Do not start with your messiest task

A complicated business workflow is easier after you have watched Claude complete a smaller task. Start with a workflow you can understand, inspect, and repeat.

Claude Cowork works better when the workspace is not a junk drawer. Before you ask for the task, gather the source material into one clear project folder and remove anything Claude does not need.

INPUTS

Source files Claude should read, such as notes, transcripts, PDFs, spreadsheets, screenshots, or exports.

REFERENCE

Optional brand voice, examples, style rules, client notes, product details, or background information.

OUTPUTS

The place where Claude should save the final file, summary, table, report, or presentation draft.

You do not need this exact folder structure, but you do need clear boundaries. Claude should know what to read, what to ignore, and where the finished result belongs.

Project-Folder/
|-- INPUTS/
|   |-- meeting-notes.md
|   |-- customer-feedback.csv
|   `-- product-background.pdf
|-- REFERENCE/
|   |-- brand-voice.md
|   `-- past-example.md
`-- OUTPUTS/

Use copied files while learning

When you are testing a new Cowork workflow, work from duplicate files instead of originals. Once the process is reliable, you can decide whether it is safe enough for higher-value work.

A good Claude Cowork prompt gives more than a request. It gives Claude a work order. The prompt should explain the outcome, source material, process, output format, approval rules, and save location.

Use this Cowork prompt formula

Prompt part What to include
Goal The single result you want Claude to produce.
Sources The files, folders, links, notes, or connected materials Claude may use.
Process The steps Claude should follow before writing or changing anything.
Output The format, sections, level of detail, and filename you expect.
Boundaries What Claude should avoid, ask about, or get approval for first.
Review How Claude should summarize what it did when finished.

Copyable Claude Cowork prompt template

I want you to complete one Cowork task.

Goal:
[Describe the finished result I need.]

Use only these sources:
[Name the folder, files, links, or project context Claude may use.]

Before changing or creating files:
1. Inspect the relevant sources.
2. Tell me your plan.
3. Confirm the exact output filename and location.
4. Wait for my approval.

Output requirements:
- Format: [Markdown, Word-style outline, spreadsheet, CSV, slide outline, etc.]
- Audience: [Who this is for.]
- Tone: [Plain, executive, friendly, technical, etc.]
- Include: [Required sections.]
- Exclude: [Anything to avoid.]

Boundaries:
- Do not delete files.
- Do not use unrelated folders.
- Ask before using web search, connected apps, plugins, or any source I did not name.
- If information is missing, list the gaps instead of guessing.

When finished:
Save the final output in [folder] as [filename].
Then give me a short completion note with what you created, where it was saved, and what I should review.

The most important line

Ask Claude to confirm the output filename and location before it starts. That one sentence prevents many messy Cowork results.

One of the biggest differences between chatting with Claude and using Claude Cowork is that Cowork can take actions. Do not approve a plan just because it sounds confident. Check whether it matches the actual job.

  • Does Claude understand the goal?
  • Is it using the correct files or project?
  • Is it avoiding folders, apps, websites, or data you did not approve?
  • Will the output be saved in the right place?
  • Is the proposed format useful for the way you will use the result?
  • Does the task require any sensitive, external, or irreversible action?

If the plan is too vague, ask Claude to rewrite it before continuing.

Pause before starting. Rewrite your plan as a numbered checklist with:
1. The files or sources you will inspect
2. The work you will perform
3. The files you will create or edit
4. Anything you will not touch
5. The exact output filename and folder

Do not begin the task until I approve this revised plan.

Watch for scope creep

If Claude starts asking for broad folder access, extra apps, unrelated web sources, or permissions that do not match the task, narrow the job before approving.

Claude Cowork can run for longer than a normal chat response. You do not need to micromanage every move, but you should pay attention to the shape of the work.

Good signs during a Cowork task

  • Claude is reading the files you expected.
  • It is following the plan it proposed.
  • It is asking before using new sources or taking broader actions.
  • It is creating intermediate notes, outlines, or checks when the task is complex.
  • It reports uncertainty instead of pretending every detail is known.

Reasons to interrupt

Wrong source

Claude starts using a file, folder, website, or connector that was not part of the assignment.

Wrong scope

The task expands from one deliverable into broad cleanup, research, account action, or unrelated analysis.

Wrong output

Claude is building a response that will not be useful in the format, tone, or level of detail you need.

Pause. The task is drifting from what I asked.

Return to this scope only:
[Restate the original task.]

Use only:
[Restate the approved files or sources.]

Do not continue with:
[Name the action, folder, source, or direction to stop.]

Give me a revised plan before proceeding.

Do not treat a Cowork output as finished just because Claude says the task is complete. Open the file, inspect it, and compare it against the original request.

Use this review checklist

  • The file exists in the right folder.
  • The filename matches what you requested.
  • The output includes every required section.
  • The format is usable without major cleanup.
  • Claims, numbers, names, links, dates, and quotes are marked for verification when needed.
  • Claude did not include sensitive or irrelevant information.
  • The completion note explains what was created and what you should check next.

If the result is close but not done, give revision instructions inside the same task thread so Claude can use the context it already gathered.

Revise the saved output before we consider this complete.

Keep:
[What is working.]

Change:
[What needs improvement.]

Add:
[Missing sections, examples, citations, tables, or details.]

Remove:
[Anything off-topic, redundant, risky, or too vague.]

After revising, save the updated version to the same output file and summarize exactly what changed.

Save the best prompt

When a Cowork task works well, save the prompt that produced it. That prompt can become a reusable skill, project instruction, or scheduled workflow later.

The real value of Claude Cowork appears when you stop inventing the process from scratch every time. A repeatable workflow gives Claude the same structure, rules, and output format each time you run the task.

After a successful task, capture the system

  • What source files did Claude need?
  • What instructions made the output better?
  • What mistakes did you have to correct?
  • What should Claude ask before doing next time?
  • What exact output format should repeat?
  • Where should completed outputs be saved?
Turn this successful task into a reusable workflow.

Create a clean instruction file I can reuse later. Include:
1. Workflow name
2. Best use case
3. Required input files
4. Step-by-step process
5. Approval points
6. Output format
7. Quality checklist
8. Things Claude should avoid

Save it in my project folder as:
workflow-instructions.md

Over time, these saved workflows become your personal operating system for Cowork. You can keep them as instruction files, project rules, reusable prompts, or Academy-style skills.

Claude Cowork includes features that can make workflows more powerful, but each one expands what Claude can use or remember. Add them gradually.

P Projects

Use projects when a set of tasks belongs to the same client, business area, content engine, research theme, or recurring process.

S Schedules

Use schedules only after the task works manually. Start with low-risk summaries, reports, reminders, or recurring research briefs.

/ Skills and plugins

Use skills and plugins when they clearly support the workflow. Review permissions and avoid unfamiliar sources until you trust them.

Do not automate a messy task

A scheduled task repeats the instructions you give it. If the manual version is unclear, unreliable, or too broad, scheduling it will make the problem repeat on a calendar.

For changing product details, use Anthropic’s current documentation on Cowork projects and plugins in Claude. For the complete practical workflow, follow our guide to scheduling recurring tasks in Claude Cowork.

Practical Claude Cowork examples

Use these examples as starting points. Replace the folder names, audience, output format, and review requirements with your own details.

Example 1: Turn meeting notes into an action plan

Use the files in INPUTS/meeting-notes to create a client-ready action plan.

Before writing, inspect the files and tell me:
1. Which meetings are represented
2. Any missing context
3. Your proposed structure

After I approve, create a Markdown document with:
- Executive summary
- Decisions made
- Open questions
- Action items with owner and due date if available
- Risks or dependencies
- Recommended next meeting agenda

Save the final file in OUTPUTS as client-action-plan.md.
Do not invent owners or deadlines. Mark anything unclear as "Needs confirmation."

Example 2: Create a weekly business briefing

Create a weekly business briefing from the files in INPUTS/weekly-updates.

Use only the files in this project folder unless I approve another source.

The briefing should include:
1. Top priorities
2. Metrics or numbers mentioned
3. Customer or audience signals
4. Problems to address
5. Recommended next actions

Write it for a busy founder who wants the important points first.
Save it in OUTPUTS as weekly-business-brief.md.
After saving, list any claims I should verify before sharing.

Example 3: Compare research files and build a decision table

Review the research files in INPUTS/vendor-research and create a comparison table.

Before creating the output, identify:
1. Which vendors are represented
2. Which criteria appear in the source files
3. Which criteria are missing or inconsistent

After I approve, create a table with:
- Vendor
- Best fit
- Key strengths
- Key concerns
- Pricing notes if present
- Missing information
- My recommended next step

Save the output in OUTPUTS as vendor-comparison.md.
Do not browse the web unless I approve it.

Example 4: Clean up a copied project folder

I want you to organize the files inside TEST-FOLDER only.

Before moving anything:
1. List the current file types and folder structure.
2. Recommend a new folder structure.
3. Tell me exactly which files you would move or rename.
4. Wait for approval.

Rules:
- Do not delete files.
- Do not touch any folder outside TEST-FOLDER.
- Preserve original filenames unless I approve a rename.
- Create an index file explaining the final organization.

After approval, organize the copied folder and save the index as TEST-FOLDER/file-index.md.

How to use Claude Cowork safely

Claude Cowork can read, create, edit, organize, and interact with approved resources. That is exactly why it is useful, and exactly why it deserves more care than a normal chatbot prompt.

Beginner safety rules

  • Use a dedicated working folder instead of giving broad access to your whole computer.
  • Use copies of important files until the workflow is proven.
  • Avoid sensitive financial, legal, health, personal, credential, or client-confidential material while testing.
  • Ask Claude to explain the plan before it creates, edits, moves, or uses connected tools.
  • Use “Ask before acting” for new workflows, unfamiliar sources, and anything you want to watch closely.
  • Do not schedule tasks that send messages, make purchases, change accounts, delete files, or touch sensitive systems.
  • Review outputs before sharing, publishing, sending, uploading, or making decisions from them.

Prompt injection matters more with agents

If Claude reads a website, email, document, comment, or file that contains malicious hidden instructions, those instructions may try to manipulate the task. Keep Cowork away from untrusted sources when it also has permission to take meaningful actions.

For the most current safety guidance, review Anthropic’s official Use Claude Cowork safely article.

Common Claude Cowork mistakes

Mistake Better habit
Giving Claude a broad goal like “help with my business.” Give one finished outcome, one folder, one format, and one review checklist.
Letting Claude browse or inspect extra sources without a reason. Name the approved sources and require permission before adding more.
Approving a vague plan. Ask for a numbered plan with files, actions, output location, and boundaries.
Using Cowork for quick text answers. Use Chat for quick answers and Cowork for file-based, multi-step, saved deliverables.
Scheduling a workflow before testing it manually. Run the task several times, fix the instructions, then consider scheduling.
Trusting the output without checking it. Open the saved file and verify facts, formatting, sources, and omissions.

What to learn next

Once you can run a basic Cowork task reliably, the next step is building a small set of repeatable workflows around the work you already do every week. Start with one workflow for planning, one for research, one for document creation, and one for review.

Claude Cowork FAQs

What is the best way to use Claude Cowork?

The best way to use Claude Cowork is to treat it like a supervised work session. Choose one outcome, provide the relevant files, ask Claude to propose a plan, approve only the actions you understand, and review the saved output before using it.

What should I use Claude Cowork for first?

Start with a low-risk but useful task such as summarizing meeting notes, creating a research brief, comparing documents, organizing copied files, or turning scattered notes into an action plan. Avoid sensitive or irreversible work until you trust the workflow.

Is Claude Cowork better than normal Claude Chat?

Claude Cowork is better for multi-step work involving files, folders, saved outputs, projects, schedules, or connected tools. Normal Claude Chat is usually better for quick questions, drafting, rewriting, brainstorming, and simple advice.

How do I write better Claude Cowork prompts?

Write Cowork prompts like work orders. Include the goal, approved sources, required steps, output format, save location, boundaries, and review instructions. Ask Claude to confirm its plan before it creates or edits files.

Can Claude Cowork edit my files?

Claude Cowork can work with files you give it permission to access, including creating, editing, organizing, and saving outputs. Use a dedicated working folder, avoid broad access, and review any planned file changes before approving them.

Can Claude Cowork run recurring tasks?

Yes. Claude Cowork supports scheduled tasks on eligible paid plans. Remote scheduled tasks can run without your computer awake or Claude Desktop open, but schedules that need local files, local apps, browser access, or computer use still need the desktop app connected. Test a workflow manually before scheduling it and keep scheduled tasks low-risk.

Is Claude Cowork safe for business files?

Claude Cowork can be useful for business files, but it should be used carefully. Start with copied, low-risk materials, avoid sensitive data while testing, grant the minimum access needed, and keep a human responsible for review and decisions.

What should I do if Claude Cowork starts going in the wrong direction?

Pause the task, restate the original scope, name the approved sources, tell Claude what to stop doing, and ask for a revised plan before it continues. If the task involves sensitive material or unexpected actions, stop it completely and inspect the workspace.

Official Claude Cowork references

Claude Cowork changes quickly, so confirm current access, safety, schedule, project, and plugin details in Anthropic’s official documentation before publishing or teaching a workflow that depends on a specific feature.

  • Get started with Claude Cowork
  • Use Claude Cowork safely
  • Organize your tasks with projects in Claude Cowork
  • Schedule recurring tasks in Claude Cowork
  • Use plugins in Claude

# How to Use Claude Cowork for Real Work
**Claude Cowork is most useful when you use it as a supervised workspace for real business tasks.** Give Claude a clear outcome, the right files, a focused working area, and a good review process before you rely on the result.
This guide starts after setup. If you can open Cowork inside Claude Desktop and run a task, use this walkthrough to choose better business tasks, write stronger Cowork prompts, review plans and outputs, and build repeatable workflows for research, summaries, reports, spreadsheets, file organization, recurring briefings, and project support.
**Still setting it up?** Start with our [free Claude Cowork setup guide](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/setup-guides/claude-cowork/) first. This article intentionally skips installation, requirements, and starter-folder setup so it can focus on using Cowork after setup. For the broader definition, read [what Claude Cowork is and how it works](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/what-is-claude-cowork/).
Quick answer
## How to use Claude Cowork in one workflow
Use Claude Cowork by choosing one specific outcome, giving Claude only the files and context it needs, asking for a plan before actions, approving deliberately, monitoring progress, and reviewing the saved output. Use Claude Chat for quick answers. Use Cowork for multi-step work with files, saved deliverables, projects, schedules, or repeatable instructions.
Once Claude Cowork is available in Claude Desktop, the real skill is learning how to assign clear, reviewable work instead of treating it like ordinary chat.
## When to use Claude Cowork instead of Claude Chat
The easiest way to waste Cowork is to use it for work that normal Claude Chat could handle faster. Cowork is an agentic workspace. That means it is better for jobs where Claude needs to inspect files, take several steps, save a deliverable, run a recurring process, or coordinate a project over time.
| Use normal Claude Chat when… | Use Claude Cowork when… | | --- | --- | | You need a quick answer, draft, rewrite, explanation, or brainstorm. | You need Claude to work across files, folders, links, notes, or project context. | | The final output can stay inside the chat window. | The final output should be saved as a document, spreadsheet, presentation, report, or organized file. | | The task has one or two simple steps. | The task has multiple steps, decisions, checks, and a reviewable end result. | | You are asking for advice or text only. | You are delegating a workflow that should continue while you supervise at a higher level. | | You do not need folder access, project memory, plugins, schedules, or file creation. | You want to turn the process into a repeatable task, project routine, or scheduled workflow. |
**Simple rule**
If you only need words, use Chat. If you need Claude to work with a set of materials and return a finished work product, use Cowork.
## The Claude Cowork operating loop
Good Cowork sessions follow a simple loop. This is the pattern to repeat until it feels natural.
1 **Choose one outcome**
Decide exactly what should exist when Claude is done: a summary, plan, table, deck outline, cleaned folder, or report.
2 **Limit the context**
Give Claude only the files, notes, links, and instructions that belong to this task.
3 **Ask for a plan**
Before Claude edits or creates files, ask it to describe the work it intends to do.
4 **Approve deliberately**
Let Claude proceed only when the plan, folder, output format, and risk level make sense.
5 **Steer while it works**
Interrupt or redirect if Claude starts using the wrong source, scope, tone, format, or level of detail.
6 **Review the result**
Open the output, check the facts and formatting, and decide whether the task is worth saving as a repeatable workflow.
Your first real Cowork workflow should be useful, but not fragile. Avoid starting with taxes, legal decisions, client-confidential data, account changes, purchases, outbound emails, or anything difficult to undo.
Look for a task that has five traits:
* It has a clear finish line. * It uses files or notes you can safely share with Claude. * The output is easy for you to inspect. * A mistake would be inconvenient, not catastrophic. * The process could become useful again in the future.
**Good first Cowork task**
Turn three meeting notes into a client-ready action plan saved as a Markdown or Word document.
**Good first Cowork task**
Review a folder of research notes and create a structured brief with key themes, quotes to verify, and next steps.
**Good first Cowork task**
Organize a test folder of copied documents into clear subfolders and create an index of what moved where.
**Do not start with your messiest task**
A complicated business workflow is easier after you have watched Claude complete a smaller task. Start with a workflow you can understand, inspect, and repeat.
Claude Cowork works better when the workspace is not a junk drawer. Before you ask for the task, gather the source material into one clear project folder and remove anything Claude does not need.
**INPUTS**
Source files Claude should read, such as notes, transcripts, PDFs, spreadsheets, screenshots, or exports.
**REFERENCE**
Optional brand voice, examples, style rules, client notes, product details, or background information.
**OUTPUTS**
The place where Claude should save the final file, summary, table, report, or presentation draft.
You do not need this exact folder structure, but you do need clear boundaries. Claude should know what to read, what to ignore, and where the finished result belongs.
``` Project-Folder/ |-- INPUTS/ | |-- meeting-notes.md | |-- customer-feedback.csv | `-- product-background.pdf |-- REFERENCE/ | |-- brand-voice.md | `-- past-example.md `-- OUTPUTS/ ```
**Use copied files while learning**
When you are testing a new Cowork workflow, work from duplicate files instead of originals. Once the process is reliable, you can decide whether it is safe enough for higher-value work.
A good Claude Cowork prompt gives more than a request. It gives Claude a work order. The prompt should explain the outcome, source material, process, output format, approval rules, and save location.
### Use this Cowork prompt formula
| Prompt part | What to include | | --- | --- | | Goal | The single result you want Claude to produce. | | Sources | The files, folders, links, notes, or connected materials Claude may use. | | Process | The steps Claude should follow before writing or changing anything. | | Output | The format, sections, level of detail, and filename you expect. | | Boundaries | What Claude should avoid, ask about, or get approval for first. | | Review | How Claude should summarize what it did when finished. |
### Copyable Claude Cowork prompt template
``` I want you to complete one Cowork task.
Goal: [Describe the finished result I need.]
Use only these sources: [Name the folder, files, links, or project context Claude may use.]
Before changing or creating files: 1. Inspect the relevant sources. 2. Tell me your plan. 3. Confirm the exact output filename and location. 4. Wait for my approval.
Output requirements: - Format: [Markdown, Word-style outline, spreadsheet, CSV, slide outline, etc.] - Audience: [Who this is for.] - Tone: [Plain, executive, friendly, technical, etc.] - Include: [Required sections.] - Exclude: [Anything to avoid.]
Boundaries: - Do not delete files. - Do not use unrelated folders. - Ask before using web search, connected apps, plugins, or any source I did not name. - If information is missing, list the gaps instead of guessing.
When finished: Save the final output in [folder] as [filename]. Then give me a short completion note with what you created, where it was saved, and what I should review. ```
**The most important line**
Ask Claude to confirm the output filename and location before it starts. That one sentence prevents many messy Cowork results.
One of the biggest differences between chatting with Claude and using Claude Cowork is that Cowork can take actions. Do not approve a plan just because it sounds confident. Check whether it matches the actual job.
* Does Claude understand the goal? * Is it using the correct files or project? * Is it avoiding folders, apps, websites, or data you did not approve? * Will the output be saved in the right place? * Is the proposed format useful for the way you will use the result? * Does the task require any sensitive, external, or irreversible action?
If the plan is too vague, ask Claude to rewrite it before continuing.
``` Pause before starting. Rewrite your plan as a numbered checklist with: 1. The files or sources you will inspect 2. The work you will perform 3. The files you will create or edit 4. Anything you will not touch 5. The exact output filename and folder
Do not begin the task until I approve this revised plan. ```
**Watch for scope creep**
If Claude starts asking for broad folder access, extra apps, unrelated web sources, or permissions that do not match the task, narrow the job before approving.
Claude Cowork can run for longer than a normal chat response. You do not need to micromanage every move, but you should pay attention to the shape of the work.
### Good signs during a Cowork task
* Claude is reading the files you expected. * It is following the plan it proposed. * It is asking before using new sources or taking broader actions. * It is creating intermediate notes, outlines, or checks when the task is complex. * It reports uncertainty instead of pretending every detail is known.
### Reasons to interrupt
**Wrong source**
Claude starts using a file, folder, website, or connector that was not part of the assignment.
**Wrong scope**
The task expands from one deliverable into broad cleanup, research, account action, or unrelated analysis.
**Wrong output**
Claude is building a response that will not be useful in the format, tone, or level of detail you need.
``` Pause. The task is drifting from what I asked.
Return to this scope only: [Restate the original task.]
Use only: [Restate the approved files or sources.]
Do not continue with: [Name the action, folder, source, or direction to stop.]
Give me a revised plan before proceeding. ```
Do not treat a Cowork output as finished just because Claude says the task is complete. Open the file, inspect it, and compare it against the original request.
### Use this review checklist
* The file exists in the right folder. * The filename matches what you requested. * The output includes every required section. * The format is usable without major cleanup. * Claims, numbers, names, links, dates, and quotes are marked for verification when needed. * Claude did not include sensitive or irrelevant information. * The completion note explains what was created and what you should check next.
If the result is close but not done, give revision instructions inside the same task thread so Claude can use the context it already gathered.
``` Revise the saved output before we consider this complete.
Keep: [What is working.]
Change: [What needs improvement.]
Add: [Missing sections, examples, citations, tables, or details.]
Remove: [Anything off-topic, redundant, risky, or too vague.]
After revising, save the updated version to the same output file and summarize exactly what changed. ```
**Save the best prompt**
When a Cowork task works well, save the prompt that produced it. That prompt can become a reusable skill, project instruction, or scheduled workflow later.
The real value of Claude Cowork appears when you stop inventing the process from scratch every time. A repeatable workflow gives Claude the same structure, rules, and output format each time you run the task.
### After a successful task, capture the system
* What source files did Claude need? * What instructions made the output better? * What mistakes did you have to correct? * What should Claude ask before doing next time? * What exact output format should repeat? * Where should completed outputs be saved?
``` Turn this successful task into a reusable workflow.
Create a clean instruction file I can reuse later. Include: 1. Workflow name 2. Best use case 3. Required input files 4. Step-by-step process 5. Approval points 6. Output format 7. Quality checklist 8. Things Claude should avoid
Save it in my project folder as: workflow-instructions.md ```
Over time, these saved workflows become your personal operating system for Cowork. You can keep them as instruction files, project rules, reusable prompts, or Academy-style skills.
Claude Cowork includes features that can make workflows more powerful, but each one expands what Claude can use or remember. Add them gradually.
P **Projects**
Use projects when a set of tasks belongs to the same client, business area, content engine, research theme, or recurring process.
S **Schedules**
Use schedules only after the task works manually. Start with low-risk summaries, reports, reminders, or recurring research briefs.
/ **Skills and plugins**
Use skills and plugins when they clearly support the workflow. Review permissions and avoid unfamiliar sources until you trust them.
**Do not automate a messy task**
A scheduled task repeats the instructions you give it. If the manual version is unclear, unreliable, or too broad, scheduling it will make the problem repeat on a calendar.
For changing product details, use Anthropic’s current documentation on [Cowork projects](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14116274-organize-your-tasks-with-projects-in-claude-cowork) and [plugins in Claude](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13837440-use-plugins-in-claude). For the complete practical workflow, follow our guide to [scheduling recurring tasks in Claude Cowork](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/schedule-recurring-tasks-in-claude-cowork/).
## Practical Claude Cowork examples
Use these examples as starting points. Replace the folder names, audience, output format, and review requirements with your own details.
### Example 1: Turn meeting notes into an action plan
``` Use the files in INPUTS/meeting-notes to create a client-ready action plan.
Before writing, inspect the files and tell me: 1. Which meetings are represented 2. Any missing context 3. Your proposed structure
After I approve, create a Markdown document with: - Executive summary - Decisions made - Open questions - Action items with owner and due date if available - Risks or dependencies - Recommended next meeting agenda
Save the final file in OUTPUTS as client-action-plan.md. Do not invent owners or deadlines. Mark anything unclear as "Needs confirmation." ```
### Example 2: Create a weekly business briefing
``` Create a weekly business briefing from the files in INPUTS/weekly-updates.
Use only the files in this project folder unless I approve another source.
The briefing should include: 1. Top priorities 2. Metrics or numbers mentioned 3. Customer or audience signals 4. Problems to address 5. Recommended next actions
Write it for a busy founder who wants the important points first. Save it in OUTPUTS as weekly-business-brief.md. After saving, list any claims I should verify before sharing. ```
### Example 3: Compare research files and build a decision table
``` Review the research files in INPUTS/vendor-research and create a comparison table.
Before creating the output, identify: 1. Which vendors are represented 2. Which criteria appear in the source files 3. Which criteria are missing or inconsistent
After I approve, create a table with: - Vendor - Best fit - Key strengths - Key concerns - Pricing notes if present - Missing information - My recommended next step
Save the output in OUTPUTS as vendor-comparison.md. Do not browse the web unless I approve it. ```
### Example 4: Clean up a copied project folder
``` I want you to organize the files inside TEST-FOLDER only.
Before moving anything: 1. List the current file types and folder structure. 2. Recommend a new folder structure. 3. Tell me exactly which files you would move or rename. 4. Wait for approval.
Rules: - Do not delete files. - Do not touch any folder outside TEST-FOLDER. - Preserve original filenames unless I approve a rename. - Create an index file explaining the final organization.
After approval, organize the copied folder and save the index as TEST-FOLDER/file-index.md. ```
## How to use Claude Cowork safely
Claude Cowork can read, create, edit, organize, and interact with approved resources. That is exactly why it is useful, and exactly why it deserves more care than a normal chatbot prompt.
Use permission settings conservatively while you are learning. A slower review process is better than letting an unclear task run too freely.

## Common Claude Cowork mistakes
| Mistake | Better habit | | --- | --- | | Giving Claude a broad goal like “help with my business.” | Give one finished outcome, one folder, one format, and one review checklist. | | Letting Claude browse or inspect extra sources without a reason. | Name the approved sources and require permission before adding more. | | Approving a vague plan. | Ask for a numbered plan with files, actions, output location, and boundaries. | | Using Cowork for quick text answers. | Use Chat for quick answers and Cowork for file-based, multi-step, saved deliverables. | | Scheduling a workflow before testing it manually. | Run the task several times, fix the instructions, then consider scheduling. | | Trusting the output without checking it. | Open the saved file and verify facts, formatting, sources, and omissions. |

item.text: Free AI Social Media Post Generator Skill The free AI Social Media Post Generator skill Paste in one idea, note, link, transcript, or rough draft — get back three ready-to-publish posts, each written natively for its platform: a community-minded Facebook post, an insight-led LinkedIn post, and a punchy Instagram post with hashtags. Copy it as a prompt, or install it as a real SKILL.md file. This Social Media Post Generator is a free AI skill that turns one idea, note, URL, transcript, existing post, or rough draft into multiple ready-to-publish posts — one written natively for Facebook, one for LinkedIn, and one for Instagram. Paste in what you want to say, and it returns three posts that each sound like they were written for that platform, not one message pasted everywhere. It writes the same three-post shape every time you run it, so the posts you make this week are as structured as the batch you’ll make next month. That’s the difference between a skill and a one-off prompt: the platform conventions, the hook rules, and the honesty guardrails don’t drift when you come back. It writes copy only — it does not design graphics, schedule, or publish, and it will never invent a statistic, quote, or result to fill a gap. Use it as a copy-paste prompt in any AI chat, or install the ready-made SKILL.md file so it runs on command in Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini Spark. No coding required. The Social Media Post Generator skill takes one input — an idea, a note, a link’s text, a transcript, or a rough draft — and returns ready-to-publish posts written natively for each platform: a community-minded Facebook post, an insight-led LinkedIn post, and a punchy Instagram post with hashtags. It writes copy only — no images, no scheduling, no posting — and it will never invent a statistic, quote, price, or result. Where a post needs a real number or link you didn’t give it, it writes [YOUR INPUT] and lists every gap at the end. It works only from the text you paste in — it can’t browse the web or open a link on its own. You still review and publish the posts in whatever tool you already use. Two ways to get the Social Media Post Generator skill Three native posts in about five minutes Content repurposing, weekly content plan, customer feedback, market research Social Media Post Generator skill: what it needs and what it returns What it isA free AI skill — a reusable set of instructions — that turns one input into posts written natively for each platform. It comes as a copy-paste prompt and as a ready-made SKILL.md file. Who it’s forOwners who need today’s post and do not want the same paragraph pasted onto three different platforms. What you give itOne input — an idea, a note, the text of a link, a transcript, or a rough draft — plus your brand voice. What you get backA community-minded Facebook post, an insight-led LinkedIn post, an Instagram post, one improvement to test, and a “Needs Your Input” list. What it will not doIt cannot read your link, see your page, or check trending topics — paste the text in. It never invents a statistic, quote, testimonial, result, price, date, or client name, and it does not schedule or publish. Time to first postsAbout five minutes. One idea becomes three posts that fit each platform By the end of this AI skill guide, you’ll have the Social Media Post Generator ready to use — as a copy-paste prompt in any AI chat, or installed as a SKILL.md file that runs on command. It handles the part of posting that eats the most time: turning a single idea into posts that each read like they were written for Facebook, LinkedIn, and Instagram, instead of the same caption dropped everywhere. ONE IDEA, MULTIPLIED INTO THREE NATIVE POSTS (example) Input idea: “We just launched our new beginner-friendly AI setup guides so anyone can start using AI agents without knowing how to code.” Facebook version (community & engagement) Want to build your first AI agent but have zero coding experience? We’ve got you covered! We just launched our brand-new, step-by-step AI Setup Guides. They’re 100% beginner-friendly and designed to help you get Claude, Gemini, or ChatGPT fully set up in minutes. No complex jargon, no terminal commands — just clear, bite-sized steps so you can start building right away. Which AI tool are you trying to master first? Let me know in the comments! LinkedIn version (professional insight & value) The biggest barrier to adopting AI in business isn’t the technology — it’s the setup friction. A one-line idea works too; it just leans more on you to fill in the specifics.
Can it read my link, see my page, or check trending topics?
**No — it cannot open a link or browse; paste the text in.** No — and it won’t pretend to. It works only from the text you paste into the chat. It can’t open a URL, log into a social account, or look up what’s trending in real time. If you want it to work from an article or video, paste the text or transcript rather than just a link. That honest boundary is deliberate: it’s better than a tool that quietly guesses at content it can’t actually see.
Will it invent stats, quotes, or results?
**No. It writes a “Needs Your Input” list instead of inventing a proof point.** No. It uses only what you provide. Where a post would be stronger with a real number, testimonial, or result you didn’t give it, it writes `[YOUR INPUT]` and lists every gap at the end under “Needs Your Input.” A made-up statistic or fake quote on a public post is a real trust and legal problem, so the skill is specifically instructed to leave an honest blank instead of filling it.
Which AI tools does it work with?
**Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini Spark all work, plus most general AI chat tools.** Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini Spark all work, and so do most general AI chat tools. The prompt writes the same three posts in any of them. The SKILL.md file installs as a saved skill in Claude and Gemini Spark; in ChatGPT you can use a Project or native Skills to keep it handy.
Can it schedule or publish the posts for me automatically?
**No — it drafts, you publish.** No. This skill writes the copy — you review it and publish it in whatever scheduler or app you already use. Automatic posting means connecting an AI agent to your social accounts, which is a bigger, connected-agent setup. If that’s what you want, our [Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/) walks you through building agents that plug into your tools, with setup help along the way.

What are AI website skills?

Are these AI website skills free?

What’s the difference between the UX Review skill and the Website Copy Refresh skill?

One judges the words, the other judges where they sit. Indirectly, and honestly. Yes — these skills are written as plain instructions, so they carry across assistants. How is this different from a tool like Wix ADI or a web designer?

Different jobs. A site builder gives you a template and hosting; a designer gives you a custom look and their time. **One judges the words, the other judges where they sit.** The [AI Website Copy Refresh Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/website-copy-refresh/) reads your page as writing — is the headline doing work, is the benefit clear, is there proof, is the call to action specific — and rewrites the weak parts. The [AI UX Review Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/ux-review/) reads it as an experience — can a stranger find the button, does the page run in the order they need, does it fall apart on a phone. A page can have excellent copy and still fail because the only call to action is below three screens of scrolling. If your writing is solid and it still doesn’t convert, that’s the UX review’s job.
Do these build the website for me, or do I still need a website builder?
**They write and review your site; they don’t host it.** You still publish in WordPress, Squarespace, Framer, Webflow, or whatever you already use — those tools display the page, and these skills decide what it says and whether it works. Think of it as the copywriter and the reviewer, not the hosting. The [AI Website Builder Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/website-builder/) gives you the whole plan; your builder ships it.
Do I need to know how to code or design to use these?
**No — every skill here is plain language.** Paste your details or your page, get back copy, structure, or feedback in plain English. The Brand Style Guide skill works best when you paste a sample of your own writing, and the SEO Metadata skill pastes its results into your SEO plugin — but none of it involves code or design software. The UX Review skill reads a page the way a visitor would, so you don’t need design training to act on what it finds.
Will these help my website rank on Google?
**Indirectly, and honestly.** The [AI SEO Audit Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/seo-audit/) finds the on-page problems worth fixing, and the [AI SEO Metadata Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/seo-metadata/) writes clean titles, descriptions, slugs, and alt text — which help search engines understand your page and help people click it once it ranks. But rankings depend on your whole site, your content, and your competition. No skill promises a position, and none can see your live rankings. They give you the best possible on-page work; the ranking is still earned.
Can I use these skills in Claude or Gemini Spark too?
**Yes — these skills are written as plain instructions, so they carry across assistants.** Website copy is long-form work, so Claude is a natural home, but each one works in ChatGPT and Gemini Spark as well. You can browse the same skills organized for [Claude](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/claude/), [ChatGPT](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/chatgpt/), and [Gemini Spark](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gemini-spark/), with setup steps tailored to each.
How is this different from a tool like Wix ADI or a web designer?
**Different jobs.** A site builder gives you a template and hosting; a designer gives you a custom look and their time. These skills give you the thinking in between — what the pages should be, what the words should say, and whether the result is clear — which is the part both of those assume you already have. Use the skills to plan and write, then publish in whatever builder you like, or hand a designer a much clearer brief.

Try a rendered browser view or a visual inspection if you have one. Only if that still fails, say so plainly and ask them to paste the copy in. Never describe a page you have not actually read. 2. PROCESS

# SEO Audit

When this skill runs, audit one page and tell the user what to fix first, in plain language, ranked by what matters most.

## Before you start

If the user gave you a URL, try to open it. Do not assume a page is private or blocked just because the first attempt returns a blank page, a loading shell, or a login-looking screen — plenty of sites render client-side and defeat a basic page reader. Try a stronger method if you have one: a rendered browser view, a browser control tool, a screenshot or visual inspection, or scrolling the page.

If you still cannot read it after trying properly, say so in one sentence and ask them to paste the copy in. Never audit a page you have not actually read, and never describe content you are guessing at.

If you do not know who the page is for or what it should be found for, ask for those two things before auditing.

## Process

1. Establish what the page is about, who it is for, and what action it wants.
2. Name what is genuinely working, pointing at the specific section or sentence.
3. Identify the 2-4 biggest gaps, ordered by impact.
4. Write 1-2 quick wins: a concrete instruction, why it matters, effort, and impact.
5. Suggest 2-5 keyword or content ideas with the intent behind each.
6. Close with one clear next step and anything you still need from the user.

## What to look at

- **Search clarity** — does the page say what it does, who it helps, and what it costs or delivers?
- **Headline and positioning** — is there a specific audience and a specific outcome, or vague language like "Solutions" and "Helping You Grow"?
- **Content depth** — enough substance to rank? Missing examples, FAQs, proof, use cases?
- **Content gaps** — a page, section, or resource that should exist and doesn't.
- **Trust and conversion** — a clear call to action, proof, testimonials, a next step.
- **Visible technical issues only** — confusing navigation, unclear URLs, links that look broken, missing image descriptions. Do not speculate about what you cannot see.

## Rules

- Never invent a search volume, keyword difficulty, traffic figure, or ranking position. Label every estimate as an estimate.
- Never promise a ranking, a position, or a timeline.
- Do not claim something is broken without evidence on the page.
- Do not rewrite the body copy — if the copy is the problem, say so in one line.
- Do not write the title tag or meta description here; that is a separate job.
- You cannot check live rankings, open Search Console, or crawl a whole site. Say so when it limits what you can conclude.
- Explain every SEO term in plain language.
- No fear-based advice. Do not make the user feel behind.
- Keep it short enough to act on. Three real fixes beat twenty listed ones.

## Output format

### Summary
One or two sentences on the overall situation.

### What's Working Well
The genuine strengths, specifically named.

### What Needs Improvement
The 2-4 biggest issues, most important first.

### Quick Wins
For each: what to do, why it matters, estimated effort (10 minutes / 30 minutes / 1 hour / under 2 hours), impact (Low / Medium / High).

### Keyword & Content Ideas
For each: the phrase, the search intent, the opportunity level, what to create.

### Your Next Step
One clear action — not a list of options.

### Needs Your Input
Anything the audit needs that the page did not provide.

When the audit is finished, offer to review another page if that makes sense.

MY PAGE: - Page copy or URL: [paste the page text, or the URL if your AI can browse] - Who it's for: [the customer this page is written for] - What I want it found for: [the phrase or topic, or write "not sure"] ```

``` --- name: seo-audit description: Audit one web page and return a prioritized list of what to fix first — what's working, the biggest gaps, quick wins with effort and impact, and keyword ideas with search intent. Use this when the user asks for an SEO audit, a website audit, asks to check my SEO, asks why a page isn't ranking, asks what to fix on a page, or asks for keyword or content ideas for a page they already have. ---
# SEO Audit
When this skill runs, audit one page and tell the user what to fix first, in plain language, ranked by what matters most.
## Before you start
If the user gave you a URL, try to open it. Do not assume a page is private or blocked just because the first attempt returns a blank page, a loading shell, or a login-looking screen — plenty of sites render client-side and defeat a basic page reader. Try a stronger method if you have one: a rendered browser view, a browser control tool, a screenshot or visual inspection, or scrolling the page.
If you still cannot read it after trying properly, say so in one sentence and ask them to paste the copy in. Never audit a page you have not actually read, and never describe content you are guessing at.
If you do not know who the page is for or what it should be found for, ask for those two things before auditing.
## Process
1. Establish what the page is about, who it is for, and what action it wants. 2. Name what is genuinely working, pointing at the specific section or sentence. 3. Identify the 2-4 biggest gaps, ordered by impact. 4. Write 1-2 quick wins: a concrete instruction, why it matters, effort, and impact. 5. Suggest 2-5 keyword or content ideas with the intent behind each. 6. Close with one clear next step and anything you still need from the user.
## What to look at
- **Search clarity** — does the page say what it does, who it helps, and what it costs or delivers? - **Headline and positioning** — is there a specific audience and a specific outcome, or vague language like "Solutions" and "Helping You Grow"? - **Content depth** — enough substance to rank? Missing examples, FAQs, proof, use cases? - **Content gaps** — a page, section, or resource that should exist and doesn't. - **Trust and conversion** — a clear call to action, proof, testimonials, a next step. - **Visible technical issues only** — confusing navigation, unclear URLs, links that look broken, missing image descriptions. Do not speculate about what you cannot see.
## Rules
- Never invent a search volume, keyword difficulty, traffic figure, or ranking position. Label every estimate as an estimate. - Never promise a ranking, a position, or a timeline. - Do not claim something is broken without evidence on the page. - Do not rewrite the body copy — if the copy is the problem, say so in one line. - Do not write the title tag or meta description here; that is a separate job. - You cannot check live rankings, open Search Console, or crawl a whole site. Say so when it limits what you can conclude. - Explain every SEO term in plain language. - No fear-based advice. Do not make the user feel behind. - Keep it short enough to act on. Three real fixes beat twenty listed ones.
## Output format
### Summary One or two sentences on the overall situation.
### What's Working Well The genuine strengths, specifically named.
### What Needs Improvement The 2-4 biggest issues, most important first.
### Quick Wins For each: what to do, why it matters, estimated effort (10 minutes / 30 minutes / 1 hour / under 2 hours), impact (Low / Medium / High).
### Keyword & Content Ideas For each: the phrase, the search intent, the opportunity level, what to create.
### Your Next Step One clear action — not a list of options.
### Needs Your Input Anything the audit needs that the page did not provide.
When the audit is finished, offer to review another page if that makes sense. ```

It decides what to post, where, and when — it does not write the finished posts (use the Social Media Post Generator for net-new posts or Content Repurposing to fill slots from content you already have). It plans only from what you provide; it can’t see your analytics, so any posting-time suggestion is a general guideline it labels as such, not your data — and it never schedules or posts anything. # Weekly Content Plan
When this skill runs, turn the user's goal, channels, and topics into a realistic one-week content calendar.
## Process
1. Confirm the week's ONE main goal, the channels, how often the user can realistically post, and any topics, offers, or events. 2. Pick a single weekly theme that ties the posts together and builds toward the goal. 3. Lay out a day-by-day calendar. For each slot give the day, channel, format, a one-line hook, and a CTA tied to the goal. 4. Keep it realistic for a small team — vary the effort and leave one flexible slot for timely content. 5. Mark which slots can be filled from existing content versus which are net-new. 6. State assumptions clearly, especially about timing.
## Rules
- Use ONLY what the user provides. Never invent audience size, follower counts, or analytics data. - You cannot see the user's analytics. Label any posting-time suggestion as a general guideline, not their data. - Do not write the finished posts here — this is the plan. Name the hook and CTA; leave drafting to a post-writing skill. - Keep the plan achievable. A plan the user can't keep up with is worse than a lighter one they can. - Do not schedule or post anything. Produce a calendar for human review.
## Output format
### This Week's Goal & Theme The goal in one line, and the theme.
### The Calendar Day by day: channel, format, hook, CTA.
### Make It From What You Have Which slots can reuse existing content, which are net-new.
### Assumptions Anything assumed, especially timing.
### What To Decide Choices left to the user before the week starts.
If the user hasn't given a goal or channels, ask for them before building the calendar. ```

## Weekly Content Plan skill: frequently asked questions
Is this AI content calendar skill free?
