ChatGPT Projects are available on free and paid plans, Claude skills are available when code execution is enabled, and Gemini Spark skills currently require Google AI Ultra, or Google AI Pro in the US.
What do I need to give it?
**Your goal for the week, the channels you actually post on, and the topics you want covered.** Three things get you a strong plan: your main goal for the week, the channels you post on, and how often you can realistically post. Add a few topics, offers, or upcoming events and it will build the week around them. A sentence for each is enough — you don’t need a brief.

**No — it plans the slots; the Post Generator and Repurposing skills write them.** No — and that’s on purpose. Can it schedule or post the content for me?

# ✅ Your AI Platform Update Watcher

You are an expert AI Platform Update Watcher.

Your job is to help beginners, founders, creators, educators, coaches, consultants, small business owners, and AI community builders stay current on important AI product updates without checking many websites manually.

Keep the process clear, practical, accurate, and beginner-friendly.

Do not overwhelm the user with too many technical details.

## Main Goal

Create a useful AI update brief that tracks recent updates from:

1. Claude
2. Claude Cowork
3. Claude Skills
4. Gemini and Gemini Spark
5. Google AI
6. Google Workspace with Gemini
7. NotebookLM
8. ChatGPT
9. OpenAI

Always focus on what changed, why it matters, and what someone can do with the update.

## Persona

Expert, practical, clear, and strategic.

You understand AI tools, release notes, product updates, AI agents, connectors, scheduled tasks, creator workflows, business workflows, and beginner-friendly explanations.

You help the user turn AI updates into useful actions, workflow ideas, and content ideas.

## Tone

Professional, concise, direct, and warm/beginner-friendly.

Use light emojis in section headers only when helpful.

Do not overuse emojis.

## Formatting Rules

Use clean Markdown.

Use:

- ## for main sections
- ### for each platform update
- Bullets for lists
- Short paragraphs
- Clear labels
- Direct source URLs
- Release dates when available

Avoid:

- Long technical explanations
- Rumors presented as facts
- Generic AI hype
- Repeating the same update
- Unsupported claims
- Long tables unless the user asks

## If the User Says "Hi" or Starts Vaguely

Use this welcome message:

Welcome. I am your AI Platform Update Watcher. 
I help you track important updates from Claude, Gemini/Gemini Spark, Google AI, NotebookLM, ChatGPT, and OpenAI.

I can create:

1. A daily AI update brief
2. A weekly AI update digest
3. A release notes summary
4. A "what changed and why it matters" report
5. AI workflow ideas based on new features

Tell me what you need, or choose one of these:

- Check the last 24 hours
- Check the last 7 days
- Check Claude updates only
- Check Gemini and Google updates only
- Check all major AI platform updates

## If the User Gives a Clear Request

If the user gives a date range, platform, source, or update type, begin immediately.

If the user does not specify a date range, default to:

- Last 24 hours for daily briefings
- Last 7 days for weekly digests

If the user does not specify platforms, check all supported platforms in this order:

1. Claude / Anthropic
2. Gemini / Google AI / Google Workspace / NotebookLM
3. ChatGPT / OpenAI

## Source Priority

Check official sources first.

### Claude / Anthropic Sources

- https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12138966-release-notes
- https://www.anthropic.com/news
- https://support.claude.com/en/collections/18031719-features-and-capabilities
- https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13854387-schedule-recurring-tasks-in-claude-cowork
- https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13837440-use-plugins-in-claude-cowork
- https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512180-use-skills-in-claude

### Gemini / Google AI / Google Workspace Sources

- https://gemini.google/release-notes/
- https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/gemini/
- https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/ai/
- https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/
- https://support.google.com/gemini/
- https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/changelog

### NotebookLM Sources

- https://notebooklm.google/
- https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/
- https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/search/label/NotebookLM

### ChatGPT / OpenAI Sources

- https://help.openai.com/en/articles/6825453-chatgpt-release-notes
- https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9624314-model-release-notes
- https://openai.com/news/

## What to Look For

Prioritize updates related to:

- AI agents
- Claude Cowork
- Claude Skills
- Gemini apps
- Gemini agents
- Google Workspace integrations
- Gmail, Docs, Drive, Calendar, Sheets, Keep, and Tasks
- NotebookLM
- ChatGPT tools
- OpenAI model updates
- scheduled tasks
- connectors
- file access
- browser access
- memory
- automation
- productivity workflows
- creator workflows
- business workflows
- education workflows

Ignore:

- Small bug fixes unless they affect major workflows
- Pure API updates unless the user asked for developer updates
- Old updates outside the requested date range
- Vague hype
- Unverified rumors
- Duplicate announcements

## Accuracy Rules

- Do not invent updates.
- Do not invent release dates.
- Do not claim a feature is available unless the source clearly says it is available.
- If the release date is not visible, write: Release date: Not clearly listed
- Always include the source URL for each update.
- Separate official updates from commentary or rumors.
- If a source cannot be accessed, say so clearly.
- If no meaningful updates are found, say so clearly.
- Keep the brief concise and useful.

## Required Output Format

Use this structure unless the user asks for something different.

[Insert date range]

Give an excellent 2 bullet concise 1 sentence per bullet easy-to-read overview of the most important updates found.

If there are no meaningful official updates in the requested date range, use this:

No major official updates found for this date range.

# ✅ Your AI Platform Update Watcher
You are an expert AI Platform Update Watcher.
Your job is to help beginners, founders, creators, educators, coaches, consultants, small business owners, and AI community builders stay current on important AI product updates without checking many websites manually.
Keep the process clear, practical, accurate, and beginner-friendly.
Do not overwhelm the user with too many technical details.
## Main Goal
Create a useful AI update brief that tracks recent updates from:
1. Claude 2. Claude Cowork 3. Claude Skills 4. Gemini and Gemini Spark 5. Google AI 6. Google Workspace with Gemini 7. NotebookLM 8. ChatGPT 9. OpenAI
Always focus on what changed, why it matters, and what someone can do with the update.
## Persona
Expert, practical, clear, and strategic.
You understand AI tools, release notes, product updates, AI agents, connectors, scheduled tasks, creator workflows, business workflows, and beginner-friendly explanations.
You help the user turn AI updates into useful actions, workflow ideas, and content ideas.
## Tone
Professional, concise, direct, and warm/beginner-friendly.
Use light emojis in section headers only when helpful.
Do not overuse emojis.
## Formatting Rules
Use clean Markdown.
Use:
- ## for main sections - ### for each platform update - Bullets for lists - Short paragraphs - Clear labels - Direct source URLs - Release dates when available
Avoid:
- Long technical explanations - Rumors presented as facts - Generic AI hype - Repeating the same update - Unsupported claims - Long tables unless the user asks
## If the User Says "Hi" or Starts Vaguely
Use this welcome message:
Welcome. I am your AI Platform Update Watcher. I help you track important updates from Claude, Gemini/Gemini Spark, Google AI, NotebookLM, ChatGPT, and OpenAI.
I can create:
1. A daily AI update brief 2. A weekly AI update digest 3. A release notes summary 4. A "what changed and why it matters" report 5. AI workflow ideas based on new features
Tell me what you need, or choose one of these:
- Check the last 24 hours - Check the last 7 days - Check Claude updates only - Check Gemini and Google updates only - Check all major AI platform updates
## If the User Gives a Clear Request
If the user gives a date range, platform, source, or update type, begin immediately.
If the user does not specify a date range, default to:
- Last 24 hours for daily briefings - Last 7 days for weekly digests
If the user does not specify platforms, check all supported platforms in this order:
1. Claude / Anthropic 2. Gemini / Google AI / Google Workspace / NotebookLM 3. ChatGPT / OpenAI
## Source Priority
Check official sources first.
### Claude / Anthropic Sources
- https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12138966-release-notes - https://www.anthropic.com/news - https://support.claude.com/en/collections/18031719-features-and-capabilities - https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13854387-schedule-recurring-tasks-in-claude-cowork - https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13837440-use-plugins-in-claude-cowork - https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512180-use-skills-in-claude
### Gemini / Google AI / Google Workspace Sources
- https://gemini.google/release-notes/ - https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/gemini/ - https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/ai/ - https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/ - https://support.google.com/gemini/ - https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/changelog
### NotebookLM Sources
- https://notebooklm.google/ - https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/ - https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/search/label/NotebookLM
### ChatGPT / OpenAI Sources
- https://help.openai.com/en/articles/6825453-chatgpt-release-notes - https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9624314-model-release-notes - https://openai.com/news/
## What to Look For
Prioritize updates related to:
- AI agents - Claude Cowork - Claude Skills - Gemini apps - Gemini agents - Google Workspace integrations - Gmail, Docs, Drive, Calendar, Sheets, Keep, and Tasks - NotebookLM - ChatGPT tools - OpenAI model updates - scheduled tasks - connectors - file access - browser access - memory - automation - productivity workflows - creator workflows - business workflows - education workflows
Ignore:
- Small bug fixes unless they affect major workflows - Pure API updates unless the user asked for developer updates - Old updates outside the requested date range - Vague hype - Unverified rumors - Duplicate announcements

- Do not invent updates. - Do not invent release dates. - Do not claim a feature is available unless the source clearly says it is available. - If the release date is not visible, write: Release date: Not clearly listed - Always include the source URL for each update. - Separate official updates from commentary or rumors. - If a source cannot be accessed, say so clearly. - If no meaningful updates are found, say so clearly. - Keep the brief concise and useful.

# Website Builder

When this skill runs, turn the user's business details into a complete, publish-ready website plan built around one conversion goal.

## Process

1. Read the inputs and identify the single conversion goal the whole site should drive toward. Everything else serves it.
2. If the business, audience, or conversion goal is missing or vague, ask two or three short clarifying questions before writing anything. Ask no more than three.
3. Plan the site map first — 5 to 7 core pages in the order a real visitor moves through them.
4. Write the hero: one benefit-led H1, a one-sentence subhead, and one CTA.
5. Write three to four landing sections. Each gets an H2, a short intro, and either three bullets or a two-column comparison.
6. Write the SEO title and meta description inside their character limits.
7. Write an FAQ of five questions this audience actually asks before buying — objections, not trivia.
8. Finish with the single change most likely to lift conversion, based only on what the user told you.

## Rules

- Use only the details the user provides. Never invent a statistic, testimonial, client name, logo, award, or case study result.
- Where a real proof point is needed but was not supplied, write [YOUR INPUT] instead of inventing one. An honest gap is useful; a fabricated number is not.
- Every headline is benefit-led, never feature-led.
- Plain language over jargon. Aim for a grade eight reading level.
- Every CTA starts with an action verb: Book, Get, Start, See, Try.
- One conversion goal drives every section. No secondary CTAs above the fold.
- If the user pasted existing copy, quote the lines that already work verbatim. Do not rewrite what is not broken.
- Return copy and structure only. Do not write HTML or CSS.
- You cannot browse the web. You cannot open the user's live site or a competitor's URL — work only from copy the user pastes in.
- Do not claim a specific result, ranking, or conversion rate. You are proposing copy, not forecasting performance.

## Output format

### Site Map
5-7 pages in journey order. One line of purpose each.

### Hero
H1, subhead, and CTA button label.

### Landing Sections
3-4 sections. Each: H2, short intro, then bullets or a comparison.

### SEO Title
60 characters or fewer. Show the character count.

### Meta Description
155 characters or fewer, benefit-led, includes the conversion goal. Show the character count.

### FAQ
5 questions, each with a two-sentence answer.

### One Improvement
The single highest-impact change, and why it matters for this business.

### Needs Your Input
Every [YOUR INPUT] placeholder you used, listed so nothing ships unfilled.

If the user has not given you the business, audience, and conversion goal, ask for those three before writing anything.

Do not write HTML or CSS. - You cannot browse the web. You cannot open the user's live site or a competitor's URL — work only from copy the user pastes in. - Do not claim a specific result, ranking, or conversion rate. You are proposing copy, not forecasting performance.
## Output format
### Site Map 5-7 pages in journey order. One line of purpose each.
### Hero H1, subhead, and CTA button label.
### Landing Sections 3-4 sections. Each: H2, short intro, then bullets or a comparison.
### SEO Title 60 characters or fewer. Show the character count.
### Meta Description 155 characters or fewer, benefit-led, includes the conversion goal. Show the character count.
### FAQ 5 questions, each with a two-sentence answer.
### One Improvement The single highest-impact change, and why it matters for this business.
### Needs Your Input Every [YOUR INPUT] placeholder you used, listed so nothing ships unfilled.
If the user has not given you the business, audience, and conversion goal, ask for those three before writing anything. ```
Copying the block above costs nothing and needs no account. A free account saves this file to your library so you can download it again from any device — and [All Access](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/all-access/) does the same for every other skill.
**Not sure which to use?**
Start with **Format 1** — you’ll have a page planned in ten minutes with nothing to set up. Install **Format 2** once you know you’re building more than one page, because that’s where running the same instructions every time actually pays. Copied the SKILL.md already? Here’s exactly where it goes in each platform:
[Where It Goes →](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/website-builder/#install)
Part 3 of 5
## Where the SKILL.md goes in Claude, ChatGPT & Gemini Spark
**In Claude it becomes a custom Skill (or a `SKILL.md` file under `.claude/skills/`); in Gemini Spark it goes on the Skills page; in ChatGPT it goes into a Project’s instructions, or a native Skill if you have access.**
### AI skill or prompt? Which one beginners should use
Both formats above contain the same instructions — the only difference is whether your AI has to be reminded every time. Use the prompt for a one-off page, install the SKILL.md once you’re building a site and want the same structure without pasting anything.
For the full breakdown of how a skill differs from a prompt and from a full AI agent, read [what an AI agent skill is](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent-skill/). If you already have a website prompt you like, [turning a prompt into an AI skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/turn-a-prompt-into-an-ai-skill/) takes about ten minutes.
The prompt works everywhere with no setup. If you copied the **SKILL.md** file instead, here’s exactly where it goes in each platform. Website copy is long-form work, so we lead with Claude — but it plans a page the same way in all three.
**Claude**
1. Copy the SKILL.md block above. 2. **Claude app:** create a custom Skill and paste it in — name it `website-builder`. 3. **Claude Code:** save it as `.claude/skills/website-builder/SKILL.md` in your project, or `~/.claude/skills/website-builder/SKILL.md` to use it everywhere. The folder name is what names the skill. 4. Say “help me plan my website” — the `description` line lets Claude fire it on its own.
Prefer no setup? The prompt above works in the Claude app right now. [Browse all free Claude skills →](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/claude/)
**ChatGPT**
1. **Have ChatGPT Skills?** Create a new Skill and paste the SKILL.md in — the description makes it fire on its own. 2. **No Skills access? Use a Project — it’s the quick way.** New Project → Project menu → **Project settings**. 3. Paste everything _below_ the `---` frontmatter into the Project instructions. Projects ignore frontmatter, so the description is just for you. 4. Keep every page of the site in that one Project so the voice stays consistent across them.
Projects work on free and paid plans; native Skills are in beta on eligible work and education plans. New to this? Read [how to use ChatGPT skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-use-chatgpt-skills/) or [how to create a ChatGPT skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-create-a-chatgpt-skill/). [Browse all free ChatGPT skills →](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/chatgpt/)
**Gemini Spark**
1. Open Gemini Spark and go to the **Skills** page. 2. Choose **Create manually**, or upload the SKILL.md file directly. 3. Use `website-builder` as the name and paste the `description` line from the file into the description field — that field is what makes Spark apply it automatically. 4. Select the skill with `/` or `@`, or just describe the page you need.
Gemini Spark skills currently require Google AI Ultra, or Google AI Pro in the US, plus an eligible account and region. [Browse all free Gemini Spark skills →](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gemini-spark/)
**Fill the conversion goal field properly and everything else improves**
Of the six inputs, the conversion goal does the most work — it’s what decides the page order, the CTA, and what gets cut. “Book a 15-minute call” produces a different site than “buy the $49 template.” If you put two goals in that field, you’ll get a site that half-argues for both. Pick one, run it, then run it again for the second if you really need both.
Part 4 of 5
## How to plan a website page in any AI tool
**Say “help me plan my website,” give it your business, audience, and single conversion goal, and answer the two or three questions it asks before it writes.**
Once the SKILL.md is installed, just ask in plain language — “help me plan my website.” Because of the `description` line, Claude and Gemini Spark can offer the skill on their own the moment you describe a page you’re writing. In ChatGPT, open your Website Builder Project and start a new chat.
* Open Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini Spark and start a new chat. * Ask it to plan your website page in plain language, or select the skill. * Fill in all six inputs — especially the single conversion goal. * Answer its two or three clarifying questions before it writes anything. * Read “Needs Your Input,” go get those real numbers and quotes, and re-run.
**New to AI assistants?** Start with our [free AI setup guides](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/setup-guides/) to get Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini Spark ready first — then come back and add this skill in minutes. If you’d rather not do it alone, [All Access](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/all-access/) includes the setup help and every skill’s ready-made file.
Try this starter request — copy it, paste it, then fill in your details:

Ask me clarifying questions first if anything above is vague. Use only what I've told you — write [YOUR INPUT] instead of inventing any number, quote, or credential, and list every gap at the end. ```

## Website Builder skill: frequently asked questions
Is this AI website builder skill free?
**Yes — the prompt is free with no account at all, and the SKILL.md file is free with a free account.** Both the copy-paste prompt and the SKILL.md file are completely free. Optional reusable features may depend on the AI tool and plan you use. ChatGPT Projects are available on free and paid plans, Claude skills are available when code execution is enabled, and Gemini Spark skills currently require Google AI Ultra, or Google AI Pro in the US.
Does it actually build the website?
**No. It writes the plan and the words; your website builder publishes them.** That’s deliberate. It returns copy and structure: the site map, the headlines, the sections, the metadata, the FAQ. You still publish it in WordPress, Squarespace, Framer, Webflow, or whatever you already use. Those tools know how to display a page; they don’t know what it should say. This skill fills the container, and the builder ships it.
Can it look at my current website or my competitors’ sites?
**No — it cannot browse the web or open any URL.** It works only from what you paste into the chat — it can’t browse the web or open a URL, and it won’t pretend otherwise. If you want it to work from your existing copy, paste the copy itself rather than a link. For competitor positioning, run the [Competitor Research skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/competitor-research/) first and paste its notes into the Competitors field.
Will it invent testimonials or statistics?
**No. It is specifically instructed to leave an honest gap instead of inventing a proof point.** It uses only the details you provide. Where a page genuinely needs a proof point you didn’t give it — a client count, a quote, a certification, a result — it writes `[YOUR INPUT]` and lists every one of those gaps at the end under “Needs Your Input.” A fabricated testimonial on a live site is a real problem, so the skill is specifically instructed to leave an honest hole instead.
What do I need to have ready before I run it?
**Three things, really: what your business does, who it’s for, and the single action you want visitors to take.** Six inputs in total, and only those three are essential: what your business does, who it’s for, and the **single** action you want visitors to take. Brand voice, existing copy, and competitor URLs make the output sharper but aren’t required. The conversion goal is the one that changes everything — if you put two goals in that field, you’ll get a site that half-argues for both.
Why does the first output sound generic?
**Yes — the prompt is free with no account at all, and the SKILL.md file is free with a free account.** Usually because the brand voice and audience fields were left thin. “Small business owners” produces generic copy; “restaurant owners who’ve been burned by a generalist accountant” produces specific copy. The other reason is stopping after one pass — the second run, where you say “tighten the hero, cut the third section, rewrite the FAQ in my voice,” is where it stops sounding like everyone else’s website.
How is this different from using website prompts?
**Different shape, same goal: a prompt gets one good page, the skill gets the same structure every time.** Different shape, same goal. A prompt gets you one good page; this skill gets you the same structure on every page, because the site map logic, headline rules, and output format are saved rather than retyped. If you’d rather work prompt-by-prompt in Claude specifically, the [best Claude Fable 5 website prompts](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-fable-5-website-prompts/) covers that approach — and [how to create a website with an AI skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-create-a-website-with-ai-skill/) explains the full method behind this one.
Should I use this or the Landing Page, SEO Metadata, or Copy Refresh skill?
**Use this one to plan the whole site, then the specialist skill for the page you want to finish.** Use this one to plan a whole site and get a solid first draft of every page. Then reach for the specialist skill for the part you want to take further: the [Landing Page skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/landing-page/) takes one offer and builds a single page all the way down; the [SEO Metadata skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/seo-metadata/) turns any finished page into a character-perfect title, meta, slug, and alt text; and the [Website Copy Refresh skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/website-copy-refresh/) fixes a page you already have. This skill gets the whole site standing; those three make individual pages excellent.
Will I be charged during the free 7-day trial?
**No. You verify a card at checkout, $0 is charged for seven days, and you can cancel in one click from your account.** If you stay past day seven it’s $14/mo. Nothing on this page is affected either way — the Website Builder prompt and the full SKILL.md text stay free to copy whether you ever start a trial or not.
Do I need an account to use this skill?
**Not to copy it.** The prompt and the full SKILL.md text are on this page in plain sight — copy either and use it immediately. A free account only matters if you want the ready-made `.md` file saved to your library so you can download it again from another device. The file for every _other_ skill comes with [All Access](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/all-access/).
Which AI tools does it work with?
**No. You verify a card, $0 is charged for seven days, and you can cancel in one click.** Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini Spark all work. Website copy is long-form, so Claude is the most natural home, but the prompt plans a page identically in all three. The SKILL.md file installs as a saved skill in Claude and Gemini Spark; in ChatGPT you can use a Project or native Skills.

item.text: Claude Desktop vs Gemini Spark: Which Is Better? (2026) Claude Desktop vs Gemini Spark is really a choice between two different visions of an AI coworker. Claude Desktop gives Claude a home on your Mac or Windows PC, with Cowork for multi-step tasks, local files, connectors, plugins, browser access, and optional computer control. Gemini Spark is Google’s personal AI agent, built to coordinate tasks across Gemini, Google Workspace, the web, schedules, and — on Mac — the folders you approve. Both can research, work with files, use saved skills, and handle recurring work. But their strengths are not identical. Claude is the more flexible desktop operator; Spark is the more natural Google-life operator. This comparison explains the difference in plain English, including where each one runs, what it can access, which accounts qualify, and which tool is the better fit for specific business workflows. Claude Desktop vs Gemini Spark — the short verdict Choose Claude Desktop if you want an AI agent that can work across local files and many different desktop apps, you use Windows, you depend on Microsoft Office, or you want a flexible system of connectors, plugins, skills, and computer use. Choose Gemini Spark if you use a personal Google Account and most of your work already lives in Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Tasks, and Keep. On a Mac, both can work with approved local folders. Claude wins on breadth; Spark wins on native Google context. For many beginners, the right answer is whichever one already connects to the tools where their work lives. The Important Distinction Most Comparisons Miss Claude Desktop and Gemini Spark are not exactly the same type of product. Claude Desktop is an application. It includes normal Claude Chat and can also provide access to Claude Cowork, Claude Code, local connectors, plugins, and desktop-specific capabilities. Gemini Spark is an agent mode inside Gemini Apps on the web, mobile, and Mac. The closest like-for-like comparison is therefore Claude Cowork inside Claude Desktop vs Gemini Spark. Cowork and Spark are the parts that accept a goal, plan multiple steps, use tools and files, and return a finished result. When this article says Claude can organize a folder, use a connector, schedule a task, or control an app, it is referring to Cowork or another eligible agentic mode inside Claude Desktop — not an ordinary one-response chat. If you are specifically looking for a Gemini Spark alternative, Cowork is the Claude feature to evaluate. Comparing Spark only with ordinary Claude Chat would leave out the local files, schedules, plugins, and multi-step task execution that make the two products real competitors. The simplest mental model Claude Desktop is a workbench. Cowork is the agent working at that bench. Gemini Spark is the agent. On Mac, the Gemini app gives Spark its desktop workbench. That is why the products overlap heavily even though their names describe different layers. Claude Desktop vs Gemini Spark: Side-by-Side Comparison This table reflects officially documented capabilities available on July 26, 2026. Beta features, plan access, languages, and supported regions can change, so verify any must-have feature before subscribing. Feature Claude Desktop with Cowork Gemini Spark Best choice What it is Desktop app containing Chat, Cowork, Claude Code, connectors, skills, and plugins Personal AI agent inside Gemini Apps Different product layers Desktop operating systems macOS and Windows for the full documented Cowork desktop experience Mac app for local desktop work; web and mobile for cloud tasks Claude for Windows Local files Reads and writes inside folders you connect Analyzes, edits, renames, and reorganizes connected Mac folders Tie on Mac Desktop app control Computer use can click, type, and navigate approved apps in research preview Mac tasks span connected folders and supported Connected Apps; direct desktop control is narrower Claude Google Workspace Google Workspace connectors, plus other connectors and plugins Deep native fit with Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Tasks, Keep, and Personal Intelligence Spark Microsoft 365 Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook add-ins; can coordinate across supported apps Not its native center of gravity Claude Reusable skills Built-in, custom, and organization-provisioned skills; can use the open SKILL.md format Creates, uploads, combines, downloads, and automatically invokes Spark skills Tie; Claude is broader, Spark is simpler Extensions Connectors, desktop extensions, plugins, and skills Connected Apps, custom apps, Personal Intelligence, and skills Claude for flexibility Scheduled tasks Recurring Cowork tasks using connectors, skills, plugins, and account files Time-based and event-based schedules across Spark sources Spark for event triggers; otherwise tie Remote local tasks Dispatch can send work from mobile to the desktop; local access needs the computer awake and app open Another signed-in device can start tasks on the Mac; local Mac access needs the app running Tie Finished business files Strong native creation of DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, PDF, charts, and other files Strong Google Workspace outputs and local file operations; output depends on the task and connected app Claude for Office files; Spark for Google-native work Account type Personal and eligible organization plans Personal Google Account only for now; not work or school accounts Claude for teams Best overall fit Cross-app, file-heavy, document-heavy, or technically flexible workflows Personal Google Workspace automation and ongoing life/work monitoring Depends where your work lives Our overall verdict Claude Desktop is the stronger general-purpose desktop agent. It covers more operating systems and offers a broader path from local files to browsers, desktop apps, Microsoft 365, connectors, plugins, and code. Gemini Spark is the stronger personal Google agent. If Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Tasks, Keep, and Google context already organize your day, Spark removes more friction because those systems are its native environment. Local Files and Desktop Control On a Mac, both tools can work inside folders you explicitly connect. That means either one can handle practical tasks such as sorting a Downloads folder, renaming files, extracting information from invoices, or saving a finished report. The important difference is what happens around those files. Where Claude Desktop is stronger Claude Cowork can combine local folder access with connectors, browser work, plugins, and — on eligible Pro and Max plans — computer use. Computer use lets Claude click, type, and navigate approved desktop apps when no direct connector is available. Anthropic says Cowork tries the most precise route first: connector, then browser, then screen interaction. That makes Claude the better fit when a workflow crosses unrelated tools. For example: read a local CSV, check an internal dashboard, update a spreadsheet, and produce a presentation. The computer-use layer is powerful but still a research preview, and Anthropic warns that screen interaction is slower and less reliable than direct connectors. Where Gemini Spark is stronger Gemini Spark on Mac is unusually clear about folder boundaries: Spark can only view the files and directories you add to its Connected folders toolbar. It can analyze, edit, rename, or reorganize those items, and it creates temporary backup files while working. Google says you can recover those backups before the next task; they are deleted when a new task starts or after 24 hours. Spark’s standout local workflow is the bridge between desktop files and Google Workspace. Google gives the example of using invoices saved on a Mac to create a budget spreadsheet and scheduling it to update. If the destination is already a Google Sheet, Gmail message, Calendar event, or Drive workflow, Spark has the shorter path. Local-file verdict: tie for basic folder work on Mac. Choose Claude for workflows that spread across desktop apps. Choose Spark for workflows that start on your Mac and finish inside Google Workspace. If you use Windows, Claude is the practical choice because Spark’s local-folder experience is currently tied to the Gemini app for Mac. Connected Apps and Business Tools The most useful AI agent is rarely the one with the longest feature list. It is the one with reliable access to the systems that contain your real work. Claude: broader and more modular Claude supports remote connectors for cloud services and desktop extensions for local tools. It also has plugins that can package skills, connectors, and supporting resources into a single installation. That modular approach matters if your work is spread across Google Workspace, Slack, Notion, GitHub, local databases, specialized internal tools, and Microsoft 365. Claude’s Microsoft 365 story is especially strong. On supported paid plans, Claude can work through add-ins for Excel, PowerPoint, Word, and Outlook, and Anthropic documents cross-app workflows such as analyzing a workbook in Excel and using the results in a PowerPoint presentation. Gemini Spark: deeper Google context Spark can use Connected Apps, Personal Intelligence, chats, websites you are signed into, location, skills, and schedules. For a personal Google user, that can create a more coherent view of the day than a collection of separately installed integrations. Typical Spark workflows include finding an email, checking the calendar, turning notes in Keep into Tasks, monitoring a topic, or using Drive context inside a larger task. Google has also announced Spark integrations including Canva and Dropbox. Availability and supported actions can vary by account, region, device, and rollout, so confirm the exact connector you need inside your own Spark account. Connected-app verdict: Claude wins for a mixed technology stack. Spark wins if your personal workflow is already organized around Google services. Research, Browser Work, and Ongoing Monitoring Both agents can research the web, work across multiple sources, and produce cited results. The difference is the shape of the research. Claude Cowork is well suited to project-shaped research: gather information from the web, local files, connected services, and project context; reconcile it; then produce a report, spreadsheet, or presentation. This is a strong fit for competitor analysis, client research, due diligence, and one-off reports where the finished deliverable matters as much as the findings. Gemini Spark is well suited to monitoring-shaped research: keep watching a topic, react when a condition is met, and send an update. Google specifically positions Spark for ongoing news tracking and real-time updates involving areas such as sports, finance, shopping, and weather. Spark can also use a remote browser and websites where you are signed in, with confirmations for consequential actions. Research verdict: use Claude for deep synthesis across mixed files and polished deliverables. Use Spark for research connected to Google context, live topics, or an ongoing trigger. Either can do both; this is about the path of least resistance. Schedules and Background Tasks Claude Cowork and Gemini Spark both support recurring tasks, and both separate cloud work from tasks that need access to your physical computer. Claude Cowork schedules Claude can schedule daily briefings, weekly reports, recurring research, file processing, and other tasks using connectors, skills, installed plugins, and files saved to the Claude account. Cloud schedules can run even when the computer is asleep. A scheduled task that needs a local file, local connector, browser, or desktop app still needs the relevant desktop connection. Gemini Spark schedules Spark supports normal time-based schedules and event-based instructions. Google’s examples include a morning briefing built from email, calendar, and Drive, or a workflow that reacts when an email from a manager contains an action item. A saved Spark skill can be attached to a schedule so the output follows your preferred method every time. Scheduling verdict: Spark has the edge when the trigger lives in the Google ecosystem or depends on an event. Claude has the edge when the scheduled workflow needs a wider mix of tools, custom plugins, or polished cross-format deliverables. Skills, Plugins, and Customization Both platforms now support reusable skills: saved instructions, context, templates, and supporting files that teach the agent how to complete a repeatable task. Both can invoke an enabled skill automatically when a request matches. Claude skills Claude offers Anthropic-built skills for Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and PDF work; custom skills you upload; and organization-provisioned skills for Team and Enterprise users. Skills can work in Chat, Cowork, and supported Microsoft 365 add-ins. Claude also supports plugins, which can bundle skills with connectors and other components for a larger workflow. Gemini Spark skills Spark lets you create a skill with Gemini, start from a template, write one manually, or upload a SKILL.md or ZIP. You can combine multiple skills in a task, download a skill as a ZIP, and attach a skill to a scheduled workflow. Google currently limits native skills to Gemini Spark and eligible Spark accounts. The useful portability story is that both platforms understand the SKILL.md pattern. A well-written plain-text skill can move between them with small platform-specific changes. Our free Claude Skill to Gemini Spark converter helps adjust an existing skill when the instructions or tool references need translating. Customization verdict: tie for everyday no-code skills. Claude wins when the workflow needs a richer plugin or connector stack. Spark wins when the skill is part of a simple task-and-schedule system inside Gemini. Documents, Spreadsheets, and Finished Outputs Claude has a clear advantage when the required deliverable is a professional file. Anthropic documents direct creation and editing of Excel spreadsheets, PowerPoint presentations, Word documents, PDFs, charts, and data-analysis outputs. Cowork can combine several source files and save a finished deliverable to an approved folder. Spark is strongest when the output belongs in the Google ecosystem: a Workspace-centered plan, calendar action, organized Drive workflow, email-related task, or spreadsheet fed by connected context. On Mac, it can also edit local files and move information between the desktop and connected services. Output verdict: choose Claude for DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, PDF, complex analysis, and multi-format client deliverables. Choose Spark when the result should stay active inside Gmail, Calendar, Tasks, Keep, Drive, or another supported Connected App. Devices, Plans, and Availability Availability may decide this comparison before features do. Claude Desktop vs Gemini Spark: Which Is Better? (2026)

Claude Desktop vs Gemini Spark is really a choice between two different visions of an AI coworker. Claude Desktop gives Claude a home on your Mac or Windows PC, with Cowork for multi-step tasks, local files, connectors, plugins, browser access, and optional computer control. Gemini Spark is Google’s personal AI agent, built to coordinate tasks across Gemini, Google Workspace, the web, schedules, and — on Mac — the folders you approve.

Both can research, work with files, use saved skills, and handle recurring work. But their strengths are not identical. Claude is the more flexible desktop operator; Spark is the more natural Google-life operator. This comparison explains the difference in plain English, including where each one runs, what it can access, which accounts qualify, and which tool is the better fit for specific business workflows.

Quick answer

Claude Desktop vs Gemini Spark — the short verdict

Choose Claude Desktop if you want an AI agent that can work across local files and many different desktop apps, you use Windows, you depend on Microsoft Office, or you want a flexible system of connectors, plugins, skills, and computer use. Choose Gemini Spark if you use a personal Google Account and most of your work already lives in Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Tasks, and Keep. On a Mac, both can work with approved local folders. Claude wins on breadth; Spark wins on native Google context. For many beginners, the right answer is whichever one already connects to the tools where their work lives.

The Important Distinction Most Comparisons Miss

Claude Desktop and Gemini Spark are not exactly the same type of product. Claude Desktop is an application. It includes normal Claude Chat and can also provide access to Claude Cowork, Claude Code, local connectors, plugins, and desktop-specific capabilities. Gemini Spark is an agent mode inside Gemini Apps on the web, mobile, and Mac.

The closest like-for-like comparison is therefore Claude Cowork inside Claude Desktop vs Gemini Spark. Cowork and Spark are the parts that accept a goal, plan multiple steps, use tools and files, and return a finished result. When this article says Claude can organize a folder, use a connector, schedule a task, or control an app, it is referring to Cowork or another eligible agentic mode inside Claude Desktop — not an ordinary one-response chat.

If you are specifically looking for a Gemini Spark alternative, Cowork is the Claude feature to evaluate. Comparing Spark only with ordinary Claude Chat would leave out the local files, schedules, plugins, and multi-step task execution that make the two products real competitors.

The simplest mental model

Claude Desktop is a workbench. Cowork is the agent working at that bench. Gemini Spark is the agent. On Mac, the Gemini app gives Spark its desktop workbench. That is why the products overlap heavily even though their names describe different layers.

Claude Desktop vs Gemini Spark: Side-by-Side Comparison

This table reflects officially documented capabilities available on July 26, 2026. Beta features, plan access, languages, and supported regions can change, so verify any must-have feature before subscribing.

Feature Claude Desktop with Cowork Gemini Spark Best choice
What it is Desktop app containing Chat, Cowork, Claude Code, connectors, skills, and plugins Personal AI agent inside Gemini Apps Different product layers
Desktop operating systems macOS and Windows for the full documented Cowork desktop experience Mac app for local desktop work; web and mobile for cloud tasks Claude for Windows
Local files Reads and writes inside folders you connect Analyzes, edits, renames, and reorganizes connected Mac folders Tie on Mac
Desktop app control Computer use can click, type, and navigate approved apps in research preview Mac tasks span connected folders and supported Connected Apps; direct desktop control is narrower Claude
Google Workspace Google Workspace connectors, plus other connectors and plugins Deep native fit with Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Tasks, Keep, and Personal Intelligence Spark
Microsoft 365 Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook add-ins; can coordinate across supported apps Not its native center of gravity Claude
Reusable skills Built-in, custom, and organization-provisioned skills; can use the open SKILL.md format Creates, uploads, combines, downloads, and automatically invokes Spark skills Tie; Claude is broader, Spark is simpler
Extensions Connectors, desktop extensions, plugins, and skills Connected Apps, custom apps, Personal Intelligence, and skills Claude for flexibility
Scheduled tasks Recurring Cowork tasks using connectors, skills, plugins, and account files Time-based and event-based schedules across Spark sources Spark for event triggers; otherwise tie
Remote local tasks Dispatch can send work from mobile to the desktop; local access needs the computer awake and app open Another signed-in device can start tasks on the Mac; local Mac access needs the app running Tie
Finished business files Strong native creation of DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, PDF, charts, and other files Strong Google Workspace outputs and local file operations; output depends on the task and connected app Claude for Office files; Spark for Google-native work
Account type Personal and eligible organization plans Personal Google Account only for now; not work or school accounts Claude for teams
Best overall fit Cross-app, file-heavy, document-heavy, or technically flexible workflows Personal Google Workspace automation and ongoing life/work monitoring Depends where your work lives

Our overall verdict

Claude Desktop is the stronger general-purpose desktop agent. It covers more operating systems and offers a broader path from local files to browsers, desktop apps, Microsoft 365, connectors, plugins, and code. Gemini Spark is the stronger personal Google agent. If Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Tasks, Keep, and Google context already organize your day, Spark removes more friction because those systems are its native environment.

Local Files and Desktop Control

On a Mac, both tools can work inside folders you explicitly connect. That means either one can handle practical tasks such as sorting a Downloads folder, renaming files, extracting information from invoices, or saving a finished report. The important difference is what happens around those files.

Where Claude Desktop is stronger

Claude Cowork can combine local folder access with connectors, browser work, plugins, and — on eligible Pro and Max plans — computer use. Computer use lets Claude click, type, and navigate approved desktop apps when no direct connector is available. Anthropic says Cowork tries the most precise route first: connector, then browser, then screen interaction.

That makes Claude the better fit when a workflow crosses unrelated tools. For example: read a local CSV, check an internal dashboard, update a spreadsheet, and produce a presentation. The computer-use layer is powerful but still a research preview, and Anthropic warns that screen interaction is slower and less reliable than direct connectors.

Where Gemini Spark is stronger

Gemini Spark on Mac is unusually clear about folder boundaries: Spark can only view the files and directories you add to its Connected folders toolbar. It can analyze, edit, rename, or reorganize those items, and it creates temporary backup files while working. Google says you can recover those backups before the next task; they are deleted when a new task starts or after 24 hours.

Spark’s standout local workflow is the bridge between desktop files and Google Workspace. Google gives the example of using invoices saved on a Mac to create a budget spreadsheet and scheduling it to update. If the destination is already a Google Sheet, Gmail message, Calendar event, or Drive workflow, Spark has the shorter path.

Local-file verdict: tie for basic folder work on Mac. Choose Claude for workflows that spread across desktop apps. Choose Spark for workflows that start on your Mac and finish inside Google Workspace. If you use Windows, Claude is the practical choice because Spark’s local-folder experience is currently tied to the Gemini app for Mac.

Connected Apps and Business Tools

The most useful AI agent is rarely the one with the longest feature list. It is the one with reliable access to the systems that contain your real work.

Claude: broader and more modular

Claude supports remote connectors for cloud services and desktop extensions for local tools. It also has plugins that can package skills, connectors, and supporting resources into a single installation. That modular approach matters if your work is spread across Google Workspace, Slack, Notion, GitHub, local databases, specialized internal tools, and Microsoft 365.

Claude’s Microsoft 365 story is especially strong. On supported paid plans, Claude can work through add-ins for Excel, PowerPoint, Word, and Outlook, and Anthropic documents cross-app workflows such as analyzing a workbook in Excel and using the results in a PowerPoint presentation.

Gemini Spark: deeper Google context

Spark can use Connected Apps, Personal Intelligence, chats, websites you are signed into, location, skills, and schedules. For a personal Google user, that can create a more coherent view of the day than a collection of separately installed integrations.

Typical Spark workflows include finding an email, checking the calendar, turning notes in Keep into Tasks, monitoring a topic, or using Drive context inside a larger task. Google has also announced Spark integrations including Canva and Dropbox. Availability and supported actions can vary by account, region, device, and rollout, so confirm the exact connector you need inside your own Spark account.

Connected-app verdict: Claude wins for a mixed technology stack. Spark wins if your personal workflow is already organized around Google services.

Research, Browser Work, and Ongoing Monitoring

Both agents can research the web, work across multiple sources, and produce cited results. The difference is the shape of the research.

Claude Cowork is well suited to project-shaped research: gather information from the web, local files, connected services, and project context; reconcile it; then produce a report, spreadsheet, or presentation. This is a strong fit for competitor analysis, client research, due diligence, and one-off reports where the finished deliverable matters as much as the findings.

Gemini Spark is well suited to monitoring-shaped research: keep watching a topic, react when a condition is met, and send an update. Google specifically positions Spark for ongoing news tracking and real-time updates involving areas such as sports, finance, shopping, and weather. Spark can also use a remote browser and websites where you are signed in, with confirmations for consequential actions.

Research verdict: use Claude for deep synthesis across mixed files and polished deliverables. Use Spark for research connected to Google context, live topics, or an ongoing trigger. Either can do both; this is about the path of least resistance.

Schedules and Background Tasks

Claude Cowork and Gemini Spark both support recurring tasks, and both separate cloud work from tasks that need access to your physical computer.

Claude Cowork schedules

Claude can schedule daily briefings, weekly reports, recurring research, file processing, and other tasks using connectors, skills, installed plugins, and files saved to the Claude account. Cloud schedules can run even when the computer is asleep. A scheduled task that needs a local file, local connector, browser, or desktop app still needs the relevant desktop connection.

Gemini Spark schedules

Spark supports normal time-based schedules and event-based instructions. Google’s examples include a morning briefing built from email, calendar, and Drive, or a workflow that reacts when an email from a manager contains an action item. A saved Spark skill can be attached to a schedule so the output follows your preferred method every time.

Scheduling verdict: Spark has the edge when the trigger lives in the Google ecosystem or depends on an event. Claude has the edge when the scheduled workflow needs a wider mix of tools, custom plugins, or polished cross-format deliverables.

Skills, Plugins, and Customization

Both platforms now support reusable skills: saved instructions, context, templates, and supporting files that teach the agent how to complete a repeatable task. Both can invoke an enabled skill automatically when a request matches.

Claude skills

Claude offers Anthropic-built skills for Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and PDF work; custom skills you upload; and organization-provisioned skills for Team and Enterprise users. Skills can work in Chat, Cowork, and supported Microsoft 365 add-ins. Claude also supports plugins, which can bundle skills with connectors and other components for a larger workflow.

Gemini Spark skills

Spark lets you create a skill with Gemini, start from a template, write one manually, or upload a SKILL.md or ZIP. You can combine multiple skills in a task, download a skill as a ZIP, and attach a skill to a scheduled workflow. Google currently limits native skills to Gemini Spark and eligible Spark accounts.

The useful portability story is that both platforms understand the SKILL.md pattern. A well-written plain-text skill can move between them with small platform-specific changes. Our free Claude Skill to Gemini Spark converter helps adjust an existing skill when the instructions or tool references need translating.

Customization verdict: tie for everyday no-code skills. Claude wins when the workflow needs a richer plugin or connector stack. Spark wins when the skill is part of a simple task-and-schedule system inside Gemini.

Documents, Spreadsheets, and Finished Outputs

Claude has a clear advantage when the required deliverable is a professional file. Anthropic documents direct creation and editing of Excel spreadsheets, PowerPoint presentations, Word documents, PDFs, charts, and data-analysis outputs. Cowork can combine several source files and save a finished deliverable to an approved folder.

Spark is strongest when the output belongs in the Google ecosystem: a Workspace-centered plan, calendar action, organized Drive workflow, email-related task, or spreadsheet fed by connected context. On Mac, it can also edit local files and move information between the desktop and connected services.

Output verdict: choose Claude for DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, PDF, complex analysis, and multi-format client deliverables. Choose Spark when the result should stay active inside Gmail, Calendar, Tasks, Keep, Drive, or another supported Connected App.

Devices, Plans, and Availability

Availability may decide this comparison before features do.

Requirement Claude Desktop / Cowork Gemini Spark
Desktop platform Claude Desktop on macOS and Windows; current Windows Cowork setup has additional system requirements Gemini app on Mac for local files; Spark also works on supported web and mobile apps
Plan Cowork requires an eligible paid Claude plan; ordinary Claude file creation is available more broadly Google AI Pro or Ultra. Pro qualified only in the US until July 2026; Google then expanded Pro access to 160+ additional countries, so Pro and Ultra now have essentially the same country footprint
Account Personal accounts plus supported Team and Enterprise organizations Personal Google Account; work and school accounts are not currently eligible
Age 18 or older under Claude’s current access requirements 18 or older
Location and language Available in Claude-supported locations; individual features can vary by plan and rollout Unavailable in the EEA, Nigeria, Switzerland, and UK; Ultra supports all Gemini app languages, while Pro language support varies by country
Required setting Permissions depend on the folder, connector, plugin, or app being used Keep Activity must be on

Spark’s personal-account restriction is a major decision factor

Gemini itself supports work and school accounts in many contexts, but Google’s current Spark requirements say Spark is not available when signed in with a work or school Google Account. If you need organization-managed access today, Claude Team or Enterprise is the more direct path. Check the Gemini Spark availability guide for the latest country and account changes.

Privacy, Permissions, and Safety

Both products can take actions that are more consequential than generating text. When an agent can edit a file, send information to an app, click through a website, or run on a schedule, the cost of a mistake increases.

Claude’s safety model

Cowork limits local file access to connected folders and checks local tool calls against the permissions you grant. Computer use asks before accessing new applications, supports an app blocklist, and can be stopped at any point. Anthropic also warns that computer use has no sandbox between Claude and an approved desktop app, takes screenshots to understand the screen, and remains vulnerable to mistakes and prompt-injection attempts.

Spark’s safety model

Spark on Mac limits file access to Connected folders. Google says Spark is designed to ask for permission before permanent deletion and before sending or sharing files with third parties. The help documentation also warns that Spark may make changes by default when asked to operate on connected files, and that a connected public cloud drive can expose information to other people with access to that drive.

Spark uses information from tasks, schedules, skills, its remote browser and computer, Connected Apps, Personal Intelligence, and websites it interacts with. Google requires Keep Activity to be on. Review the Gemini Apps Privacy Hub before connecting sensitive sources.

Use the same beginner rule in either tool

Connect one dedicated test folder, use copies of important files, keep approvals on, and supervise the first few runs. Do not begin with your whole Documents folder, a shared company drive, financial accounts, health information, or a workflow that sends, deletes, purchases, or publishes without review.

Which One Is Better for Your Use Case?

Feature lists are useful, but actual work makes the decision clearer.

Your main job Better starting point Why
Organize files on a Mac Either Both work with explicitly connected folders; Spark adds temporary backups, while Claude offers broader follow-on tools
Organize files on Windows Claude Desktop Claude documents the full Cowork desktop experience on Windows; Spark local files currently require the Mac app
Daily Gmail and Calendar brief Gemini Spark Google services, schedules, and personal context are Spark’s native environment
Create a client-ready Word report Claude Desktop Claude has dedicated document skills and direct DOCX creation
Build and format an Excel model Claude Desktop Claude has native Excel file creation plus an Excel add-in on supported plans
Turn Keep notes into Tasks Gemini Spark Keep and Tasks are native Connected Apps in the Google ecosystem
Work across mixed desktop apps Claude Desktop Connectors, browser use, and optional computer control provide more routes
Monitor a topic and react to an event Gemini Spark Spark emphasizes ongoing tracking and event-based schedules
Build a custom reusable workflow Either Both support native skills and a portable SKILL.md pattern
Deploy to a managed business team Claude Spark currently requires a personal Google Account; Claude supports Team and Enterprise controls
Lowest-friction first agent Whichever matches your existing stack Integrating with the tools you already use matters more than winning every feature row

Claude Desktop or Gemini Spark: The Final Decision

Use these questions in order:

  1. Do you use Windows for local agent work? Choose Claude Desktop.
  2. Is this for a work or school Google account? Spark is not currently eligible; choose Claude or wait for access to expand.
  3. Does most of the workflow live in Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Tasks, and Keep? Choose Gemini Spark.
  4. Does the workflow cross local files, browsers, desktop apps, or several non-Google tools? Choose Claude Desktop.
  5. Is the finished result a Word document, Excel model, PowerPoint deck, or PDF? Start with Claude.
  6. Is the task an ongoing monitor or event-driven Google workflow? Start with Spark.
  7. Are you still unsure? Test the same low-risk task in both using the same skill, source files, and acceptance criteria.

The bottom line: Claude Desktop is the better all-purpose desktop AI agent for most mixed-tool business workflows. Gemini Spark is the better specialist for eligible personal Google users. The strongest reason to choose Claude is flexibility; the strongest reason to choose Spark is native context. Choose based on where your work lives, not which logo you prefer.
