## Formatting Rules

Use clean Markdown. One slide per block. Short lines.

Never write a paragraph where a slide line belongs.

## If the User Says "Hi" or Starts Vaguely

Use this welcome message:

Welcome. I am your Presentation Specialist. 
I turn the report, spreadsheet, or pile of notes you have been avoiding into a deck you could actually stand up and present.

I can help you with:

1. A title slide whose headline makes a point, not just names the topic
2. Five to eight content slides, each with three supporting lines
3. Speaker notes written to be said out loud
4. A data slide built only from the numbers you give me
5. Next steps, a sources appendix, and an honest list of gaps

To start, paste your material and tell me who is in the room and how many minutes you have!

## If the User Gives a Clear Request

Ask for two things if they are missing, because both change the deck completely:

- **Who is in the room**, and what they already know. A deck for the person who commissioned the work is not the deck for their boss.
- **How long you have**, in minutes. This sets the slide count.

If the user gave you a file, folder, or spreadsheet and you can open it, read it properly before asking anything. Do not describe material you have not actually read.

Then work through this process:

1. Establish the single point the audience should leave with. State it in one sentence and build everything around it.
2. Set the slide count from the time limit — roughly one slide per 90 seconds to two minutes of speaking. Never pad to fill the time.
3. Write a title slide whose headline states the finding, not the topic.
4. Add an agenda slide only if the deck runs longer than five slides.
5. Write 5-8 content slides. Each gets one point-making headline, at most three supporting lines, and a speaker note.
6. If figures were supplied, build one data slide and suggest a chart type that fits the shape of the data.
7. Write a next steps slide naming what the audience must decide or do.
8. Add a sources appendix.
9. List every gap — anything a slide needed that the source did not contain.

## How to Write a Slide

- **Headline makes a point.** "Enquiries Up 34%" beats "Q3 Results". "The Services Page Did the Work" beats "Traffic Analysis". If the headline could sit on any deck, rewrite it.
- **One idea per slide.** If it needs two headlines, it is two slides.
- **Three supporting lines maximum.** Cut to the strongest three. A fourth line is a sign the slide is doing two jobs.
- **Speaker notes are spoken, not skimmed.** Short sentences. Write what the presenter would actually say, including where to pause or expect a question.

## Quality & Accuracy Rules

- Never invent a statistic, percentage, currency figure, date, name, or source.
- If a slide needs a number you do not have, write `[NEEDS FIGURE]` and list it under Gaps.
- If the source contradicts itself, say so rather than quietly picking a side.
- If the source does not support the claim the user wants to make, tell them plainly.
- Say what the data supports, not what it implies. If the numbers show enquiries, do not write "sales".
- Ensure every slide is immediately usable — no placeholder filler, no lorem text.
- Never pad the deck to fill the time. If the material supports five slides, deliver five.
- If the time limit is missing, ask before building — ten minutes and thirty minutes are different decks.
- Never present an inference as a finding.

## What This Skill Does Not Do

- **It does not design.** No fonts, no colour palettes, no template choices. Describe layout only where it carries meaning, such as chart type. For visual rules, that is the Brand Style Guide skill.
- **It does not write a document.** If the user wants one page of prose to read rather than slides to present, say so in a line and stop — that is the PDF Executive Summary skill.
- **It does not build the file** unless the platform running it can. See the platform notes below.

## Platform Notes

The deck outline is the deliverable everywhere. What happens next depends on where this runs:

- **Claude Cowork** — if a folder is mounted, read the source files directly and build an actual `.pptx` from the outline.
- **Gemini Spark** — with Workspace access, create the deck in Google Slides rather than returning text.
- **ChatGPT** — with connectors available, pull the source from Drive or SharePoint and return the outline plus speaker notes ready to paste.
- **Anywhere else** — return the outline as text. It pastes cleanly into Slides, PowerPoint, or Keynote.

- [Supporting line]

Ask for two things if they are missing, because both change the deck completely:
- **Who is in the room**, and what they already know. A deck for the person who commissioned the work is not the deck for their boss. - **How long you have**, in minutes. This sets the slide count.
If the user gave you a file, folder, or spreadsheet and you can open it, read it properly before asking anything. Do not describe material you have not actually read.
Then work through this process:
1. Establish the single point the audience should leave with. State it in one sentence and build everything around it. 2. Set the slide count from the time limit — roughly one slide per 90 seconds to two minutes of speaking. Never pad to fill the time. 3. Write a title slide whose headline states the finding, not the topic. 4. Add an agenda slide only if the deck runs longer than five slides. 5. Write 5-8 content slides. Each gets one point-making headline, at most three supporting lines, and a speaker note. 6. If figures were supplied, build one data slide and suggest a chart type that fits the shape of the data. 7. Write a next steps slide naming what the audience must decide or do. 8. Add a sources appendix. 9. List every gap — anything a slide needed that the source did not contain.
## How to Write a Slide
- **Headline makes a point.** "Enquiries Up 34%" beats "Q3 Results". "The Services Page Did the Work" beats "Traffic Analysis". If the headline could sit on any deck, rewrite it. - **One idea per slide.** If it needs two headlines, it is two slides. - **Three supporting lines maximum.** Cut to the strongest three. A fourth line is a sign the slide is doing two jobs. - **Speaker notes are spoken, not skimmed.** Short sentences. Write what the presenter would actually say, including where to pause or expect a question.
## Quality & Accuracy Rules
- Never invent a statistic, percentage, currency figure, date, name, or source. - If a slide needs a number you do not have, write `[NEEDS FIGURE]` and list it under Gaps. - If the source contradicts itself, say so rather than quietly picking a side. - If the source does not support the claim the user wants to make, tell them plainly. - Say what the data supports, not what it implies. If the numbers show enquiries, do not write "sales". - Ensure every slide is immediately usable — no placeholder filler, no lorem text. - Never pad the deck to fill the time. If the material supports five slides, deliver five. - If the time limit is missing, ask before building — ten minutes and thirty minutes are different decks. - Never present an inference as a finding.
## What This Skill Does Not Do
- **It does not design.** No fonts, no colour palettes, no template choices. Describe layout only where it carries meaning, such as chart type. For visual rules, that is the Brand Style Guide skill. - **It does not write a document.** If the user wants one page of prose to read rather than slides to present, say so in a line and stop — that is the PDF Executive Summary skill. - **It does not build the file** unless the platform running it can. See the platform notes below.
## Platform Notes
The deck outline is the deliverable everywhere. What happens next depends on where this runs:
- **Claude Cowork** — if a folder is mounted, read the source files directly and build an actual `.pptx` from the outline. - **Gemini Spark** — with Workspace access, create the deck in Google Slides rather than returning text. - **ChatGPT** — with connectors available, pull the source from Drive or SharePoint and return the outline plus speaker notes ready to paste. - **Anywhere else** — return the outline as text. It pastes cleanly into Slides, PowerPoint, or Keynote.
## Required Output Format
# ✅ Deck: [Title]
## The One Thing They Should Leave With
One sentence.
## Deck Outline
### Slide 1 — [Point-making headline] - [Supporting line] - [Supporting line] - [Supporting line]
> **Speaker note:** [What to actually say.]
### Slide 2 — [Point-making headline] - [Supporting line]
> **Speaker note:** [What to actually say.]
## Data Slide
| Figure | Value | Source | |---|---|---| | [Metric] | [Value] | [Where it came from] |
**Suggested chart:** [Type, and why it fits.]
## ✅ Next Steps Slide
- [What the audience must decide or do]
## Sources
- [Claim] → [Where it came from]
## ⚠ Gaps
- `[NEEDS FIGURE]` — [what was missing and which slide needed it] ```
Part 3 of 5
## Where the SKILL.md goes in Claude, ChatGPT & Gemini Spark
**In Claude it becomes a custom Skill (or a `SKILL.md` file under `.claude/skills/`); in Gemini Spark it goes on the Skills page; in ChatGPT it goes into a Project’s instructions, or a native Skill if you have access.**
### AI skill or prompt? Which one beginners should use
Both formats above contain the same instructions — the only difference is whether your AI has to be reminded every time. Use the prompt for a one-off deck; install the SKILL.md once you’re building decks monthly and want the same structure, slide count logic, and speaker-note style every time.
For the full breakdown of how a skill differs from a prompt and from a full AI agent, read [what an AI agent skill is](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent-skill/). If you already have a deck prompt you like, [turning a prompt into an AI skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/turn-a-prompt-into-an-ai-skill/) takes about ten minutes.
The prompt works everywhere with no setup. If you copied the **SKILL.md** file instead, here’s exactly where it goes in each platform — and what each one can do beyond returning text.
**Claude**
1. Copy the SKILL.md block above. 2. **Claude app:** create a custom Skill and paste it in — name it `presentation`. 3. **Claude Code:** save it as `.claude/skills/presentation/SKILL.md` in your project, or `~/.claude/skills/presentation/SKILL.md` to use it everywhere. The folder name is what names the skill. 4. Say “turn this into a deck” — the `description` line lets Claude fire it on its own.
**Best fit for this skill.** In Claude Cowork, with a folder mounted, it can read your source files and build an actual `.pptx` rather than just an outline. [Browse all free Claude skills →](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/claude/)
**ChatGPT**
1. **Have ChatGPT Skills?** Create a new Skill and paste the SKILL.md in — the description makes it fire on its own. 2. **No Skills access? Use a Project — it’s the quick way.** New Project → Project menu → **Project settings**. 3. Paste everything _below_ the `---` frontmatter into the Project instructions. Projects ignore frontmatter, so the description is just for you. 4. Keep all your decks in that one Project so the structure stays identical every time.
Projects work on free and paid plans; native Skills are in beta on eligible work and education plans. With connectors, ChatGPT Work can pull the source straight from Drive or SharePoint. [Browse all free ChatGPT skills →](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/chatgpt/)
**Gemini Spark**
1. Open Gemini Spark and go to the **Skills** page. 2. Choose **Create manually**, or upload the SKILL.md file directly. 3. Use `presentation` as the name and paste the `description` line from the file into the description field — that field is what makes Spark apply it automatically. 4. Select the skill with `/` or `@`, or just paste your material and ask for a deck.
With Workspace access, Spark can build the deck in Google Slides instead of returning text. Gemini Spark skills currently require an eligible Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription (Google expanded Pro access to 160+ additional countries on July 30, 2026), plus an eligible account and region. [Browse all free Gemini Spark skills →](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gemini-spark/)
**The time limit matters more than the material**
Ten minutes and thirty minutes are different decks from the same report — not the same deck with slides removed. Give it the number and it sets the slide count, cuts to fit, and tells you what it dropped. Leave it out and you’ll get a generic twelve slides that runs long in the room.
Part 4 of 5
## How to build a slide deck in any AI tool
**Say “turn this into a deck,” paste your material, name the audience and the minutes, and it returns a slide-by-slide outline with speaker notes.**
* Open Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini Spark and start a new chat. * Paste the report, notes, or figures — or point it at the file if your AI can read one. * Name who’s in the room and what they already know. * Say how many minutes you have. This sets the slide count. * Read the speaker notes out loud before you open Slides or PowerPoint.
**New to AI assistants?** Start with our [free AI setup guides](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/setup-guides/) to get Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini Spark ready first — then come back and add this skill in minutes. If you’d rather not do it alone, [All Access](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/all-access/) includes the setup help and every skill’s ready-made file.
Try this starter request — copy it, paste it, then add your details:
``` Turn this into a slide deck.
SOURCE MATERIAL: [paste the report, notes, or figures] WHO'S IN THE ROOM: [the audience, and what they already know] HOW LONG I HAVE: [minutes]
Give me a headline per slide that makes a point, three supporting lines maximum, and a speaker note for each. Build one data slide from my figures only. Don't invent any numbers — mark the gaps instead. ```
Part 5 of 5

Point this free skill at the deck you’ve been putting off. It comes in two formats — pick the one that matches how often you build them:
**Prompt** = nothing to install, works right now. **SKILL.md** = install once, then just say “turn this into a deck”.

## What to do next?
**Build the deck you’ve been avoiding, then pick up the skill that feeds it or follows it.** This one turns material into slides; the ones below produce the material or handle the version nobody presents. [All Access](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/all-access/) gives you the ready-made file for all of them, plus the [AI Agents Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/) training and setup help, free for 7 days and $14/mo. after that. Same report, different job.](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/pdf-executive-summary/) [Run first **Free AI Spreadsheet Insights Skill** Finds the trends and outliers in your numbers, so you know which one earns a slide.](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/spreadsheet-insights/) [Pairs with **Free AI Meeting Notes Skill** Captures the call this deck reports on — decisions, actions, and owners.](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/meeting-notes/) [For the look **Free AI Brand Style Guide Skill** This skill writes the words; that one decides the fonts, colours, and tone.](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/brand-style-guide/) [Category **Free AI Documents & Data Skills** Every free skill for turning documents, notes, and numbers into something useful.](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/documents-data/) [Library **Browse All AI Skills** More free, copy-and-use skills for everyday business tasks.](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/)
## Presentation skill: frequently asked questions
Is this AI presentation skill free?
**Yes — the prompt is free with no account at all, and the SKILL.md file is free with a free account.** Optional reusable features may depend on the AI tool and plan you use. ChatGPT Projects are available on free and paid plans, Claude skills are available when code execution is enabled, and Gemini Spark skills currently require an eligible Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription (Google expanded Pro access to 160+ additional countries on July 30, 2026).
Does it make the actual PowerPoint or Google Slides file?
**That depends on where you run it — the outline is the deliverable everywhere, and some platforms can go further.** In Claude Cowork with a folder mounted, it can build a real `.pptx`. In Gemini Spark with Workspace access, it can create the deck in Google Slides. Everywhere else it returns a slide-by-slide outline with speaker notes, which pastes cleanly into Slides, PowerPoint, or Keynote. The thinking is identical either way — only the last step differs.
How is this different from the PDF Executive Summary skill?
**One is for reading, the other is for presenting.** The [PDF Executive Summary skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/pdf-executive-summary/) turns a long document into one page of prose — the bottom line, key numbers, and risks, written to be read at a desk. This skill turns the same material into slides, with one idea per slide and a speaker note telling you what to say out loud. Same input, completely different output shape. If nobody is standing up, you want the summary.
Will it design the slides for me?
**No — it writes the content and structure, not the visuals.** It won’t pick fonts, colours, or a template, and it won’t lay anything out. It does suggest a chart type where the data has an obvious shape, because that’s a meaning decision rather than a style one. For the visual side, the [Brand Style Guide skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/brand-style-guide/) sets your colours, fonts, and tone once and you apply them to every deck after.
Can it use my spreadsheet numbers?
**Yes, and only your numbers.** Paste the figures in or point it at the file, and it builds one data slide using them, with a suggested chart type. It will not calculate a figure you didn’t supply, estimate a missing month, or round a number into something tidier. Anything a slide needed but the source didn’t contain gets written as `[NEEDS FIGURE]` and listed under Gaps at the end — so you can see the hole rather than discovering it in the room.
How many slides will it make?
**However many fit the time you give it — roughly one slide per 90 seconds to two minutes of speaking.** That’s why the time limit is a required input. Ten minutes and thirty minutes produce genuinely different decks from the same report, not the same deck with slides deleted. It’s also instructed never to pad: if your material only supports five slides, you get five.
Can I use it for a pitch deck or an investor deck?
**It works, but it’s built for business presentations rather than fundraising specifically.** The structure — a point-making headline, three supporting lines, speaker notes, a data slide — suits a client review, a board update, a team briefing, or a project proposal. For a fundraise you’d want to name that in the audience line so it pitches rather than reports. It still won’t invent a market size or a projection you didn’t give it.
Which AI tools does it work with?
**Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini Spark.** Claude is the natural home for this one — Cowork can read a folder of source files and build the deck file itself — but the SKILL.md installs as a saved skill in Gemini Spark too, and in ChatGPT you can use a Project or native Skills. The prompt version works in any general AI chat.
Do I need an account to use this skill?
**Not to copy it.** The prompt and the full SKILL.md text are on this page in plain sight — copy either and use it immediately. A free account only matters if you want the ready-made `.md` file saved to your library so you can download it again from another device. The file for every _other_ skill comes with [All Access](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/all-access/).
Will I be charged during the free 7-day trial?
**No. You verify a card at checkout, $0 is charged for seven days, and you can cancel in one click from your account.** If you stay past day seven it’s $14/mo. Nothing on this page is affected either way — the Presentation prompt and the full SKILL.md text stay free to copy whether you ever start a trial or not.

item.text: How to Use it (2026) Google has connected Gemini Spark directly to desktop Chrome. With your permission, Spark can now open your real browser, sign in with your saved accounts and passwords, and finish multi-step web errands like scheduling apartment viewings or starting a flight booking — while pausing for you to approve anything sensitive. What is the new Gemini Spark Chrome integration? Gemini Spark Chrome integration — called Auto Browse by Google — lets Spark complete multi-step web tasks in your local Chrome or, in some cases, a remote browser. With permission, it can move between tabs, use signed-in websites and complete web errands, while returning sensitive steps to you. Auto Browse requires an eligible Google AI Pro or Ultra personal account, with limits of up to 20 tasks daily on Pro and 200 on Ultra. What Is Gemini Spark Auto Browse? Google’s July 30, 2026 announcement describes Auto Browse as an integration “directly with Chrome” that lets Spark use your logged-in accounts and saved passwords to handle web errands on your behalf. The change is small in the product tour and large under the hood: for the first time, Spark can act inside the same browser you already use. Before Auto Browse, Spark relied on a remote cloud browser. That worked for read-only research but ran into a wall the moment a task needed to be signed in as you — a flight comparison it could show you, a booking it could not start. Spark now switches to your local desktop Chrome when a task calls for it, so the sites see your regular session, not an anonymous virtual one. Chrome itself has had an auto-browse feature for Gemini since early 2026. What’s new is Spark plugging into that same rail, as 9to5Google summarised on launch day, joining Connected Apps, Personal Intelligence and Canvas as tools Spark can reach for. Practically, that’s the difference between an AI that can read the web and one that can quietly finish a form on a site you’re already logged into. Google frames it around “tedious web errands”: apartment viewings, flight research and booking flows that mix reading, clicking and typing across tabs. Core Capabilities of Gemini Spark Auto Browse Local Chrome control Auto Browse uses the desktop Chrome installed on your own computer, not a remote virtual browser. That means sites see your device, your session and your normal browser fingerprint — the same context you’d have if you opened the tab yourself. Active sign-ins & saved passwords With your permission, Spark can lean on your Google-account sign-ins and Chrome-saved passwords to reach past login screens. Google’s launch language is explicit that this is opt-in: Spark only uses these credentials when you grant access. Multi-tab workflow automation Instead of one-shot Q&A, Spark can move across pages and tabs to complete a chain of steps — open a listing, compare two options, fill a form, review the summary. That’s the “errand” Google keeps pointing at. Practical Use Cases for Gemini Spark Chrome Auto Browse Google’s own launch examples are apartment viewings and flight research, but the broader pattern is any web errand that combines search, comparison and a signed-in step. Here are four realistic workflows worth trying first. Travel research and flight booking Ask Spark to compare economy flights from your home airport to a specific city across two dates, filter by non-stop routes under a duration cap, then start the booking on your preferred airline. Spark can open the airline site, apply your loyalty number from your saved profile, and load the seat-selection screen — then hand off to you to confirm and pay. Apartment or housing viewings Google calls this out by name. Spark can open a saved listing site, sift through short-listed rentals, and start the viewing-request form on your behalf. Because it’s using your local Chrome, it can use the listing account you’re already logged into rather than starting a fresh anonymous session. Reservations and event bookings Restaurant tables, ticketed events, gym classes — any recurring “book me the earliest slot that meets these rules” task fits Auto Browse well. Spark opens the reservation platform in Chrome, applies your filters, and pauses at the confirmation step for you to check the party size, seat, or date one last time. Recurring shopping and price checks Ask Spark to check three retailers for a specific product, apply the coupon you’ve saved in Chrome’s autofill, and load the cart at the best price. It can read prices, run a comparison, and get the checkout flow ready — while stopping before the actual payment, which Google routes back to you. Security and Boundaries: What Auto Browse Won’t Do Because Auto Browse touches your real browser session, Google is deliberate about where it draws the line. The key safeguard is the human-in-the-loop pause: Google says Spark keeps you in the loop “on sensitive actions, such as payments, by handing the task back to you”. Spark can load a checkout screen, but it will not click Pay for you. Google’s documentation also calls out protection against prompt injection — the class of attack where a malicious page hides instructions that try to hijack the agent. Google links Auto Browse’s protections to its broader agentic-security architecture. Access is opt-in. Google’s launch post states Spark uses your logged-in accounts and saved passwords “with your permission”, and the “Gemini and auto browse” indicator appears in Chrome’s top bar only after you grant access. If you never approve Auto Browse, Spark keeps using its previous remote browser. Google’s support documentation goes further than the launch blog and names the actions Auto Browse hands back to you. It says Gemini may ask for your intervention when finalizing financial transactions, accepting terms of service, or creating an account. It also aims to request confirmation before sending communications, modifying your data, submitting web forms, scheduling events, or accessing sites with highly sensitive financial or health data. That is a broader pause list than “payments” alone, and it is worth knowing before you hand over an errand. What Auto Browse won’t do: buy something without asking, sign into accounts you haven’t saved in Chrome, or replace a human eye on money-moving forms. It carries the tedious part of the errand up to the confirmation step — not a fully autonomous shopper. Availability: Where Auto Browse Is Rolling Out Auto Browse is rolling out first to Google AI Pro and Google AI Ultra subscribers in the United States, with Google stating that additional regions will follow “in the future”. Even in the US, rollout is gradual — if you don’t see it yet, the feature may simply not have reached your account. This launch runs alongside a much broader move: on the same day, Google expanded Gemini Spark access on Google AI Pro to over 160 additional countries. The Auto Browse feature itself is US-first, but the underlying Spark agent is now available to Pro subscribers in most Gemini Apps countries. For the current supported-country list, exclusions and plan requirements, see the Gemini Spark availability guide, which tracks Google’s Help Center changes. Gemini Spark Auto Browse Requirements Google published a dedicated Auto Browse support page on Chrome Help that spells out the full eligibility list. Every item below has to be true — missing any one of them is the usual reason Auto Browse never appears: You are 18 or over and in the United States. Google states the age and country rule explicitly; there is no waitlist to join. You are eligible for and have opted in to Gemini in Chrome. Auto Browse rides on the Gemini in Chrome surface, so that has to be switched on first. You are running the latest version of Chrome on desktop. Your device language is set to English. This one catches people out — a US account on a non-English system language will not see Auto Browse. You have Google AI Pro or Google AI Ultra on a personal account. You are signed in to Chrome with a personal Google Account. Chrome Safe Browsing is set to Enhanced or Standard protection. If you have turned Safe Browsing off, Auto Browse will not run. Where Auto Browse does not work Google also lists the situations the feature is deliberately excluded from. Auto Browse is not available in Incognito mode, and it is not available if you sign in to Chrome with a school Google Account. It also does not run in Live chats, or in Gemini in Chrome on iPhone and iPad. As Google puts it, only Gemini Spark in desktop Chrome can use auto browse. How many Auto Browse requests do you get per day? Auto Browse is metered, and the cap depends on your plan. Google’s support documentation gives two figures: up to 20 requests per day on Google AI Pro, and up to 200 requests per day on Google AI Ultra. That ten-fold gap is the clearest practical reason to consider Ultra if you intend to lean on Auto Browse for daily work rather than the occasional errand. PlanAuto Browse accessDaily request limit Google AI Free Not included — Google AI Pro Included, US only Up to 20 requests per day Google AI Ultra Included, US only Up to 200 requests per day How to Try Gemini Spark Chrome Auto Browse Confirm you have a qualifying plan. Auto Browse currently requires Google AI Pro or Google AI Ultra on a personal Google Account, and you must be 18 or over and in the US. Check your access on the Gemini Spark availability page if you’re unsure. Update Chrome to the latest desktop version. Auto Browse rides on Chrome desktop specifically. Open Chrome, go to the About page from the menu, and let it install any pending update before you start. Check the two settings people forget. Set your device language to English, and make sure Chrome’s Safe Browsing is on Enhanced or Standard protection. Google lists both as hard requirements, and either one being wrong will hide Auto Browse entirely. Opt in to Gemini in Chrome. Auto Browse sits on top of the Gemini in Chrome surface, so enable that first and sign in to Chrome itself with your personal Google Account — not a work or school one. Open Gemini Spark on desktop. Sign in with the personal Google Account tied to your Google AI subscription and switch to Spark. If Spark is new to you, the how to use Gemini Spark guide walks through Tasks, Skills and Schedules first. Grant Auto Browse permission when Spark asks. The first time Spark needs to drive your local Chrome, it will ask for permission. Approving it turns on the “Gemini and auto browse” indicator in Chrome’s top bar so you can see when the agent is active. Describe your errand in natural language. Ask Spark to research three flight options and start the booking on your preferred airline, or to open a saved apartment listing and request a viewing. Stay near the screen for the first few tasks so you can approve the sensitive steps quickly. How Auto Browse Compares to Other AI Browser Agents Gemini Spark isn’t the only agent that can drive a browser — it’s one of several approaches, each with different trade-offs. ChatGPT-based browser agents like the Atlas surface run inside their own browser experience and pair well with the wider ChatGPT plugin and Skills ecosystem. Perplexity’s Comet is a purpose-built agentic browser that leans on Perplexity’s answer engine to move across sites. Anthropic’s Computer Use is broader still: it lets Claude drive an entire computer, not just a browser, but running it usually means a virtual machine and more setup. Spark’s differentiator is that it works inside the desktop Chrome you already use — no separate agentic browser to install, no VM to spin up. That’s a strength for anyone whose life lives inside Chrome and Google, and a limitation if you prefer another browser. Which one is “better” depends less on the model and more on where your accounts already sit. Related articles and skills Browse the full Gemini Spark skills library Every free, ready-to-install Skill built for Gemini Spark — email, meetings, research, content and more. See Gemini Spark availability by country Plans, supported countries, exclusions and eligibility rules for Google AI Pro and Ultra. Learn Gemini Spark step by step at AI Agents Academy The training path built for beginners — Tasks, Skills, Schedules and now Auto Browse. The 12 best Gemini Spark skills for business Install-first companion — the reusable Skills to pair with Spark’s new Chrome integration. How to use Gemini Spark The broader operating guide — Tasks, Skills, Schedules, monitoring and safe workflow building. Gemini Spark on Mac How Spark’s Mac desktop app works — and how it complements Chrome Auto Browse on the web. Frequently asked questions about Gemini Spark Chrome Auto Browse Does Gemini Spark Auto Browse work in browsers other than Chrome? Not currently. Google’s launch post specifies Chrome desktop as the browser Spark integrates with. There is no announcement about Firefox, Safari or Edge support for Auto Browse, and Google’s documentation refers only to Chrome. Spark can still run its previous remote-browser tasks in the background, but the “drive your local browser” capability is Chrome-only for now. Will Auto Browse make purchases without asking? No. Google says Spark keeps you in the loop “on sensitive actions, such as payments, by handing the task back to you”. In practice, Spark can load a checkout screen and populate the cart, but it stops and returns control to you before the actual payment step. Treat that pause as the design intent, not a bug. How many Auto Browse requests do you get per day? How to Use it (2026)

Google has connected Gemini Spark directly to desktop Chrome. With your permission, Spark can now open your real browser, sign in with your saved accounts and passwords, and finish multi-step web errands like scheduling apartment viewings or starting a flight booking — while pausing for you to approve anything sensitive.

Quick answer

What is the new Gemini Spark Chrome integration?

Gemini Spark Chrome integration — called Auto Browse by Google — lets Spark complete multi-step web tasks in your local Chrome or, in some cases, a remote browser. With permission, it can move between tabs, use signed-in websites and complete web errands, while returning sensitive steps to you. Auto Browse requires an eligible Google AI Pro or Ultra personal account, with limits of up to 20 tasks daily on Pro and 200 on Ultra.

What Is Gemini Spark Auto Browse?

Google’s July 30, 2026 announcement describes Auto Browse as an integration “directly with Chrome” that lets Spark use your logged-in accounts and saved passwords to handle web errands on your behalf. The change is small in the product tour and large under the hood: for the first time, Spark can act inside the same browser you already use.

Before Auto Browse, Spark relied on a remote cloud browser. That worked for read-only research but ran into a wall the moment a task needed to be signed in as you — a flight comparison it could show you, a booking it could not start. Spark now switches to your local desktop Chrome when a task calls for it, so the sites see your regular session, not an anonymous virtual one.

Chrome itself has had an auto-browse feature for Gemini since early 2026. What’s new is Spark plugging into that same rail, as 9to5Google summarised on launch day, joining Connected Apps, Personal Intelligence and Canvas as tools Spark can reach for.

Practically, that’s the difference between an AI that can read the web and one that can quietly finish a form on a site you’re already logged into. Google frames it around “tedious web errands”: apartment viewings, flight research and booking flows that mix reading, clicking and typing across tabs.

Core Capabilities of Gemini Spark Auto Browse

Local Chrome control

Auto Browse uses the desktop Chrome installed on your own computer, not a remote virtual browser. That means sites see your device, your session and your normal browser fingerprint — the same context you’d have if you opened the tab yourself.

Active sign-ins & saved passwords

With your permission, Spark can lean on your Google-account sign-ins and Chrome-saved passwords to reach past login screens. Google’s launch language is explicit that this is opt-in: Spark only uses these credentials when you grant access.

Multi-tab workflow automation

Instead of one-shot Q&A, Spark can move across pages and tabs to complete a chain of steps — open a listing, compare two options, fill a form, review the summary. That’s the “errand” Google keeps pointing at.

Practical Use Cases for Gemini Spark Chrome Auto Browse

Google’s own launch examples are apartment viewings and flight research, but the broader pattern is any web errand that combines search, comparison and a signed-in step. Here are four realistic workflows worth trying first.

Travel research and flight booking

Ask Spark to compare economy flights from your home airport to a specific city across two dates, filter by non-stop routes under a duration cap, then start the booking on your preferred airline. Spark can open the airline site, apply your loyalty number from your saved profile, and load the seat-selection screen — then hand off to you to confirm and pay.

Apartment or housing viewings

Google calls this out by name. Spark can open a saved listing site, sift through short-listed rentals, and start the viewing-request form on your behalf. Because it’s using your local Chrome, it can use the listing account you’re already logged into rather than starting a fresh anonymous session.

Reservations and event bookings

Restaurant tables, ticketed events, gym classes — any recurring “book me the earliest slot that meets these rules” task fits Auto Browse well. Spark opens the reservation platform in Chrome, applies your filters, and pauses at the confirmation step for you to check the party size, seat, or date one last time.

Recurring shopping and price checks

Ask Spark to check three retailers for a specific product, apply the coupon you’ve saved in Chrome’s autofill, and load the cart at the best price. It can read prices, run a comparison, and get the checkout flow ready — while stopping before the actual payment, which Google routes back to you.

Security and Boundaries: What Auto Browse Won’t Do

Because Auto Browse touches your real browser session, Google is deliberate about where it draws the line. The key safeguard is the human-in-the-loop pause: Google says Spark keeps you in the loop “on sensitive actions, such as payments, by handing the task back to you”. Spark can load a checkout screen, but it will not click Pay for you.

Google’s documentation also calls out protection against prompt injection — the class of attack where a malicious page hides instructions that try to hijack the agent. Google links Auto Browse’s protections to its broader agentic-security architecture.

Access is opt-in. Google’s launch post states Spark uses your logged-in accounts and saved passwords “with your permission”, and the “Gemini and auto browse” indicator appears in Chrome’s top bar only after you grant access. If you never approve Auto Browse, Spark keeps using its previous remote browser.

Google’s support documentation goes further than the launch blog and names the actions Auto Browse hands back to you. It says Gemini may ask for your intervention when finalizing financial transactions, accepting terms of service, or creating an account. It also aims to request confirmation before sending communications, modifying your data, submitting web forms, scheduling events, or accessing sites with highly sensitive financial or health data. That is a broader pause list than “payments” alone, and it is worth knowing before you hand over an errand.

What Auto Browse won’t do: buy something without asking, sign into accounts you haven’t saved in Chrome, or replace a human eye on money-moving forms. It carries the tedious part of the errand up to the confirmation step — not a fully autonomous shopper.

Availability: Where Auto Browse Is Rolling Out

Auto Browse is rolling out first to Google AI Pro and Google AI Ultra subscribers in the United States, with Google stating that additional regions will follow “in the future”. Even in the US, rollout is gradual — if you don’t see it yet, the feature may simply not have reached your account.

This launch runs alongside a much broader move: on the same day, Google expanded Gemini Spark access on Google AI Pro to over 160 additional countries. The Auto Browse feature itself is US-first, but the underlying Spark agent is now available to Pro subscribers in most Gemini Apps countries. For the current supported-country list, exclusions and plan requirements, see the Gemini Spark availability guide, which tracks Google’s Help Center changes.

Gemini Spark Auto Browse Requirements

Google published a dedicated Auto Browse support page on Chrome Help that spells out the full eligibility list. Every item below has to be true — missing any one of them is the usual reason Auto Browse never appears:

  • You are 18 or over and in the United States. Google states the age and country rule explicitly; there is no waitlist to join.
  • You are eligible for and have opted in to Gemini in Chrome. Auto Browse rides on the Gemini in Chrome surface, so that has to be switched on first.
  • You are running the latest version of Chrome on desktop.
  • Your device language is set to English. This one catches people out — a US account on a non-English system language will not see Auto Browse.
  • You have Google AI Pro or Google AI Ultra on a personal account.
  • You are signed in to Chrome with a personal Google Account.
  • Chrome Safe Browsing is set to Enhanced or Standard protection. If you have turned Safe Browsing off, Auto Browse will not run.

Where Auto Browse does not work

Google also lists the situations the feature is deliberately excluded from. Auto Browse is not available in Incognito mode, and it is not available if you sign in to Chrome with a school Google Account. It also does not run in Live chats, or in Gemini in Chrome on iPhone and iPad. As Google puts it, only Gemini Spark in desktop Chrome can use auto browse.

How many Auto Browse requests do you get per day?

Auto Browse is metered, and the cap depends on your plan. Google’s support documentation gives two figures: up to 20 requests per day on Google AI Pro, and up to 200 requests per day on Google AI Ultra. That ten-fold gap is the clearest practical reason to consider Ultra if you intend to lean on Auto Browse for daily work rather than the occasional errand.

How to Try Gemini Spark Chrome Auto Browse

  1. Confirm you have a qualifying plan. Auto Browse currently requires Google AI Pro or Google AI Ultra on a personal Google Account, and you must be 18 or over and in the US. Check your access on the Gemini Spark availability page if you’re unsure.
  2. Update Chrome to the latest desktop version. Auto Browse rides on Chrome desktop specifically. Open Chrome, go to the About page from the menu, and let it install any pending update before you start.
  3. Check the two settings people forget. Set your device language to English, and make sure Chrome’s Safe Browsing is on Enhanced or Standard protection. Google lists both as hard requirements, and either one being wrong will hide Auto Browse entirely.
  4. Opt in to Gemini in Chrome. Auto Browse sits on top of the Gemini in Chrome surface, so enable that first and sign in to Chrome itself with your personal Google Account — not a work or school one.
  5. Open Gemini Spark on desktop. Sign in with the personal Google Account tied to your Google AI subscription and switch to Spark. If Spark is new to you, the how to use Gemini Spark guide walks through Tasks, Skills and Schedules first.
  6. Grant Auto Browse permission when Spark asks. The first time Spark needs to drive your local Chrome, it will ask for permission. Approving it turns on the “Gemini and auto browse” indicator in Chrome’s top bar so you can see when the agent is active.
  7. Describe your errand in natural language. Ask Spark to research three flight options and start the booking on your preferred airline, or to open a saved apartment listing and request a viewing. Stay near the screen for the first few tasks so you can approve the sensitive steps quickly.

How Auto Browse Compares to Other AI Browser Agents

Gemini Spark isn’t the only agent that can drive a browser — it’s one of several approaches, each with different trade-offs. ChatGPT-based browser agents like the Atlas surface run inside their own browser experience and pair well with the wider ChatGPT plugin and Skills ecosystem. Perplexity’s Comet is a purpose-built agentic browser that leans on Perplexity’s answer engine to move across sites. Anthropic’s Computer Use is broader still: it lets Claude drive an entire computer, not just a browser, but running it usually means a virtual machine and more setup.

Spark’s differentiator is that it works inside the desktop Chrome you already use — no separate agentic browser to install, no VM to spin up. That’s a strength for anyone whose life lives inside Chrome and Google, and a limitation if you prefer another browser. Which one is “better” depends less on the model and more on where your accounts already sit.

Related articles and skills

Browse the full Gemini Spark skills library Every free, ready-to-install Skill built for Gemini Spark — email, meetings, research, content and more. See Gemini Spark availability by country Plans, supported countries, exclusions and eligibility rules for Google AI Pro and Ultra. Learn Gemini Spark step by step at AI Agents Academy The training path built for beginners — Tasks, Skills, Schedules and now Auto Browse. The 12 best Gemini Spark skills for business Install-first companion — the reusable Skills to pair with Spark’s new Chrome integration. How to use Gemini Spark The broader operating guide — Tasks, Skills, Schedules, monitoring and safe workflow building. Gemini Spark on Mac How Spark’s Mac desktop app works — and how it complements Chrome Auto Browse on the web.

Not currently. Google’s launch post specifies Chrome desktop as the browser Spark integrates with. There is no announcement about Firefox, Safari or Edge support for Auto Browse, and Google’s documentation refers only to Chrome. Spark can still run its previous remote-browser tasks in the background, but the “drive your local browser” capability is Chrome-only for now.

If you plan to use Auto Browse as part of a daily routine rather than for occasional errands, that 20-versus-200 gap is the main argument for Ultra.

The two that trip people most often are the English device-language rule and Safe Browsing being switched off. Auto Browse also will not run in Incognito mode, on a school Google Account, in Live chats, or in Gemini in Chrome on iPhone or iPad. If everything checks out, the rollout may simply not have reached your account yet.

No. Google states that Auto Browse is not available if you sign in to Chrome with a school Google Account, and the requirements list specifies a personal Google Account with Google AI Pro or Ultra attached. If your browser is signed in to a managed account, switch to a Chrome profile using your personal account before trying again.

What plans include Auto Browse?

The Chrome Auto Browse feature is rolling out to those tiers in the United States first, with additional regions to follow. Even if Gemini Spark itself is now available on Google AI Pro in your country (Google extended Pro access to over 160 additional countries on July 30, 2026), the Chrome Auto Browse feature may not have arrived there yet. Check the availability tracker for current status.

Only with your permission. Google’s documentation states that Spark uses your logged-in accounts and saved passwords with your permission to complete web errands. Google’s support documentation sets a daily cap by plan: up to 20 requests per day on Google AI Pro, and up to 200 requests per day on Google AI Ultra. Google AI Free does not include Auto Browse at all. If you plan to use Auto Browse as part of a daily routine rather than for occasional errands, that 20-versus-200 gap is the main argument for Ultra.
Why is Gemini Spark Auto Browse not working for me?
Almost always a missed requirement rather than a bug. Work through Google’s checklist: you must be 18 or over and in the US, opted in to Gemini in Chrome, running the latest desktop Chrome, with your device language set to English, Google AI Pro or Ultra on a personal account, signed in to Chrome with that personal account, and Safe Browsing set to Enhanced or Standard. The two that trip people most often are the English device-language rule and Safe Browsing being switched off. Auto Browse also will not run in Incognito mode, on a school Google Account, in Live chats, or in Gemini in Chrome on iPhone or iPad. If everything checks out, the rollout may simply not have reached your account yet.
Does Auto Browse work with a work or school Google Account?
No. Google states that Auto Browse is not available if you sign in to Chrome with a school Google Account, and the requirements list specifies a personal Google Account with Google AI Pro or Ultra attached. If your browser is signed in to a managed account, switch to a Chrome profile using your personal account before trying again.
What plans include Auto Browse?
Google AI Pro and Google AI Ultra subscribers on an eligible personal Google Account. The Chrome Auto Browse feature is rolling out to those tiers in the United States first, with additional regions to follow. Google doesn’t publish a standalone Auto Browse SKU — it’s a Spark feature on those plans.
Is Auto Browse available in my country?
Google says Auto Browse is rolling out in the US first, with plans to expand to additional regions. Even if Gemini Spark itself is now available on Google AI Pro in your country (Google extended Pro access to over 160 additional countries on July 30, 2026), the Chrome Auto Browse feature may not have arrived there yet. Check the [availability tracker](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/gemini-spark-availability/) for current status.
Can Auto Browse see my saved passwords?
Only with your permission. Google’s documentation states that Spark uses your logged-in accounts and saved passwords with your permission to complete web errands. Access is opt-in per Google’s launch language, and Chrome shows a “Gemini and auto browse” indicator in the top bar whenever Spark is driving. If you don’t grant permission, Spark falls back to its earlier remote-browser behaviour.
How is this different from ChatGPT Atlas or Perplexity Comet?
ChatGPT Atlas and Perplexity Comet are agentic browser experiences you open separately from your normal browser. Gemini Spark’s Auto Browse plugs into the desktop Chrome you already use — there’s no dedicated agentic browser to install. The trade-off is that Spark is tightly tied to Google accounts and Chrome, whereas the others are more standalone. None is universally better; the right fit depends on which accounts and browser your work already lives in.
## Get Started With Gemini Spark

item.text: Free AI Blog Post Skill: Claude, ChatGPT, & Gemini The free AI Blog Post skill Give it one phrase you want to be found for and it works out what someone typing that actually wants, builds the outline, then writes the draft — in your voice, with the gaps marked instead of invented. The step between “I should blog about that” and a page you can publish. This AI blog post skill turns a single keyword or topic into a publish-ready draft — starting with what the person searching that phrase actually wants, then the outline, then the writing. It’s the missing step between deciding to write something and having something to publish. Most AI blog drafts fail for the same two reasons: they answer a topic instead of a question, and they sound like every other AI blog draft. This skill fixes the first by reading the search intent before writing a word, and the second by asking for a sample of your own writing and matching it — with a banned-phrase list for the tells that give AI away. It also refuses to make things up. If a section needs a statistic, a case study, or a price you didn’t supply, it marks the gap rather than inventing a plausible number. That’s the difference between a draft you can edit and a draft you have to fact-check line by line. Use it as a copy-paste prompt in any AI chat, or install the ready-made SKILL.md file so it runs on command in ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini Spark. No coding required. The AI Blog Post skill takes one keyword or topic, plus who the post is for and what you want them to do after reading, and returns a complete draft: a read on the search intent behind the phrase, three working title options, a full H2/H3 outline, the written post, suggested internal links, and a list of anything it could not source. It writes one new long-form page from a topic — which is different from its neighbours. The Weekly Content Plan skill decides what to publish and when; the Content Repurposing skill turns something you already wrote into other formats; the SEO Metadata skill writes the title tag and meta description once the page is finished. This one starts from nothing but a phrase. It never invents a statistic, a study, a quote, or a customer example — it marks the gap and asks. Give it a sample of your own writing and it matches your voice instead of producing the usual AI cadence. Two ways to get the Blog Post skill Paste into ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini Spark One draft in about fifteen minutes SEO audit, SEO metadata, content repurposing, social posts, content planning Blog Post skill: what it needs and what it returns What it isA free AI skill — a reusable set of instructions — that turns one keyword or topic into an outline and a publish-ready draft. It comes as a copy-paste prompt and as a ready-made SKILL.md file. Who it’s forBusiness owners, marketers, and service providers who need to publish regularly and don’t have a writer. No SEO background needed — it explains what it’s doing as it goes. What you give itThe keyword or topic, who the post is for, and what you want them to do after reading. Optionally a sample of your own writing — that one input is what stops the draft sounding like AI. What you get backA read on the search intent behind the phrase, three working title options, a full H2/H3 outline, the written draft, suggested internal links, and a list of anything it could not source. Works withChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini Spark. The prompt runs on free plans; the SKILL.md installs as a saved skill in Claude and Gemini Spark, or as a Project in ChatGPT. What it will not doIt writes one new post from a topic — it does not plan your publishing calendar (that’s Weekly Content Plan), reshape something you already wrote (that’s Content Repurposing), or write the title tag and meta description (that’s SEO Metadata). It never invents a statistic, study, quote, or customer example — it marks the gap and asks. What it costsThe prompt is free with no account. The SKILL.md file is free with a free account. The downloadable file for every other skill comes with All Access: free for 7 days, then only $14/mo., cancel anytime. Time to first resultAbout fifteen minutes for a first draft. One phrase becomes a page you can actually publish By the end of this AI skill guide, you’ll have the Blog Post skill ready to use — as a copy-paste prompt in any AI chat, or installed as a SKILL.md file that runs on command. It handles the two things that make AI drafts unusable: writing to a topic instead of a question, and sounding like a machine. DRAFT — keyword: “how often should you service a bike” (example) Search intent: Informational, with a buying decision hiding behind it. Someone typing this owns a bike and suspects they’ve neglected it. They want a number, then permission to relax or a nudge to book. Answer the number in the first two sentences or they leave. Title options: “How Often Should You Service a Bike? A Straight Answer” · “Bike Servicing: How Often, and How to Tell It’s Overdue” · “How Often Your Bike Actually Needs a Service” Outline: The short answer (lead with it) → What changes the number: mileage, weather, storage → Five signs it’s overdue → What a service actually includes → What you can do yourself → When to stop DIY-ing → FAQ Opening lines of the draft: “Once a year if you ride occasionally, every six months if you ride most weeks, and straight away if the gears are skipping. That’s the honest answer, and for most people the first one is enough. What changes it is less about time and more about what you’re riding through…” Internal links suggested: the workshop services page from “what a service actually includes” · the winter riding post from the weather section · the contact page from “when to stop DIY-ing” Couldn’t source: Your actual service price and turnaround time · whether you do collection and drop-off · the brands you’re certified for — left blank in the draft, not guessed. How to use the Blog Post AI skill in 3 steps Pick a format, give it the keyword plus a sample of your own writing, then fill the gaps it marks instead of letting it guess. That’s the whole method — the detail is below. The Blog Post skill is an AI skill — a reusable set of instructions. It comes in two formats below, and they contain the same thinking. Use the prompt for one post today. Use the SKILL.md file if you publish regularly and want every post to hold the same structure and voice. Copy the prompt for a one-off post, or copy the SKILL.md file to install it permanently. Both are below — same instructions, different packaging. Give it the keyword and a writing sample The keyword sets the intent; two or three paragraphs of your own writing set the voice. Skip the sample and you’ll get competent, generic prose — the exact thing readers scroll past. Fill the gaps before you publish It marks every place it needed a fact it didn’t have. Those blanks are where your actual expertise goes — and they’re what makes the post worth reading. Then run the SEO Metadata skill on the finished page. Paste this into ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini Spark, add your keyword at the bottom, and send. Works on free plans. Best if you want one post rather than a repeatable process. You are an expert content writer who writes for small businesses. Your job is to turn one keyword or topic into a blog post that answers what the searcher actually wants, in the business owner's own voice, without inventing anything. PROCESS 1. Read the keyword and work out the search intent behind it. Say what kind of intent it is and what the person typing it actually wants. If the intent is unclear, ask before writing. 2. Decide what the post must answer in the first three sentences. Most searches have one question underneath them - answer it immediately, not after 400 words of preamble. 3. Offer three working title options. Plain language, no colons stacked on colons, no "Ultimate Guide" unless it genuinely is one. 4. Build an H2/H3 outline. Order the sections the way the reader needs them, not the way the topic is organised. 5. Write the draft. Match the writing sample if one was given. If not, write plainly and say you have not matched a voice. 6. Suggest internal links - which sections should link out, and to what kind of page. 7. List everything you could not source. RULES - Never invent a statistic, a study, a survey result, a quote, a customer name, a case study, or a price. If a section needs one, write [NEEDS: what you need] and list it at the end. - Answer the question early. Do not withhold the answer to increase reading time. - Match the sample's sentence length, vocabulary, and level of formality. If the sample uses contractions, use them. - Never open with "In today's fast-paced world", "In the ever-evolving landscape", "Whether you're a seasoned", or any variation. No "delve", "leverage", "seamless", "robust", "unlock the power", "game-changer", "it's important to note". - Do not repeat the keyword unnaturally. Write it the way a person would say it. - Vary sentence length. Two short sentences beat one long one with a semicolon. - No section should exist only to hit a word count. If a heading has nothing real under it, cut the heading. - Write at the reading level of the audience described, not at the level that sounds most impressive. - Do not write the title tag or meta description here. That is a separate job. OUTPUT FORMAT ### Search intent What kind, and what the person actually wants. ### The question to answer first One sentence. ### Title options Three. ### Outline H2s and H3s. ### Draft The full post. ### Internal links to add Which section, and what kind of page it should point to. ### Couldn't source Everything marked [NEEDS: ...] in the draft. MY POST: - Keyword or topic: [the phrase you want to be found for] - Who it's for: [the reader, and what they already know] - What I want them to do after reading: [book, buy, enquire, subscribe, just trust you] - Writing sample (optional but recommended): [paste 2-3 paragraphs you have written] This is the same skill packaged as a proper SKILL.md — the format Claude and Gemini Spark use for saved skills. The description line at the top is the important part: it tells your AI when to run this on its own, so you can just say “write a blog post about…” and it fires. Paste the whole block into a new file called SKILL.md, or straight into your platform’s skill instructions. --- name: blog-post-expert description: Turn one keyword or topic into a publish-ready blog post - search intent, three title options, an H2/H3 outline, the full draft in the user's own voice, internal link suggestions, and a list of anything that could not be sourced. Use this when the user asks to write a blog post, write an article, draft a post about a keyword, create an SEO content brief, or turn a topic or keyword idea into content. --- # ✅ Your Blog Post Specialist You are an expert Blog Post Specialist. Your job is to turn one keyword or topic into a publish-ready draft that answers what the searcher actually wants, in the user's own voice, without inventing anything. ## Main Goal Turn one keyword or topic into a draft the user could publish after filling in the blanks. Answer the real question behind the search, sound like the user, and invent nothing. ## Persona Expert, practical, clear, strategic, and detail-oriented. You understand search intent, content structure, and how small business owners actually write. You turn a single phrase into a finished draft with the gaps honestly marked. ## Tone Professional, concise, direct, and warm/beginner-friendly. Use light emojis in section headers only when helpful. Do not overuse emojis. ## Formatting Rules Use clean Markdown. Short sections, simple headings, bullets for steps or rules. Never bury the answer. Never pad to hit a word count. ## If the User Says "Hi" or Starts Vaguely Use this welcome message: Welcome. I am your Blog Post Specialist. I turn one keyword or topic into a publish-ready draft that sounds like you, not like AI. I can help you with: 1. Search intent — what the person typing your keyword actually wants 2. Three working title options 3. A full H2/H3 outline in reader order 4. The written draft, matched to your voice 5. Internal links and a list of anything I could not source To start, give me your keyword, who it's for, and paste two or three paragraphs of your own writing! ## If the User Gives a Clear Request Ask for anything missing from these three: - **The keyword or topic.** Required. - **Who the post is for**, and what they already know. - **What the reader should do after reading** — book, buy, enquire, subscribe, or simply trust them. Then ask for one optional thing that matters more than people expect: **two or three paragraphs of their own writing**. It is the difference between a draft they edit and a draft they rewrite. If they decline, write plainly and say at the end that you did not match a voice. Then work through this process: 1. **Read the intent, not the topic.** Say what kind of search it is — informational, comparison, commercial, navigational, or a how-to — and what the person typing it actually wants. Many phrases have a decision hiding behind an innocent question. Name it. 2. **Decide the question to answer first.** Write it in one sentence. It goes in the opening lines of the draft, not halfway down. 3. **Offer three working titles.** Plain language. No stacked colons. No "Ultimate Guide" unless it genuinely is one. 4. **Build the outline.** H2s and H3s ordered the way the reader needs them, not the way the subject is conventionally organised. 5. **Write the draft**, matching the sample. 6. **Suggest internal links** — which section, and what kind of page it should point to. 7. **List everything you could not source.** ## Voice Rules - Match the sample's sentence length, vocabulary, and formality. If they use contractions, use contractions. - **Never open with**: "In today's fast-paced world", "In the ever-evolving landscape", "Whether you're a seasoned", "Picture this", or any variation. - **Never use**: delve, leverage, seamless, robust, unlock the power, game-changer, tapestry, testament to, it's important to note, in conclusion. - Vary sentence length deliberately. Two short sentences beat one long one joined by a semicolon. - Write at the audience's reading level, not the level that sounds most impressive. - Cut any sentence that could appear in a post on any other topic. ## Structure Rules - Answer the question early. Do not withhold it to increase time on page. - No section exists to hit a word count. If a heading has nothing real underneath it, delete the heading. - Do not repeat the keyword unnaturally. Write it the way a person would say it out loud. - One idea per paragraph. Three or four sentences maximum. ## Quality & Accuracy Rules - Never invent a statistic, study, survey, quote, customer name, case study, testimonial, award, or price. - Where a section needs a fact you do not have, write `[NEEDS: the specific thing]` inline and collect them all at the end. Those blanks are where the user's real expertise goes — they are a feature, not a failure. - Do not present a general claim as a researched one. "Most people find" is not a statistic. - If the topic requires professional qualification to answer safely — legal, medical, financial — say so and write around it rather than through it. - Ensure the draft is immediately usable once the blanks are filled. - If no writing sample was given, say plainly at the end that you did not match a voice. - If the keyword's intent is genuinely unclear, ask before writing rather than guessing. - Never claim the post is optimised for a ranking. You improve the odds; you do not promise a position. ## What This Skill Does Not Do - **It does not plan a calendar.** What to publish and when is the Weekly Content Plan skill. - **It does not reshape existing content.** Turning one asset into many formats is the Content Repurposing skill. This one starts from a phrase, not from something already written. - **It does not write metadata.** The title tag, meta description, slug, and alt text for the finished page are the SEO Metadata skill's job. ## Required Output Format # ✅ Blog Post Draft: [Keyword] ## Search Intent What kind of search this is, and what the person typing it actually wants. ## The Question to Answer First One sentence. This goes in the opening lines. ## Title Options 1. [Option one] 2. [Option two] 3. [Option three] ## Outline - **H2:** [Section] - H3: [Sub-section] - **H2:** [Section] ## ✍ Draft [The full post, matched to the user's voice.] ## Internal Links to Add | Section | Link to what kind of page | |---|---| | [Section] | [Page type] | ## ⚠ Couldn't Source - `[NEEDS: ...]` — [where it appears in the draft] Where the SKILL.md goes in ChatGPT, Claude & Gemini Spark In ChatGPT it goes into a Project’s instructions, or a native Skill if you have access; in Claude it becomes a custom Skill (or a SKILL.md file under .claude/skills/); in Gemini Spark it goes on the Skills page. Both formats above contain the same instructions — the only difference is whether your AI has to be reminded every time. Use the prompt for one post; install the SKILL.md once you’re publishing regularly and want the voice rules, banned phrases, and structure to hold across every post without re-pasting them. For the full breakdown of how a skill differs from a prompt and from a full AI agent, read what an AI agent skill is. If you already have a writing prompt you like, turning a prompt into an AI skill takes about ten minutes. The prompt works everywhere with no setup. If you copied the SKILL.md file instead, here’s exactly where it goes in each platform. Upload your writing samples to the Project once. Every post you draft in it inherits the voice without re-pasting. Best fit for this skill. One Project per publication keeps voice, structure, and banned phrases consistent across every post. Projects work on free and paid plans. Browse all free ChatGPT skills → Claude app: create a custom Skill and paste it in — name it blog-post. Claude Code: save it as .claude/skills/blog-post/SKILL.md in your project, or ~/.claude/skills/blog-post/SKILL.md to use it everywhere. The folder name is what names the skill. Say “write a blog post about…” — the description line lets Claude fire it on its own. Long-form is Claude’s strength, and in Cowork it can pull source material from a mounted folder. Browse all free Claude skills → Use blog-post as the name and paste the description line from the file into the description field — that field is what makes Spark apply it automatically. Select the skill with / or @, or just give it a keyword and ask for a post. With Workspace access, Spark can draft straight into a Google Doc. Gemini Spark skills currently require an eligible Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription (Google expanded Pro access to 160+ additional countries on July 30, 2026), plus an eligible account and region. Browse all free Gemini Spark skills → The writing sample is the whole game Everything else in this skill is structure, and structure is easy. What makes a post yours is sentence rhythm, the words you’d never use, and how directly you say things. Two or three paragraphs of your own writing gives the AI all of that. Skip it and you’ll get something competent, correct, and completely forgettable — which is the one outcome that doesn’t help you. How to write a blog post with AI in any tool Say “write a blog post about,” give it the keyword, the reader, and a sample of your writing, and it returns intent, titles, an outline, and the draft. Open ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini Spark and start a new chat. Give it the keyword or topic you want to be found for. Name the reader and what they already know. Paste two or three paragraphs of your own writing. Fill in every [NEEDS: …] blank before you publish. New to AI assistants? KEYWORD OR TOPIC: [the phrase you want to be found for] WHO IT'S FOR: [the reader, and what they already know] WHAT I WANT THEM TO DO AFTER: [book, buy, enquire, subscribe, or just trust me] MY WRITING SAMPLE: [paste 2-3 paragraphs you have written] Read the search intent first and answer the real question in the opening lines. PROCESS

# ✅ Your Blog Post Specialist

You are an expert Blog Post Specialist.

Your job is to turn one keyword or topic into a publish-ready draft that answers what the searcher actually wants, in the user's own voice, without inventing anything.

## Main Goal

Turn one keyword or topic into a draft the user could publish after filling in the blanks. Answer the real question behind the search, sound like the user, and invent nothing.

## Persona

Expert, practical, clear, strategic, and detail-oriented.

You understand search intent, content structure, and how small business owners actually write.

You turn a single phrase into a finished draft with the gaps honestly marked.

## Tone

Professional, concise, direct, and warm/beginner-friendly.

Use light emojis in section headers only when helpful.

Do not overuse emojis.

## Formatting Rules

Use clean Markdown. Short sections, simple headings, bullets for steps or rules.

Never bury the answer. Never pad to hit a word count.

## If the User Says "Hi" or Starts Vaguely

Use this welcome message:

Welcome. I am your Blog Post Specialist. 
I turn one keyword or topic into a publish-ready draft that sounds like you, not like AI.

I can help you with:

1. Search intent — what the person typing your keyword actually wants
2. Three working title options
3. A full H2/H3 outline in reader order
4. The written draft, matched to your voice
5. Internal links and a list of anything I could not source

To start, give me your keyword, who it's for, and paste two or three paragraphs of your own writing!

## If the User Gives a Clear Request

Ask for anything missing from these three:

- **The keyword or topic.** Required.
- **Who the post is for**, and what they already know.
- **What the reader should do after reading** — book, buy, enquire, subscribe, or simply trust them.

Then ask for one optional thing that matters more than people expect: **two or three paragraphs of their own writing**. It is the difference between a draft they edit and a draft they rewrite. If they decline, write plainly and say at the end that you did not match a voice.

Then work through this process:

1. **Read the intent, not the topic.** Say what kind of search it is — informational, comparison, commercial, navigational, or a how-to — and what the person typing it actually wants. Many phrases have a decision hiding behind an innocent question. Name it.
2. **Decide the question to answer first.** Write it in one sentence. It goes in the opening lines of the draft, not halfway down.
3. **Offer three working titles.** Plain language. No stacked colons. No "Ultimate Guide" unless it genuinely is one.
4. **Build the outline.** H2s and H3s ordered the way the reader needs them, not the way the subject is conventionally organised.
5. **Write the draft**, matching the sample.
6. **Suggest internal links** — which section, and what kind of page it should point to.
7. **List everything you could not source.**

## Voice Rules

- Match the sample's sentence length, vocabulary, and formality. If they use contractions, use contractions.
- **Never open with**: "In today's fast-paced world", "In the ever-evolving landscape", "Whether you're a seasoned", "Picture this", or any variation.
- **Never use**: delve, leverage, seamless, robust, unlock the power, game-changer, tapestry, testament to, it's important to note, in conclusion.
- Vary sentence length deliberately. Two short sentences beat one long one joined by a semicolon.
- Write at the audience's reading level, not the level that sounds most impressive.
- Cut any sentence that could appear in a post on any other topic.

## Structure Rules

- Answer the question early. Do not withhold it to increase time on page.
- No section exists to hit a word count. If a heading has nothing real underneath it, delete the heading.
- Do not repeat the keyword unnaturally. Write it the way a person would say it out loud.
- One idea per paragraph. Three or four sentences maximum.

## Quality & Accuracy Rules

- Never invent a statistic, study, survey, quote, customer name, case study, testimonial, award, or price.
- Where a section needs a fact you do not have, write `[NEEDS: the specific thing]` inline and collect them all at the end. Those blanks are where the user's real expertise goes — they are a feature, not a failure.
- Do not present a general claim as a researched one. "Most people find" is not a statistic.
- If the topic requires professional qualification to answer safely — legal, medical, financial — say so and write around it rather than through it.
- Ensure the draft is immediately usable once the blanks are filled.
- If no writing sample was given, say plainly at the end that you did not match a voice.
- If the keyword's intent is genuinely unclear, ask before writing rather than guessing.
- Never claim the post is optimised for a ranking. You improve the odds; you do not promise a position.

## What This Skill Does Not Do

- **It does not plan a calendar.** What to publish and when is the Weekly Content Plan skill.
- **It does not reshape existing content.** Turning one asset into many formats is the Content Repurposing skill. This one starts from a phrase, not from something already written.
- **It does not write metadata.** The title tag, meta description, slug, and alt text for the finished page are the SEO Metadata skill's job.

## Required Output Format

# ✅ Blog Post Draft: [Keyword]

##  Search Intent

What kind of search this is, and what the person typing it actually wants.

##  The Question to Answer First

One sentence. This goes in the opening lines.

##  Title Options

1. [Option one]
2. [Option two]
3. [Option three]

##  Outline

- **H2:** [Section]
  - H3: [Sub-section]
- **H2:** [Section]

## ✍ Draft

[The full post, matched to the user's voice.]

##  Internal Links to Add

| Section | Link to what kind of page |
|---|---|
| [Section] | [Page type] |

## ⚠ Couldn't Source

- `[NEEDS: ...]` — [where it appears in the draft]

Is this AI blog post skill free?

How is this different from the Content Repurposing skill?

This one starts from a phrase; that one starts from something you already wrote. The Content Repurposing skill takes one finished asset — a post, a video, a webinar — and turns it into other formats. This skill has nothing to work from except a keyword and your expertise, so it has to decide what the post should say in the first place. Use them in order: write the post here, then repurpose it there.

How is this different from the Weekly Content Plan skill?

One decides what to write; this one writes it. The Weekly Content Plan skill builds the calendar — topics, formats, and when each goes out. It stops at the plan. This skill takes one line off that calendar and turns it into an actual draft. They’re designed to hand off to each other.

Do I need to know SEO to use it?

No — it does the SEO thinking and explains it as it goes. The first thing it returns is a read on the search intent behind your phrase: what kind of search it is, and what the person typing it actually wants. That’s the part most people get wrong, and it’s why so many posts answer a topic instead of a question. You don’t need to know the terminology; you just need to know your subject.

Will it make up statistics or sources?

Where a section genuinely needs one, it writes [NEEDS: the specific thing] inline and collects every one of them at the end. Those blanks are the point — they’re exactly where your real experience goes, and they’re what makes the finished post worth reading instead of interchangeable.

Can it write the meta description too?

Deliberately not — that’s a separate job and a separate skill.
