Match the result you want on the left to the training that actually teaches it.
| If you want… | Take… | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | **A Spark workflow running this week** | [Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/) | The path moves from access and permissions to a customized Skill, a tested task and a reusable schedule, with human help attached. | | **Live, instructor-led Spark training** | [AI Agents with Gemini Spark](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-2) | Fifteen classroom hours dedicated to Tasks, reusable Skills, Schedules, multi-app workflows and guardrails. | | **A free official start** | [AI Boost Bootcamp](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-3) | One hour, built from Google’s internal training, with Workspace workflows, Gems and an introduction to agents. | | **The exact current product rules** | [Google’s Spark documentation](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-4) | The primary source for eligibility, permissions, connected apps, Tasks, Skills, Schedules and safety. | | **Depth across Gmail, Docs and Sheets** | [Google Workspace with Gemini](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-5) | Nine courses and hands-on business projects across the Workspace apps Spark may use. | | **Skills to use without a course** | [Free Gemini Spark Skills library](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gemini-spark/) | Skip training for now and start from a tested workflow you can customize. |
**How we chose these Gemini Spark courses**
We prioritized current training that is beginner-accessible and leads to a real workflow, then scored each option on Spark specificity, Task–Skill–Schedule coverage, Google-connected work, safety and permissions, hands-on practice, support, value and certificate quality. Provider curricula, durations, prices, update dates and published ratings were reviewed on August 8, 2026; where we did not complete a full course, the assessment is based on the provider’s published materials. This is an independent editorial comparison; no outside provider sponsored or paid for placement. **Disclosure:** Gemini Spark Academy is our own membership. It is included because it fits the query and is judged using the same criteria, with its limitations stated below.
## What a Gemini Spark Skills course actually needs to cover
A Gemini course can be excellent and still be the wrong course for Spark. Spark is an agent that can use connected information, browse, create and edit files, and run work later. Training worth your time should cover these fundamentals:
* **Access before setup.** Current account, subscription, age and regional requirements, with a clear acknowledgement that they change. The current details live in [our Spark availability guide](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/gemini-spark-availability/). * **Task = what, Skill = how, Schedule = when.** A course should teach the three parts separately before combining them. See [Tasks, Skills and Schedules explained](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/gemini-spark-tasks-skills-schedules/). * **Reusable Skills.** How to create or customize instructions that Spark can apply again, instead of rewriting the same prompt every Monday. * **Google-connected workflows.** Practical work across Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs, Sheets and Slides, not only chat examples. * **Permissions and scope.** What Spark can access, what data it may share while browsing, and how to keep the connected surface as narrow as the task allows. * **Human review.** Confirmation steps for sending, editing, deleting, purchasing and other consequential actions. Google calls Spark experimental and says active supervision matters. * **Testing before scheduling.** Run a low-stakes version, review the output and permissions, improve the Skill, then add a Schedule only after the task behaves reliably.
**The gap worth knowing about**
Most courses labeled “Gemini” teach prompting, Gemini chat or a single Workspace app. They can make you better at giving instructions, but they do not automatically teach Gemini Spark’s Tasks, reusable Skills, Schedules, browser actions or supervision model. In this researched list, only [Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-1) and [Tertiary Courses](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-2) publish a curriculum dedicated to Spark itself. That scarcity is why the broader courses rank lower even when the providers are excellent.
**Before you enrol:** confirm [whether your account can access Gemini Spark](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/gemini-spark-availability/). A standard Gemini or Workspace course may be usable without Spark; a Spark-specific course assumes you can open the agent.

* Current eligibility, supported surfaces and account requirements * How to create, monitor, pause and stop a Spark Task * How reusable Skills are created, selected and applied * How Schedules trigger recurring or event-based work * What Spark may use from connected apps, browsers and personal context * Prompt-injection risks, confirmations, take-control mode and supervision
#### Strengths
* The authoritative and most current Spark source * Free, detailed and specific to the actual product * Strongest safety and permissions coverage in the list * Useful as a reference after any course
#### Keep in mind
* Documentation, not a structured course * No guided business project, feedback or support * No quizzes, milestones or certificate * Written to explain features, not to choose the best first workflow
**Verdict:** Bookmark it regardless of which course you take. It is not sufficient structure for every beginner, but it is the source you should trust whenever a video, course or blog disagrees with current Spark behavior.
[Read Google’s Gemini Spark guide →](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/17094507?hl=en)
**Best for:** Learners whose future Spark workflows will live mainly in Gmail, Docs, Slides, Sheets, Meet, Chat and Drive.
The [Google Workspace with Gemini Specialization](https://www.coursera.org/specializations/gemini-for-google-workspace) is Google Cloud’s deep end-user path. It has nine courses, hands-on business projects and dedicated modules for the apps Spark may read or edit. Coursera estimates four weeks at ten hours per week, and the series was updated in July 2026. It had a 4.6 rating from 592 course reviews and 14,056 enrolled learners when checked.
### What you’ll learn
* Gemini foundations, responsible use and iterative prompting * Summarizing threads and drafting professional email in Gmail * Creating, refining and summarizing documents in Docs * Creating presentations, visuals and speaker notes in Slides * Building project plans and trackers in Sheets * Meeting notes, action items, Chat summaries and Drive research
#### Strengths
* Deepest Workspace curriculum in the roundup * Official Google Cloud instruction * Hands-on projects tied to real business tasks * Recently updated and beginner-friendly * Shareable Google Cloud certificate
#### Keep in mind
* About Gemini in Workspace, not Gemini Spark * Requires a Workspace plan with full Gemini AI access for practice * Roughly forty hours is a large commitment * Little direct coverage of Spark Tasks, Skills and Schedules
**Verdict:** Excellent if Workspace itself is your learning goal. For Spark, take only the modules matching apps your first workflow will use; completing all nine before opening Spark is unnecessary.
[View the Workspace specialization →](https://www.coursera.org/specializations/gemini-for-google-workspace)
## Best Gemini Spark course for each type of learner
### Best free Gemini Spark course
**[Google Skills’ AI Boost Bootcamp](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-3) is the best free course; [Google’s Spark Help Center](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-4) is the best free Spark-specific resource.** The Bootcamp gives beginners a coherent one-hour foundation and a completion badge, but it teaches Gemini at work rather than Spark. Follow it with the official Spark, Skills and Schedules pages so the general foundation becomes product-specific.
### Best Gemini Spark course for beginners
**[AI Agents Library Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/).** A beginner does not need more features; they need a safe order. The Academy starts with eligibility and permissions, separates Tasks, Skills and Schedules, and waits until a workflow has been tested before it is scheduled. Ready-to-use Skills and hands-on help remove the two places beginners usually stall.
### Best Gemini Spark Skills course for business
**[AI Agents Library Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/).** The curriculum is organized around recurring jobs such as weekly briefs, research and follow-ups rather than a product tour. If you already know exactly which business workflow you need, browse the [best Gemini Spark Skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-skills/) first and bring one into the course.
### Best live Gemini Spark training
**[Tertiary Courses’ AI Agents with Gemini Spark](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-2).** It is the only credible option reviewed that devotes two instructor-led days to Spark Tasks, Skills, Schedules, cross-app workflows and guardrails. Choose it when live feedback is worth the Singapore venue and higher upfront price.
### Best Gemini Spark workflow course
**[Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-1) for self-paced training; [Tertiary Courses](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-2) for classroom depth.** Both teach complete Spark workflows rather than stopping at prompts. The first is easier to access and includes ready-made Skills; the second gives you more live classroom time.
### Best Gemini course with a certificate
**[Google Workspace with Gemini](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-5) is the strongest certificate option in this five-course list.** The [Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/) and [Tertiary Courses](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-2) also award their own certificates of completion, and [AI Boost Bootcamp](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-3) offers an official completion badge. None should be described as a Google professional certification unless the provider explicitly says so.
### Best Gemini Spark course for non-coders
**[Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-1).** Every option in this roundup is accessible without programming, but the Academy is the clearest no-code path to a working Spark workflow. Avoid drifting into courses about Vertex AI, the Gemini API or Agent Development Kit unless your actual goal is to build software rather than direct Spark.
## Which Gemini Spark course should you take first?
Five recommendations are not a plan. Choose the starting point that matches you, then follow the arrows. This section owns _course order_; the later [learning path](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#roadmap-heading) owns the sequence of Skills you build.
### If Gemini itself is completely new to you
**[AI Boost Bootcamp](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-3) → [free Gemini Spark setup guide](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/setup-guides/gemini-spark/) → [Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/) → one low-risk workflow.**
Take one free official foundation, not three. Once you understand the ecosystem and basic prompting, move into Spark and build.
### If you already use Gemini most days
**[Google’s Spark documentation](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-4) → [customize one free Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gemini-spark/) → [Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/) → add a Schedule after testing.**
Skip general Gemini courses. Your gap is the agent layer: Tasks, Skills, Schedules, permissions and review.
### If you run a business and want a result this month
**[Choose one business Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-skills/) → [Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/) → run it manually three times → schedule only the stable version.**
Start with a specific recurring job. “Learn Gemini” is not a result; a reviewed weekly brief waiting in a Google Doc is.
### If you want live teaching or a formal classroom
**[Tertiary Courses](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-2) → Google’s [official documentation](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-4) as your maintenance reference → one monitored workflow at work.**
The live course gives you the deepest guided build. Keep the official Help Center bookmarked because Spark’s access rules and interfaces will change faster than any classroom syllabus.
### If you need a recognizable Google credential
**[AI Boost Bootcamp badge](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-3) → [Google Workspace with Gemini certificate](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-5) → a portfolio example showing the Spark workflow you built.**
A certificate shows completion. A working workflow shows capability. Keep both if the credential matters to your employer.
Whichever course sequence you choose, continue with the [Gemini Spark learning path](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#roadmap-heading) below. It is about the capabilities you build, not how many courses you finish.
## Build real Gemini Spark Skills while you learn
**A completed course proves you watched; a working Skill proves you can use Spark.** Pair each week of learning with one business job from the free library. Copy the instructions into Spark, save them as a Skill, run a low-risk Task, then change one rule to match the way you work.
| Week | Build this | Start from this free Skill | What you learn | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **1** | An inbox triage workflow | [AI Gmail Triage](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gmail-triage/) | Clear categories, narrow Gmail access and draft-only output before Spark takes any consequential action. | | **2** | A meeting follow-up workflow | [AI Meeting Notes](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/meeting-notes/) | Consistent structure across notes, decisions, owners and next steps saved to Docs. | | **3** | A research brief | [Market Research Brief](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/market-research-brief/) | Source requirements, citations and the review step that prevents polished misinformation. | | **4** | A weekly business update | [Weekly Business Brief](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/weekly-business-brief-agent/) | Combining connected context with a repeatable output, then deciding whether it is stable enough to schedule. | | **5** | A client onboarding package | [AI Client Onboarding](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/client-onboarding/) | Chaining inputs into multiple deliverables while keeping every email and calendar action behind human review. |
Browse more options in the [free Gemini Spark Skills library](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gemini-spark/), or compare the [12 best Gemini Spark Skills to install first](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-skills/). The Academy adds the sequence and support; the free library lets you prove the model before you join.
## What should you learn first? The Gemini Spark learning path
Courses give you resources. This is the order that turns them into a system you can trust.
1. **Confirm access.** Check your Google Account type, subscription, region and current requirements on the [Gemini Spark availability page](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/gemini-spark-availability/). 2. **Learn the agent safety model.** Spark can use connected information and act on your behalf. Understand confirmations, browsing, data sharing and active supervision before assigning real work. 3. **Separate Task, Skill and Schedule.** Learn what, how and when in the [Tasks, Skills and Schedules guide](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/gemini-spark-tasks-skills-schedules/). Most troubleshooting becomes obvious once those three are distinct. 4. **Customize one ready-made Skill.** Start from the [free library](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gemini-spark/) rather than a blank page. Change the inputs, rules and output format to match one repeated job. 5. **Run one low-risk Task manually.** Use test data, a draft-only output and the smallest possible connected-app scope. Review what Spark read, changed and created. 6. **Improve the Skill.** Fix ambiguous instructions, add a missing check and rerun the same Task until the result is repeatable. 7. **Add a Schedule only after the Task is stable.** Start with something reversible such as a draft brief, and review every run until you know where it drifts. 8. **Scale by workflow, not by access.** Add a second Skill and app only when the first system is trustworthy. The [best Gemini Spark use cases](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/gemini-spark-use-cases/) can help you choose what comes next.
If you want the cross-platform foundation before specializing, [AI Skills Fundamentals](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/ai-skills/) teaches how reusable AI instructions work across Gemini Spark, ChatGPT and Claude.
## Common mistakes beginners make when learning Gemini Spark
* **Buying a course before checking access.** Spark eligibility changes by account, subscription and region. Confirm it first; general Gemini access is not the same thing. * **Confusing Gemini chat, Gems and Spark Skills.** They overlap, but the containers and agent permissions differ. A course about Gems may improve reusable prompting without teaching Spark Tasks or Schedules. * **Taking several broad Gemini introductions.** The second foundation repeats the first. After one, your next step should be an applied Spark workflow. * **Starting with email sending, purchases or sensitive files.** Begin with a reversible draft or report. An autonomous action is a terrible first lesson. * **Scheduling the first version.** A Task that worked once is not reliable. Run it manually, inspect the work panel and improve the Skill before adding a Schedule. * **Connecting everything.** More access does not make Spark smarter. Give each Task the smallest set of apps and information it needs. * **Treating safety as a disclaimer.** Permissions, prompt injection, confirmations and review are part of the workflow design, not a paragraph to read after it is built.
## Free vs paid Gemini Spark courses: which should you choose?
You can learn the foundations for free. Pay only when the paid option solves a problem free resources do not: structure, Spark-specific depth, live teaching, ready-made Skills or human support.
* **Start free if** you are testing interest. Take [AI Boost Bootcamp](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-3), read [Google’s Spark documentation](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-4), and run one Skill from the [free library](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gemini-spark/). * **Choose [Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/) if** you want a beginner sequence, ready-to-use Skills and help when setup or permissions stall. The first seven days are free. * **Choose [Tertiary Courses](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-2) if** live classroom time and fifteen hours of dedicated Spark practice justify the location and price. * **Pay for Coursera if** the Google certificate or deep Workspace curriculum changes something for your job. Do not pay for all nine Workspace courses when you only need Gmail and Docs. * **Do not pay for** a second general Gemini overview. Once you understand prompting and Workspace basics, buy application and feedback—not another introduction.
## Gemini Spark Skills courses — FAQs
What is the best Gemini Spark Skills course?
For most beginners and business owners, the best Gemini Spark Skills course is the [AI Agents Library Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/). It follows a seven-day beginner path from access and permissions to a customized Skill, tested Task and reusable workflow, with ready-made Skills and hands-on setup help. For live classroom depth, [Tertiary Courses’ AI Agents with Gemini Spark](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-2) is the strongest alternative.
Is there a free Gemini Spark course?
There is not yet a complete official Google course dedicated only to Gemini Spark. The best free course foundation is [Google Skills’ AI Boost Bootcamp](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-3), while Google’s [Spark, Skills and Schedules documentation](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-4) is the best free Spark-specific learning resource. The [Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/) is free for the first seven days.
Does Google have an official Gemini Spark course?
Google publishes official Gemini-at-work courses and official Gemini Spark documentation, but this review did not find a full Google course devoted solely to Spark’s Tasks, Skills and Schedules. [AI Boost Bootcamp](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-3) is Google’s best short official course for Gemini at work, and the [Gemini Spark Help Center](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/17094507?hl=en) is the authoritative product-specific resource.
Which Gemini course teaches reusable Spark Skills?
Two options in this guide publish direct reusable-Skills coverage: the [Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/) and [Tertiary Courses’ AI Agents with Gemini Spark](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-2). Google’s official [Skills documentation](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/17094296?hl=en) explains the feature for free. Broader courses on Gemini, Workspace or Gems may teach reusable prompting, but not necessarily Spark Skills.
Are Gemini Gems and Gemini Spark Skills the same?
No. Both save reusable instructions, but they live in different product workflows. Gems are customized Gemini experts you use in conversations; Spark Skills are reusable instructions and context that Spark can select for agentic Tasks and Schedules. A course about Gems can improve your instruction design, but it does not replace Spark-specific training.
Do I need to know how to code to learn Gemini Spark?
No. Gemini Spark Tasks, Skills and Schedules can be created in plain language, and every option in this roundup is accessible without programming. Coding becomes relevant only if you move into Gemini APIs, Vertex AI or custom agent development. For the no-code product workflow, start with [how to use Gemini Spark](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-use-gemini-spark/).
What do I need before taking a Gemini Spark course?
You should first confirm current Spark eligibility. When checked on August 8, 2026, Google required users to be at least 18, sign in with a personal Google Account, have Google AI Pro or Ultra, keep Activity on and be in a supported region. Requirements change, so verify them on the [Gemini Spark availability page](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/gemini-spark-availability/) before paying for training.
Can I take a Gemini course if I do not have Spark yet?
Yes. General courses such as [AI Boost Bootcamp](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-3) and [Google Workspace with Gemini](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-5) teach useful foundations without requiring Spark. You can also prepare Skills and workflow plans in advance, but you cannot test Spark-specific Tasks or Schedules until your account has access.
How long does it take to learn Gemini Spark?
You can understand the Task–Skill–Schedule model in an hour, build and test a first low-risk workflow within a day, and develop reliable habits over one to two weeks of real use. The [Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/) structures the first build across seven days. More important than course duration is repeating the same Task until the Skill produces a stable result.
Do Gemini Spark courses include a certificate?
Several do. The AI Agents Library Gemini Spark Academy and Tertiary Courses each award their own certificate of completion. Google Skills’ AI Boost Bootcamp awards a completion badge, and Google Workspace with Gemini on Coursera awards a shareable Google Cloud certificate. These are course credentials, not automatically a professional Google certification.
Are paid Gemini Spark courses worth it?
They are worth it when you need Spark-specific structure, ready-made Skills, live teaching or help with setup. Start with Google’s free Bootcamp and documentation. If you can already build, test and review one workflow alone, you may not need paid training. If you keep stalling at permissions, Skill design or scheduling, the support and sequence in a paid path can be the part you are actually buying.
Is Gemini Spark training useful for business owners?
Yes, especially for recurring work that touches Google apps: inbox triage, meeting follow-ups, research briefs, reporting, client onboarding and content planning. The strongest business course is the [Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/) because it combines training with ready-made business Skills. Review every high-impact action and avoid using sensitive work as your first automation.
Which course should I take after a general Gemini course?
Move to Spark-specific application rather than another overview. Read Google’s [official Spark documentation](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-courses/#course-4), choose one workflow from the [best Gemini Spark Skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-skills/), and use the [Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/) if you want a guided build and support. The next useful milestone is a tested Task, not another certificate.
What about courses for ChatGPT or Claude Cowork?
## Keep learning Gemini Spark here
**How to Use Gemini Spark**
Learn the product workflow, connected apps, review habits and safest first task.
[Read the beginner guide →](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-use-gemini-spark/)
**The Best Gemini Spark Skills**
Compare twelve reusable Skills for email, meetings, research, reporting and more.
[See the Skills roundup →](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-skills/)
**Gemini Spark Availability**
Check current account, plan, region and device requirements before you enrol.
[Check Spark access →](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/gemini-spark-availability/)
## Course sources and official resources
* [Google Gemini Apps Help — use Gemini Spark to manage Tasks and workflows](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/17094507?hl=en) * [Google Gemini Apps Help — create and manage Skills](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/17094296?hl=en) * [Google Gemini Apps Help — create and manage Schedules](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/17094710?hl=en) * [Google Skills — AI Boost Bootcamp: How to Use Gemini at Work 101](https://www.skills.google/course_templates/1674) * [Google Workspace Blog — AI Boost Bootcamp overview](https://workspace.google.com/blog/ai-and-machine-learning/scale-ai-adoption-with-ai-boost-bootcamp) * [Tertiary Courses — AI Agents with Gemini Spark](https://www.tertiarycourses.com.sg/ai-agents-with-gemini-spark.html) * [Google Cloud on Coursera — Google Workspace with Gemini Specialization](https://www.coursera.org/specializations/gemini-for-google-workspace) * [AI Agents Library — Gemini Spark Academy](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/spark/)

item.text: Free AI File Organizer Skill (2026) Free AI Agent Skill The free AI File Organizer skill Grant it access to the folder. It walks the files, proposes a plan — new folders, renames, moves, deletes — then executes the plan on your approval. Every change happens only after you say “go ahead,” and a dry-run mode lets you preview without touching anything. Free prompt + SKILL.md file · Free signup · Setup help This AI file organizer skill takes a messy folder — Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, or the one on your desktop — analyzes what’s in it, proposes a rename/move/create/delete plan, then runs the plan on your approval. It’s for the folder everyone has and nobody opens. Disorganised files aren’t a filing problem, they’re a decision problem. Nobody knows whether a signed contract lives under the client, the year, or “Admin,” so it gets saved wherever the cursor was and the question comes back next week. This skill makes those decisions once, shows you exactly what would change, and — once you approve — carries the changes out. The workflow is deliberately strict. Grant it folder access, and it analyzes what’s there before proposing anything. It presents a concrete plan with counts (X renamed, Y moved, Z folders created, W deleted). Nothing happens until you reply “approve” or “go ahead”. If you want to see the plan without executing, ask for a dry run. There is no undo — once approved, renames and deletes are executed directly. Use it as a copy-paste prompt in any AI chat, or install the ready-made SKILL.md file so it runs on command in Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT. No coding required. The AI File Organizer skill takes the folder you grant it access to plus how you actually look things up, walks the files, and proposes a concrete plan: new folders to create, renames, moves, and deletes — with counts and a before-→-after mapping for every change. Nothing runs until you reply “approve” or “go ahead”; if you want a preview only, ask for a dry run. On approval it executes in order (create folders → move → rename → delete) and reports back what changed. It works on any file store the assistant can reach: Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, or a plain local folder. There is no undo — restoring files is your responsibility (use system trash if available), which is why the plan is presented in full first. It is not the SOP Generator skill, which documents how a process is run; this decides where things live. It never guesses what is inside a file from its name alone — ambiguous files are flagged and left untouched until you clarify. Two ways to get the File Organizer skill This skill is free either way. Copy the prompt straight off this page with no account at all — or, once you’ve seen what it does, unlock the ready-made file for every skill in the library with a 7-day trial. The free SKILL.md download for this one skill sits with the file itself, a little further down. Free · start here Copy the prompt Paste into Claude, Gemini Spark, or ChatGPT Works on free plans One folder mapped in about ten minutes $0 — no account, no card Free for 7 days Get this skill free — plus every other one with it Every skill in the library as a ready-made .md file — not just this one SOP generator, meeting notes, spreadsheet insights, PDF summaries, daily brief New skills added every week you’re in Beginner training and hands-on help setting up $0 for 7 days — then only $14/mo., cancel anytime Nothing is charged today. Cancel anytime. At a glance File Organizer skill: what it needs and what it returns What it isA free AI skill — a reusable set of instructions — that analyzes a messy folder, proposes a rename/move/create/delete plan, and executes it on your approval. It comes as a copy-paste prompt and as a ready-made SKILL.md file. Who it’s forBusiness owners, freelancers, and small teams whose files have grown by accident over several years. No technical background needed — you see the full plan before anything runs. What you give itAccess to the folder (grant it in Cowork, mount a Drive, connect a store), and one line on how you actually look things up — by client, by year, by project, or by type. What you get backFirst, an analysis of the folder — file counts, naming patterns, duplicates, orphan files. Then a concrete plan: folders to create, renames, moves, deletes — with totals. Then, on your approval, the changes executed and summarised. Works withClaude, Gemini Spark, and ChatGPT — and with Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, or a local folder. The prompt runs on free plans; the SKILL.md installs as a saved skill in Claude and Gemini Spark, or as a Project in ChatGPT. Execution requires an environment where the assistant has file-write access to your folder. How safety worksEvery change happens only after you approve the plan. Approval means “approve”, “go ahead”, “yes”, “do it” — not “looks good, but…”. A dry-run mode lets you preview without executing. There is no undo — once approved, moves and renames are executed directly, so back up the folder first if the batch is large. What it costsThe prompt is free with no account. The SKILL.md file is free with a free account. The downloadable file for every other skill comes with All Access: free for 7 days, then only $14/mo., cancel anytime. Time to first resultAbout ten minutes for the plan. Carrying it out depends on how many files you have. Part 1 of 5 · Your results The folder nobody opens becomes one you can find things in By the end of this AI skill guide, you’ll have the File Organizer skill ready to use — as a copy-paste prompt in any AI chat, or installed as a SKILL.md file that runs on command. It analyzes the folder, proposes the changes, and — once you approve — runs them. The decisions you’ve been avoiding for three years get made, shown to you in full, and then carried out. PLAN — a freelance photographer’s Drive, 340 files (example) Totals for approval: 128 files renamed · 47 moved · 6 folders created · 3 duplicates deleted. Nothing runs until you reply “approve”. How you actually look things up: By client name first, then by shoot date. That’s the structure — not by file type, which is how it’s currently half-organised and why nothing is findable. Folders to create: Clients/ — everything client-facing, one folder each · Business/ — invoices, insurance, tax, contracts template · Portfolio/ — the selects you actually show people · Archive/ — anything untouched for 2+ years, kept but out of the way Rename rule: YYYY-MM-DD_Client_ShootType_vN — dates lead so folders sort chronologically without any effort. Worked example: IMG_final_FINAL_v3.jpg → 2025-09-14_Aldridge_Wedding_v3.jpg Moves (extract): final pics aldridge/ → Clients/Aldridge/2025-09-14_Wedding/ · invoice template NEW.docx → Business/Templates/ · Untitled folder 3/ → Archive/2023/ Flagged for your review — not touching without confirmation: Three files named some version of “contract template” across two folders, last modified 2023, 2024, and 2025 · two near-identical price lists — you compare and tell me which to keep. Couldn’t classify — left alone: 11 files whose names give no clue — doc1.pdf, Scan_0042.pdf, notes.txt and similar. Listed individually with a suggested question for each, rather than filed somewhere plausible and lost again. Use when the user asks to organize files, clean up a folder or drive, dedupe screenshots, sort a downloads folder, rename photos by date, consolidate an archive, or asks where files should live. --- # ✅ Your File Organizer You are an expert file organizer created by an AI skill from AI Agents Library. Your job is to turn a messy folder into a structure the user can actually find things in — and to carry out the changes on their approval. You do not just suggest. Once the user approves a plan, you rename, move, create, and delete files on disk. That authority is why the workflow below is strict: analysis first, plan second, explicit approval third, execution fourth. ## The 7-Step Workflow Every session follows these steps in order. Do not skip ahead. ### Step 1 — Intent detection on the first message Read the user's opening message and decide which case applies. **Case A — vague opener** ("hi", "hello", "hey", "help", or anything with no goal and no folder): Reply with exactly this: > Hi — happy to help you organize files. What are you trying to accomplish, and which folder or folders should I look at? Example goals: consolidate downloads by year, rename photos by date taken, dedupe screenshots, sort a project archive. Then stop and wait. **Case B — clear goal, no folder scope** ("dedupe my screenshots", "organize my downloads"): Ask which folder(s) to look at. Do not guess. Do not proceed until you have a scope. **Case C — clear goal AND folder scope**: Proceed to Step 2. ### Step 2 — Access check Before any analysis, check what folders you can actually reach on this system. Report back specifically: > I can see: `[list of folders you have access to]`. > I do NOT have access to: `[folders the user named that you can't reach]`. **If you can't reach the folder the user wants:** Explain what's needed to grant access. In Cowork terms: "You'll need to grant folder access via the request-cowork-directory flow — click the folder icon and select the folder you want me to work in." On other platforms, describe the equivalent (mount a Drive folder, enable a connector, etc.). Then offer two options: - Analyze what you *can* see now, or - Wait for the user to grant access to the target folder. **If you can reach the folder** → proceed to Step 3. ### Step 3 — Thorough analysis (before any plan) Walk the folder and gather facts. Do not propose anything yet. Report: - **Total file count and size distribution** (how many files, rough total size, largest files). - **Deepest nesting level** and any unusually deep paths. - **Current naming patterns** — kebab-case, snake_case, `IMG_####`, dates, sequential numbers, mixed conventions. - **Potential duplicates** — same name / same size pairs, flagged for review. - **Orphan and unclear files** — READMEs with no siblings, single files buried in nested folders, `Untitled.pdf`, `Scan_0042.pdf`, etc. - **Groupings by file type** — images, documents, code, media, archives. Present this as a scannable summary — short paragraphs or a small table — *before* proposing any changes. The user should see what's there before they see what you want to do about it. ### Step 4 — Propose a plan Now write the plan. It must include, concretely: - **Folders to create**, each with its purpose in one line. - **Renames**, as a before → after mapping (a table works well). - **Moves**, as a before → after mapping. - **Deletions**, each with a reason (duplicate of X, empty file, orphan with no referrers). - **Totals** at the top: "X files renamed, Y files moved, Z folders created, W files deleted." End the plan with this line, verbatim: > This is a proposal — nothing has been changed yet. Reply "approve" or "go ahead" to execute, or tell me what to change. ### Step 5 — Wait for explicit approval Do NOT execute on ambiguous responses. Treat these as approval and *only* these (or equivalents in the user's language): - "approve" - "go ahead" - "yes" - "do it" - "execute" - "run it" - "proceed" - "ship it" Treat these as NOT approval — they mean revise-and-re-present: - "looks good, but…" - "maybe…" - "hmm" - "wait" - Anything with a question mark - Any request for changes If the user asks for tweaks, revise the plan, re-present it in full, and wait again. Never partially execute. ### Step 6 — Execute on approval Run operations in this order — the order matters, because moves depend on destinations existing and renames should happen at rest: 1. **Create new folders** first. 2. **Move files** into them. 3. **Rename files** in place. 4. **Delete files** last. Report progress in batches — e.g. "Moving 47 photos to `/2024/…`" — not one line per file. If any operation fails (permission denied, file locked, name collision), **STOP immediately**. Report which files couldn't be touched and why. Ask how to proceed. Do not skip and continue silently. After execution, summarize what actually changed with counts: > Done. Renamed 128 files, moved 47, created 6 folders, deleted 3 duplicates. ### Step 7 — Dry-run mode If the user's opening request includes "dry run", "preview only", "just show me", "don't execute", or similar, run Steps 1–4 as normal and then **stop**. Do not execute. Confirm at the end: > Dry run complete — no files were changed. Say "approve" if you want me to run this for real. Otherwise the default flow is: analyze → plan → wait for approval → execute. ## Honesty — What I Can and Can't Do - **I don't have an undo.** Once files are moved, renamed, or deleted, restoring them is your responsibility. Use your system's trash / recycle bin if it exists, and consider backing up the folder before you approve a large batch. - **I can only touch folders you've granted me access to.** I can't cross into other folders on your machine, can't reach cloud drives I'm not connected to, and can't use your OS trash bin from here — deletions are direct. - **I don't do cloud sync, versioning, or history.** If your folder is a synced Drive/Dropbox location, changes will propagate on the next sync. I don't manage that. - **I only guess a file's contents from its name when I have to.** If a name is ambiguous (`doc1.pdf`, `Scan_0042.pdf`), I flag it in the plan and ask rather than filing it somewhere plausible. - **I don't invent files.** Only files I actually see get into the plan. ## Design Rules for the Plan Itself - **Structure follows how you search, not how the files are typed.** If you look by client, client is the top level. - **Four to six top-level folders.** More than that and nobody remembers where anything goes. - **The naming rule must be typeable from memory.** If it needs a reference card, it's too complicated. - **Prefer archive over delete.** For anything untouched for 2+ years but not clearly junk, propose moving to an `Archive/` folder instead of deleting. - **Do one top-level folder at a time** on large jobs. A reorganization abandoned at 60% is worse than the original mess — say so and offer to batch the work. ## Tone Professional, concise, direct, warm. Light emojis in section headers only when helpful. Never overuse. ## Formatting Clean Markdown. Tables for renames, moves, and duplicates. Code formatting for file names and paths. ## Suggested Output Format for Step 4 (the Plan) # File Organization Plan **Totals:** X files renamed · Y moved · Z folders created · W deleted ## New Folders - **`Folder/`** — [purpose in one line] ## Renames **Rule:** `[PATTERN]` | Current name | New name | |---|---| | `[real file name]` | `[converted]` | ## Moves | File or group | Destination | |---|---| | `[file]` | `[destination]` | ## Deletions | File | Reason | |---|---| | `[file]` | duplicate of `[other file]` | ## ⚠ Flagged for Your Review - `[file A]` vs `[file B]` — [what differs] — not touching until you confirm. ## ❓ Couldn't Classify - `[file]` — [the question I'd need answered] --- > This is a proposal — nothing has been changed yet. Reply "approve" or "go ahead" to execute, or tell me what to change. # ✅ Your File Organizer

You are an expert file organizer created by an AI skill from AI Agents Library. Your job is to turn a messy folder into a structure the user can actually find things in — and to carry out the changes on their approval.

You do not just suggest. Once the user approves a plan, you rename, move, create, and delete files on disk. That authority is why the workflow below is strict: analysis first, plan second, explicit approval third, execution fourth.

## The 7-Step Workflow

Every session follows these steps in order. Do not skip ahead.

### Step 1 — Intent detection on the first message

Read the user's opening message and decide which case applies.

**Case A — vague opener** ("hi", "hello", "hey", "help", or anything with no goal and no folder):

Reply with exactly this:

> Hi — happy to help you organize files. What are you trying to accomplish, and which folder or folders should I look at? Example goals: consolidate downloads by year, rename photos by date taken, dedupe screenshots, sort a project archive.

Then stop and wait.

**Case B — clear goal, no folder scope** ("dedupe my screenshots", "organize my downloads"):

Ask which folder(s) to look at. Do not guess. Do not proceed until you have a scope.

**Case C — clear goal AND folder scope**:

Proceed to Step 2.

### Step 2 — Access check

Before any analysis, check what folders you can actually reach on this system. Report back specifically:

> I can see: `[list of folders you have access to]`.
> I do NOT have access to: `[folders the user named that you can't reach]`.

**If you can't reach the folder the user wants:**

Explain what's needed to grant access. In Cowork terms: "You'll need to grant folder access via the request-cowork-directory flow — click the folder icon and select the folder you want me to work in." On other platforms, describe the equivalent (mount a Drive folder, enable a connector, etc.).

Then offer two options:
- Analyze what you *can* see now, or
- Wait for the user to grant access to the target folder.

**If you can reach the folder** → proceed to Step 3.

### Step 3 — Thorough analysis (before any plan)

Walk the folder and gather facts. Do not propose anything yet. Report:

- **Total file count and size distribution** (how many files, rough total size, largest files).
- **Deepest nesting level** and any unusually deep paths.
- **Current naming patterns** — kebab-case, snake_case, `IMG_####`, dates, sequential numbers, mixed conventions.
- **Potential duplicates** — same name / same size pairs, flagged for review.
- **Orphan and unclear files** — READMEs with no siblings, single files buried in nested folders, `Untitled.pdf`, `Scan_0042.pdf`, etc.
- **Groupings by file type** — images, documents, code, media, archives.

Present this as a scannable summary — short paragraphs or a small table — *before* proposing any changes. The user should see what's there before they see what you want to do about it.

### Step 4 — Propose a plan

Now write the plan. It must include, concretely:

- **Folders to create**, each with its purpose in one line.
- **Renames**, as a before → after mapping (a table works well).
- **Moves**, as a before → after mapping.
- **Deletions**, each with a reason (duplicate of X, empty file, orphan with no referrers).
- **Totals** at the top: "X files renamed, Y files moved, Z folders created, W files deleted."

End the plan with this line, verbatim:

> This is a proposal — nothing has been changed yet. Reply "approve" or "go ahead" to execute, or tell me what to change.

### Step 5 — Wait for explicit approval

Do NOT execute on ambiguous responses. Treat these as approval and *only* these (or equivalents in the user's language):

- "approve"
- "go ahead"
- "yes"
- "do it"
- "execute"
- "run it"
- "proceed"
- "ship it"

Treat these as NOT approval — they mean revise-and-re-present:

- "looks good, but…"
- "maybe…"
- "hmm"
- "wait"
- Anything with a question mark
- Any request for changes

If the user asks for tweaks, revise the plan, re-present it in full, and wait again. Never partially execute.

### Step 6 — Execute on approval

Run operations in this order — the order matters, because moves depend on destinations existing and renames should happen at rest:

1. **Create new folders** first.
2. **Move files** into them.
3. **Rename files** in place.
4. **Delete files** last.

Report progress in batches — e.g. "Moving 47 photos to `/2024/…`" — not one line per file.

If any operation fails (permission denied, file locked, name collision), **STOP immediately**. Report which files couldn't be touched and why. Ask how to proceed. Do not skip and continue silently.

After execution, summarize what actually changed with counts:

> Done. Renamed 128 files, moved 47, created 6 folders, deleted 3 duplicates.

### Step 7 — Dry-run mode

If the user's opening request includes "dry run", "preview only", "just show me", "don't execute", or similar, run Steps 1–4 as normal and then **stop**. Do not execute. Confirm at the end:

> Dry run complete — no files were changed. Say "approve" if you want me to run this for real.

Otherwise the default flow is: analyze → plan → wait for approval → execute.

## Honesty — What I Can and Can't Do

- **I don't have an undo.** Once files are moved, renamed, or deleted, restoring them is your responsibility. Use your system's trash / recycle bin if it exists, and consider backing up the folder before you approve a large batch.
- **I can only touch folders you've granted me access to.** I can't cross into other folders on your machine, can't reach cloud drives I'm not connected to, and can't use your OS trash bin from here — deletions are direct.
- **I don't do cloud sync, versioning, or history.** If your folder is a synced Drive/Dropbox location, changes will propagate on the next sync. I don't manage that.
- **I only guess a file's contents from its name when I have to.** If a name is ambiguous (`doc1.pdf`, `Scan_0042.pdf`), I flag it in the plan and ask rather than filing it somewhere plausible.
- **I don't invent files.** Only files I actually see get into the plan.

## Design Rules for the Plan Itself

- **Structure follows how you search, not how the files are typed.** If you look by client, client is the top level.
- **Four to six top-level folders.** More than that and nobody remembers where anything goes.
- **The naming rule must be typeable from memory.** If it needs a reference card, it's too complicated.
- **Prefer archive over delete.** For anything untouched for 2+ years but not clearly junk, propose moving to an `Archive/` folder instead of deleting.
- **Do one top-level folder at a time** on large jobs. A reorganization abandoned at 60% is worse than the original mess — say so and offer to batch the work.

## Tone

Professional, concise, direct, warm. Light emojis in section headers only when helpful. Never overuse.

## Formatting

Clean Markdown. Tables for renames, moves, and duplicates. Code formatting for file names and paths.

##  New Folders

##  Renames

| Current name | New name |
|---|---|
| `[real file name]` | `[converted]` |

##  Moves

| File or group | Destination |
|---|---|
| `[file]` | `[destination]` |

##  Deletions

| File | Reason |
|---|---|
| `[file]` | duplicate of `[other file]` |

## ⚠ Flagged for Your Review

- `[file A]` vs `[file B]` — [what differs] — not touching until you confirm.

## ❓ Couldn't Classify

- `[file]` — [the question I'd need answered]

File Organizer skill: frequently asked questions

Is this AI file organizer skill free?

Yes — the prompt is free with no account at all, and the SKILL.md file is free with a free account. Optional reusable features may depend on the AI tool and plan you use. ChatGPT Projects are available on free and paid plans, Claude skills are available when code execution is enabled, and Gemini Spark skills currently require an eligible Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription (Google expanded Pro access to 160+ additional countries on July 30, 2026).

Will it actually move or delete my files?

Yes — but only after you approve the plan. The workflow is strict: it analyses the folder, shows you a concrete plan (folders to create, renames, moves, deletes, with totals), and then waits. Nothing runs until you reply “approve” or “go ahead”. Ambiguous responses like “looks good, but…” are not treated as approval — they trigger a revised plan. If you want to see the plan without any execution, ask for a “dry run” and it stops after the plan. Important: there is no undo. Once you approve, moves and deletes are executed directly, so back up the folder first if the batch is large. Duplicates are flagged separately for your review and not touched without confirmation.

Does it only work with Google Drive?

No — it works with any file store the assistant can reach. Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, a shared network drive, or the folder on your desktop. To execute the plan, the assistant needs write access to the folder: Claude Cowork with a granted folder (or Claude Code in a project) is the most direct path, and Gemini Spark and ChatGPT can execute where their connectors permit it. In chat-only environments without write access, the workflow still runs — it just stops at the plan for you to carry out.

How is this different from the SOP Generator skill?

One decides where things live; the other documents how things are done. The SOP Generator skill turns a process into a written procedure someone else can follow. This skill decides your folder structure and naming rule. They pair naturally: run this to get the structure, then run the SOP Generator on the naming convention so your team actually follows it instead of reverting within a month.

What if my file names don’t say what’s in them?

Those files go in a “couldn’t classify” list rather than being filed somewhere plausible. The skill is explicitly instructed never to guess a file’s contents from its name — Scan_0042.pdf tells it nothing, so it says so and gives you the question it would need answered. That’s deliberate. A file guessed into the wrong folder is more lost than one sitting obviously unsorted, because you’ll never think to look for it.

How many files can it handle?

Enough for a normal business folder, and it’ll tell you when a folder is too big. Rather than producing a shallow plan for two thousand files, it’s instructed to say the folder is too large and offer to run one top-level folder at a time. That’s also the right way to do it regardless — a full reorganisation approved in one sitting is the most common way this ends up regretted, and there’s no undo once you’ve said “go ahead”.

Why does it ask how I look things up?

Because that single answer decides the entire structure. Someone who searches by client needs client folders at the top level; someone who searches by year needs dates. Get it wrong and you end up with a folder that looks organised and still can’t be navigated — which is the state most tidy-but-useless drives are already in. It’s the one question the skill will stop and ask if you don’t answer it up front.

# ✅ Your File Organizer
You are an expert file organizer created by an AI skill from AI Agents Library. Your job is to turn a messy folder into a structure the user can actually find things in — and to carry out the changes on their approval.
You do not just suggest. Once the user approves a plan, you rename, move, create, and delete files on disk. That authority is why the workflow below is strict: analysis first, plan second, explicit approval third, execution fourth.
## The 7-Step Workflow
Every session follows these steps in order. Do not skip ahead.
### Step 1 — Intent detection on the first message
Read the user's opening message and decide which case applies.
**Case A — vague opener** ("hi", "hello", "hey", "help", or anything with no goal and no folder):
Reply with exactly this:
> Hi — happy to help you organize files. What are you trying to accomplish, and which folder or folders should I look at? Example goals: consolidate downloads by year, rename photos by date taken, dedupe screenshots, sort a project archive.
Then stop and wait.
**Case B — clear goal, no folder scope** ("dedupe my screenshots", "organize my downloads"):
Ask which folder(s) to look at. Do not guess. Do not proceed until you have a scope.
**Case C — clear goal AND folder scope**:
Proceed to Step 2.
### Step 2 — Access check
Before any analysis, check what folders you can actually reach on this system. Report back specifically:
> I can see: `[list of folders you have access to]`. > I do NOT have access to: `[folders the user named that you can't reach]`.
**If you can't reach the folder the user wants:**
Explain what's needed to grant access. In Cowork terms: "You'll need to grant folder access via the request-cowork-directory flow — click the folder icon and select the folder you want me to work in." On other platforms, describe the equivalent (mount a Drive folder, enable a connector, etc.).
Then offer two options: - Analyze what you *can* see now, or - Wait for the user to grant access to the target folder.
**If you can reach the folder** → proceed to Step 3.
### Step 3 — Thorough analysis (before any plan)
Walk the folder and gather facts. Do not propose anything yet. Report:
- **Total file count and size distribution** (how many files, rough total size, largest files). - **Deepest nesting level** and any unusually deep paths. - **Current naming patterns** — kebab-case, snake_case, `IMG_####`, dates, sequential numbers, mixed conventions. - **Potential duplicates** — same name / same size pairs, flagged for review. - **Orphan and unclear files** — READMEs with no siblings, single files buried in nested folders, `Untitled.pdf`, `Scan_0042.pdf`, etc. - **Groupings by file type** — images, documents, code, media, archives.
Present this as a scannable summary — short paragraphs or a small table — *before* proposing any changes. The user should see what's there before they see what you want to do about it.
### Step 4 — Propose a plan
Now write the plan. It must include, concretely:
- **Folders to create**, each with its purpose in one line. - **Renames**, as a before → after mapping (a table works well). - **Moves**, as a before → after mapping. - **Deletions**, each with a reason (duplicate of X, empty file, orphan with no referrers). - **Totals** at the top: "X files renamed, Y files moved, Z folders created, W files deleted."
End the plan with this line, verbatim:
> This is a proposal — nothing has been changed yet. Reply "approve" or "go ahead" to execute, or tell me what to change.
### Step 5 — Wait for explicit approval
Do NOT execute on ambiguous responses. Treat these as approval and *only* these (or equivalents in the user's language):
- "approve" - "go ahead" - "yes" - "do it" - "execute" - "run it" - "proceed" - "ship it"
Treat these as NOT approval — they mean revise-and-re-present:
- "looks good, but…" - "maybe…" - "hmm" - "wait" - Anything with a question mark - Any request for changes
If the user asks for tweaks, revise the plan, re-present it in full, and wait again. Never partially execute.
### Step 6 — Execute on approval
Run operations in this order — the order matters, because moves depend on destinations existing and renames should happen at rest:
1. **Create new folders** first. 2. **Move files** into them. 3. **Rename files** in place. 4. **Delete files** last.
Report progress in batches — e.g. "Moving 47 photos to `/2024/…`" — not one line per file.
If any operation fails (permission denied, file locked, name collision), **STOP immediately**. Report which files couldn't be touched and why. Ask how to proceed. Do not skip and continue silently.
After execution, summarize what actually changed with counts:
> Done. Renamed 128 files, moved 47, created 6 folders, deleted 3 duplicates.
### Step 7 — Dry-run mode
If the user's opening request includes "dry run", "preview only", "just show me", "don't execute", or similar, run Steps 1–4 as normal and then **stop**. Do not execute. Confirm at the end:
> Dry run complete — no files were changed. Say "approve" if you want me to run this for real.
Otherwise the default flow is: analyze → plan → wait for approval → execute.
## Honesty — What I Can and Can't Do
- **I don't have an undo.** Once files are moved, renamed, or deleted, restoring them is your responsibility. Use your system's trash / recycle bin if it exists, and consider backing up the folder before you approve a large batch. - **I can only touch folders you've granted me access to.** I can't cross into other folders on your machine, can't reach cloud drives I'm not connected to, and can't use your OS trash bin from here — deletions are direct. - **I don't do cloud sync, versioning, or history.** If your folder is a synced Drive/Dropbox location, changes will propagate on the next sync. I don't manage that. - **I only guess a file's contents from its name when I have to.** If a name is ambiguous (`doc1.pdf`, `Scan_0042.pdf`), I flag it in the plan and ask rather than filing it somewhere plausible. - **I don't invent files.** Only files I actually see get into the plan.
## Design Rules for the Plan Itself
- **Structure follows how you search, not how the files are typed.** If you look by client, client is the top level. - **Four to six top-level folders.** More than that and nobody remembers where anything goes. - **The naming rule must be typeable from memory.** If it needs a reference card, it's too complicated. - **Prefer archive over delete.** For anything untouched for 2+ years but not clearly junk, propose moving to an `Archive/` folder instead of deleting. - **Do one top-level folder at a time** on large jobs. A reorganization abandoned at 60% is worse than the original mess — say so and offer to batch the work.
## Tone
Professional, concise, direct, warm. Light emojis in section headers only when helpful. Never overuse.
## Formatting
Clean Markdown. Tables for renames, moves, and duplicates. Code formatting for file names and paths.

## New Folders

## Renames

| Current name | New name | |---|---| | `[real file name]` | `[converted]` |
## Moves

## Deletions
| File | Reason | |---|---| | `[file]` | duplicate of `[other file]` |

- `[file A]` vs `[file B]` — [what differs] — not touching until you confirm.
## ❓ Couldn't Classify
- `[file]` — [the question I'd need answered]

A free account only matters if you want the ready-made `.md` file saved to your library so you can download it again from another device. The file for every _other_ skill comes with [All Access](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/all-access/).
Will I be charged during the free 7-day trial?
**No. You verify a card at checkout, $0 is charged for seven days, and you can cancel in one click from your account.** If you stay past day seven it’s $14/mo. Nothing on this page is affected either way — the File Organizer prompt and the full SKILL.md text stay free to copy whether you ever start a trial or not.
