item.text: How to Schedule Tasks in ChatGPT Work (2026) ChatGPT Work’s Scheduled Tasks feature lets you run a tested prompt on a recurring cadence — hourly, daily, weekly, or a custom RFC 5545 recurrence rule — by opening Scheduled, pasting the prompt, and choosing whether each run starts a fresh chat or returns to an existing conversation. As of August 2026, it’s available in the Scheduled view on ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare and Edu workspaces, and every run is reviewable afterwards from the same Scheduled view — which behaves like an inbox and flags the runs that need your attention. Quick answer: Scheduled Tasks in ChatGPT Work is a recurring-run feature that turns any tested prompt into a background job on a schedule you define. It works by pointing ChatGPT at a source and cadence, running unattended, and reporting back in the Scheduled inbox only when there’s something worth reading. You need an eligible ChatGPT Work plan, a prompt you’ve already tested manually, and a clear rule for what counts as important enough to report. The setting that decides whether a scheduled task actually works is not the day or the time. It is where the task runs. A task created on ChatGPT web can use uploads, connected tools, skills and plugins while your laptop is shut — but it cannot reach a folder on your computer. A task that depends on local files has to run on the desktop app, which means the machine stays on and the app stays open. This guide covers only scheduling, triggering and monitoring. If you are still deciding whether to use Work at all, start with what ChatGPT Work is and how it differs from regular Chat. Prefer structured lessons before you set anything up? Our ChatGPT Training for Beginners path walks through workspace setup, installing reusable ChatGPT skill files, and putting a first workflow on a schedule. How do you schedule a task in ChatGPT Work? Test the prompt once in a normal chat and confirm the output is reviewable. Open Scheduled and create a new task, or ask ChatGPT in the chat to schedule it for you. Paste the tested prompt and state what counts as worth reporting. Choose the cadence — hourly, daily, weekly, a custom schedule, or a recurrence rule. Decide whether each run starts a new chat or returns to this one, then save and review the first few runs. Scheduled tasks run unattended, so the prompt has to answer questions you will not be there to answer. Say what to check, what to ignore, what counts as important, and when to stop. Standalone vs In-Chat Scheduled Tasks ChatGPT Work has two shapes of scheduled task, and picking the wrong one is the most common reason a schedule produces output nobody reads. The difference is memory: whether each run begins from a blank slate or inherits everything already discussed in a conversation. Standalone scheduled task Scheduled task inside a chat What each run does Starts a new chat from the saved prompt Returns to the same chat and reuses its context Where results appear As separate runs in Scheduled In the original conversation Best cadence Daily, weekly, monthly, or a custom rule Minute-based loops, or a daily/weekly check-in Use it for Monday competitor updates, monthly analytics summaries, recurring reports Waiting on a long-running job, polling a source, continuing a research loop Watch out for The prompt must carry all its own context — nothing is remembered The chat grows over time, and old context can start to skew results A useful rule: if you would be annoyed to receive the same information twice, use a standalone task and give it explicit change criteria. If you would be confused receiving it without the earlier conversation, schedule it inside the chat. Where Scheduled Tasks Run: Web vs Desktop This is the constraint that quietly breaks schedules. ChatGPT Work is available on the web and in the desktop app, and the two do not have the same reach. Capability ChatGPT web ChatGPT desktop app Runs while your computer is off Yes No — the machine and app must stay available Local folders and files No direct access Yes, for tasks scoped to a local project Uploads, connected tools, skills, plugins Yes Yes Manage tasks in Scheduled Yes, where enabled for your workspace Yes, from the sidebar A web task cannot read your hard drive Scheduled tasks on the web have no local folder available between runs. If a task needs source material, keep it somewhere the task can actually reach: attached to the task prompt, inside a skill, uploaded, or in a connected service. Pointing a web schedule at “the spreadsheet on my desktop” produces a confident, useless run. The Scheduled management interface is not available in the Codex CLI or the IDE extension. Use ChatGPT on the web or the desktop app to create and manage schedules. There are two setup paths. You can build the task yourself in Scheduled, or you can simply describe it in a chat and let ChatGPT create it — including drafting the prompt, choosing whether runs return to the current chat, and updating the task later when the scope changes. Run the prompt manually in a normal chat first. OpenAI recommends this explicitly, and it is the step people skip. You are checking three things: that the prompt is scoped tightly enough, that the model and tools behave the way you expected, and that the output is something you can actually review in under a minute. A prompt that needs a follow-up question to be useful will fail on a schedule, because there is nobody there to answer it. If you don’t have a prompt to test yet, start with our free AI News skill — it’s a ready-made prompt, so what you’re testing in step one is real wording instead of a blank page. Open Scheduled and create a new task, then paste the prompt you just tested. Or stay in the conversation and ask. Describe the work, the schedule, and whether each run should return to the current chat or start a new one — ChatGPT can draft the prompt, pick the destination, and update the task later when the cadence or scope changes. This is usually faster right after a successful test run, because the working context already exists. Recurring work needs tighter instructions than a live session. State which sources may be used, the period to cover, the method to follow, the output format, and — most importantly — what counts as important enough to report and what should be ignored. If the task should sometimes produce nothing at all, say so directly. “If nothing meaningful changed, reply with one line saying so” is the single most valuable sentence in a recurring prompt. Use the free productivity AI skill prompts here to not start from scratch. Pick the frequency from the options available in your account, or build a custom schedule. Then confirm the destination: a standalone task that reports into Scheduled, or an in-chat task that returns to the existing conversation. Match the cadence to how often the underlying information actually changes — not to how often you would like an update. A daily check on a source that changes monthly produces twenty-nine runs of noise and one you stop reading. Daily earns its place when the inputs genuinely turn over every day, which is why a morning AI Daily Brief skill works on a schedule and a market summary rarely does. Save the task and open the first completed run from Scheduled. Check whether it used the intended sources, covered the right period, followed the format, and separated verified facts from assumptions. OpenAI’s guidance is to review the first few outputs and then adjust the prompt, tools or cadence if results are too broad. Treat the first three runs as a trial, not as delivery. Cadence, Custom Schedules and RRULE Triggers Standard cadences cover most business workflows: hourly, daily, weekly. Two options go further. Minute-based intervals, for chats that are waiting on something Scheduled tasks inside a chat can use minute-based intervals. This is built for active follow-up loops rather than reporting — checking whether a long-running operation has finished, or polling a connected source until a specific thing changes. Give these a stopping condition, or you have built something that runs forever. Custom schedules and recurrence rules When the built-in options do not fit, standalone tasks support custom schedule controls, and an advanced schedule can be expressed as an RFC 5545 recurrence rule (RRULE) — the same calendar standard behind repeating events in Google Calendar and Outlook. OpenAI documents this example, which runs at 9:00 on the first day of every month: RRULE:FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTHDAY=1;BYHOUR=9;BYMINUTE=0 Because RRULE is a published standard rather than a ChatGPT-specific syntax, the usual building blocks apply: FREQ sets the unit, INTERVAL skips periods, BYDAY picks weekdays, and BYHOUR with BYMINUTE sets the time. A weekday-morning briefing, for instance, is FREQ=DAILY;BYDAY=MO,TU,WE,TH,FR with the hour you want. Confirm the rule behaved as intended by checking the next scheduled run time after you save it. Schedule around your review habit, not the clock A report that lands at 6:00 a.m. Monday gets read. The same report at 4:00 p.m. Friday does not. Set the trigger for shortly before you would naturally look at that kind of information. The Recurring Task Prompt Framework A schedule is only a trigger. The prompt decides whether run number twenty is as useful as run number one. This framework gives ChatGPT the five things an unattended run needs: timing, sources, method, output, and a reporting threshold. Task name: [SHORT DESCRIPTIVE NAME] Goal: [The business outcome, not the activity. "Know if a competitor changed pricing," not "check the pricing page."] Approved sources: - [Connected tool, upload, skill, or URL 1] - [Source 2] - Cover only [time period, e.g. the last 7 days] Method: 1. [First required step] 2. Compare what you find against [baseline, prior run, or criteria] 3. Remove duplicates and separate confirmed facts from assumptions Report only if: [The specific change threshold. e.g. "a price changed, a new feature shipped, or a competitor published a comparison page."] If nothing meets this bar, reply with a single line saying so. Output format: [Bulleted summary / table / short brief], under [N] words. Flag anything uncertain under a heading called "Needs review." Never do without asking me first: Send messages, publish anything, change records, make purchases, or delete data. The last two blocks are what make a schedule survivable. Without a reporting threshold you get noise; without an action boundary you get an agent taking consequential steps at 3:00 a.m. with nobody watching. If you find yourself pasting the same framework repeatedly, that is the signal to turn it into a reusable skill instead — see how to turn a prompt into an AI skill. How to Build a Monitor That Stays Quiet A monitor is not a separate ChatGPT feature. It is a scheduled task with a reporting threshold: ChatGPT checks a source repeatedly and tells you only when something crosses the bar you defined. Everything that makes monitors useful lives in that definition. A vague monitor reports every run, which trains you to ignore it. A well-defined one might stay silent for three weeks and then earn its place with a single message. Specify all five of these: Define Weak version Version that works What to check “Watch our competitor” “Check the pricing page and the changelog at [URL]” How often “Regularly” “Every weekday at 7:00 a.m.” What counts “Anything important” “A price change, a new plan tier, or a removed feature” What to ignore (unspecified) “Blog posts, job listings, and copy edits” When to stop (never) “Stop after the migration ships, or after 30 days” Monitors that watch a public web source are a natural fit for a task created on the web, since they do not need anything on your computer and should keep running while it is closed. Managing Runs: Pause, Edit, Resume, Delete The Scheduled view is the control panel and the inbox at once. It lists tasks by status — active, paused, completed — alongside recent runs, and shows an unread indicator when a run has something that needs your attention. Review a run — open it from Scheduled to see what the task actually did, not just its conclusion. Edit — update the instructions or cadence, then review the next run before trusting it again. An edited prompt is an untested prompt. Pause — stops future runs while keeping the task. The right move for seasonal workflows or while you rewrite instructions. Delete — for workflows that are genuinely finished. If you are unsure, pause instead. Schedules accumulate quietly. A monthly review of the Scheduled list — pausing anything you have stopped reading — keeps both the noise and the usage down, since agent-style runs consume more than ordinary chat messages. Permissions and Unattended Runs Scheduled tasks run when you are not there, using your default permission settings. That is the entire benefit and the entire risk in one sentence. Where organization policy allows it, scheduled tasks run without pausing to ask for approval. In managed workspaces, admins can enforce requirements that override this and force scheduled runs back to the approval behaviour of your selected permission mode. If a scheduled task is behaving more conservatively than you expect, workspace policy is the first thing to check — see OpenAI’s permissions documentation. Grant the narrowest access that lets the task succeed Start restrictive and widen only when a run genuinely fails without it. Require explicit human approval before anything consequential and hard to reverse: sending messages, publishing, sharing files, changing records, making purchases, or deleting data. A scheduled task that only reads and reports is very difficult to regret. Check the model on older scheduled tasks Scheduled tasks pinned to gpt-5.4 or gpt-5.4-mini with ChatGPT sign-in need updating before those models retire on August 31, 2026. OpenAI’s stated replacements are gpt-5.6-terra for gpt-5.4 and gpt-5.6-luna for gpt-5.4-mini. Tasks left on a retired model are the kind of thing you discover through silence. Skills Worth Putting on a Schedule Scheduled tasks can use skills, and pairing the two is what makes a recurring workflow maintainable: the skill holds the method, the schedule holds the timing. Change the method once and every future run inherits it. In the desktop app you can invoke a specific skill directly in the task prompt using $skill-name, which is worth doing whenever the workflow should not depend on automatic tool selection. These free skills are all built around work that repeats on a natural cadence: Skill Natural cadence What the run produces Weekly Business Brief Weekly, Monday morning Decisions, blockers, owners and deadlines in one brief Competitor Research Weekly or monthly What changed since the last run, with sources AI News Research Daily or weekday mornings Filtered industry updates, not a raw feed Gmail Triage Daily What needs a reply, sorted by urgency Customer Feedback Weekly or monthly Themes and sentiment shifts across recent feedback Market Research Brief Monthly or quarterly A structured brief on a defined market question New to skills entirely? Start with how to use ChatGPT skills, or how to create your own ChatGPT skill if you already know the workflow you want to repeat. If Skills are not showing in your account, that is a plan and workspace question covered in ChatGPT Skills availability. Why a Scheduled Task Did Not Run Most failures trace back to a handful of causes, and nearly all of them are environmental rather than a problem with the prompt. Symptom Likely cause Fix Nothing ran overnight A desktop task that needs local files, on a machine that was asleep Move it to the web if it does not need local files, or keep the computer on and the app running Ran, but found nothing The task cannot reach the source — a web task pointed at a local folder Attach the material to the task, put it in a skill, upload it, or use a connected service Reports every single run No reporting threshold in the prompt Add explicit change criteria and permission to report nothing Output drifted over time An in-chat task accumulating stale context Switch to a standalone task so each run starts clean Stops at an approval prompt Workspace policy requires approval for unattended runs Confirm the admin policy, or narrow the task to read-and-report only No Scheduled option at all Using the Codex CLI or IDE extension, or the feature is not enabled for the workspace Use ChatGPT on the web or the desktop app, and check with your admin Working in more than one AI tool? The equivalent setup for Google’s assistant is covered in Gemini Spark tasks, skills and schedules. Can ChatGPT Work run tasks on a recurring schedule? Yes. ChatGPT Work supports scheduled tasks that run in the background on a recurring cadence. You manage them from the Scheduled view, which lists active, paused and completed tasks along with their recent runs. A scheduled task can also use skills and plugins, so a repeatable method and current data can run together. What is the difference between a standalone scheduled task and one inside a chat? A standalone scheduled task starts a new chat from its saved prompt on every run and reports each result separately in Scheduled. A scheduled task inside a chat returns to that same conversation and reuses its existing context. Use standalone for independent recurring reports, and in-chat when continuity matters — such as waiting for a long-running job to finish. Do ChatGPT Work scheduled tasks run when my computer is off? It depends where the task was created. Tasks created on ChatGPT web can keep running while your computer is off, because they rely on uploads, connected tools, skills and plugins rather than your machine. A task scoped to local files in the desktop app needs the computer powered on and the ChatGPT app running at the scheduled time. Can a scheduled task use files on my computer? Only on the desktop app. Scheduled tasks in the ChatGPT desktop app can work with local projects, and the files must still be available on disk when the run starts. Scheduled tasks on the web cannot work directly in a folder on your computer, so keep required source material in the task prompt, a skill, an upload, or a connected service. How do I set a custom schedule in ChatGPT Work? Standalone scheduled tasks offer custom schedule controls beyond the standard hourly, daily and weekly options. For an advanced schedule you can supply an RFC 5545 recurrence rule (RRULE) — the same standard used by calendar apps. OpenAI’s documented example, RRULE:FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTHDAY=1;BYHOUR=9;BYMINUTE=0, runs the task at 9:00 on the first day of every month. What is a ChatGPT Work monitor? A monitor is not a separate product or feature. It is a scheduled task written so that ChatGPT repeatedly checks a source and reports only when something meaningful changes. To work properly, the prompt must state what to check, how often, what counts as important, what to ignore, and when to stop. Without those, the monitor reports on every run and quickly gets ignored. Can I ask ChatGPT to create a scheduled task for me? Yes. You can create and update scheduled tasks directly from a chat by describing the work, the schedule, and whether each run should return to the current chat or start a new one. ChatGPT can draft the prompt, choose the destination, and update the task later when its scope or cadence changes. Skills can also create and update scheduled tasks. Do scheduled tasks ask for approval before taking actions? Scheduled tasks run unattended using your default permission settings, and where organization policy allows it they run without pausing for approval. Admin-enforced requirements in a managed workspace can override this and return scheduled runs to the approval behaviour of your selected permission mode. Grant the narrowest access a task needs, and require human approval before anything consequential or hard to reverse. How do I pause or stop a recurring ChatGPT task? Open Scheduled, select the task, and pause it to stop future runs while keeping the task available to resume later. Delete it only when the workflow is genuinely finished. Reviewing the Scheduled list once a month and pausing anything you have stopped reading keeps both the noise and the usage down, since agent-style runs consume more than ordinary chat messages. Why did my scheduled task stop working after an update? Check which model the task is pinned to. Scheduled tasks using gpt-5.4 or gpt-5.4-mini with ChatGPT sign-in need updating before those models retire on August 31, 2026 — OpenAI’s replacements are gpt-5.6-terra and gpt-5.6-luna. Also confirm the task can still reach its sources, since a moved file or a revoked connector will produce runs that complete but find nothing. Official Sources and Next Steps Fact-checked August 3, 2026. ChatGPT Work is changing quickly. Confirm anything business-critical against OpenAI’s current documentation before you rely on a schedule. Scheduled tasks — OpenAI documentation Get started with ChatGPT Work Build skills for ChatGPT Permissions and access

  Standalone scheduled task Scheduled task inside a chat
What each run does Starts a new chat from the saved prompt Returns to the same chat and reuses its context
Where results appear As separate runs in Scheduled In the original conversation
Best cadence Daily, weekly, monthly, or a custom rule Minute-based loops, or a daily/weekly check-in

Capability ChatGPT web ChatGPT desktop app
Runs while your computer is off Yes No — the machine and app must stay available
Local folders and files No direct access Yes, for tasks scoped to a local project
Uploads, connected tools, skills, plugins Yes Yes
Manage tasks in Scheduled Yes, where enabled for your workspace Yes, from the sidebar

A web task cannot read your hard drive

If the task should sometimes produce nothing at all, say so directly. “If nothing meaningful changed, reply with one line saying so” is the single most valuable sentence in a recurring prompt.

Use the free productivity AI skill prompts here to not start from scratch.

Pick the frequency from the options available in your account, or build a custom schedule. Then confirm the destination: a standalone task that reports into Scheduled, or an in-chat task that returns to the existing conversation.

Match the cadence to how often the underlying information actually changes — not to how often you would like an update. Save the task and open the first completed run from Scheduled. Check whether it used the intended sources, covered the right period, followed the format, and separated verified facts from assumptions.

Cadence, Custom Schedules and RRULE Triggers

Standard cadences cover most business workflows: hourly, daily, weekly. Two options go further.

Scheduled tasks inside a chat can use minute-based intervals. This is built for active follow-up loops rather than reporting — checking whether a long-running operation has finished, or polling a connected source until a specific thing changes. OpenAI documents this example, which runs at 9:00 on the first day of every month:

A weekday-morning briefing, for instance, is FREQ=DAILY;BYDAY=MO,TU,WE,TH,FR with the hour you want. Confirm the rule behaved as intended by checking the next scheduled run time after you save it.

Schedule around your review habit, not the clock

A report that lands at 6:00 a.m. Monday gets read. The same report at 4:00 p.m. Friday does not. Set the trigger for shortly before you would naturally look at that kind of information.

The Recurring Task Prompt Framework

A schedule is only a trigger. The prompt decides whether run number twenty is as useful as run number one. This framework gives ChatGPT the five things an unattended run needs: timing, sources, method, output, and a reporting threshold.

Task name: [SHORT DESCRIPTIVE NAME]

Goal:
[The business outcome, not the activity. "Know if a competitor
changed pricing," not "check the pricing page."]

Approved sources:
- [Connected tool, upload, skill, or URL 1]
- [Source 2]
- Cover only [time period, e.g. the last 7 days]

Method:
1. [First required step]
2. Compare what you find against [baseline, prior run, or criteria]
3. Remove duplicates and separate confirmed facts from assumptions

Report only if:
[The specific change threshold. e.g. "a price changed, a new
feature shipped, or a competitor published a comparison page."]
If nothing meets this bar, reply with a single line saying so.

Output format:
[Bulleted summary / table / short brief], under [N] words.
Flag anything uncertain under a heading called "Needs review."

Never do without asking me first:
Send messages, publish anything, change records, make purchases,
or delete data.

The last two blocks are what make a schedule survivable. Without a reporting threshold you get noise; without an action boundary you get an agent taking consequential steps at 3:00 a.m. with nobody watching.

If you find yourself pasting the same framework repeatedly, that is the signal to turn it into a reusable skill instead — see how to turn a prompt into an AI skill.

How to Build a Monitor That Stays Quiet

A monitor is not a separate ChatGPT feature. It is a scheduled task with a reporting threshold: ChatGPT checks a source repeatedly and tells you only when something crosses the bar you defined. Everything that makes monitors useful lives in that definition.

A vague monitor reports every run, which trains you to ignore it. A well-defined one might stay silent for three weeks and then earn its place with a single message. Specify all five of these:

Define Weak version Version that works
What to check “Watch our competitor” “Check the pricing page and the changelog at [URL]”
How often “Regularly” “Every weekday at 7:00 a.m.”
What counts “Anything important” “A price change, a new plan tier, or a removed feature”
What to ignore (unspecified) “Blog posts, job listings, and copy edits”
When to stop (never) “Stop after the migration ships, or after 30 days”

Monitors that watch a public web source are a natural fit for a task created on the web, since they do not need anything on your computer and should keep running while it is closed.

Managing Runs: Pause, Edit, Resume, Delete

The Scheduled view is the control panel and the inbox at once. It lists tasks by status — active, paused, completed — alongside recent runs, and shows an unread indicator when a run has something that needs your attention.

  • Review a run — open it from Scheduled to see what the task actually did, not just its conclusion.
  • Edit — update the instructions or cadence, then review the next run before trusting it again. An edited prompt is an untested prompt.
  • Pause — stops future runs while keeping the task. The right move for seasonal workflows or while you rewrite instructions.
  • Delete — for workflows that are genuinely finished. If you are unsure, pause instead.

Schedules accumulate quietly. A monthly review of the Scheduled list — pausing anything you have stopped reading — keeps both the noise and the usage down, since agent-style runs consume more than ordinary chat messages.

Permissions and Unattended Runs

Scheduled tasks run when you are not there, using your default permission settings. That is the entire benefit and the entire risk in one sentence.

Where organization policy allows it, scheduled tasks run without pausing to ask for approval. In managed workspaces, admins can enforce requirements that override this and force scheduled runs back to the approval behaviour of your selected permission mode. If a scheduled task is behaving more conservatively than you expect, workspace policy is the first thing to check — see OpenAI’s permissions documentation.

Grant the narrowest access that lets the task succeed

Start restrictive and widen only when a run genuinely fails without it. Require explicit human approval before anything consequential and hard to reverse: sending messages, publishing, sharing files, changing records, making purchases, or deleting data. A scheduled task that only reads and reports is very difficult to regret.

Check the model on older scheduled tasks

Scheduled tasks pinned to gpt-5.4 or gpt-5.4-mini with ChatGPT sign-in need updating before those models retire on August 31, 2026. OpenAI’s stated replacements are gpt-5.6-terra for gpt-5.4 and gpt-5.6-luna for gpt-5.4-mini. Tasks left on a retired model are the kind of thing you discover through silence.

Skills Worth Putting on a Schedule

Scheduled tasks can use skills, and pairing the two is what makes a recurring workflow maintainable: the skill holds the method, the schedule holds the timing. Change the method once and every future run inherits it. In the desktop app you can invoke a specific skill directly in the task prompt using $skill-name, which is worth doing whenever the workflow should not depend on automatic tool selection.

These free skills are all built around work that repeats on a natural cadence:

Skill Natural cadence What the run produces
Weekly Business Brief Weekly, Monday morning Decisions, blockers, owners and deadlines in one brief
Competitor Research Weekly or monthly What changed since the last run, with sources
AI News Research Daily or weekday mornings Filtered industry updates, not a raw feed
Gmail Triage Daily What needs a reply, sorted by urgency
Customer Feedback Weekly or monthly Themes and sentiment shifts across recent feedback
Market Research Brief Monthly or quarterly A structured brief on a defined market question

New to skills entirely? Start with how to use ChatGPT skills, or how to create your own ChatGPT skill if you already know the workflow you want to repeat. If Skills are not showing in your account, that is a plan and workspace question covered in ChatGPT Skills availability.

Why a Scheduled Task Did Not Run

Most failures trace back to a handful of causes, and nearly all of them are environmental rather than a problem with the prompt.

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Nothing ran overnight A desktop task that needs local files, on a machine that was asleep Move it to the web if it does not need local files, or keep the computer on and the app running
Ran, but found nothing The task cannot reach the source — a web task pointed at a local folder Attach the material to the task, put it in a skill, upload it, or use a connected service
Reports every single run No reporting threshold in the prompt Add explicit change criteria and permission to report nothing
Output drifted over time An in-chat task accumulating stale context Switch to a standalone task so each run starts clean
Stops at an approval prompt Workspace policy requires approval for unattended runs Confirm the admin policy, or narrow the task to read-and-report only
No Scheduled option at all Using the Codex CLI or IDE extension, or the feature is not enabled for the workspace Use ChatGPT on the web or the desktop app, and check with your admin

Working in more than one AI tool? The equivalent setup for Google’s assistant is covered in Gemini Spark tasks, skills and schedules.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can ChatGPT Work run tasks on a recurring schedule?

Yes. ChatGPT Work supports scheduled tasks that run in the background on a recurring cadence. You manage them from the Scheduled view, which lists active, paused and completed tasks along with their recent runs. A scheduled task can also use skills and plugins, so a repeatable method and current data can run together.

What is the difference between a standalone scheduled task and one inside a chat?

A standalone scheduled task starts a new chat from its saved prompt on every run and reports each result separately in Scheduled. A scheduled task inside a chat returns to that same conversation and reuses its existing context. Use standalone for independent recurring reports, and in-chat when continuity matters — such as waiting for a long-running job to finish.

Do ChatGPT Work scheduled tasks run when my computer is off?

It depends where the task was created. Tasks created on ChatGPT web can keep running while your computer is off, because they rely on uploads, connected tools, skills and plugins rather than your machine. A task scoped to local files in the desktop app needs the computer powered on and the ChatGPT app running at the scheduled time.

Can a scheduled task use files on my computer?

Only on the desktop app. Scheduled tasks in the ChatGPT desktop app can work with local projects, and the files must still be available on disk when the run starts. Scheduled tasks on the web cannot work directly in a folder on your computer, so keep required source material in the task prompt, a skill, an upload, or a connected service.

How do I set a custom schedule in ChatGPT Work?

Standalone scheduled tasks offer custom schedule controls beyond the standard hourly, daily and weekly options. For an advanced schedule you can supply an RFC 5545 recurrence rule (RRULE) — the same standard used by calendar apps. OpenAI’s documented example, RRULE:FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTHDAY=1;BYHOUR=9;BYMINUTE=0, runs the task at 9:00 on the first day of every month.

What is a ChatGPT Work monitor?

A monitor is not a separate product or feature. It is a scheduled task written so that ChatGPT repeatedly checks a source and reports only when something meaningful changes. To work properly, the prompt must state what to check, how often, what counts as important, what to ignore, and when to stop. Without those, the monitor reports on every run and quickly gets ignored.

Can I ask ChatGPT to create a scheduled task for me?

Yes. You can create and update scheduled tasks directly from a chat by describing the work, the schedule, and whether each run should return to the current chat or start a new one. ChatGPT can draft the prompt, choose the destination, and update the task later when its scope or cadence changes. Skills can also create and update scheduled tasks.

Do scheduled tasks ask for approval before taking actions?

Scheduled tasks run unattended using your default permission settings, and where organization policy allows it they run without pausing for approval. Admin-enforced requirements in a managed workspace can override this and return scheduled runs to the approval behaviour of your selected permission mode. Grant the narrowest access a task needs, and require human approval before anything consequential or hard to reverse.

How do I pause or stop a recurring ChatGPT task?

Open Scheduled, select the task, and pause it to stop future runs while keeping the task available to resume later. Delete it only when the workflow is genuinely finished. Reviewing the Scheduled list once a month and pausing anything you have stopped reading keeps both the noise and the usage down, since agent-style runs consume more than ordinary chat messages.

Why did my scheduled task stop working after an update?

Check which model the task is pinned to. Scheduled tasks using gpt-5.4 or gpt-5.4-mini with ChatGPT sign-in need updating before those models retire on August 31, 2026 — OpenAI’s replacements are gpt-5.6-terra and gpt-5.6-luna. Also confirm the task can still reach its sources, since a moved file or a revoked connector will produce runs that complete but find nothing.

Official Sources and Next Steps

# How to Schedule Tasks in ChatGPT Work (2026)
**ChatGPT Work’s Scheduled Tasks feature lets you run a tested prompt on a recurring cadence — hourly, daily, weekly, or a custom RFC 5545 recurrence rule — by opening _Scheduled_, pasting the prompt, and choosing whether each run starts a fresh chat or returns to an existing conversation.** As of August 2026, it’s available in the Scheduled view on ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare and Edu workspaces, and every run is reviewable afterwards from the same Scheduled view — which behaves like an inbox and flags the runs that need your attention.
**Quick answer:** Scheduled Tasks in ChatGPT Work is a recurring-run feature that turns any tested prompt into a background job on a schedule you define. It works by pointing ChatGPT at a source and cadence, running unattended, and reporting back in the Scheduled inbox only when there’s something worth reading. You need an eligible ChatGPT Work plan, a prompt you’ve already tested manually, and a clear rule for what counts as important enough to report.
The setting that decides whether a scheduled task actually works is not the day or the time. It is **where the task runs**. A task created on ChatGPT web can use uploads, connected tools, skills and plugins while your laptop is shut — but it cannot reach a folder on your computer. A task that depends on local files has to run on the desktop app, which means the machine stays on and the app stays open.
This guide covers only scheduling, triggering and monitoring. If you are still deciding whether to use Work at all, start with [what ChatGPT Work is and how it differs from regular Chat](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/what-is-chatgpt-work/). Prefer structured lessons before you set anything up? Our [ChatGPT Training for Beginners](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/academy/chatgpt/) path walks through workspace setup, installing reusable ChatGPT skill files, and putting a first workflow on a schedule.
Quick answer
## How do you schedule a task in ChatGPT Work?
1. Test the prompt once in a normal chat and confirm the output is reviewable. 2. Open **Scheduled** and create a new task, or ask ChatGPT in the chat to schedule it for you. 3. Paste the tested prompt and state what counts as worth reporting. 4. Choose the cadence — hourly, daily, weekly, a custom schedule, or a recurrence rule. 5. Decide whether each run starts a new chat or returns to this one, then save and review the first few runs.
Scheduled tasks run unattended, so the prompt has to answer questions you will not be there to answer. Say what to check, what to ignore, what counts as important, and when to stop.
## Standalone vs In-Chat Scheduled Tasks
ChatGPT Work has two shapes of scheduled task, and picking the wrong one is the most common reason a schedule produces output nobody reads. The difference is memory: whether each run begins from a blank slate or inherits everything already discussed in a conversation.
| | Standalone scheduled task | Scheduled task inside a chat | | --- | --- | --- | | What each run does | Starts a new chat from the saved prompt | Returns to the same chat and reuses its context | | Where results appear | As separate runs in **Scheduled** | In the original conversation | | Best cadence | Daily, weekly, monthly, or a custom rule | Minute-based loops, or a daily/weekly check-in | | Use it for | Monday competitor updates, monthly analytics summaries, recurring reports | Waiting on a long-running job, polling a source, continuing a research loop | | Watch out for | The prompt must carry all its own context — nothing is remembered | The chat grows over time, and old context can start to skew results |
A useful rule: if you would be annoyed to receive the same information twice, use a standalone task and give it explicit change criteria. If you would be confused receiving it without the earlier conversation, schedule it inside the chat.
## Where Scheduled Tasks Run: Web vs Desktop
This is the constraint that quietly breaks schedules. ChatGPT Work is available on the web and in the desktop app, and the two do not have the same reach.
| Capability | ChatGPT web | ChatGPT desktop app | | --- | --- | --- | | Runs while your computer is off | Yes | No — the machine and app must stay available | | Local folders and files | No direct access | Yes, for tasks scoped to a local project | | Uploads, connected tools, skills, plugins | Yes | Yes | | Manage tasks in **Scheduled** | Yes, where enabled for your workspace | Yes, from the sidebar |
**A web task cannot read your hard drive**
Scheduled tasks on the web have no local folder available between runs. If a task needs source material, keep it somewhere the task can actually reach: attached to the task prompt, inside a skill, uploaded, or in a connected service. Pointing a web schedule at “the spreadsheet on my desktop” produces a confident, useless run.
The Scheduled management interface is not available in the Codex CLI or the IDE extension. Use ChatGPT on the web or the desktop app to create and manage schedules.
There are two setup paths. You can build the task yourself in **Scheduled**, or you can simply describe it in a chat and let ChatGPT create it — including drafting the prompt, choosing whether runs return to the current chat, and updating the task later when the scope changes.
Run the prompt manually in a normal chat first. OpenAI recommends this explicitly, and it is the step people skip. You are checking three things: that the prompt is scoped tightly enough, that the model and tools behave the way you expected, and that the output is something you can actually review in under a minute.
A prompt that needs a follow-up question to be useful will fail on a schedule, because there is nobody there to answer it.
If you don’t have a prompt to test yet, start with our [free AI News skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/ai-news-agent/) — it’s a ready-made prompt, so what you’re testing in step one is real wording instead of a blank page.
Open **Scheduled** and create a new task, then paste the prompt you just tested.
Or stay in the conversation and ask. Describe the work, the schedule, and whether each run should return to the current chat or start a new one — ChatGPT can draft the prompt, pick the destination, and update the task later when the cadence or scope changes. This is usually faster right after a successful test run, because the working context already exists.
Recurring work needs tighter instructions than a live session. State which sources may be used, the period to cover, the method to follow, the output format, and — most importantly — what counts as important enough to report and what should be ignored.
If the task should sometimes produce nothing at all, say so directly. “If nothing meaningful changed, reply with one line saying so” is the single most valuable sentence in a recurring prompt.
**Use the [free productivity AI skill prompts here](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/productivity/) to not start from scratch.**
Pick the frequency from the options available in your account, or build a custom schedule. Then confirm the destination: a standalone task that reports into **Scheduled**, or an in-chat task that returns to the existing conversation.
Match the cadence to how often the underlying information actually changes — not to how often you would like an update. A daily check on a source that changes monthly produces twenty-nine runs of noise and one you stop reading. Daily earns its place when the inputs genuinely turn over every day, which is why a morning [AI Daily Brief skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/daily-brief/) works on a schedule and a market summary rarely does.
Save the task and open the first completed run from **Scheduled**. Check whether it used the intended sources, covered the right period, followed the format, and separated verified facts from assumptions.
OpenAI’s guidance is to review the first few outputs and then adjust the prompt, tools or cadence if results are too broad. Treat the first three runs as a trial, not as delivery.
## Cadence, Custom Schedules and RRULE Triggers
Standard cadences cover most business workflows: hourly, daily, weekly. Two options go further.
### Minute-based intervals, for chats that are waiting on something
Scheduled tasks inside a chat can use minute-based intervals. This is built for active follow-up loops rather than reporting — checking whether a long-running operation has finished, or polling a connected source until a specific thing changes. Give these a stopping condition, or you have built something that runs forever.
### Custom schedules and recurrence rules
When the built-in options do not fit, standalone tasks support custom schedule controls, and an advanced schedule can be expressed as an **RFC 5545 recurrence rule (RRULE)** — the same calendar standard behind repeating events in Google Calendar and Outlook.
OpenAI documents this example, which runs at 9:00 on the first day of every month:
``` RRULE:FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTHDAY=1;BYHOUR=9;BYMINUTE=0 ```
Because RRULE is a published standard rather than a ChatGPT-specific syntax, the usual building blocks apply: `FREQ` sets the unit, `INTERVAL` skips periods, `BYDAY` picks weekdays, and `BYHOUR` with `BYMINUTE` sets the time. A weekday-morning briefing, for instance, is `FREQ=DAILY;BYDAY=MO,TU,WE,TH,FR` with the hour you want. Confirm the rule behaved as intended by checking the next scheduled run time after you save it.
**Schedule around your review habit, not the clock**
A report that lands at 6:00 a.m. Monday gets read. The same report at 4:00 p.m. Friday does not. Set the trigger for shortly before you would naturally look at that kind of information.
## The Recurring Task Prompt Framework
A schedule is only a trigger. The prompt decides whether run number twenty is as useful as run number one. This framework gives ChatGPT the five things an unattended run needs: timing, sources, method, output, and a reporting threshold.
``` Task name: [SHORT DESCRIPTIVE NAME]
Goal: [The business outcome, not the activity. "Know if a competitor changed pricing," not "check the pricing page."]
Approved sources: - [Connected tool, upload, skill, or URL 1] - [Source 2] - Cover only [time period, e.g. the last 7 days]
Method: 1. [First required step] 2. Compare what you find against [baseline, prior run, or criteria] 3. Remove duplicates and separate confirmed facts from assumptions
Report only if: [The specific change threshold. e.g. "a price changed, a new feature shipped, or a competitor published a comparison page."] If nothing meets this bar, reply with a single line saying so.
Output format: [Bulleted summary / table / short brief], under [N] words. Flag anything uncertain under a heading called "Needs review."
Never do without asking me first: Send messages, publish anything, change records, make purchases, or delete data. ```
The last two blocks are what make a schedule survivable. Without a reporting threshold you get noise; without an action boundary you get an agent taking consequential steps at 3:00 a.m. with nobody watching.
If you find yourself pasting the same framework repeatedly, that is the signal to turn it into a reusable skill instead — see [how to turn a prompt into an AI skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/turn-a-prompt-into-an-ai-skill/).

A vague monitor reports every run, which trains you to ignore it. A well-defined one might stay silent for three weeks and then earn its place with a single message. Specify all five of these:
| Define | Weak version | Version that works | | --- | --- | --- | | What to check | “Watch our competitor” | “Check the pricing page and the changelog at \[URL\]” | | How often | “Regularly” | “Every weekday at 7:00 a.m.” | | What counts | “Anything important” | “A price change, a new plan tier, or a removed feature” | | What to ignore | (unspecified) | “Blog posts, job listings, and copy edits” | | When to stop | (never) | “Stop after the migration ships, or after 30 days” |

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to complete a ChatGPT course?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most focused beginner courses take between 90 minutes and a weekend. The AI Agents Library ChatGPT Academy runs about 3 hours across six modules, DeepLearning.AI's prompt-engineering short course is 1h 40m, and OpenAI Academy's free foundations are self-paced (typically one to two evenings each). Longer certificate courses like Vanderbilt's Coursera path are a roughly 19-hour commitment across six modules.

mainEntity.name: Do ChatGPT courses cover Skills, Projects, and workflows?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only some do. As of August 2026, OpenAI's free Using Skills guide and the AI Agents Library ChatGPT Academy are the two on this list that treat Skills as a first-class topic alongside Projects and workflows. Most legacy prompt-engineering courses predate Skills and don't mention SKILL.md at all — check the syllabus for the words 'Skill' and 'workflow' before enrolling.

mainEntity.name: Are there ChatGPT courses that come with downloadable skill files?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The AI Agents Library ChatGPT Academy ships with 25+ ready-to-install ChatGPT Skills, and the AI Agents Library All Access Pass unlocks the full library across ChatGPT, Claude Cowork and Gemini Spark. Free copy-paste versions of many workflows are also available in the free ChatGPT Skills library — install one before you finish the course and you already have working leverage.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a paid ChatGPT plan for these courses?

acceptedAnswer.text: The lessons themselves can be studied on any ChatGPT plan, including free. The free copy-paste versions can be adapted for many free AI chat plans. Native Skill installation, Claude Cowork, Gemini Spark, connected tools and advanced automation features may require an eligible paid plan. Confirm plan-eligibility in ChatGPT Skills availability before buying training that assumes access you may not have.

mainEntity.name: How is a ChatGPT course different from ChatGPT Skills?

acceptedAnswer.text: A ChatGPT course teaches you how to use ChatGPT well; a ChatGPT Skill is a reusable SKILL.md file you install into ChatGPT so it does one specific job the same way every time. Courses build knowledge; Skills build leverage. The best training combines the two — you leave with the principles and with installed workflows already running. The AI Agents Library ChatGPT Training for Beginners path is built around that combination.

mainEntity.name: What is the best ChatGPT Skills course?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most beginners and business owners, the best ChatGPT Skills course is the AI Agents Library ChatGPT Academy, because it combines six beginner modules with 25+ ready-to-install Skills and real human support — so you finish with working workflows rather than notes. If you want the official fundamentals for free, OpenAI Academy's AI Foundations is the best free starting course, and OpenAI's free Using Skills guide is the best free training on Skills specifically.

mainEntity.name: Is there a free ChatGPT course?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, several. OpenAI Academy offers three free official courses — AI Foundations, Applied AI Foundations, and Agents and Workflows — each with a free completion certificate. OpenAI's Using Skills guide is free, DeepLearning.AI's prompt engineering short course is free, and Vanderbilt's Coursera course is free to audit. The ChatGPT Academy is also free for your first 7 days.

mainEntity.name: Does OpenAI have an official ChatGPT course?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. OpenAI Academy is OpenAI's own free learning platform and currently publishes three public courses: AI Foundations for people new to AI, Applied AI Foundations for turning prompts into repeatable workflows, and Agents and Workflows for directing agent-assisted work. Each issues a free course-completion certificate. OpenAI also runs live sessions, including short Skill Labs, with replays posted afterwards.

mainEntity.name: What is a ChatGPT Skill, and why does it need its own course?

acceptedAnswer.text: OpenAI defines a skill as a reusable, shareable workflow that tells ChatGPT how to do a specific task — you define the process once, in a plain-text SKILL.md file, and it is applied reliably whenever that task comes up. It needs separate teaching because prompting and Skill design are different disciplines: prompting is about one good result now, Skills are about the same good result every time. Most ChatGPT courses were written before Skills existed and only teach the first.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to know how to code to learn ChatGPT Skills?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A SKILL.md file is written in Markdown — plain text with a few symbols like # for headings and - for lists. You can write one in any text editor, and you can ask ChatGPT to draft the first version for you. Every course in this guide except DeepLearning.AI's, which assumes basic Python, is fully no-code.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to learn ChatGPT Skills?

acceptedAnswer.text: About 15 minutes to understand what a Skill is, an hour or two to install one and run it on real work, and roughly a weekend to finish a structured beginner path — the ChatGPT Academy runs about three hours across six modules. Becoming genuinely fluent takes two to three weeks of using Skills on real jobs. The gap between finishing a course and saving time is almost always the step most people skip: building one Skill for a job you genuinely repeat.

mainEntity.name: Which ChatGPT course teaches reusable Skills?

acceptedAnswer.text: Very few, which is the main finding of this guide. OpenAI's free Using Skills guide is the authoritative explainer, and Applied AI Foundations teaches the workflow thinking behind Skills. For building and installing them against your own work, the AI Agents Library ChatGPT Academy is the applied option — you finish with working Skills rather than an understanding of Skills. You can also install proven ones straight from the free ChatGPT Skills library.

mainEntity.name: Are paid ChatGPT courses worth it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sometimes — but start free. OpenAI Academy and the Using Skills guide will teach you the fundamentals at no cost. A paid course earns its money when you want structure, business-specific examples, a recognised certificate, or a human to ask when you get stuck. For most business owners, support and ready-made Skills deliver more than another set of videos. What is rarely worth paying for is a second prompting course.

mainEntity.name: Do ChatGPT courses include a certificate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many do. All three OpenAI Academy courses issue a free course-completion certificate, and the AI Agents Library ChatGPT Academy issues a certificate of completion. Vanderbilt's Coursera course offers a paid, shareable certificate; Udemy issues a certificate of completion; DeepLearning.AI's certificate requires a paid membership tier. Note the distinction OpenAI itself draws: a course-completion certificate is not a formal OpenAI certification. Certificate terms change, so confirm on the provider's enrolment page before you sign up.

mainEntity.name: Can I learn ChatGPT Skills without a Business or Enterprise plan?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can learn the concepts on any plan — OpenAI's Using Skills guide, the Academy courses and beginner articles all cost nothing and assume nothing. Installing Skills into a workspace is a different matter and depends on your plan tier. Check ChatGPT Skills availability before buying training that assumes access you may not have.

mainEntity.name: Is ChatGPT training good for business owners?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is arguably better suited to business owners than to developers. The recurring, low-judgement work that eats an owner's week — weekly reporting, inbox triage, proposal drafts, client updates, content planning — is exactly what Skills handle well, and none of it needs code. The catch is that it rewards people who commit to one workflow rather than experimenting broadly. OpenAI's free small business program is a good place to see what that looks like in practice.

mainEntity.name: Which course should I take after OpenAI Academy?

acceptedAnswer.text: OpenAI teaches you the product; the natural next step teaches you what to build with it. For business workflows, reusable Skills and scheduled work, the ChatGPT Academy picks up roughly where the free curriculum stops. If you want prompting depth instead, take Vanderbilt's Coursera course or DeepLearning.AI's short course. Do not take two foundation courses back to back — the second will mostly repeat the first.

mainEntity.name: Is there a ChatGPT certification?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not in the sense most people mean. OpenAI Academy issues free course-completion certificates, and OpenAI has been explicit that those are not a formal OpenAI certification. Third-party certificates from Coursera, Udemy and LinkedIn Learning are certificates of completion from those platforms, not from OpenAI. If a credential matters for a job or a client, Vanderbilt's Coursera certificate carries the most recognisable name. If capability matters more than the credential, a Skill running in your business proves more than any of them.

mainEntity.name: What about courses for Claude or Gemini?

acceptedAnswer.text: The same logic applies — look for training that ends in something reusable. We compare the equivalent Claude options in our guide to the best Claude Cowork courses. If you use more than one tool, AI Skills Fundamentals teaches the cross-platform skill format first, so what you learn is not stranded on one platform.

Every pick lists who it is best for, the format and price, what you will actually learn, honest pros and limitations, and a clear verdict — so you can pick training that matches your goal, your budget, and how much time you have. Last updated August 2026. All course info verified against current provider offerings. Why “Skills courses” and not just “ChatGPT courses”? Because the gap for most people is no longer prompting. A ChatGPT Skill is a reusable, shareable workflow — a plain-text SKILL.md file that tells ChatGPT how to do one job the same way every time. A course that only teaches prompting leaves you re-explaining yourself forever. A course that teaches Skills leaves you with something that keeps working after the course ends. That distinction is the yardstick used to rank everything below. The 9 best ChatGPT Skills courses in 2026 The best ChatGPT Skills course depends on whether you want practical business workflows, prompt engineering, official training, or reusable Skills you can install the same day. Beginners often benefit most from structured learning that includes real projects rather than only videos. If you take one free course and build one real Skill from it, you are ahead of almost everyone who finished five. Who this guide is for Business owners, professionals, marketers and complete beginners who want to learn ChatGPT Skills through structured training rather than piecing it together from scattered videos. What a ChatGPT Skills course actually needs to cover Most “ChatGPT courses” were written for a product that no longer exists. They teach prompting into a blank chat box. ChatGPT now runs reusable Skills, holds context in Projects, connects to your real tools, and runs work on a schedule — and those are the parts that actually save time. A course worth your hours should cover all seven of these: Prompting fundamentals. Clear instructions, useful context, and reviewing what comes back. Everything else sits on top of this. The plain-text playbook itself: what the skill does, required inputs, step-by-step instructions, required output format, and the final checks. It is Markdown and portable, which is why a Skill you write today survives tool changes. Projects and standing context. The difference between a Skill, a Project and a custom GPT, and when each one is the right container. If a course blurs those three, it will teach you to build the wrong thing.
