How to Use Gemini Spark: Complete Guide (2026)

Learning how to use Gemini Spark starts with understanding that Spark is not simply another Gemini chat mode. It is Google’s personal AI agent for managing multi-step tasks, recurring workflows, connected apps, websites, files, skills, and schedules under your direction.

Instead of asking one question and receiving one response, you give Spark a defined outcome. Spark can plan the work, use approved sources, complete multiple steps, request input when necessary, and continue eligible tasks in the background.

This complete guide explains how to access Gemini Spark, create your first task, monitor its progress, build reusable skills, add schedules, connect supported Google services, and use Spark safely.

New to Gemini Spark? If you have not opened Spark yet, start with the Free Gemini Spark Setup Guide for Beginners. This article is the broader operating guide for tasks, skills, schedules, monitoring, and safe workflow building.

Prefer a structured learning path with guided practice? Compare the best Gemini Spark Skills courses for beginners. The roundup covers dedicated Spark training, free official resources and broader Gemini courses; this page remains the step-by-step operating guide.

In this complete Gemini Spark guide:

  1. What you need before using Gemini Spark
  2. How to access Gemini Spark
  3. How to use Gemini Spark step by step
  4. How to write an effective Spark task
  5. How to monitor and manage tasks
  6. Tasks vs. skills vs. schedules
  7. Gemini Spark skills: quick overview
  8. How to create a Gemini Spark schedule
  9. What Spark can do with Google Workspace
  10. Gemini Spark examples and use cases
  11. How to use Gemini Spark safely
  12. Current limits and restrictions
  13. Common Gemini Spark problems
  14. Frequently asked questions

What you need before using Gemini Spark

Gemini Spark is available inside the Gemini app, but it does not automatically appear on every Google Account. Gemini Spark requires a personal Google Account, age 18 or older, Keep Activity enabled, and an eligible Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription. Spark is now available to Pro subscribers in more than 160 additional countries, although availability, supported languages and individual features can vary by region.

To use Gemini Spark, you currently need:

  • A personal Google Account that you manage yourself
  • An eligible Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription (Google says Pro access expanded to 160+ additional countries on July 30, 2026)
  • To be at least 18 years old
  • Gemini Apps Keep Activity turned on
  • A supported Spark language — Google AI Ultra works in all Gemini Apps languages; Pro language support varies by country
  • Access from a currently supported location
  • The Gemini web app, Gemini mobile app, or the Gemini app for macOS if you are eligible for the beta

Availability can change. Review the Gemini Spark availability guide for current account, country, subscription, and language information.

Quick answer

To use Gemini Spark, open Gemini, select Change mode, switch to Spark, and open Tasks. Describe the result you want, add any required files, Google Drive content, notebooks, connected apps, or skills, and submit the task. Review Spark’s progress regularly and take control before sensitive or important actions.

How to access Gemini Spark

Gemini Spark is accessed from inside Gemini rather than through a separate Spark website or standalone application. Google now also offers Spark in beta inside the Gemini app for macOS for eligible subscribers on an eligible Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription (Google expanded Pro access to 160+ additional countries on July 30, 2026).

1

Open Gemini

Use the Gemini web app, an eligible mobile app, or the Gemini app for macOS beta.

2

Switch modes

Select Change mode and then choose Switch to Spark.

3

Open Tasks

Create a new task or open an existing Spark task thread.

  1. Go to Gemini, open the Gemini mobile app, or open the Gemini app for macOS if you have access.
  2. Sign in using your eligible personal Google Account.
  3. Open the Gemini sidebar or navigation menu.
  4. Select Change mode.
  5. Select Switch to Spark.
  6. Open Tasks.
  7. Enter the task you want Spark to manage.

The interface may look slightly different on web, Android, iPhone, iPad, or macOS, but the overall process is similar.

How to use Gemini Spark step by step

Your first Spark workflow should be useful, easy to verify, and relatively low-risk. Research, summaries, document organization, and planning are generally better starting points than purchases, deletions, account changes, or external communications.

Before creating your first workflow, review the difference between Gemini Spark Tasks, Skills, and Schedules.

1

Choose one clear outcome

Do not begin with a vague request such as “help me manage my business.” Choose one result that you can recognize and verify when it is complete.

  • Create a weekly summary of important AI news.
  • Review meeting notes and create an action list.
  • Compare selected documents in a structured table.
  • Organize research from selected Drive files.
  • Create a weekly content-planning brief.

2

Define what a successful result looks like

Decide what Spark must deliver before writing the task. A clear completion standard makes the workflow easier to evaluate.

  • What is the main goal?
  • Which information should Spark use?
  • Which steps are essential?
  • What should the final output include?
  • What should Spark exclude?
  • Which actions require your approval?

3

Write detailed task instructions

Explain the goal, approved sources, important steps, required output, timing, and guardrails. You do not need technical language, but you do need enough detail for Spark to understand what completion means.

4

Add the necessary sources and skills

Spark can use information from supported sources that you make available. Add only the context required to complete the task.

  • Upload supported files.
  • Add selected files from Google Drive.
  • Add a supported notebook.
  • Use approved Connected Apps.
  • Connect permitted desktop folders in the Gemini app for macOS when the task needs local files.
  • Reference an existing skill by entering a slash or at symbol.

5

Submit the task

Review your instructions and attached sources, then submit the task. Spark will begin planning and completing the work. Stay available in case it needs clarification, permission, or browser takeover.

6

Monitor the task

Open the task thread and work panel to review completed steps, current progress, planned steps, files, schedules, connected apps, and any input Spark needs from you.

7

Review and improve the result

Identify what Spark misunderstood, omitted, or formatted incorrectly. Improve the instructions, add examples, narrow the sources, and test the workflow again before converting it into a reusable skill or schedule.

How to write an effective Gemini Spark task

Strong Spark instructions normally contain six elements: the goal, sources, process, output, guardrails, and timing.

Goal

State the exact result Spark should accomplish.

Sources

Identify which files, apps, messages, websites, notebooks, or skills it may use.

Process

Explain the important steps and evaluation criteria.

Output

Define the required structure, format, detail, and destination.

Guardrails

State what Spark must not do without approval.

Timing

Explain when the result is needed or whether the task should repeat.

Example Gemini Spark task

Copy and customize this Spark instruction

Create a weekly AI news brief for a small business owner. GOAL Identify the most important AI agent and productivity updates from the past seven days. SOURCES Use reputable primary sources and official company announcements whenever possible. PROCESS 1. Find the most meaningful updates. 2. Remove duplicate stories and minor announcements. 3. Explain what changed. 4. Explain why each update matters to a business owner. 5. Identify one practical action from each major update. OUTPUT Create a concise brief containing: – Executive summary – Five most important updates – Why each update matters – Practical action ideas – Source links – Three related content ideas GUARDRAILS Do not publish, send, purchase, subscribe, delete, or change account settings. Ask for my approval before taking any external action.

How to improve a weak Spark task

When the first result is too generic, add:

  • A required heading or table structure
  • Specific sources and date ranges
  • An example of a strong result
  • Rules for prioritizing information
  • Information that must be excluded
  • The expected length and detail level
  • Actions that require your approval

Want examples before writing your own task? Browse Gemini Spark guides and Gemini Spark skills to see how clear goals, sources, process, output, guardrails, and timing work in real workflows.

How to monitor and manage Gemini Spark tasks

Spark can continue working on eligible tasks in the background, but it should not be treated as an agent you never need to check.

Open the task thread and work panel

  1. Open Gemini.
  2. Switch to Spark.
  3. Select Tasks.
  4. Open the task thread you want to review.
  5. Open the progress chip or task work panel.

Review Spark’s progress

The progress area can show completed steps, the current step, and planned steps. This allows you to identify misunderstandings before Spark reaches an important action.

Review files Spark read or updated

The work panel can show files Spark read, created, or changed. Open important files and verify facts, formatting, calculations, and actions before relying on the result.

Take control of the remote browser

Some Spark tasks can use a remote browser. You can observe the browser, take control, complete a step yourself, and then return control to Gemini.

Use browser takeover when a website requires a password, payment details, sensitive information, confirmation, or another action that you should complete personally.

Do not enter passwords, payment information, or highly sensitive information directly into a Spark task thread. Take control of the browser and enter necessary information directly on the website instead.

Gemini Spark tasks vs. skills vs. schedules

Tasks, skills, and schedules are the three main building blocks of Gemini Spark. A simple way to remember them is: task equals what, skill equals how, and schedule equals when.

Spark featureWhat it controlsExampleBest use
TaskThe complete goal or projectCreate this week’s business intelligence briefWhen you want Spark to produce a defined outcome
SkillReusable instructions and context for completing workAlways format briefs using my preferred structureWhen you repeat the same rules, style, or process
ScheduleThe time or condition that triggers a taskRun the business brief every Monday morningAfter the task has been tested and is safe to automate

Test a task manually before scheduling it. Once the task produces dependable results, save its repeatable method as a skill. Add a schedule only after you understand how the workflow behaves.

Gemini Spark skills: quick overview

A Gemini Spark skill is a saved set of reusable instructions and supporting context that teaches Gemini how you want a certain type of work completed. Spark can apply a relevant active skill automatically, or you can select one for a specific task.

You can add a skill four ways: let Create with Gemini draft it for you, start from a Recommended template, Create manually, or upload a SKILL.md file. Whichever you pick, a strong skill needs a clear name, a description of when to use it, step-by-step instructions, the output format, and an example.

Want the full walkthrough? Our complete guide on how to create a Gemini Spark skill covers every method step by step, plus a reusable instructions template and how to test and refine your skill.

How to create a Gemini Spark schedule

A schedule tells Spark when to run a task. A workflow can run at a selected time or in response to a supported condition.

Create a schedule conversationally

  1. Open Gemini and switch to Spark.
  2. Open Tasks.
  3. Describe what Spark should do.
  4. State when or under which condition it should run.
  5. Submit the instruction.
  6. Review the task and its schedule.

Example scheduled Spark task

Every Monday morning, review the business updates in the selected Gmail label and project files in the selected Drive folder. Create a weekly brief containing: 1. Major updates 2. Decisions that need to be made 3. Missed deadlines or risks 4. This week’s priorities 5. A suggested action list Do not send emails, modify files, delete information, or create calendar events without asking for my approval.

Create a time-based schedule manually

  1. Open Gemini and switch to Spark.
  2. Open Schedules.
  3. Select Create manually.
  4. Enter a schedule name.
  5. Choose when it should run.
  6. Enter the task instructions.
  7. Create the schedule.
  8. Use Run now to test it before relying on it.

Manual schedule creation is designed for time-based schedules. Gmail-triggered schedules and monitors can be created through conversational instructions.

Types of Gemini Spark schedules

  • Time-based schedules: Run once, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, or yearly.
  • Gmail-triggered schedules: Run when an email satisfies a supported Gmail filter.
  • Monitors: Check a condition periodically throughout the day and act when the condition is satisfied.

Monitors are not instant alerts. Spark generally checks monitor conditions every few hours, so monitors are not appropriate for urgent, rapidly changing, or highly time-sensitive events.

Manage a Spark schedule

Use the Schedules page or the related task thread to review, edit, pause, resume, run, or delete a schedule. Review scheduled workflows regularly instead of assuming every unattended run will behave exactly as expected.

What Gemini Spark can do with Google Workspace

Spark can work with supported Google Workspace services when Google Workspace is connected to Gemini Apps and the required permissions are enabled.

Google’s June 2026 Spark update also expanded connected apps beyond the core Workspace flow. Google says Tasks and Keep are being added, along with Canva, Dropbox, Instacart, OpenTable, Zillow Rentals, and support for custom Model Context Protocol connections. Treat each connector as account- and rollout-dependent until it appears in your own Spark settings.

Gmail

Search and summarize email threads, draft replies, organize selected messages, and use supported Gmail conditions to trigger workflows.

Google Calendar

Review availability, help plan meetings, respond to supported invitations, and prepare calendar-related actions.

Google Drive

Search for files, review selected file content, locate recent documents, and organize supported information.

Google Docs

Create drafts, add summaries, organize notes, and work with supported document content.

Google Sheets

Create and organize spreadsheets containing structured data, tables, and supported formulas.

Google Slides

Prepare presentation drafts and organize slide content from approved instructions and sources.

Google Tasks

Turn approved action items into task lists and keep follow-up work organized when the connector is available.

Google Keep

Use selected notes as lightweight context for reminders, checklists, and recurring workflow instructions.

Available apps and actions can change based on your account, connected services, permissions, device, location, and Google’s current feature support. Review Spark’s work before allowing it to edit, delete, send, schedule, purchase, or publish anything.

Gemini Spark examples and use cases

Gemini Spark is best suited to workflows with a clear outcome, repeatable process, and information you are comfortable allowing Spark to use.

Research assistant

Research a topic, compare sources, track updates, and create a cited summary.

Weekly business brief

Summarize selected messages, files, deadlines, risks, and priorities.

Content planning

Review approved topics and create a structured weekly content plan.

Inbox organization

Summarize selected emails, identify action items, and organize recurring newsletters.

Document organization

Review selected Drive files and organize important information in a table.

Meeting follow-up

Turn approved meeting notes into decisions, owners, priorities, and next steps.

How to get better results from Gemini Spark

Start with a narrow task

“Manage my business” is too broad. “Review these five files and create a table of unresolved decisions” is focused and testable.

Specify the sources

Tell Spark which Gmail label, Drive folder, files, websites, notebook, date range, or skill it should use.

Define the final deliverable

State whether you want a summary, table, document, spreadsheet, presentation, email draft, action list, or another format.

Explain how information should be evaluated

Define what counts as important, credible, urgent, relevant, complete, duplicated, or outside the task’s scope.

Provide examples

A sample output, heading structure, writing style, or table format can improve a workflow more than adding vague directions such as “make it better.”

Separate preparation from external action

Ask Spark to research, organize, compare, and draft first. Require approval before it sends, publishes, purchases, books, deletes, submits, or changes anything.

How to use Gemini Spark safely

Spark can work with connected apps, files, websites, browser sessions, remote computer data, and other authorized information. That makes it more capable than an ordinary chatbot, but it also requires stronger supervision.

  • Start with low-risk and reversible tasks.
  • Connect only the information required for the task.
  • Review important instructions before submitting them.
  • Monitor tasks involving private information.
  • Do not type passwords into task threads.
  • Do not type payment information into task threads.
  • Use browser takeover for sensitive steps.
  • Require approval before sending or publishing.
  • Check files and messages Spark creates or changes.
  • Pause schedules you are no longer actively using.

Be aware of prompt injection

An AI agent may encounter hidden or misleading instructions inside websites, messages, documents, code, or other content. Those instructions may attempt to redirect the agent away from your original request.

Closely supervise tasks involving unfamiliar websites, connected accounts, sensitive documents, purchases, deletions, or actions where a mistake would have a meaningful consequence.

Understand how Spark uses and stores data

Spark may process information from your tasks, schedules, skills, Connected Apps, Personal Intelligence, websites, remote browser, and remote computer. Remote browser information can include page content and cookies used to keep you signed in. Remote computer information can include files, code, and task-related data.

Spark may share information required to complete a task with connected services, websites, and other third parties. Only provide access to information that is necessary for the workflow.

You can delete saved remote browser data and manage or clear remote computer information from your Gemini Spark settings.

What happens when you turn Gemini Spark off

Turning Spark off deletes saved remote browser and remote computer data. Your tasks and schedules are paused rather than deleted, and your chats are not automatically deleted.

If you turn Spark back on, paused tasks and schedules may resume automatically. Review active schedules before re-enabling Spark so an older workflow does not restart unexpectedly.

Current Gemini Spark limits and restrictions

Gemini Spark remains an experimental product. Understanding its current limits will help you avoid creating workflows that are too urgent, sensitive, or complex to run reliably without supervision.

15 concurrent tasks

Spark currently allows up to 15 tasks to run at the same time.

50 active schedules

You can currently maintain up to 50 active Spark schedules.

Approximate start times

Scheduled tasks may not begin at the exact moment requested.

Periodic monitoring

Monitors generally check conditions every few hours rather than continuously.

Scheduled tasks may also be delayed by usage limits or periods of high demand. Avoid using Spark schedules or monitors for emergencies, security alerts, immediate purchasing, fast-moving prices, or other situations where a delay could create a meaningful problem.

Common Gemini Spark problems

Gemini Spark is not showing on my account

Confirm that you are using an eligible personal Google Account, have Google AI Ultra (or Google AI Pro in the US), are at least 18, have Keep Activity enabled, are using a language your plan supports, and are accessing Gemini from a currently supported location.

My task stopped or needs attention

Open the task thread and work panel. Spark may need clarification, confirmation, access to a file, permission to use an app, or for you to take control of the remote browser.

My scheduled task did not run

Check whether the schedule is paused, Spark is enabled, your usage limit was reached, or 15 other tasks were already running. Schedule start times are approximate and may also be delayed during periods of high demand.

I cannot create another schedule

Spark currently supports up to 50 active schedules. Pause or delete an existing schedule before creating or resuming another one.

The output is too generic

Add a required format, source rules, date range, selection criteria, examples, exclusions, and a clearer definition of completion.

Spark used the wrong information

Narrow the approved sources. Name the exact Drive folder, files, Gmail label, website, notebook, date range, or skill Spark should use.

Spark is taking an action I do not want

Stop the task or take control of the remote browser. Then update the instructions to state which actions are prohibited or require confirmation.

Frequently asked questions about using Gemini Spark

How do I start using Gemini Spark?

If you are brand new, follow the Free Gemini Spark Setup Guide for Beginners first. Once Spark is available on your account, open Gemini with an eligible personal account, select Change mode, switch to Spark, open Tasks, describe the outcome you want Spark to manage, add the required files, apps, notebooks, or skills, submit the task, and monitor its progress.

Do I need coding experience to use Gemini Spark?

No. Gemini Spark uses conversational instructions and supports no-code workflows. You still need to define a clear goal, provide the right context, structure the workflow, and review the agent’s work.

What is the difference between a task, skill, and schedule?

A task is the complete goal Spark should manage. A skill contains reusable instructions explaining how work should be completed. A schedule determines when or under which condition the task should run.

Can Gemini Spark work with Google Workspace apps?

Spark can use supported Google Workspace services when Workspace is connected to Gemini Apps and the necessary permissions are enabled. Supported apps and actions can vary by account, settings, platform, and Google’s current feature support.

Can Gemini Spark continue working when my computer is turned off?

Spark is designed to continue eligible cloud-based tasks in the background. Tasks that need local files in the Gemini app for macOS require your Mac to stay on, awake, and connected while they run. You should still return regularly to review progress, respond to requests for input, and supervise important workflows.

Should I schedule my first Gemini Spark task?

It is better to test a new workflow manually first. Improve the instructions until the task produces dependable results, then schedule it only when it is safe and appropriate to run without constant supervision.

How many Gemini Spark tasks can run at the same time?

Spark currently allows up to 15 tasks to run concurrently. A scheduled task may not begin if 15 other tasks are already running.

How many active Gemini Spark schedules can I create?

Spark currently supports up to 50 active schedules. You must pause or delete an existing schedule before creating or resuming another schedule after reaching the limit.

Is Gemini Spark safe to use?

Spark provides monitoring, remote-browser controls, and browser takeover, but it is still an experimental AI agent that can make mistakes. Begin with low-risk tasks, limit access, avoid entering sensitive information in task threads, and supervise important actions.

What should I create first with Gemini Spark?

Start with a focused workflow that is useful and easy to verify, such as a research summary, weekly business brief, meeting-action list, document comparison, inbox summary, or content plan.

Official Google resources

  • Use Gemini Spark to manage tasks and workflows
  • Find and manage Gemini Spark tasks
  • Create and manage Gemini Spark schedules
  • Create and manage Gemini Spark skills
  • Gemini Spark updates: macOS launch, connected apps and more
  • Gemini Apps Privacy Hub

Editorial note: Gemini Spark is an experimental product. Features, interface labels, regional availability, account requirements, limits, connected apps, and supported actions may change. AI Agents Library is an independent educational resource and is not affiliated with Google.

Define the required structure, format, detail, and destination.
Guardrails
State what Spark must not do without approval.
Timing
Explain when the result is needed or whether the task should repeat.
### Example Gemini Spark task
Copy and customize this Spark instruction
Create a weekly AI news brief for a small business owner. GOAL Identify the most important AI agent and productivity updates from the past seven days. SOURCES Use reputable primary sources and official company announcements whenever possible. PROCESS 1. Find the most meaningful updates. 2. Remove duplicate stories and minor announcements. 3. Explain what changed. 4. Explain why each update matters to a business owner. 5. Identify one practical action from each major update. OUTPUT Create a concise brief containing: – Executive summary – Five most important updates – Why each update matters – Practical action ideas – Source links – Three related content ideas GUARDRAILS Do not publish, send, purchase, subscribe, delete, or change account settings. Ask for my approval before taking any external action.
### How to improve a weak Spark task
When the first result is too generic, add:
* A required heading or table structure * Specific sources and date ranges * An example of a strong result * Rules for prioritizing information * Information that must be excluded * The expected length and detail level * Actions that require your approval
**Want examples before writing your own task?** Browse [Gemini Spark guides](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/category/gemini-spark/) and [Gemini Spark skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gemini-spark/) to see how clear goals, sources, process, output, guardrails, and timing work in real workflows.
## How to monitor and manage Gemini Spark tasks
Spark can continue working on eligible tasks in the background, but it should not be treated as an agent you never need to check.
### Open the task thread and work panel
1. Open Gemini. 2. Switch to Spark. 3. Select **Tasks**. 4. Open the task thread you want to review. 5. Open the progress chip or task work panel.
### Review Spark’s progress
The progress area can show completed steps, the current step, and planned steps. This allows you to identify misunderstandings before Spark reaches an important action.
### Review files Spark read or updated
The work panel can show files Spark read, created, or changed. Open important files and verify facts, formatting, calculations, and actions before relying on the result.
### Take control of the remote browser
Some Spark tasks can use a remote browser. You can observe the browser, take control, complete a step yourself, and then return control to Gemini.
Use browser takeover when a website requires a password, payment details, sensitive information, confirmation, or another action that you should complete personally.
**Do not enter passwords, payment information, or highly sensitive information directly into a Spark task thread.** Take control of the browser and enter necessary information directly on the website instead.
## Gemini Spark tasks vs. skills vs. schedules
Tasks, skills, and schedules are the three main building blocks of Gemini Spark. A simple way to remember them is: **task equals what, skill equals how, and schedule equals when.**
| Spark feature | What it controls | Example | Best use | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Task** | The complete goal or project | Create this week’s business intelligence brief | When you want Spark to produce a defined outcome | | **Skill** | Reusable instructions and context for completing work | Always format briefs using my preferred structure | When you repeat the same rules, style, or process | | **Schedule** | The time or condition that triggers a task | Run the business brief every Monday morning | After the task has been tested and is safe to automate |
Test a task manually before scheduling it. Once the task produces dependable results, save its repeatable method as a skill. Add a schedule only after you understand how the workflow behaves.
## Gemini Spark skills: quick overview
A Gemini Spark skill is a saved set of reusable instructions and supporting context that teaches Gemini how you want a certain type of work completed. Spark can apply a relevant active skill automatically, or you can select one for a specific task.
You can add a skill four ways: let **Create with Gemini** draft it for you, start from a **Recommended** template, **Create manually**, or upload a `SKILL.md` file. Whichever you pick, a strong skill needs a clear name, a description of when to use it, step-by-step instructions, the output format, and an example.
**Want the full walkthrough?** Our complete guide on [how to create a Gemini Spark skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-create-a-gemini-spark-skill/) covers every method step by step, plus a reusable instructions template and how to test and refine your skill.
How to create your first Gemini Spark skill
## How to create a Gemini Spark schedule
A schedule tells Spark when to run a task. A workflow can run at a selected time or in response to a supported condition.
### Create a schedule conversationally
1. Open Gemini and switch to Spark. 2. Open **Tasks**. 3. Describe what Spark should do. 4. State when or under which condition it should run. 5. Submit the instruction. 6. Review the task and its schedule.
Example scheduled Spark task
Every Monday morning, review the business updates in the selected Gmail label and project files in the selected Drive folder. Create a weekly brief containing: 1. Major updates 2. Decisions that need to be made 3. Missed deadlines or risks 4. This week’s priorities 5. A suggested action list Do not send emails, modify files, delete information, or create calendar events without asking for my approval.
### Create a time-based schedule manually
1. Open Gemini and switch to Spark. 2. Open **Schedules**. 3. Select **Create manually**. 4. Enter a schedule name. 5. Choose when it should run. 6. Enter the task instructions. 7. Create the schedule. 8. Use **Run now** to test it before relying on it.
Manual schedule creation is designed for time-based schedules. Gmail-triggered schedules and monitors can be created through conversational instructions.
### Types of Gemini Spark schedules
* **Time-based schedules:** Run once, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, or yearly. * **Gmail-triggered schedules:** Run when an email satisfies a supported Gmail filter. * **Monitors:** Check a condition periodically throughout the day and act when the condition is satisfied.
**Monitors are not instant alerts.** Spark generally checks monitor conditions every few hours, so monitors are not appropriate for urgent, rapidly changing, or highly time-sensitive events.
### Manage a Spark schedule
Use the Schedules page or the related task thread to review, edit, pause, resume, run, or delete a schedule. Review scheduled workflows regularly instead of assuming every unattended run will behave exactly as expected.
How to schedule a task or skill to run automatically with Gemini Spark.
## What Gemini Spark can do with Google Workspace
Spark can work with supported Google Workspace services when Google Workspace is connected to Gemini Apps and the required permissions are enabled.
[Google’s June 2026 Spark update](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-app/gemini-spark-updates-june-2026/) also expanded connected apps beyond the core Workspace flow. Google says Tasks and Keep are being added, along with Canva, Dropbox, Instacart, OpenTable, Zillow Rentals, and support for custom Model Context Protocol connections. Treat each connector as account- and rollout-dependent until it appears in your own Spark settings.
Gmail
Search and summarize email threads, draft replies, organize selected messages, and use supported Gmail conditions to trigger workflows.
Google Calendar
Review availability, help plan meetings, respond to supported invitations, and prepare calendar-related actions.
Google Drive
Search for files, review selected file content, locate recent documents, and organize supported information.
Google Docs
Create drafts, add summaries, organize notes, and work with supported document content.
Google Sheets
Create and organize spreadsheets containing structured data, tables, and supported formulas.
Google Slides
Prepare presentation drafts and organize slide content from approved instructions and sources.
Google Tasks
Turn approved action items into task lists and keep follow-up work organized when the connector is available.
Google Keep
Use selected notes as lightweight context for reminders, checklists, and recurring workflow instructions.
Available apps and actions can change based on your account, connected services, permissions, device, location, and Google’s current feature support. Review Spark’s work before allowing it to edit, delete, send, schedule, purchase, or publish anything.
## Gemini Spark examples and use cases
Gemini Spark is best suited to workflows with a clear outcome, repeatable process, and information you are comfortable allowing Spark to use.
Research assistant
Research a topic, compare sources, track updates, and create a cited summary.
Weekly business brief
Summarize selected messages, files, deadlines, risks, and priorities.
Content planning
Review approved topics and create a structured weekly content plan.
Inbox organization
Summarize selected emails, identify action items, and organize recurring newsletters.
Document organization
Review selected Drive files and organize important information in a table.
Meeting follow-up
Turn approved meeting notes into decisions, owners, priorities, and next steps.
## How to get better results from Gemini Spark
### Start with a narrow task
“Manage my business” is too broad. “Review these five files and create a table of unresolved decisions” is focused and testable.
### Specify the sources
Tell Spark which Gmail label, Drive folder, files, websites, notebook, date range, or skill it should use.
### Define the final deliverable
State whether you want a summary, table, document, spreadsheet, presentation, email draft, action list, or another format.
### Explain how information should be evaluated
Define what counts as important, credible, urgent, relevant, complete, duplicated, or outside the task’s scope.
### Provide examples
A sample output, heading structure, writing style, or table format can improve a workflow more than adding vague directions such as “make it better.”
### Separate preparation from external action
Ask Spark to research, organize, compare, and draft first. Require approval before it sends, publishes, purchases, books, deletes, submits, or changes anything.
## How to use Gemini Spark safely
Spark can work with connected apps, files, websites, browser sessions, remote computer data, and other authorized information. That makes it more capable than an ordinary chatbot, but it also requires stronger supervision.
* Start with low-risk and reversible tasks. * Connect only the information required for the task. * Review important instructions before submitting them. * Monitor tasks involving private information. * Do not type passwords into task threads. * Do not type payment information into task threads. * Use browser takeover for sensitive steps. * Require approval before sending or publishing. * Check files and messages Spark creates or changes. * Pause schedules you are no longer actively using.
### Be aware of prompt injection
An AI agent may encounter hidden or misleading instructions inside websites, messages, documents, code, or other content. Those instructions may attempt to redirect the agent away from your original request.
Closely supervise tasks involving unfamiliar websites, connected accounts, sensitive documents, purchases, deletions, or actions where a mistake would have a meaningful consequence.
### Understand how Spark uses and stores data
Spark may process information from your tasks, schedules, skills, Connected Apps, Personal Intelligence, websites, remote browser, and remote computer. Remote browser information can include page content and cookies used to keep you signed in. Remote computer information can include files, code, and task-related data.
Spark may share information required to complete a task with connected services, websites, and other third parties. Only provide access to information that is necessary for the workflow.
You can delete saved remote browser data and manage or clear remote computer information from your Gemini Spark settings.
### What happens when you turn Gemini Spark off
Turning Spark off deletes saved remote browser and remote computer data. Your tasks and schedules are paused rather than deleted, and your chats are not automatically deleted.
If you turn Spark back on, paused tasks and schedules may resume automatically. Review active schedules before re-enabling Spark so an older workflow does not restart unexpectedly.
## Current Gemini Spark limits and restrictions
Gemini Spark remains an experimental product. Understanding its current limits will help you avoid creating workflows that are too urgent, sensitive, or complex to run reliably without supervision.
15 concurrent tasks
Spark currently allows up to 15 tasks to run at the same time.
50 active schedules
You can currently maintain up to 50 active Spark schedules.
Approximate start times
Scheduled tasks may not begin at the exact moment requested.
Periodic monitoring
Monitors generally check conditions every few hours rather than continuously.
Scheduled tasks may also be delayed by usage limits or periods of high demand. Avoid using Spark schedules or monitors for emergencies, security alerts, immediate purchasing, fast-moving prices, or other situations where a delay could create a meaningful problem.
## Common Gemini Spark problems
### Gemini Spark is not showing on my account
Confirm that you are using an eligible personal Google Account, have Google AI Ultra (or Google AI Pro in the US), are at least 18, have Keep Activity enabled, are using a language your plan supports, and are accessing Gemini from a currently supported location.
### My task stopped or needs attention
Open the task thread and work panel. Spark may need clarification, confirmation, access to a file, permission to use an app, or for you to take control of the remote browser.
### My scheduled task did not run
Check whether the schedule is paused, Spark is enabled, your usage limit was reached, or 15 other tasks were already running. Schedule start times are approximate and may also be delayed during periods of high demand.
### I cannot create another schedule
Spark currently supports up to 50 active schedules. Pause or delete an existing schedule before creating or resuming another one.
### The output is too generic
Add a required format, source rules, date range, selection criteria, examples, exclusions, and a clearer definition of completion.
### Spark used the wrong information
Narrow the approved sources. Name the exact Drive folder, files, Gmail label, website, notebook, date range, or skill Spark should use.
### Spark is taking an action I do not want
Stop the task or take control of the remote browser. Then update the instructions to state which actions are prohibited or require confirmation.
## Frequently asked questions about using Gemini Spark
### How do I start using Gemini Spark?
If you are brand new, follow the [Free Gemini Spark Setup Guide for Beginners](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/setup-guides/gemini-spark/) first. Once Spark is available on your account, open Gemini with an eligible personal account, select Change mode, switch to Spark, open Tasks, describe the outcome you want Spark to manage, add the required files, apps, notebooks, or skills, submit the task, and monitor its progress.
### Do I need coding experience to use Gemini Spark?
No. Gemini Spark uses conversational instructions and supports no-code workflows. You still need to define a clear goal, provide the right context, structure the workflow, and review the agent’s work.
### What is the difference between a task, skill, and schedule?
A task is the complete goal Spark should manage. A skill contains reusable instructions explaining how work should be completed. A schedule determines when or under which condition the task should run.
### Can Gemini Spark work with Google Workspace apps?
Spark can use supported Google Workspace services when Workspace is connected to Gemini Apps and the necessary permissions are enabled. Supported apps and actions can vary by account, settings, platform, and Google’s current feature support.
### Can Gemini Spark continue working when my computer is turned off?
Spark is designed to continue eligible cloud-based tasks in the background. Tasks that need local files in the Gemini app for macOS require your Mac to stay on, awake, and connected while they run. You should still return regularly to review progress, respond to requests for input, and supervise important workflows.
### Should I schedule my first Gemini Spark task?
It is better to test a new workflow manually first. Improve the instructions until the task produces dependable results, then schedule it only when it is safe and appropriate to run without constant supervision.
### How many Gemini Spark tasks can run at the same time?
Spark currently allows up to 15 tasks to run concurrently. A scheduled task may not begin if 15 other tasks are already running.
### How many active Gemini Spark schedules can I create?
Spark currently supports up to 50 active schedules. You must pause or delete an existing schedule before creating or resuming another schedule after reaching the limit.
### Is Gemini Spark safe to use?
Spark provides monitoring, remote-browser controls, and browser takeover, but it is still an experimental AI agent that can make mistakes. Begin with low-risk tasks, limit access, avoid entering sensitive information in task threads, and supervise important actions.
### What should I create first with Gemini Spark?
Start with a focused workflow that is useful and easy to verify, such as a research summary, weekly business brief, meeting-action list, document comparison, inbox summary, or content plan.
Official Google resources
* [Use Gemini Spark to manage tasks and workflows](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/17094507) * [Find and manage Gemini Spark tasks](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/17094196) * [Create and manage Gemini Spark schedules](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/17094710) * [Create and manage Gemini Spark skills](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/17094296) * [Gemini Spark updates: macOS launch, connected apps and more](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-app/gemini-spark-updates-june-2026/) * [Gemini Apps Privacy Hub](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961)
_Editorial note: Gemini Spark is an experimental product. Features, interface labels, regional availability, account requirements, limits, connected apps, and supported actions may change. AI Agents Library is an independent educational resource and is not affiliated with Google._

item.text: The 15 Best ChatGPT Skills for Business Owners (2026) Most business owners don’t have a ChatGPT problem — they have a repetition problem. The same follow-up email, the same weekly report, the same competitor check, rewritten from scratch every single time. A ChatGPT skill fixes that: you save the process once, and ChatGPT can follow the same method more consistently whenever you ask. This guide covers the 15 skills worth setting up first, what problem each one actually solves, and roughly how much time it gives you back. Most are free, take minutes to add, and need no coding. If you’d rather skim what’s available first, browse the full ChatGPT skills library — or grab the 15 free AI skills download pack and install a curated cross-platform starter set in under a minute. Want to see what these workflows actually look like in practice? Explore 15 ChatGPT Skills examples with real inputs, workflows, and outputs. Quick answer What are the best ChatGPT skills for business owners? The best ChatGPT skills for business owners automate the work you repeat every week: client follow-ups, competitor checks, industry news, customer feedback, and inbox triage. Start with the AI Follow-Up Email Skill if deals go quiet, the AI Competitor Research Skill if you’re making pricing calls blind, and the AI Gmail Triage Skill if email eats your morning. Pick one, use it for a week, then add the next. New to ChatGPT and want structured lessons alongside the skills? See our roundup of the best ChatGPT courses to learn Skills — nine step-by-step ChatGPT courses for beginners, from free official OpenAI paths to full training with support. Comparing workflows across every major agent? Start with the complete guide to the best AI Skills for business owners, then use this platform-specific list to decide which ones fit ChatGPT best. Looking specifically for small-business marketing workflows? See the best ChatGPT marketing skills for content, social media, customer research, landing pages, websites, and brand voice. A ChatGPT skill saves your process once, so the same task doesn’t cost you an hour every week. What Are ChatGPT Skills? A ChatGPT Skill is a reusable workflow that ChatGPT can apply when relevant. Skills can be distributed independently or packaged inside a plugin with connected apps and app templates. Each Skill defines three things: when to use it, the steps to follow, and the format of the result. Save it once, and ChatGPT can produce more consistent output without making you re-explain the method in every new chat. For a concrete example, the AI Follow-Up Email ChatGPT Skill tells ChatGPT when a follow-up is needed, the steps to draft one, and the exact format the finished email should take. That’s the difference between a prompt and a skill. A prompt is a single request you retype. A skill is the saved method behind it. If you want the deeper distinction, see what an AI agent skill is. Interface update: Skills are in the Plugin Directory OpenAI replaced the App Directory with the Plugin Directory on July 9, 2026. To find workspace Skills, open Plugins in the ChatGPT sidebar, then select the Skills tab. Older screenshots may still show an App Directory or a standalone Skills destination; the public-facing term ChatGPT Skills is still accurate. Read this first: Skills aren’t on every plan — but you can still use all of these OpenAI’s native Skills feature isn’t on every plan, and it’s easy to go hunting for a button that isn’t there. If you want the full picture — which plans have it, where the tab lives, and the five usual reasons it doesn’t appear — see ChatGPT Skills availability: which plans have it and why it may not be showing. Either way, it doesn’t block you. ChatGPT Projects are available on free and paid plans, and project instructions override your global custom instructions — so pasting any skill below into a Project’s instructions gives you a practical reusable setup without native Skills. Not identical to the built-in feature, but for instruction-based workflows it does the job. Quick Comparison: All 15 Skills at a Glance Time saved is an estimate — it depends entirely on your volume. Treat it as a guide to what to fix first, not a promise. Skill Best for Est. time saved Difficulty Works with AI Follow-Up Email Skill Deals and clients going cold 1–2 hrs/week Beginner ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI Competitor Research Skill Pricing and positioning calls 2–3 hrs/report Beginner ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI Customer Feedback Skill Reviews and survey replies piling up 2–3 hrs/month Beginner ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI News Agent Skill Staying current without the doomscroll 1–2 hrs/week Beginner ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI Gmail Triage Skill An inbox that eats your morning 3–5 hrs/week Beginner ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI Spreadsheet Insights Skill Data you export but never read 1–3 hrs/month Beginner ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI Weekly Business Brief Skill Knowing where the business stands 1–2 hrs/week Beginner ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI SOP Generator Skill Processes trapped in your head 2–4 hrs/SOP Beginner ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI Social Media Post Skill Posting consistently without a team 2–4 hrs/week Beginner ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI Cold Outreach Email Skill Filling the top of the pipeline 2–3 hrs/week Intermediate ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI Market Research Brief Skill Testing a new offer or market 3–4 hrs/brief Intermediate ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI Credit Saver Skill Wasting messages on vague prompts 1–2 hrs/week Beginner ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI Client Proposal Skill Proposals that take days to send 1–2 hrs/proposal Beginner ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI Meeting Notes Skill Messy notes, forgotten action items 2–3 hrs/week Beginner ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark AI Monthly Business Review Skill The month-end review you keep skipping 2–3 hrs/month Beginner ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini Spark The 15 Best ChatGPT Skills for Business Owners Ordered by how many business owners the problem actually affects — not by how impressive the skill sounds. Start at the top. What it does: Turns raw meeting notes or a short context line into a clear client follow-up — thank-you, decisions made, action items with owners, and a specific next step. Why business owners use it: Most deals don’t die from a bad pitch. They die in the silence afterward. The follow-up is the highest-leverage email you send, and it’s the one most likely to be put off until tomorrow. Real-world example: After a discovery call, a freelancer pastes her scribbled notes and gets a follow-up she can send in under a minute — with the next step already proposed. Expected outcome: Follow-ups are easier to send promptly and in a consistent format. What it does: Runs a structured competitor check — positioning, pricing, offers, messaging — and returns what changed and what it means for you. Why business owners use it: Competitor research usually happens in a panic, right after you lose a deal. Run on a schedule instead, it becomes an early warning system. Real-world example: Before a pricing change, an agency owner runs the skill on three rivals and finds two have quietly added a service she still charges extra for. Expected outcome: You make pricing and positioning calls with evidence, not vibes. What it does: Reads reviews, survey replies, or support messages in bulk and pulls out the themes — what people love, what they complain about, and what’s quietly costing you sales. Why business owners use it: Feedback is only useful in aggregate. One angry review is noise; the same complaint eleven times is a roadmap — and nobody has time to spot that by hand. Real-world example: A shop owner pastes three months of reviews and learns “shipping was slow” appears in a third of them — a fixable problem she’d been reading past. Expected outcome: You act on patterns instead of reacting to whoever shouted loudest. What it does: Pulls the news that matters in your industry into a short digest — what happened, why it matters to you, and what (if anything) to do about it. Why business owners use it: Staying informed has quietly become a part-time job. This gives you the signal without the two hours of scrolling that usually comes attached. Real-world example: Every Monday, a marketing lead gets a five-item digest on her industry — and skips the newsletters entirely. Expected outcome: You stay current in ten minutes instead of an afternoon. What it does: Reads a batch of emails and sorts them by what actually needs you — urgent replies, things to delegate, things to archive — with a suggested next action for each. Why business owners use it: Email isn’t hard, it’s relentless. The cost isn’t answering messages; it’s deciding, forty times a morning, which message matters. This makes that decision once. Real-world example: A consultant pastes in 30 overnight emails and gets back five that need her personally today, eight to hand to her VA, and the rest flagged as noise — before her first coffee. Expected outcome: You open your inbox with a plan instead of a backlog. What it does: Paste your rows — sales, expenses, survey answers, ad numbers — and get the story the spreadsheet is telling: the headline trend, the outliers worth explaining, the totals that matter, and what to look at next. Plain English, no formulas. OpenAI now supports Skills directly inside ChatGPT for Excel and Google Sheets. This means the workflow can run beside the workbook rather than requiring users to paste rows into a separate conversation. Why business owners use it: Most owners have the data already. What they don’t have is an hour to sit with it, or the confidence that they’d spot the right thing if they did. This skill closes the gap between exporting a report and actually understanding it. Real-world example: Open the sales workbook in Excel or Google Sheets, invoke the Spreadsheet Insights Skill with @, and ask it to identify the months, products, or discounts driving the largest changes. Expected outcome: You stop exporting reports you never read, and start making decisions from numbers you already had. What it does: Takes your scattered updates — numbers, notes, wins, problems — and returns one structured weekly brief: what moved, what’s stuck, and what needs a decision. Why business owners use it: Most owners are busy enough to lose the thread of their own business. A weekly brief forces the fifteen minutes of thinking that prevents a bad quarter. Real-world example: On Friday, a shop owner pastes the week’s sales figures and a few notes, and gets a brief that flags a supplier issue she’d stopped noticing. Expected outcome: You start Monday knowing your three priorities, not guessing them. What it does: Turns a process you describe out loud into a clean, step-by-step standard operating procedure someone else could actually follow. Why business owners use it: You can’t delegate what only lives in your head. Writing SOPs is the task everyone agrees matters and nobody ever starts, because a blank document is intimidating. Real-world example: An owner talks through how she onboards a new client, pastes that ramble in, and gets an SOP her new hire can run on day one. Expected outcome: The processes in your head become processes your team can run. What it does: Turns one idea, article, or update into ready-to-post copy for Facebook, LinkedIn, and Instagram — each written for how that platform actually reads. Why business owners use it: Consistency beats brilliance on social, and consistency is exactly what breaks first when you get busy. This removes the blank-page cost of showing up. Real-world example: A freelancer feeds in a client win and gets a LinkedIn post, an Instagram caption, and a Facebook update — three platforms from one story. Expected outcome: You post regularly without it becoming a second job. What it does: Writes a specific, researched cold email built around the prospect’s situation — not a template with their first name dropped into it. Why business owners use it: Cold outreach fails when it’s obviously mass-produced. The bottleneck is the research and personalization, and that’s exactly the part this handles. Real-world example: A consultant pastes a prospect’s website and role, and gets an email that references their actual situation and asks for a small, easy yes. Expected outcome: Outreach that reads like a person wrote it, at a volume a person couldn’t. What it does: Produces a structured brief on a market or audience — who’s in it, what they want, what they pay, and where the gaps are. Why business owners use it: Most new offers fail because nobody checked whether anyone wanted them. This makes the check cheap enough that you’ll actually do it. Real-world example: Before launching a retainer package, a consultant runs a brief on the segment and finds they buy on speed, not price — so she rebuilds the offer around turnaround time. Expected outcome: You launch into demand you’ve verified, not demand you assumed. What it does: Cleans up a messy, vague, or bloated request before you send it — so you get a usable answer on the first try instead of the fourth. Why business owners use it: Every plan has a ceiling, whether that’s message limits, usage credits, or your own patience. Most of that budget gets burned on re-asking the same question three different ways. Fixing the prompt is cheaper than fixing the output. Real-world example: An owner runs a rambling half-page request through it, gets back a tight version with the goal and format spelled out, and gets what she wanted in one message. Expected outcome: Fewer retries, less back-and-forth, better first drafts. Finish with three practical business workflows Numbers 13–15 help you move client work forward, turn meetings into action, and review the health of your business each month. They are beginner-friendly skills you can use immediately: no coding or technical setup required. What it does: Turns your discovery notes into a proposal that wins the work by being clear rather than long — their problem in their own words, your approach, exact deliverables, a timeline, the investment, and one obvious next step. Why business owners use it: Proposals are the highest-stakes writing most owners do, and they’re usually written late at night after the energy of the call has worn off. This skill keeps the structure consistent so the quality doesn’t depend on what time you sat down to write it. Real-world example: A consultant finishes a discovery call, pastes her messy notes in, and sends a clean proposal the same afternoon instead of three days later — while the conversation is still warm. Expected outcome: Proposals go out faster, read more clearly, and stop drifting into ten pages nobody finishes. What it does: Converts messy notes or a transcript into a structured summary: decisions, action items with owners and dates, open questions, and what to follow up on. Why business owners use it: The value of a meeting is what happens afterward. If the notes stay messy, the decisions quietly evaporate and get re-litigated next month. The 15 Best ChatGPT Skills for Business Owners (2026)

Most business owners don’t have a ChatGPT problem — they have a repetition problem. The same follow-up email, the same weekly report, the same competitor check, rewritten from scratch every single time. A ChatGPT skill fixes that: you save the process once, and ChatGPT can follow the same method more consistently whenever you ask.

This guide covers the 15 skills worth setting up first, what problem each one actually solves, and roughly how much time it gives you back. Most are free, take minutes to add, and need no coding. If you’d rather skim what’s available first, browse the full ChatGPT skills library — or grab the 15 free AI skills download pack and install a curated cross-platform starter set in under a minute.

Want to see what these workflows actually look like in practice? Explore 15 ChatGPT Skills examples with real inputs, workflows, and outputs.

Quick answer

What are the best ChatGPT skills for business owners?

The best ChatGPT skills for business owners automate the work you repeat every week: client follow-ups, competitor checks, industry news, customer feedback, and inbox triage. Start with the AI Follow-Up Email Skill if deals go quiet, the AI Competitor Research Skill if you’re making pricing calls blind, and the AI Gmail Triage Skill if email eats your morning. Pick one, use it for a week, then add the next.

New to ChatGPT and want structured lessons alongside the skills? See our roundup of the best ChatGPT courses to learn Skills — nine step-by-step ChatGPT courses for beginners, from free official OpenAI paths to full training with support.

Comparing workflows across every major agent? Start with the complete guide to the best AI Skills for business owners, then use this platform-specific list to decide which ones fit ChatGPT best.

Looking specifically for small-business marketing workflows? See the best ChatGPT marketing skills for content, social media, customer research, landing pages, websites, and brand voice.

What Are ChatGPT Skills?

A ChatGPT Skill is a reusable workflow that ChatGPT can apply when relevant. Skills can be distributed independently or packaged inside a plugin with connected apps and app templates. Each Skill defines three things: when to use it, the steps to follow, and the format of the result. Save it once, and ChatGPT can produce more consistent output without making you re-explain the method in every new chat. For a concrete example, the AI Follow-Up Email ChatGPT Skill tells ChatGPT when a follow-up is needed, the steps to draft one, and the exact format the finished email should take.

That’s the difference between a prompt and a skill. A prompt is a single request you retype. A skill is the saved method behind it. If you want the deeper distinction, see what an AI agent skill is.

Interface update: Skills are in the Plugin Directory

OpenAI replaced the App Directory with the Plugin Directory on July 9, 2026. To find workspace Skills, open Plugins in the ChatGPT sidebar, then select the Skills tab. Older screenshots may still show an App Directory or a standalone Skills destination; the public-facing term ChatGPT Skills is still accurate.

Read this first: Skills aren’t on every plan — but you can still use all of these

OpenAI’s native Skills feature isn’t on every plan, and it’s easy to go hunting for a button that isn’t there. If you want the full picture — which plans have it, where the tab lives, and the five usual reasons it doesn’t appear — see ChatGPT Skills availability: which plans have it and why it may not be showing.

Either way, it doesn’t block you. ChatGPT Projects are available on free and paid plans, and project instructions override your global custom instructions — so pasting any skill below into a Project’s instructions gives you a practical reusable setup without native Skills. Not identical to the built-in feature, but for instruction-based workflows it does the job.

Time saved is an estimate — it depends entirely on your volume. Treat it as a guide to what to fix first, not a promise.

What it does: Turns raw meeting notes or a short context line into a clear client follow-up — thank-you, decisions made, action items with owners, and a specific next step.

Why business owners use it: Most deals don’t die from a bad pitch. They die in the silence afterward. The follow-up is the highest-leverage email you send, and it’s the one most likely to be put off until tomorrow.

Real-world example: After a discovery call, a freelancer pastes her scribbled notes and gets a follow-up she can send in under a minute — with the next step already proposed.

Expected outcome: Follow-ups are easier to send promptly and in a consistent format.

What it does: Runs a structured competitor check — positioning, pricing, offers, messaging — and returns what changed and what it means for you.

Why business owners use it: Competitor research usually happens in a panic, right after you lose a deal. Run on a schedule instead, it becomes an early warning system.

Real-world example: Before a pricing change, an agency owner runs the skill on three rivals and finds two have quietly added a service she still charges extra for.

Expected outcome: You make pricing and positioning calls with evidence, not vibes.

What it does: Reads reviews, survey replies, or support messages in bulk and pulls out the themes — what people love, what they complain about, and what’s quietly costing you sales.

Why business owners use it: Feedback is only useful in aggregate. One angry review is noise; the same complaint eleven times is a roadmap — and nobody has time to spot that by hand.

Real-world example: A shop owner pastes three months of reviews and learns “shipping was slow” appears in a third of them — a fixable problem she’d been reading past.

Expected outcome: You act on patterns instead of reacting to whoever shouted loudest.

What it does: Pulls the news that matters in your industry into a short digest — what happened, why it matters to you, and what (if anything) to do about it.

Why business owners use it: Staying informed has quietly become a part-time job. This gives you the signal without the two hours of scrolling that usually comes attached.

Real-world example: Every Monday, a marketing lead gets a five-item digest on her industry — and skips the newsletters entirely.

Expected outcome: You stay current in ten minutes instead of an afternoon.

Why business owners use it: Email isn’t hard, it’s relentless. The cost isn’t answering messages; it’s deciding, forty times a morning, which message matters. This makes that decision once.

Real-world example: A consultant pastes in 30 overnight emails and gets back five that need her personally today, eight to hand to her VA, and the rest flagged as noise — before her first coffee.

Expected outcome: You open your inbox with a plan instead of a backlog.

What it does: Paste your rows — sales, expenses, survey answers, ad numbers — and get the story the spreadsheet is telling: the headline trend, the outliers worth explaining, the totals that matter, and what to look at next. Plain English, no formulas.

OpenAI now supports Skills directly inside ChatGPT for Excel and Google Sheets. This means the workflow can run beside the workbook rather than requiring users to paste rows into a separate conversation.

Why business owners use it: Most owners have the data already. What they don’t have is an hour to sit with it, or the confidence that they’d spot the right thing if they did. This skill closes the gap between exporting a report and actually understanding it.

Real-world example: Open the sales workbook in Excel or Google Sheets, invoke the Spreadsheet Insights Skill with @, and ask it to identify the months, products, or discounts driving the largest changes.

Expected outcome: You stop exporting reports you never read, and start making decisions from numbers you already had.

What it does: Takes your scattered updates — numbers, notes, wins, problems — and returns one structured weekly brief: what moved, what’s stuck, and what needs a decision.

Why business owners use it: Most owners are busy enough to lose the thread of their own business. A weekly brief forces the fifteen minutes of thinking that prevents a bad quarter.

Real-world example: On Friday, a shop owner pastes the week’s sales figures and a few notes, and gets a brief that flags a supplier issue she’d stopped noticing.

Expected outcome: You start Monday knowing your three priorities, not guessing them.

What it does: Turns a process you describe out loud into a clean, step-by-step standard operating procedure someone else could actually follow.

Why business owners use it: You can’t delegate what only lives in your head. Writing SOPs is the task everyone agrees matters and nobody ever starts, because a blank document is intimidating.

Real-world example: An owner talks through how she onboards a new client, pastes that ramble in, and gets an SOP her new hire can run on day one.

Expected outcome: The processes in your head become processes your team can run.

What it does: Turns one idea, article, or update into ready-to-post copy for Facebook, LinkedIn, and Instagram — each written for how that platform actually reads.

Why business owners use it: Consistency beats brilliance on social, and consistency is exactly what breaks first when you get busy. This removes the blank-page cost of showing up.

Real-world example: A freelancer feeds in a client win and gets a LinkedIn post, an Instagram caption, and a Facebook update — three platforms from one story.

Expected outcome: You post regularly without it becoming a second job.

What it does: Writes a specific, researched cold email built around the prospect’s situation — not a template with their first name dropped into it.

Why business owners use it: Cold outreach fails when it’s obviously mass-produced. The bottleneck is the research and personalization, and that’s exactly the part this handles.

Real-world example: A consultant pastes a prospect’s website and role, and gets an email that references their actual situation and asks for a small, easy yes.

Expected outcome: Outreach that reads like a person wrote it, at a volume a person couldn’t.

What it does: Produces a structured brief on a market or audience — who’s in it, what they want, what they pay, and where the gaps are.

Why business owners use it: Most new offers fail because nobody checked whether anyone wanted them. This makes the check cheap enough that you’ll actually do it.

Real-world example: Before launching a retainer package, a consultant runs a brief on the segment and finds they buy on speed, not price — so she rebuilds the offer around turnaround time.

Expected outcome: You launch into demand you’ve verified, not demand you assumed.

What it does: Cleans up a messy, vague, or bloated request before you send it — so you get a usable answer on the first try instead of the fourth.

Why business owners use it: Every plan has a ceiling, whether that’s message limits, usage credits, or your own patience. Most of that budget gets burned on re-asking the same question three different ways. Fixing the prompt is cheaper than fixing the output.

That’s the difference between a prompt and a skill. A prompt is a single request you retype. A skill is the saved method behind it. If you want the deeper distinction, see [what an AI agent skill is](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent-skill/).
**Interface update: Skills are in the Plugin Directory**
[OpenAI replaced the App Directory with the Plugin Directory](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001256-plugins-in-chatgpt-and-codex) on July 9, 2026. To find workspace Skills, open **Plugins** in the ChatGPT sidebar, then select the **Skills** tab. Older screenshots may still show an App Directory or a standalone Skills destination; the public-facing term **ChatGPT Skills** is still accurate.
**Read this first: Skills aren’t on every plan — but you can still use all of these**
OpenAI’s native Skills feature isn’t on every plan, and it’s easy to go hunting for a button that isn’t there. If you want the full picture — which plans have it, where the tab lives, and the five usual reasons it doesn’t appear — see [ChatGPT Skills availability: which plans have it and why it may not be showing](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/chatgpt-skills-availability/).
**Either way, it doesn’t block you.** ChatGPT Projects are available on free and paid plans, and project instructions override your global custom instructions — so pasting any skill below into a Project’s instructions gives you a practical reusable setup without native Skills. Not identical to the built-in feature, but for instruction-based workflows it does the job.
## Quick Comparison: All 15 Skills at a Glance
