## The 15 Best ChatGPT Skills for Business Owners
Ordered by how many business owners the problem actually affects — not by how impressive the skill sounds. Start at the top.
**What it does:** Turns raw meeting notes or a short context line into a clear client follow-up — thank-you, decisions made, action items with owners, and a specific next step.
**Why business owners use it:** Most deals don’t die from a bad pitch. They die in the silence afterward. The follow-up is the highest-leverage email you send, and it’s the one most likely to be put off until tomorrow.
**Real-world example:** After a discovery call, a freelancer pastes her scribbled notes and gets a follow-up she can send in under a minute — with the next step already proposed.
**Expected outcome:** Follow-ups are easier to send promptly and in a consistent format.
**What it does:** Runs a structured competitor check — positioning, pricing, offers, messaging — and returns what changed and what it means for you.
**Why business owners use it:** Competitor research usually happens in a panic, right after you lose a deal. Run on a schedule instead, it becomes an early warning system.
**Real-world example:** Before a pricing change, an agency owner runs the skill on three rivals and finds two have quietly added a service she still charges extra for.
**Expected outcome:** You make pricing and positioning calls with evidence, not vibes.
**What it does:** Reads reviews, survey replies, or support messages in bulk and pulls out the themes — what people love, what they complain about, and what’s quietly costing you sales.
**Why business owners use it:** Feedback is only useful in aggregate. One angry review is noise; the same complaint eleven times is a roadmap — and nobody has time to spot that by hand.
**Real-world example:** A shop owner pastes three months of reviews and learns “shipping was slow” appears in a third of them — a fixable problem she’d been reading past.
**Expected outcome:** You act on patterns instead of reacting to whoever shouted loudest.
**What it does:** Pulls the news that matters in your industry into a short digest — what happened, why it matters to you, and what (if anything) to do about it.
**Why business owners use it:** Staying informed has quietly become a part-time job. This gives you the signal without the two hours of scrolling that usually comes attached.
**Real-world example:** Every Monday, a marketing lead gets a five-item digest on her industry — and skips the newsletters entirely.
**Expected outcome:** You stay current in ten minutes instead of an afternoon.
**What it does:** Reads a batch of emails and sorts them by what actually needs you — urgent replies, things to delegate, things to archive — with a suggested next action for each.
**Why business owners use it:** Email isn’t hard, it’s relentless. The cost isn’t answering messages; it’s deciding, forty times a morning, which message matters. This makes that decision once.
**Real-world example:** A consultant pastes in 30 overnight emails and gets back five that need her personally today, eight to hand to her VA, and the rest flagged as noise — before her first coffee.
**Expected outcome:** You open your inbox with a plan instead of a backlog.
**What it does:** Paste your rows — sales, expenses, survey answers, ad numbers — and get the story the spreadsheet is telling: the headline trend, the outliers worth explaining, the totals that matter, and what to look at next. Plain English, no formulas.
OpenAI now supports Skills directly inside ChatGPT for Excel and Google Sheets. This means the workflow can run beside the workbook rather than requiring users to paste rows into a separate conversation.
**Why business owners use it:** Most owners have the data already. What they don’t have is an hour to sit with it, or the confidence that they’d spot the right thing if they did. This skill closes the gap between exporting a report and actually understanding it.
**Real-world example:** Open the sales workbook in Excel or Google Sheets, invoke the Spreadsheet Insights Skill with **@**, and ask it to identify the months, products, or discounts driving the largest changes.
**Expected outcome:** You stop exporting reports you never read, and start making decisions from numbers you already had.
**What it does:** Takes your scattered updates — numbers, notes, wins, problems — and returns one structured weekly brief: what moved, what’s stuck, and what needs a decision.
**Why business owners use it:** Most owners are busy enough to lose the thread of their own business. A weekly brief forces the fifteen minutes of thinking that prevents a bad quarter.
**Real-world example:** On Friday, a shop owner pastes the week’s sales figures and a few notes, and gets a brief that flags a supplier issue she’d stopped noticing.
**Expected outcome:** You start Monday knowing your three priorities, not guessing them.
**What it does:** Turns a process you describe out loud into a clean, step-by-step standard operating procedure someone else could actually follow.
**Why business owners use it:** You can’t delegate what only lives in your head. Writing SOPs is the task everyone agrees matters and nobody ever starts, because a blank document is intimidating.
**Real-world example:** An owner talks through how she onboards a new client, pastes that ramble in, and gets an SOP her new hire can run on day one.
**Expected outcome:** The processes in your head become processes your team can run.
**What it does:** Turns one idea, article, or update into ready-to-post copy for Facebook, LinkedIn, and Instagram — each written for how that platform actually reads.
**Why business owners use it:** Consistency beats brilliance on social, and consistency is exactly what breaks first when you get busy. This removes the blank-page cost of showing up.
**Real-world example:** A freelancer feeds in a client win and gets a LinkedIn post, an Instagram caption, and a Facebook update — three platforms from one story.
**Expected outcome:** You post regularly without it becoming a second job.
**What it does:** Writes a specific, researched cold email built around the prospect’s situation — not a template with their first name dropped into it.
**Why business owners use it:** Cold outreach fails when it’s obviously mass-produced. The bottleneck is the research and personalization, and that’s exactly the part this handles.
**Real-world example:** A consultant pastes a prospect’s website and role, and gets an email that references their actual situation and asks for a small, easy yes.
**Expected outcome:** Outreach that reads like a person wrote it, at a volume a person couldn’t.
**What it does:** Produces a structured brief on a market or audience — who’s in it, what they want, what they pay, and where the gaps are.
**Why business owners use it:** Most new offers fail because nobody checked whether anyone wanted them. This makes the check cheap enough that you’ll actually do it.
**Real-world example:** Before launching a retainer package, a consultant runs a brief on the segment and finds they buy on speed, not price — so she rebuilds the offer around turnaround time.
**Expected outcome:** You launch into demand you’ve verified, not demand you assumed.
**What it does:** Cleans up a messy, vague, or bloated request _before_ you send it — so you get a usable answer on the first try instead of the fourth.
**Why business owners use it:** Every plan has a ceiling, whether that’s message limits, usage credits, or your own patience. Most of that budget gets burned on re-asking the same question three different ways. Fixing the prompt is cheaper than fixing the output.
**Real-world example:** An owner runs a rambling half-page request through it, gets back a tight version with the goal and format spelled out, and gets what she wanted in one message.
**Expected outcome:** Fewer retries, less back-and-forth, better first drafts.
**Finish with three practical business workflows**
Numbers 13–15 help you move client work forward, turn meetings into action, and review the health of your business each month. They are beginner-friendly skills you can use immediately: no coding or technical setup required.
**What it does:** Turns your discovery notes into a proposal that wins the work by being clear rather than long — their problem in their own words, your approach, exact deliverables, a timeline, the investment, and one obvious next step.
**Why business owners use it:** Proposals are the highest-stakes writing most owners do, and they’re usually written late at night after the energy of the call has worn off. This skill keeps the structure consistent so the quality doesn’t depend on what time you sat down to write it.
**Real-world example:** A consultant finishes a discovery call, pastes her messy notes in, and sends a clean proposal the same afternoon instead of three days later — while the conversation is still warm.
**Expected outcome:** Proposals go out faster, read more clearly, and stop drifting into ten pages nobody finishes.
**What it does:** Converts messy notes or a transcript into a structured summary: decisions, action items with owners and dates, open questions, and what to follow up on.
**Why business owners use it:** The value of a meeting is what happens afterward. If the notes stay messy, the decisions quietly evaporate and get re-litigated next month.
**Real-world example:** An agency owner drops in a rambling call transcript and gets six action items with owners — which she pastes straight into her project tool.
**Expected outcome:** Every meeting ends with a record someone can act on.
**What it does:** Runs the month-end review most owners skip: what worked, what didn’t, what the numbers say, and what to change next month.
**Why business owners use it:** A weekly brief keeps you on track; a monthly review is where you notice the trend. Without one, a slow decline just looks like a normal week — twelve times in a row.
**Real-world example:** At month-end, an owner runs the review and sees her best-margin service quietly shrank to a fifth of revenue while a low-margin one grew.
**Expected outcome:** You catch the slow problems while they’re still small.
**Going further: two more technical resources**
If you’d rather build skills than copy them, two free resources are worth knowing. The [Agent Skills quickstart](https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/quickstart) walks you through writing your first skill from scratch in about fifteen minutes — it’s a tiny example, but it makes the format click permanently. And [Anthropic’s open-source skill library](https://github.com/anthropics/skills) publishes production-grade skills for Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and PDF work that you can read and adapt.
Both use a code editor, so they’re more technical than everything above. For the no-code route, see [how to create a ChatGPT skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-create-a-chatgpt-skill/).
## How to Choose the Right ChatGPT Skill
Skip the temptation to browse. Pick using the task you’re already dreading.
1. **Find the task you repeat and resent.** The best first skill isn’t the most impressive one — it’s the one attached to the job you keep pushing to tomorrow. 2. **Check it happens weekly.** A skill pays back its five-minute setup on the second or third run. If a task comes up twice a year, a plain prompt is fine. 3. **Start where the output is low-risk.** Internal work — notes, briefs, research — is a safer place to build trust than an email going to your biggest client. The [AI Meeting Notes ChatGPT skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/meeting-notes/) and the [AI Competitor Research ChatGPT skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/competitor-research/) are two obvious starting points. 4. **Use it for a full week before adding another.** Skills fail from being collected, not from being bad. 5. **Then customize it.** Once a skill is part of your week, tighten its instructions to match your voice, format, and rules. That’s when it stops feeling generic — and when you’re ready to build your own from scratch, follow [how to create a ChatGPT skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-create-a-chatgpt-skill/).
**Don’t install all fifteen today**
The people who get the most out of skills add one, use it for a week until it’s a habit, then add the next. Fifteen skills you never open are worth less than one you run every Monday.
## Start With One, Not Fifteen
Every skill here solves a problem you already have — the difference is which one is costing you the most this month. Pick that one, use it until it’s automatic, then come back for the next.
The library skills are free to copy, work in ChatGPT alongside Claude and Gemini Spark, and need no coding. Browse the full [ChatGPT skills library](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/chatgpt/) when you’re ready for more — or if you want a shorter list, see [which 15 AI skills to download first](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/ai-skills-download/) across all three platforms.
Using a different tool? See the [best Claude Skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-claude-skills/), the [best Gemini Spark Skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-gemini-spark-skills/), the [best AI Website Skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-ai-website-skills/), or return to the cross-platform [best AI Skills for business owners](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-ai-skills/).
## Frequently asked questions
What are ChatGPT skills?
A ChatGPT Skill is a reusable workflow that ChatGPT can apply when relevant. It defines when to use it, the steps to follow, and the format of the result, and it can be distributed independently or packaged inside a plugin with connected apps and app templates. It is the saved method behind a task rather than a one-off prompt you retype.
Are these ChatGPT skills free?
Yes. Every skill featured in this article is free to open, copy, and try. The optional Agent Skills quickstart and Anthropic open-source library linked in the “Going further” section are free resources too. Browse the complete collection in the [ChatGPT skills library](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/chatgpt/).
Do I need a paid ChatGPT plan to use skills?
No. Every skill on this page includes instructions you can paste into a chat or a ChatGPT Project, and Projects are available on free and paid plans. OpenAI’s native Skills feature has separate account requirements; see [OpenAI’s current Skills documentation](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001066-skills-in-chatgpt/) for the official availability and feature details, or our [ChatGPT Skills availability guide](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/chatgpt-skills-availability/) for the plain-English version. For setup steps, see [how to use ChatGPT skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-use-chatgpt-skills/).
What’s the difference between a ChatGPT skill, a project, and custom instructions?
Custom instructions are global — they apply to every conversation. A project is a workspace holding files, chats, and instructions for one area of work, and its instructions override your global ones. A skill is narrower still: a reusable method for one specific task, applied when the task matches. They layer well — a project holds the context, a skill handles the recurring job inside it. If you are using OpenAI’s agent for multi-step tasks, start with [our guide to ChatGPT Work](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/what-is-chatgpt-work/) to see how Skills, connected apps, files, deliverables, and scheduled work fit together.
Do I need to know how to code to use a ChatGPT skill?
No. All 15 business skills featured here include plain-language instructions you can copy, paste, and customize without coding. Native skill packages can also include supporting files or code for advanced workflows, but none of that is required to start using the templates in this article.
Which ChatGPT skill should I start with?
Start with the one attached to the task you’re already avoiding. If deals go quiet after calls, use the [AI Follow-Up Email Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/ai-follow-up-email-generator/). If email eats your morning, use the [AI Gmail Triage Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gmail-triage/). If you’re making pricing decisions blind, use the [AI Competitor Research Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/competitor-research/). Use one for a full week before adding another.
Can I use these skills in Claude or Gemini Spark too?
Yes. These skills are written as plain instructions, so they carry across assistants. You can browse the same skills organized for [Claude](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/claude/) and [Gemini Spark](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gemini-spark/), where the setup steps are tailored to each tool.
How do I add a skill to ChatGPT?
Copy the skill’s instructions, then add them wherever your plan supports them: as a Skill if you have that feature, or as Project instructions if you don’t (create a Project, open its settings, and paste the skill into the project instructions). Then test it on a real, messy task — not a clean example — and adjust the wording until the output matches what you wanted. For the full step-by-step — turning skills on, installing one, and editing or removing it — see [how to use ChatGPT skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-use-chatgpt-skills/). Rolling one out to a team instead? See [how to share and install ChatGPT skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-share-chatgpt-skills/).
Can I customize these skills for my business?
Yes, and you should. Use a skill as-is for the first week to see how it behaves, then tighten it: add your tone, your formatting rules, your must-include details, and anything it should never do. A well-tested custom version will usually fit your business better than a generic workflow. If you’d rather build one from scratch, see [how to create an AI skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-create-an-ai-skill/).
How much time do these ChatGPT skills actually save?
It depends entirely on your volume, which is why every estimate here is a range rather than a promise. The pattern most people see: a skill pays back its short setup by the second or third use, and the biggest wins come from the highest-frequency tasks — inbox triage, follow-ups, and meeting notes — rather than the most complex ones.

item.text:
How to Create a ChatGPT Skill in 2026 You can create a reusable ChatGPT Skill three ways: ask ChatGPT to build it, write it in the Skills editor, or upload a structured skill package. This guide shows how to turn a prompt into a saved workflow, install and test it inside ChatGPT, and download the resulting skill for reuse in compatible tools. Important: OpenAI uses several related customization features. A ChatGPT Skill is not the same as a custom GPT, a Project, or a plugin. This guide focuses on Personal Skills in ChatGPT. OpenAI also supports the Agent Skills format in Codex and the API. If you want the universal framework first, start with How to Create an AI Skill. Already have a prompt you reuse? Use how to turn a prompt into an AI skill first, then come back here to shape it into a ChatGPT skill. Not sure what to build first? See the 15 best ChatGPT skills for business owners for a ranked shortlist, then come back here to build your own. ChatGPT Skills availability OpenAI officially lists Personal Skills for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu. Check the current ChatGPT Skills availability guide for plan, admin, and device-sync details before you begin. Quick answer How do you create a ChatGPT skill? Open Plugins → Skills → Create, then choose Create with chat, Create with editor, or Upload from your computer. Define one task, when the skill should run, required inputs, ordered steps, output format, and rules. Install it, test realistic requests, and refine the trigger. For a portable file, use a skill folder whose required SKILL.md contains name, description, and the workflow instructions. What you finish with: a saved, installable workflow inside ChatGPT; optionally, a downloadable Agent Skills package you can reuse in another compatible product. A strong ChatGPT skill starts with one repeatable workflow, clear instructions, and a testable output format. What Is a ChatGPT Skill? A ChatGPT skill is a reusable workflow for a focused task. OpenAI describes skills as packages of instructions and supporting resources that help ChatGPT complete repeatable work with the right process, context, and tools. A skill can include a name, a description, workflow instructions, templates, examples, brand guidance, schemas, or connected tools. The key idea is simple: a prompt asks once; a skill saves the process. Once a skill is created and installed, OpenAI says ChatGPT can automatically use one or more skills when they are helpful. Once yours is set up, how to use ChatGPT skills walks through installing, running, editing, and removing them. For official context, see OpenAI’s Skills in ChatGPT help page and Build Skills guide. For the beginner-friendly definition of skills across every platform, read What Is an AI Agent Skill?. Need ideas before building your own? See these ChatGPT Skills examples to compare real triggers, inputs, workflows, and outputs. What You Need Before You Start Before you create a ChatGPT skill, make sure you have: A ChatGPT account with Skills access – Personal Skills are generally available for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu accounts — keep an eye out as availability expands to more plans over time. In Enterprise and Edu workspaces, an admin may need to enable Skills and related permissions. One repeatable task – choose a weekly update, client follow-up, research brief, content QA pass, documentation review, or another workflow you already repeat. A clear output format – define what “done” looks like before you build anything. Example inputs or templates – one real example makes the skill much easier to test and refine. Is a ChatGPT Skill the Same as a Custom GPT? No. They overlap, but they are not the same surface. OpenAI’s Help Center describes GPTs as custom versions of ChatGPT configured for a specific purpose, with instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, and actions. A skill is more like a reusable workflow package that ChatGPT or Codex can use when a task matches. Simple rule Use a skill when you want ChatGPT to reuse a process. Use a custom GPT when you want a named assistant experience that users can open, share, or publish in the GPT Store. How to Create a ChatGPT Skill: 7 Steps The best first ChatGPT skill is boring in the best way: one job, one process, one predictable output. Do not start with “help me with marketing.” Start with “turn raw campaign notes into a launch brief” or “draft a warm follow-up email from meeting notes.” Finish this sentence first: This skill should always ___ when I ___. That sentence becomes the foundation for the skill’s description, trigger, and test cases. The description is how ChatGPT understands when the skill applies. Make it specific, action-oriented, and full of the words you actually use when asking for the task. Weak: Helps with emails. Better: Use this skill when I provide meeting notes and ask for a client follow-up email. Turn the notes into a short, warm email with a recap, next step, and three subject line options. Clear beats clever A plain, descriptive name and description help both you and ChatGPT recognize when the skill applies. “Client Follow-Up Email” works; “Inbox Ninja” doesn’t. Save the clever name for when the purpose is already obvious. Write the process like you are training a new assistant. Include the goal, required inputs, ordered steps, output format, rules, and a review checklist. ChatGPT skill planning template: SKILL NAME [Short, specific name]
WHEN TO USE THIS SKILL Use this skill when I ask you to [repeatable task] and provide [required inputs].
GOAL Produce [specific result] using the same process and format every time.
REQUIRED INPUTS - [Input 1] - [Input 2] - [Input 3]
WORKFLOW 1. Review the inputs and identify the goal. 2. Ask one clarifying question only if a required input is missing. 3. Follow this process: - [Step A] - [Step B] - [Step C] 4. Create the output in the format below. 5. Run the review checklist before finalizing. OUTPUT FORMAT - [Section 1] - [Section 2] - [Section 3] RULES - Do not invent facts, quotes, dates, sources, or numbers. - Use [tone/style]. - Keep the output [length]. - Flag anything that needs human review. EXAMPLE Input: [Example input] Strong output: [Example output] REVIEW CHECKLIST - Did I use all required inputs? - Did I follow the workflow? - Did I match the output format? - Did I flag uncertainty instead of guessing? A ChatGPT skill can be instruction-only, but the strongest skills often include support material: a brand voice guide, a formatting template, an example output, a checklist, a schema, or a source policy. Use instructions for behavior, tone, rules, steps, and output format. Use examples to show what good output looks like. Use resources for templates, reference material, brand guidelines, or reusable checklists. Use an app when the workflow needs access to external systems, data, or actions. Use a plugin when you want to package and distribute Skills with an app or other shared workflow capabilities. Start simple. Add tools only after the instruction-only version works. How to Create a ChatGPT Skill in 2026

You can create a reusable ChatGPT Skill three ways: ask ChatGPT to build it, write it in the Skills editor, or upload a structured skill package. This guide shows how to turn a prompt into a saved workflow, install and test it inside ChatGPT, and download the resulting skill for reuse in compatible tools.

Important: OpenAI uses several related customization features. A ChatGPT Skill is not the same as a custom GPT, a Project, or a plugin. This guide focuses on Personal Skills in ChatGPT. OpenAI also supports the Agent Skills format in Codex and the API. If you want the universal framework first, start with How to Create an AI Skill.

Already have a prompt you reuse? Use how to turn a prompt into an AI skill first, then come back here to shape it into a ChatGPT skill.

Not sure what to build first? See the 15 best ChatGPT skills for business owners for a ranked shortlist, then come back here to build your own.

ChatGPT Skills availability

OpenAI officially lists Personal Skills for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu. Check the current ChatGPT Skills availability guide for plan, admin, and device-sync details before you begin.

Quick answer

How do you create a ChatGPT skill?

Open Plugins → Skills → Create, then choose Create with chat, Create with editor, or Upload from your computer. Define one task, when the skill should run, required inputs, ordered steps, output format, and rules. Install it, test realistic requests, and refine the trigger. For a portable file, use a skill folder whose required SKILL.md contains name, description, and the workflow instructions.

What you finish with: a saved, installable workflow inside ChatGPT; optionally, a downloadable Agent Skills package you can reuse in another compatible product.

What Is a ChatGPT Skill?

A ChatGPT skill is a reusable workflow for a focused task. OpenAI describes skills as packages of instructions and supporting resources that help ChatGPT complete repeatable work with the right process, context, and tools. A skill can include a name, a description, workflow instructions, templates, examples, brand guidance, schemas, or connected tools.

The key idea is simple: a prompt asks once; a skill saves the process. Once a skill is created and installed, OpenAI says ChatGPT can automatically use one or more skills when they are helpful. Once yours is set up, how to use ChatGPT skills walks through installing, running, editing, and removing them.

For official context, see OpenAI’s Skills in ChatGPT help page and Build Skills guide. For the beginner-friendly definition of skills across every platform, read What Is an AI Agent Skill?.

Need ideas before building your own? See these ChatGPT Skills examples to compare real triggers, inputs, workflows, and outputs.

What You Need Before You Start

Before you create a ChatGPT skill, make sure you have:

  • A ChatGPT account with Skills access – Personal Skills are generally available for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu accounts — keep an eye out as availability expands to more plans over time. In Enterprise and Edu workspaces, an admin may need to enable Skills and related permissions.
  • One repeatable task – choose a weekly update, client follow-up, research brief, content QA pass, documentation review, or another workflow you already repeat.
  • A clear output format – define what “done” looks like before you build anything.
  • Example inputs or templates – one real example makes the skill much easier to test and refine.

Is a ChatGPT Skill the Same as a Custom GPT?

No. They overlap, but they are not the same surface. OpenAI’s Help Center describes GPTs as custom versions of ChatGPT configured for a specific purpose, with instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, and actions. A skill is more like a reusable workflow package that ChatGPT or Codex can use when a task matches.

Simple rule

Use a skill when you want ChatGPT to reuse a process. Use a custom GPT when you want a named assistant experience that users can open, share, or publish in the GPT Store.

How to Create a ChatGPT Skill: 7 Steps

The best first ChatGPT skill is boring in the best way: one job, one process, one predictable output. Do not start with “help me with marketing.” Start with “turn raw campaign notes into a launch brief” or “draft a warm follow-up email from meeting notes.”

Finish this sentence first: This skill should always ___ when I ___.

That sentence becomes the foundation for the skill’s description, trigger, and test cases.

The description is how ChatGPT understands when the skill applies. Make it specific, action-oriented, and full of the words you actually use when asking for the task.

Weak: Helps with emails.

Better: Use this skill when I provide meeting notes and ask for a client follow-up email. Turn the notes into a short, warm email with a recap, next step, and three subject line options.

Clear beats clever

A plain, descriptive name and description help both you and ChatGPT recognize when the skill applies. “Client Follow-Up Email” works; “Inbox Ninja” doesn’t. Save the clever name for when the purpose is already obvious.

Write the process like you are training a new assistant. Include the goal, required inputs, ordered steps, output format, rules, and a review checklist.

ChatGPT skill planning template:

SKILL NAME
[Short, specific name]

WHEN TO USE THIS SKILL
Use this skill when I ask you to [repeatable task] and provide [required inputs].

GOAL
Produce [specific result] using the same process and format every time.

REQUIRED INPUTS
- [Input 1]
- [Input 2]
- [Input 3]

WORKFLOW
1. Review the inputs and identify the goal.
2. Ask one clarifying question only if a required input is missing.
3. Follow this process:
   - [Step A]
   - [Step B]
   - [Step C]
4. Create the output in the format below.
5. Run the review checklist before finalizing.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- [Section 1]
- [Section 2]
- [Section 3]

RULES
- Do not invent facts, quotes, dates, sources, or numbers.
- Use [tone/style].
- Keep the output [length].
- Flag anything that needs human review.

EXAMPLE
Input:
[Example input]

Strong output:
[Example output]

REVIEW CHECKLIST
- Did I use all required inputs?
- Did I follow the workflow?
- Did I match the output format?
- Did I flag uncertainty instead of guessing?

A ChatGPT skill can be instruction-only, but the strongest skills often include support material: a brand voice guide, a formatting template, an example output, a checklist, a schema, or a source policy.

  • Use instructions for behavior, tone, rules, steps, and output format.
  • Use examples to show what good output looks like.
  • Use resources for templates, reference material, brand guidelines, or reusable checklists.
  • Use an app when the workflow needs access to external systems, data, or actions. Use a plugin when you want to package and distribute Skills with an app or other shared workflow capabilities.

Start simple. Add tools only after the instruction-only version works. Most bad skills fail because the instructions are vague, not because they lack integrations.

Open ChatGPT, select Plugins in the sidebar, and open the Skills tab in the Plugin Directory. Select Create, then choose Create with chat, Create with editor, or Upload from your computer.

  1. Create with chat: Describe the workflow and let ChatGPT’s Skill Creator guide you.
  2. Create with editor: Write or edit the Skill directly in the Skills editor.
  3. Upload from your computer: Upload an existing Skill package.

For the simplest method, choose Create with chat and paste the planning template below.

Starter prompt:

Build me a ChatGPT skill for this repeatable workflow:

[Paste your completed skill planning template.]

Make it focused on one task. Keep it instruction-only unless a supporting template or example would make the workflow more reliable. Before finalizing, point out any vague trigger language, missing inputs, weak output formatting, or rules that need human review.

You do not need to write a SKILL.md manually when using ChatGPT’s Create with chat or Skills editor. If you are authoring manually for Codex, the API, or an uploadable skill folder, OpenAI’s build-skills documentation says a skill directory includes a required SKILL.md file with name and description, plus optional scripts, references, assets, and metadata.

How to Create a ChatGPT Skill With Chat

Create with chat is the fastest way to create a ChatGPT skill, especially for beginners. You describe the workflow, and ChatGPT’s skill creator walks you through name, description, instructions, and any supporting resources. It’s the closest thing OpenAI ships to a guided “ask ChatGPT to create a skill” flow — no manual template writing required.

  1. Open Plugins → Skills.
  2. Select Create → Create with chat.
  3. Describe the workflow you want the Skill to handle.
  4. Answer ChatGPT’s follow-up questions (audience, inputs, output format).
  5. Review the generated name, description, instructions, and resources.
  6. Install the completed Skill.
  7. Test it with two or three realistic inputs before rolling it out.

Every eligible account includes a built-in skill-creator Skill. When you ask ChatGPT to create, modify, or troubleshoot a Skill, ChatGPT automatically uses it to generate, update, or debug the Skill — even if you never install it manually.

How to Create a ChatGPT Skill With the Editor

The Skills editor is the “manual mode” for people who want direct control. Use it when Create with chat gets you 80% of the way there but you need to tighten specific pieces yourself, or when you’re revising an already-installed Skill. The editor gives you a form-style interface with every field the Skill uses.

Inside the editor you can control:

  • Skill name — how the Skill is referenced and displayed.
  • Description and triggering language — the phrasing ChatGPT matches against a user’s request.
  • Instructions — the step-by-step workflow ChatGPT follows.
  • Output format — the shape and structure of the result.
  • Examples — sample inputs and strong outputs.
  • Supporting resources — templates, checklists, brand guidelines, or schemas.
  • Later revisions — you can return to the editor any time to refine an installed Skill.

Pick the method that matches how you like to work — beginners should start with chat, and precision-minded builders should default to the editor.

Method Best for
Create with Chat Beginners and fast first drafts
Create with Editor Precise control and manual refinement
Upload Existing skill packages, Codex/API, or external files
Install Shared Skill Reusing a teammate’s approved workflow

How to Upload an Existing ChatGPT Skill

Upload is for Skills you already have as a file — for example, a package you exported from Codex, one you authored against the OpenAI API, or a Skill shared with you outside of your workspace. It takes seconds, but you should always review what you’re importing.

  1. Open Plugins → Skills → Create → Upload from your computer.
  2. Select the Skill file from your computer.
  3. Verify the imported name, description, and instructions match what you expected.
  4. Install the Skill and run a quick test.

Uploaded Skills are scanned automatically, but you should still review them yourself before installing, since a Skill may contain instructions, supporting files, or code that changes how ChatGPT behaves.

How to Download a Structured ChatGPT Skill File

OpenAI Skills follow the Agent Skills open standard, which is designed so a skill can move between compatible products. A portable skill is a folder with a required SKILL.md file and optional scripts, references, and assets folders. The SKILL.md must include a valid name and description, followed by the instructions.

Download controls vary by ChatGPT surface and workspace permission. OpenAI documents a Download action in the workspace admin Skills page; if your personal Skills menu does not show Download, use the editor to preserve the instructions or build the folder structure shown in the uploadable SKILL.md example. Do not promise a one-click export to every reader or plan.

Do not trust a skill after one clean test. Test it on three examples:

  • Easy test: a clean input where the expected output is obvious.
  • Real test: the messy kind of notes, files, or requests you actually use.
  • Edge test: missing information, conflicting instructions, or a task the skill should refuse or flag.

Watch for two things: whether ChatGPT chooses or accepts the skill for the right request, and whether the output follows the process without drifting.

Install and Test Your ChatGPT Skill

After creating the Skill, install it when prompted or manage it from your ChatGPT Skills page. Once installed, test it again with two or three realistic requests to confirm that ChatGPT selects it for the intended tasks and avoids using it for unrelated ones. Watch for both trigger accuracy and output quality — a Skill that fires on the wrong request is just as much of a problem as one that ignores the right request.

Depending on your permissions, you can keep a Skill private, share it with specific people or groups, or publish it to your workspace so teammates can install it themselves. The full walkthrough — sharing, publishing, uploading, and managing access afterward — is in how to share and install ChatGPT skills.

Refine the Skill When Results Drift

If ChatGPT misses the Skill entirely, tighten the description and triggering language. If it uses the Skill but the output drifts, fix the workflow instructions, output format, rules, or examples in the editor — or ask ChatGPT to modify the Skill for you. Do not broaden the Skill every time you notice a new use case; create a second focused Skill instead. Five small Skills are easier to trigger and maintain than one giant “business assistant” Skill.

Advanced Example: An Uploadable ChatGPT SKILL.md

You do not need to write a SKILL.md manually when using ChatGPT’s Create with chat or Skills editor. The following example is for people creating an uploadable Agent Skills package or working with Codex or the API.

---
name: client-follow-up-email
description: Use this skill when I provide meeting notes and ask for a client follow-up email. Turn the notes into a short, warm, professional email with a recap, next step, and three subject line options.
---

Goal:
Draft a client follow-up email from meeting notes.

Required inputs:
- Client name
- Meeting notes or call summary
- Desired next step

Workflow:
1. Review the notes and identify the client's goal, concern, or open question.
2. Choose the clearest next step.
3. Draft one email under 180 words.
4. Add three subject line options.
5. If a required detail is missing, list it under "Needs review" instead of guessing.

Output format:
Subject line options:
1.
2.
3.

Email draft:
[Email]

Needs review:
- [Only include if something is missing or uncertain.]

Rules:
- Do not invent pricing, dates, promises, or deliverables.
- Keep the tone warm, direct, and useful.
- Make the call to action clear.

ChatGPT Skills vs. Custom GPTs vs. Projects

If the terminology feels crowded, use the job-to-be-done:

  • Create a ChatGPT skill when you want a reusable task workflow that can be selected or triggered when needed.
  • Create a custom GPT when you want a named assistant experience with its own instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, or actions.
  • Create a Project when you want a persistent workspace for long-running work, shared files, project instructions, and related chats.
  • Create a plugin when you want an installable package containing one or more Skills, an app, or both.
Surface Best for What you create
ChatGPT skill A repeatable workflow ChatGPT should follow consistently. Instructions, resources, examples, and optionally a SKILL.md package.
Custom GPT A reusable ChatGPT assistant experience with its own name and settings. A GPT with instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, or actions.
Project Long-running work with shared files, chats, and project-specific instructions. A workspace that keeps context together across related chats.
Plugin Installing or distributing a packaged workflow across ChatGPT or Codex. An installable bundle containing one or more Skills, an app, or both; it may also include app templates.

For official GPT details, see OpenAI’s GPTs in ChatGPT and Creating and editing GPTs docs. For Projects, see OpenAI’s Projects in ChatGPT guide.

Common Mistakes When Creating a ChatGPT Skill

Mistake Better approach
Making the skill too broad Give it one job, one trigger, and one expected output.
Writing a prompt instead of a workflow Separate the goal, inputs, steps, output format, rules, and review checklist.
Using a vague description State exactly when the skill should run and what it should produce.
Adding tools before the instructions work Test the instruction-only version first, then add apps, actions, or plugins only when needed.
Skipping real-world tests Test with messy inputs, missing details, and edge cases before trusting the skill.
Confusing skills with custom GPTs Use skills for workflows and custom GPTs for named assistant experiences.

Where to Find and Reuse AI Skills

You do not have to build every workflow from scratch. Browse the ChatGPT skills gallery for examples that work in ChatGPT, or compare platform-specific formats with the Claude skills gallery and Gemini Spark skills gallery. Even when the setup steps differ, the core pattern is the same: one job, clear trigger, ordered steps, defined output, and testing.

See the Free AI News Agent Skill for an example of a reusable workflow that can be run in ChatGPT to create a structured AI update brief. Keep it labeled Works in ChatGPT until a native ChatGPT Skill package has been uploaded and tested.

Final Takeaway

A ChatGPT skill is your repeatable process, saved so ChatGPT can follow it again. Pick a task you repeat, write the trigger and workflow clearly, add one example, test it on real work, and refine until it behaves consistently. If you need a named assistant experience, build a custom GPT instead. If you need an installable package that bundles Skills with an app or other workflow capabilities, use a plugin.

# How to Create a ChatGPT Skill in 2026
**You can create a reusable ChatGPT Skill three ways: ask ChatGPT to build it, write it in the Skills editor, or upload a structured skill package.** This guide shows how to turn a prompt into a saved workflow, install and test it inside ChatGPT, and download the resulting skill for reuse in compatible tools.
**Important:** OpenAI uses several related customization features. A **ChatGPT Skill** is not the same as a **custom GPT**, a **Project**, or a **plugin**. This guide focuses on Personal Skills in ChatGPT. OpenAI also supports the Agent Skills format in Codex and the API. If you want the universal framework first, start with [How to Create an AI Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-create-an-ai-skill/).
**Already have a prompt you reuse?** Use [how to turn a prompt into an AI skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/turn-a-prompt-into-an-ai-skill/) first, then come back here to shape it into a ChatGPT skill.
**Not sure what to build first?** See [the 15 best ChatGPT skills for business owners](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/best-chatgpt-skills/) for a ranked shortlist, then come back here to build your own.
**ChatGPT Skills availability**
OpenAI officially lists Personal Skills for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu. Check the [current ChatGPT Skills availability guide](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/chatgpt-skills-availability/) for plan, admin, and device-sync details before you begin.
Quick answer
## How do you create a ChatGPT skill?
Open **Plugins → Skills → Create**, then choose **Create with chat**, **Create with editor**, or **Upload from your computer**. Define one task, when the skill should run, required inputs, ordered steps, output format, and rules. Install it, test realistic requests, and refine the trigger. For a portable file, use a skill folder whose required `SKILL.md` contains `name`, `description`, and the workflow instructions.
**What you finish with:** a saved, installable workflow inside ChatGPT; optionally, a downloadable Agent Skills package you can reuse in another compatible product.
![How to create an ai skill for chatgpt, claude, and gemini by defining a prompt, setting up instructions and tools, then testing the reusable workflow](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/claude-gemini-chatgpt-how-to-create-ai-skill.jpg "How To Create A Chatgpt Skill")
A strong ChatGPT skill starts with one repeatable workflow, clear instructions, and a testable output format.
## What Is a ChatGPT Skill?
A ChatGPT skill is a reusable workflow for a focused task. OpenAI describes skills as packages of instructions and supporting resources that help ChatGPT complete repeatable work with the right process, context, and tools. A skill can include a name, a description, workflow instructions, templates, examples, brand guidance, schemas, or connected tools.
The key idea is simple: a prompt asks once; a skill saves the process. Once a skill is created and installed, OpenAI says ChatGPT can automatically use one or more skills when they are helpful. Once yours is set up, [how to use ChatGPT skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-use-chatgpt-skills/) walks through installing, running, editing, and removing them.
For official context, see OpenAI’s [Skills in ChatGPT](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001066-skills-in-chatgpt) help page and [Build Skills](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills) guide. For the beginner-friendly definition of skills across every platform, read [What Is an AI Agent Skill?](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent-skill/).
**Need ideas before building your own?** See these [ChatGPT Skills examples](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/chatgpt-skills-examples/) to compare real triggers, inputs, workflows, and outputs.
## What You Need Before You Start
Before you create a ChatGPT skill, make sure you have:
* **A ChatGPT account with Skills access** – Personal Skills are generally available for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu accounts — keep an eye out as availability expands to more plans over time. In Enterprise and Edu workspaces, an admin may need to enable Skills and related permissions. * **One repeatable task** – choose a weekly update, client follow-up, research brief, content QA pass, documentation review, or another workflow you already repeat. * **A clear output format** – define what “done” looks like before you build anything. * **Example inputs or templates** – one real example makes the skill much easier to test and refine.
## Is a ChatGPT Skill the Same as a Custom GPT?
No. They overlap, but they are not the same surface. OpenAI’s Help Center describes GPTs as custom versions of ChatGPT configured for a specific purpose, with instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, and actions. A skill is more like a reusable workflow package that ChatGPT or Codex can use when a task matches.
**Simple rule**
Use a **skill** when you want ChatGPT to reuse a process. Use a **custom GPT** when you want a named assistant experience that users can open, share, or publish in the GPT Store.
## How to Create a ChatGPT Skill: 7 Steps
The best first ChatGPT skill is boring in the best way: one job, one process, one predictable output. Do not start with “help me with marketing.” Start with “turn raw campaign notes into a launch brief” or “draft a warm follow-up email from meeting notes.”
**Finish this sentence first:** _This skill should always \_\_\_ when I \_\_\_._
That sentence becomes the foundation for the skill’s description, trigger, and test cases.
The description is how ChatGPT understands when the skill applies. Make it specific, action-oriented, and full of the words you actually use when asking for the task.
**Weak:** Helps with emails.
**Better:** Use this skill when I provide meeting notes and ask for a client follow-up email. Turn the notes into a short, warm email with a recap, next step, and three subject line options.
**Clear beats clever**
A plain, descriptive name and description help both you and ChatGPT recognize when the skill applies. “Client Follow-Up Email” works; “Inbox Ninja” doesn’t. Save the clever name for when the purpose is already obvious.
Write the process like you are training a new assistant. Include the goal, required inputs, ordered steps, output format, rules, and a review checklist.
**ChatGPT skill planning template:**
SKILL NAME \[Short, specific name\]
WHEN TO USE THIS SKILL Use this skill when I ask you to \[repeatable task\] and provide \[required inputs\].
GOAL Produce \[specific result\] using the same process and format every time.
REQUIRED INPUTS - \[Input 1\] - \[Input 2\] - \[Input 3\]
WORKFLOW 1. Review the inputs and identify the goal. 2. Ask one clarifying question only if a required input is missing. 3. Follow this process: - \[Step A\] - \[Step B\] - \[Step C\] 4. Create the output in the format below. 5. Run the review checklist before finalizing.
OUTPUT FORMAT - \[Section 1\] - \[Section 2\] - \[Section 3\]
RULES - Do not invent facts, quotes, dates, sources, or numbers. - Use \[tone/style\]. - Keep the output \[length\]. - Flag anything that needs human review.
EXAMPLE Input: \[Example input\]
Strong output: \[Example output\]
REVIEW CHECKLIST - Did I use all required inputs? - Did I follow the workflow? - Did I match the output format? - Did I flag uncertainty instead of guessing?
A ChatGPT skill can be instruction-only, but the strongest skills often include support material: a brand voice guide, a formatting template, an example output, a checklist, a schema, or a source policy.
* **Use instructions** for behavior, tone, rules, steps, and output format. * **Use examples** to show what good output looks like. * **Use resources** for templates, reference material, brand guidelines, or reusable checklists. * **Use an app** when the workflow needs access to external systems, data, or actions. Use a **plugin** when you want to package and distribute Skills with an app or other shared workflow capabilities.
Start simple. Add tools only after the instruction-only version works. Most bad skills fail because the instructions are vague, not because they lack integrations.
Open ChatGPT, select **Plugins** in the sidebar, and open the **Skills** tab in the Plugin Directory. Select **Create**, then choose **Create with chat**, **Create with editor**, or **Upload from your computer**.
1. **Create with chat:** Describe the workflow and let ChatGPT’s Skill Creator guide you. 2. **Create with editor:** Write or edit the Skill directly in the Skills editor. 3. **Upload from your computer:** Upload an existing Skill package.
Switch from Plugins to the Skills tab, then use the add (+) menu to pick how you want to build it — chat, editor, or upload.
For the simplest method, choose **Create with chat** and paste the planning template below.
**Starter prompt:**
Build me a ChatGPT skill for this repeatable workflow:
\[Paste your completed skill planning template.\]
Make it focused on one task. Keep it instruction-only unless a supporting template or example would make the workflow more reliable. Before finalizing, point out any vague trigger language, missing inputs, weak output formatting, or rules that need human review.
You do not need to write a `SKILL.md` manually when using ChatGPT’s Create with chat or Skills editor. If you are authoring manually for Codex, the API, or an uploadable skill folder, OpenAI’s build-skills documentation says a skill directory includes a required `SKILL.md` file with `name` and `description`, plus optional scripts, references, assets, and metadata.
## How to Create a ChatGPT Skill With Chat
Create with chat is the fastest way to create a ChatGPT skill, especially for beginners. You describe the workflow, and ChatGPT’s skill creator walks you through name, description, instructions, and any supporting resources. It’s the closest thing OpenAI ships to a guided “ask ChatGPT to create a skill” flow — no manual template writing required.
1. Open Plugins → Skills. 2. Select Create → Create with chat. 3. Describe the workflow you want the Skill to handle. 4. Answer ChatGPT’s follow-up questions (audience, inputs, output format). 5. Review the generated name, description, instructions, and resources. 6. Install the completed Skill. 7. Test it with two or three realistic inputs before rolling it out.
Every eligible account includes a built-in **skill-creator Skill**. When you ask ChatGPT to create, modify, or troubleshoot a Skill, ChatGPT automatically uses it to generate, update, or debug the Skill — even if you never install it manually.
## How to Create a ChatGPT Skill With the Editor
The Skills editor is the “manual mode” for people who want direct control. Use it when Create with chat gets you 80% of the way there but you need to tighten specific pieces yourself, or when you’re revising an already-installed Skill. The editor gives you a form-style interface with every field the Skill uses.
Inside the editor you can control:
* **Skill name** — how the Skill is referenced and displayed. * **Description and triggering language** — the phrasing ChatGPT matches against a user’s request. * **Instructions** — the step-by-step workflow ChatGPT follows. * **Output format** — the shape and structure of the result. * **Examples** — sample inputs and strong outputs. * **Supporting resources** — templates, checklists, brand guidelines, or schemas. * **Later revisions** — you can return to the editor any time to refine an installed Skill.
Pick the method that matches how you like to work — beginners should start with chat, and precision-minded builders should default to the editor.
| Method | Best for | | --- | --- | | **Create with Chat** | Beginners and fast first drafts | | **Create with Editor** | Precise control and manual refinement | | **Upload** | Existing skill packages, Codex/API, or external files | | **Install Shared Skill** | Reusing a teammate’s approved workflow |
## How to Upload an Existing ChatGPT Skill
Upload is for Skills you already have as a file — for example, a package you exported from Codex, one you authored against the OpenAI API, or a Skill shared with you outside of your workspace. It takes seconds, but you should always review what you’re importing.
1. Open Plugins → Skills → Create → Upload from your computer. 2. Select the Skill file from your computer. 3. Verify the imported name, description, and instructions match what you expected. 4. Install the Skill and run a quick test.
Uploaded Skills are scanned automatically, but you should still review them yourself before installing, since a Skill may contain instructions, supporting files, or code that changes how ChatGPT behaves.
## How to Download a Structured ChatGPT Skill File
OpenAI Skills follow the Agent Skills open standard, which is designed so a skill can move between compatible products. A portable skill is a folder with a required `SKILL.md` file and optional `scripts`, `references`, and `assets` folders. The `SKILL.md` must include a valid `name` and `description`, followed by the instructions.
Download controls vary by ChatGPT surface and workspace permission. OpenAI documents a **Download** action in the workspace admin Skills page; if your personal Skills menu does not show Download, use the editor to preserve the instructions or build the folder structure shown in the [uploadable SKILL.md example](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-create-a-chatgpt-skill/#example). Do not promise a one-click export to every reader or plan.
Do not trust a skill after one clean test. Test it on three examples:
* **Easy test:** a clean input where the expected output is obvious. * **Real test:** the messy kind of notes, files, or requests you actually use. * **Edge test:** missing information, conflicting instructions, or a task the skill should refuse or flag.
Watch for two things: whether ChatGPT chooses or accepts the skill for the right request, and whether the output follows the process without drifting.
## Install and Test Your ChatGPT Skill
After creating the Skill, install it when prompted or manage it from your ChatGPT Skills page. Once installed, test it again with two or three realistic requests to confirm that ChatGPT selects it for the intended tasks and avoids using it for unrelated ones. Watch for both trigger accuracy and output quality — a Skill that fires on the wrong request is just as much of a problem as one that ignores the right request.
Depending on your permissions, you can keep a Skill private, share it with specific people or groups, or publish it to your workspace so teammates can install it themselves. The full walkthrough — sharing, publishing, uploading, and managing access afterward — is in [how to share and install ChatGPT skills](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-share-chatgpt-skills/).
## Refine the Skill When Results Drift
If ChatGPT misses the Skill entirely, tighten the description and triggering language. If it uses the Skill but the output drifts, fix the workflow instructions, output format, rules, or examples in the editor — or ask ChatGPT to modify the Skill for you. Do not broaden the Skill every time you notice a new use case; create a second focused Skill instead. Five small Skills are easier to trigger and maintain than one giant “business assistant” Skill.
## Advanced Example: An Uploadable ChatGPT SKILL.md
You do not need to write a `SKILL.md` manually when using ChatGPT’s Create with chat or Skills editor. The following example is for people creating an uploadable Agent Skills package or working with Codex or the API.
\--- name: client-follow-up-email description: Use this skill when I provide meeting notes and ask for a client follow-up email. Turn the notes into a short, warm, professional email with a recap, next step, and three subject line options. ---
Goal: Draft a client follow-up email from meeting notes.
Required inputs: - Client name - Meeting notes or call summary - Desired next step
Workflow: 1. Review the notes and identify the client's goal, concern, or open question. 2. Choose the clearest next step. 3. Draft one email under 180 words. 4. Add three subject line options. 5. If a required detail is missing, list it under "Needs review" instead of guessing.
Output format: Subject line options: 1. 2. 3.
Email draft: \[Email\]
Needs review: - \[Only include if something is missing or uncertain.\]
Rules: - Do not invent pricing, dates, promises, or deliverables. - Keep the tone warm, direct, and useful. - Make the call to action clear.
## ChatGPT Skills vs. Custom GPTs vs. Projects
If the terminology feels crowded, use the job-to-be-done:
* **Create a ChatGPT skill** when you want a reusable task workflow that can be selected or triggered when needed. * **Create a custom GPT** when you want a named assistant experience with its own instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, or actions. * **Create a Project** when you want a persistent workspace for long-running work, shared files, project instructions, and related chats. * **Create a plugin** when you want an installable package containing one or more Skills, an app, or both.
| Surface | Best for | What you create | | --- | --- | --- | | **ChatGPT skill** | A repeatable workflow ChatGPT should follow consistently. | Instructions, resources, examples, and optionally a `SKILL.md` package. | | **Custom GPT** | A reusable ChatGPT assistant experience with its own name and settings. | A GPT with instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, or actions. | | **Project** | Long-running work with shared files, chats, and project-specific instructions. | A workspace that keeps context together across related chats. | | **Plugin** | Installing or distributing a packaged workflow across ChatGPT or Codex. | An installable bundle containing one or more Skills, an app, or both; it may also include app templates. |
For official GPT details, see OpenAI’s [GPTs in ChatGPT](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8554407) and [Creating and editing GPTs](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8554397-creating-a-gpt) docs. For Projects, see OpenAI’s [Projects in ChatGPT](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-using-projects-in-chatgpt) guide.
## Common Mistakes When Creating a ChatGPT Skill
| Mistake | Better approach | | --- | --- | | Making the skill too broad | Give it one job, one trigger, and one expected output. | | Writing a prompt instead of a workflow | Separate the goal, inputs, steps, output format, rules, and review checklist. | | Using a vague description | State exactly when the skill should run and what it should produce. | | Adding tools before the instructions work | Test the instruction-only version first, then add apps, actions, or plugins only when needed. | | Skipping real-world tests | Test with messy inputs, missing details, and edge cases before trusting the skill. | | Confusing skills with custom GPTs | Use skills for workflows and custom GPTs for named assistant experiences. |
## Where to Find and Reuse AI Skills
You do not have to build every workflow from scratch. Browse the [ChatGPT skills gallery](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/chatgpt/) for examples that work in ChatGPT, or compare platform-specific formats with the [Claude skills gallery](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/claude/) and [Gemini Spark skills gallery](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/gemini-spark/). Even when the setup steps differ, the core pattern is the same: one job, clear trigger, ordered steps, defined output, and testing.
See the [Free AI News Agent Skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/skills/ai-news-agent/) for an example of a reusable workflow that can be run in ChatGPT to create a structured AI update brief. Keep it labeled **Works in ChatGPT** until a native ChatGPT Skill package has been uploaded and tested.
For a longer build written to run in ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini without changes, see this [no-code AI website skill](https://www.aiagentslibrary.com/blog/how-to-create-a-website-with-ai-skill/) — a single skill that returns a site map, hero copy, SEO metadata, and FAQs on every run.
## Final Takeaway
A ChatGPT skill is your repeatable process, saved so ChatGPT can follow it again. Pick a task you repeat, write the trigger and workflow clearly, add one example, test it on real work, and refine until it behaves consistently. If you need a named assistant experience, build a custom GPT instead. If you need an installable package that bundles Skills with an app or other workflow capabilities, use a plugin.
## Frequently Asked Questions
What is a ChatGPT skill?
A ChatGPT skill is a reusable workflow that gives ChatGPT task-specific instructions, resources, and tools for repeatable work. It helps ChatGPT follow the same process each time instead of relying on a prompt you paste manually.
How do I create a ChatGPT skill?
Choose one focused workflow, write when the skill should apply, define the steps and output format, add examples or resources, ask ChatGPT to build the skill, test it with realistic inputs, and refine it until it works consistently.
Is a ChatGPT skill the same as a custom GPT?
No. A skill is best for a repeatable workflow. A custom GPT is a named ChatGPT experience with its own instructions, knowledge, capabilities, apps, or actions, and it can be shared or published depending on eligibility.
Do I need to know how to code to create a ChatGPT skill?
No for a basic instruction-only skill. You can start by describing the workflow to ChatGPT. Coding becomes relevant only if the skill needs scripts, custom tools, APIs, or plugin packaging.
What should I put in a ChatGPT skill?
Include a clear name, a specific description of when to use it, required inputs, step-by-step instructions, output format, rules, examples, and a review checklist. Add supporting resources only when they make the workflow more reliable.
Can ChatGPT choose a skill automatically?
Yes. OpenAI’s Skills documentation says that after a skill is created and installed, ChatGPT can automatically use one or more skills when they are helpful.
When should I use a plugin instead of a skill?
Use a skill for reusable instructions around one focused workflow. Use a plugin when you need an installable bundle that can include one or more Skills, an app, or both.

item.text: How to Use ChatGPT Skills: Complete Beginner's Guide (2026) Here’s the part that surprises most people: you don’t really “run” a ChatGPT skill — it runs itself. Once a skill is turned on, ChatGPT applies it automatically the moment your request matches what the skill is for. There’s no button to press and no reminder to type. This guide walks you through the whole thing: turning skills on, adding one, letting it work, editing it when it’s close but not quite right, and removing it when you’re done. Want the bigger picture first? What Is an AI Agent Skill? explains how skills differ from prompts. Ready to make your own? See how to create a ChatGPT skill. This page is about using skills that already exist. See 15 ChatGPT Skills examples for work and business if you want practical workflows to try first. ChatGPT Skills availability OpenAI’s dedicated Skills documentation lists Personal Skills as generally available for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu users; its Plugins FAQ separately says Personal Skills in Work are available on paid plans except Free and Go. Skills are also supported in Codex and the API. Skills do not automatically sync between desktop/web and mobile — you may need to install a Skill in each place you use ChatGPT. Interface update: Skills are now inside the Plugin Directory OpenAI replaced the App Directory with the Plugin Directory on July 9, 2026. Open Plugins in the ChatGPT sidebar, then select the Skills tab in the Plugin Directory. From there, you can browse, install, manage, or open the Skills available to your workspace. Plugins can package Skills alongside apps and reusable app templates, so older screenshots may still show an App Directory or a standalone Skills destination. Quick answer To use a ChatGPT Skill, select Plugins in the sidebar, then open the Skills tab in the Plugin Directory. Add a Skill by installing one that’s shared with you, creating one, or uploading a trusted skill package. After that, start the task it’s built for and ChatGPT can apply it automatically. If the result is close but off, edit the Skill or ask ChatGPT in the chat to adjust it. To stop using one, remove or delete it. Access varies by plan, product surface, and workspace permissions; use a Project instead if the Skills tab is not available to you. The whole flow in three steps — install a skill, add it to ChatGPT, then run it. Once a skill is on, ChatGPT applies it automatically whenever your task matches. What “Using” a ChatGPT Skill Actually Means This is the one thing worth understanding before anything else: a ChatGPT Skill is a reusable workflow that ChatGPT can apply when relevant. Skills can be distributed as standalone workflows or packaged inside a plugin with connected apps and app templates. When you start a task that matches a Skill’s purpose, ChatGPT can apply it automatically — you don’t have to switch it on or repeat its instructions. So “using” a skill really means two things: making sure the right skill is available (turned on and added), and then simply doing your work. The rest of this guide is about that first part — getting skills set up so they’re ready when you need them. Do You Have Skills on Your Plan? OpenAI’s dedicated Skills page lists Personal Skills as generally available on Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, and Edu. Its newer Plugins FAQ separately says Personal Skills in Work are available on paid plans except Free and Go. Because those official pages describe different surfaces, the practical check is your current Plugins → Skills tab; see the ChatGPT Skills availability guide for the full plan-by-plan nuance. Don’t see Skills yet? Use a Project instead — it works on every plan, including Free, and gives you the same everyday benefit. Jump to the Project method below. The 5 Steps to Using a ChatGPT Skill This covers the native Skills feature. Don’t see Skills on your account yet? Skip to the Project method instead. Open ChatGPT, select Plugins in the sidebar, and open the Skills tab in the Plugin Directory — that’s where your skills live and where you add new ones. On a shared workspace (Business, Enterprise, Healthcare, or Edu), a workspace admin may need to enable Skills for your role first — so if you don’t see Skills at all, that’s the thing to ask your admin about. Not on one of those plans? Keep an eye out, since availability has been expanding over time. Open Plugins from the sidebar, select the Skills tab in the Plugin Directory, then use the add (+) menu to create a skill with chat, build one in the editor, or upload your own. You can’t use a skill you don’t have, so this is where you get one. There are two common ways: Install one that’s shared with you. Select Plugins in the sidebar, open the Skills tab, and look under Shared with me or Shared by your workspace. Open the more-options menu (•••) next to the skill and choose Install. It’s now available to run. Sharing one out to your team is a different flow — see how to share and install ChatGPT skills. Add your own. Paste a skill from our free ChatGPT skills library using ChatGPT’s build flow, or write one from scratch. The full walkthrough is in how to create a ChatGPT skill. Fastest way to start Grab a ready-made skill from the ChatGPT skills library — it’s free, and using someone else’s well-built skill is the quickest way to see how the whole thing works before you make your own. If a teammate or your workspace has already built a Skill you want to use, you don’t need to recreate it — you just install it. The whole flow is short: Open Plugins from the ChatGPT sidebar. Select the Skills tab in the Plugin Directory. Select Shared with me or Shared by [workspace name]. Open the three-dot menu beside the Skill. Select Install. Start a matching task and confirm the Skill is applied correctly. Before installing a Skill from another source, review it carefully. Uploaded Skills are scanned automatically, but OpenAI recommends reviewing the Skill yourself because it may contain instructions, supporting files, or code. How to Use a ChatGPT Skill in Excel or Google Sheets Open ChatGPT for Excel or Google Sheets and select + → Skills, or type @ followed by the Skill name. Ask ChatGPT to build, update, explain, analyze, or summarize the workbook. Spreadsheet conversations do not sync with your main ChatGPT history or memory, so provide any business rules or context the Skill needs inside the workbook session. This is the step people overthink. You don’t select the skill, switch it on, or mention it. You just start the task it was built for, and ChatGPT applies the skill on its own. For example, if you’ve added a follow-up email skill, you simply paste your meeting notes and ask for a follow-up — ChatGPT recognizes the task and uses the skill automatically. To confirm it’s working, check the output against what the skill promises: the right structure, tone, and steps. If the result already looks like the skill’s format, it’s running. If the output is nearly right but not quite — wrong tone, missing a section, too long — you don’t scrap the skill. You adjust it. Two ways: Edit it on the Skills page directly: open the skill and tighten its instructions or output format. Ask ChatGPT in the chat to modify the skill — for example, “update this skill so the email is always under 150 words.” The same flow that builds skills can update and troubleshoot them. A skill you refine a couple of times to match your voice will always outperform a generic one. This is normal, and expected. When you no longer need a skill, clear it out so ChatGPT isn’t applying something outdated. On the Skills page, open the skill and choose Delete skill to remove it permanently. Before deleting a shared Skill, check its ownership and workspace access. Depending on your permissions, you may only be able to stop using it, or the owner or administrator may need to manage broader access. Don’t See Skills Yet? Use a Project Instead If Skills haven’t reached your account yet, you can get the same everyday benefit with a Project, which is available on every plan, including Free. A Project is a workspace that holds files, chats, and instructions for one area of work, and its instructions apply to every conversation inside it. So you can take any instruction-based skill and put it to work like this: Create a new Project in ChatGPT. Open the Project’s settings and find the instructions field. Paste the skill’s instructions there. Work inside that Project — ChatGPT follows the skill’s workflow in every chat there. It’s not identical to a native Skill — native Skills can include examples and code and activate across your whole account — but for the instruction-based skills most business owners use, a Project gives you a practical, reusable setup without an upgrade. We break down the differences in full in our upcoming ChatGPT Skills vs GPTs vs Projects guide. Start by Adding One Good Skill Using ChatGPT skills comes down to a simple loop: turn skills on, add a good one, and then just do your work while ChatGPT applies it in the background.
